chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: There was no chance of going for a walk that day. We had wandered through the bare shrubbery for an hour that morning, but since lunch (Mrs. Reed dined early when there were no guests), the cold winter wind had brought such dark clouds and such relentless rain that any further time outdoors was out of the question.

I was glad of it. I never liked long walks, especially on chilly afternoons. I dreaded coming home in the raw twilight with frozen fingers and toes, my heart heavy from Bessie the nurse's scoldings, and humbled by the awareness that I was physically inferior to Eliza, John, and Georgiana Reed.

Eliza, John, and Georgiana were now gathered around their mama in the drawing room. She lay on a sofa by the fire, and with her darlings around her (for the moment neither fighting nor crying), she looked perfectly content. She had excused me from joining the group, saying that she regretted having to keep me at a distance, but that until she heard from Bessie, and could see for herself, that I was genuinely trying to develop a more sociable and childlike nature, a more appealing and lively manner—something lighter, more open, more natural—she really had to exclude me from privileges meant only for happy, well-behaved little children.
"What does Bessie say I have done?" I asked.

"Jane, I don't like arguers or questioners. Besides, there is something truly unpleasant about a child challenging her elders like that. Sit down somewhere, and until you can speak pleasantly, stay quiet."

A breakfast room adjoined the drawing room, and I slipped in there. It had a bookcase, and I quickly grabbed a book, making sure it was one full of pictures. I climbed into the window seat, tucked my feet up, and sat cross-legged. Having pulled the red curtain nearly shut, I was hidden away in double seclusion.

Folds of scarlet fabric blocked my view to the right. To the left were the clear glass panes, shielding me from but not hiding the dreary November day. Now and then, while turning the pages of my book, I studied the winter afternoon. In the distance, there was nothing but a pale blur of mist and cloud. Nearby, a scene of wet lawn and battered shrubs, with endless rain sweeping wildly before a long, mournful wind.

I went back to my book—Bewick's History of British Birds. I didn't care much for the text itself, generally speaking, but there were certain introductory pages that, young as I was, I couldn't simply skip over. They described the haunts of seabirds, the solitary rocks and headlands where only they lived, the coast of Norway dotted with islands from its southern tip, the Lindeness or Naze, all the way to the North Cape—
"Where the Northern Ocean, in vast whirls, Boils round the naked, melancholy isles Of farthest Thule; and the Atlantic surge Pours in among the stormy Hebrides."

I was equally struck by the descriptions of the bleak shores of Lapland, Siberia, Spitzbergen, Nova Zembla, Iceland, Greenland, with "the vast sweep of the Arctic Zone, and those desolate regions of barren space—that reservoir of frost and snow, where solid fields of ice, built up over centuries of winters, rising to alpine heights above heights, surround the pole and concentrate the extreme cold." Of these death-white realms I formed my own idea: shadowy, like all the half-understood notions that drift through children's minds, but strangely powerful. The words in those introductory pages connected themselves to the illustrations that followed, and gave meaning to the rock standing alone in a sea of waves and spray, to the wrecked boat stranded on a desolate coast, to the cold and ghostly moon glancing through bars of cloud at a ship just sinking.

I can't explain what feeling haunted the completely solitary churchyard, with its inscribed headstone, its gate, its two trees, its low horizon ringed by a broken wall, and its newly risen crescent moon, marking the hour of dusk.
The two ships becalmed on a lifeless sea I believed to be ghostly vessels.
The demon pinning down the thief's pack behind him—I turned past that quickly. It terrified me.
So did the black horned creature perched alone on a rock, watching a distant crowd gathered around a gallows.

Each picture told a story, often mysterious to my young mind and untrained feelings, yet always deeply fascinating. They were as interesting as the tales Bessie sometimes told on winter evenings, when she happened to be in a good mood, and when, having brought her ironing board to the nursery fire, she let us sit around it. While she pressed Mrs. Reed's lace trim and crimped her nightcap borders, she fed our eager attention with stories of love and adventure from old fairy tales and ballads—or, as I later discovered, from the pages of Pamela and Henry, Earl of Moreland.
With Bewick on my knee, I was happy then—happy at least in my own way. I feared nothing except interruption, and that came too soon. The breakfast room door opened.
"Boo! Madam Mope!" cried the voice of John Reed. Then he paused—he found the room apparently empty.
"Where the dickens is she!" he went on. "Lizzy! Georgy!" (calling to his sisters) "Joan isn't here—tell mama she's run out into the rain—bad animal!"

"Good thing I drew the curtain," I thought, fervently hoping he wouldn't find my hiding place. And John Reed wouldn't have found it on his own—he wasn't quick in either sight or thought—but Eliza stuck her head in at the door and said immediately—
"She's in the window seat, of course, Jack."
I came out at once, because I trembled at the thought of being dragged out by Jack.
"What do you want?" I asked, with awkward shyness.
"Say, 'What do you want, Master Reed?'" was the answer. "I want you to come here." He sat down in an armchair and gestured for me to come stand in front of him.

John Reed was a schoolboy of fourteen, four years older than me—I was only ten. He was big and heavy for his age, with a dull, unhealthy complexion, coarse features in a broad face, thick limbs, and large hands and feet. He constantly stuffed himself at meals, which left him with a sluggish look, bleary eyes, and flabby cheeks. He should have been at school, but his mama had brought him home for a month or two on account of his "delicate health." Mr. Miles, the headmaster, said he would do perfectly well if fewer cakes and sweets were sent from home. But his mother rejected such a harsh opinion and preferred the more flattering idea that John's sallowness was due to too much studying and, perhaps, homesickness.

John didn't have much affection for his mother and sisters, and he actively disliked me. He bullied and hurt me—not two or three times a week, not once or twice a day, but constantly. Every nerve in my body feared him, and every bit of me shrank when he came near. There were moments when his cruelty left me stunned, because I had no defense against his threats or his violence. The servants didn't want to upset their young master by taking my side, and Mrs. Reed was blind and deaf to it all. She never saw him hit me or heard him insult me, though he did both in her very presence from time to time—more often, though, behind her back.

As usual, I obeyed John and came up to his chair. He spent about three minutes sticking his tongue out at me as far as it would go. I knew he would hit me soon, and while dreading the blow, I studied the disgusting, ugly face of the person about to deliver it. I wonder if he saw that thought in my expression, because without a word, he suddenly struck me, hard. I staggered, and once I regained my balance, I stepped back a pace or two from his chair.
"That's for your rudeness in answering mama earlier," he said, "and for your sneaky way of hiding behind curtains, and for the look in your eyes just now, you rat!"
I was so used to John Reed's abuse that it never occurred to me to talk back. My only concern was how to endure the blow that would certainly follow the insult.
"What were you doing behind the curtain?" he asked.
"I was reading."
"Show me the book."
I went back to the window and brought it to him.

"You have no right to take our books. You're a dependent, mama says. You have no money—your father left you nothing. You should be begging, not living here with gentlemen's children like us, eating the same food and wearing clothes bought with our mama's money. Now I'll teach you to rummage through my bookshelves—because they are mine. The whole house belongs to me, or will in a few years. Go stand by the door, out of the way of the mirror and the windows."

I obeyed, not understanding at first what he intended. But when I saw him lift and aim the book, ready to throw it, I instinctively jumped aside with a cry of alarm—not quickly enough, though. The book was hurled, it hit me, and I fell, striking my head against the door and cutting it. The cut bled, the pain was sharp. My terror had reached its peak and broken through—other feelings took over.
"Wicked and cruel boy!" I said. "You are like a murderer—you are like a slave driver—you are like the Roman emperors!"
I had read Goldsmith's History of Rome and formed my own opinions about Nero, Caligula, and the rest. I had also drawn these comparisons in silence, never imagining I would declare them out loud.
"What! What!" he cried. "Did she say that to me? Did you hear her, Eliza and Georgiana? I'm going to tell mama! But first—"

He charged straight at me. I felt him grab my hair and my shoulder—he had tangled with a desperate creature. I truly saw in him a tyrant, a murderer. I felt a drop or two of blood from my head trickle down my neck, and the pain was sharp and stinging. For the moment, these sensations overpowered my fear, and I fought back wildly. I don't really know what I did with my hands, but he called me "Rat! Rat!" and screamed out loud. Help was close by—Eliza and Georgiana had run for Mrs. Reed, who had gone upstairs. She now arrived on the scene, followed by Bessie and the maid Abbot. We were pulled apart. I heard the words—
"Goodness! What a terror, to attack Master John like that!"
"Has anyone ever seen such a display of temper!"
Then Mrs. Reed added—
"Take her away to the red room and lock her in there." Four hands were immediately laid on me, and I was carried upstairs.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: I fought the whole way—a new thing for me, and something that only strengthened the bad opinion Bessie and Miss Abbot already had. The truth is, I was a little beside myself, or rather outside myself, as the French say. I knew that a moment's rebellion had already made me liable to strange punishments, and like any other rebel slave, I felt determined in my desperation to go all the way.
"Hold her arms, Miss Abbot—she's like a wild cat."
"Shame on you!" cried the lady's maid. "What shocking behavior, Miss Eyre, to strike a young gentleman, your benefactress's son! Your young master."
"Master! How is he my master? Am I a servant?"
"No, you are less than a servant, because you do nothing to earn your keep. Now sit down and think about what you've done."
By this time they had gotten me into the room Mrs. Reed had indicated and shoved me onto a stool. My instinct was to spring up immediately, but their four hands pinned me down.
"If you won't sit still, we'll have to tie you down," said Bessie. "Miss Abbot, lend me your garters—she'd snap mine in a second."
Miss Abbot bent to remove the necessary ties from her sturdy leg. This preparation for being bound, and the added humiliation it implied, took some of the fight out of me.
"Don't take them off," I cried. "I won't move."
To prove it, I gripped the edges of my seat with both hands.

"Make sure you don't," said Bessie. Once she was satisfied I was truly calming down, she let go of me. Then she and Miss Abbot stood with folded arms, looking darkly and doubtfully at my face, as if they questioned my sanity.
"She's never done that before," Bessie finally said, turning to Abbot.

"But it was always in her," was the reply. "I've told the Missus my opinion of this child many times, and she agreed with me. She's a sneaky little thing. I've never seen a girl her age with so much cunning."
Bessie didn't respond, but before long, speaking to me, she said—
"You should know, Miss, that you are indebted to Mrs. Reed. She provides for you. If she turned you out, you'd have to go to the poorhouse."

I had nothing to say to this. It wasn't new to me—my earliest memories included hints of the same kind. This constant reminder of my dependence had become a dull refrain in my ear, painful and crushing but only half understood. Miss Abbot joined in—

"And you shouldn't think of yourself as equal to the Misses Reed and Master Reed just because the Missus is kind enough to let you be raised alongside them. They will have a great deal of money, and you will have none. Your place is to be humble and try to make yourself pleasant to them."

"What we're telling you is for your own good," added Bessie, not unkindly. "You should try to be helpful and agreeable. Then perhaps you'd have a home here. But if you become wild and rude, the Missus will send you away, I'm sure of it."

"Besides," said Miss Abbot, "God will punish her. He might strike her dead in the middle of one of her tantrums, and then where would she go? Come, Bessie, let's leave her. I wouldn't have her heart for anything. Say your prayers, Miss Eyre, when you're alone. If you don't repent, something terrible might come down the chimney and carry you off."
They left, shutting and locking the door behind them.

The red room was a large square chamber, very rarely slept in—almost never, really, unless an overflow of visitors at Gateshead Hall made it necessary to use every available room. Yet it was one of the grandest bedrooms in the house. A bed on massive mahogany pillars, draped in deep red damask curtains, stood like a shrine at the center. The two large windows, their blinds always drawn, were half-hidden behind swags and falls of the same fabric. The carpet was red. The table at the foot of the bed was covered with a crimson cloth. The walls were a soft fawn color with a hint of pink. The wardrobe, the dressing table, and the chairs were all darkly polished old mahogany. Rising from these deep, dark surroundings, the piled mattresses and pillows of the bed gleamed high and white, spread with a snowy Marseilles counterpane. Nearly as prominent was a large cushioned armchair near the head of the bed, also white, with a footstool before it—looking, I thought, like a pale throne.

The room was cold, because it rarely had a fire. It was silent, because it was far from the nursery and kitchen. It was solemn, because everyone knew how rarely it was entered. Only the housemaid came here on Saturdays to dust the mirrors and furniture. And Mrs. Reed herself, at long intervals, visited it to check the contents of a secret drawer in the wardrobe, where she kept various documents, her jewelry box, and a portrait of her dead husband. In those last words lies the secret of the red room—the reason it remained so lonely despite its grandeur.

Mr. Reed had been dead nine years. He had drawn his last breath in this room. He had lain in state here. From here his coffin was carried out by the undertakers. And since that day, a sense of somber sanctity had kept it from being used.

The seat where Bessie and the harsh Miss Abbot had left me was a low ottoman near the marble fireplace. The bed rose before me. To my right was the tall, dark wardrobe, its polished panels catching dim, broken reflections. To my left were the curtained windows. A large mirror between them reflected the stately emptiness of the bed and room. I wasn't sure they had actually locked the door, and when I dared to move, I got up to check. They had. No prison was ever more secure. On my way back, I had to pass the mirror, and my eyes were drawn involuntarily into its depths. Everything looked colder and darker in that reflected hollow than in reality. And the strange little figure staring back at me—with a white face and white arms standing out against the gloom, and glittering, frightened eyes moving where all else was still—looked like a real ghost. It reminded me of one of those tiny spirits, half fairy, half imp, that Bessie's evening stories described coming out of lonely fern-covered hollows on the moors to appear before travelers caught out after dark. I went back to my stool.

Superstition gripped me then, but it hadn't fully won yet. My blood was still warm. The mood of the rebel slave still braced me with its bitter strength. I had to fight back a flood of memories before I could give in to the grim present.

All of John Reed's violent cruelties, all his sisters' cold indifference, all his mother's hostility, all the servants' favoritism—it all churned up in my troubled mind like dark sediment in a stirred well. Why was I always suffering, always put down, always blamed, forever condemned? Why could I never please anyone? Why was it pointless even to try? Eliza, who was stubborn and selfish, was respected. Georgiana, who had a spoiled temper, a sharp spite, and a rude, arrogant manner, was indulged by everyone. Her beauty, her pink cheeks and golden curls, seemed to enchant everyone who saw her, and to buy forgiveness for every fault. No one crossed John, let alone punished him, though he wrung the necks of pigeons, killed baby peacocks, set the dogs on the sheep, stripped the greenhouse vines of their fruit, and broke the buds off the finest plants in the conservatory. He called his mother "old girl," mocked her for her dark skin (which matched his own), blatantly ignored her wishes, and regularly tore and ruined her silk clothes—and he was still "her darling." I dared not make a single mistake. I tried to do everything right. And still I was called naughty and tiresome, sulky and sneaky, from morning to noon and from noon to night.

My head still ached and bled from the blow and the fall. No one had scolded John for hitting me without reason. And because I had fought back to stop further irrational violence, I was the one condemned by everyone.

"Unjust! Unjust!" cried my reason, forced by the agony into a power beyond my years, though it wouldn't last. And my will, equally roused, urged some desperate measure to escape unbearable oppression—like running away, or if that couldn't be done, simply refusing to eat or drink, and letting myself die.

What turmoil filled my soul that dreary afternoon! How my mind reeled and my heart rebelled! Yet in what darkness, what deep ignorance, was the inner battle fought! I couldn't answer the relentless question—why I suffered this way. Now, at a distance of—I won't say how many years—I see it clearly.

I was a misfit at Gateshead Hall. I was unlike anyone there. I had nothing in common with Mrs. Reed or her children or her chosen household. If they didn't love me, I loved them just as little. They had no reason to feel affection for someone who couldn't relate to any of them—an outsider, different in temperament, ability, and inclination. A useless thing, unable to serve their interests or add to their pleasure. A troublesome thing, harboring the seeds of resentment at their treatment and contempt for their judgment. I know that if I had been a cheerful, bright, carefree, bold, and pretty child—though equally dependent and friendless—Mrs. Reed would have tolerated my presence more easily. Her children would have felt more warmth toward me. The servants would have been less inclined to make me the nursery scapegoat.

Daylight began to fade from the red room. It was past four o'clock, and the overcast afternoon was sliding toward grim twilight. I could hear the rain still beating steadily against the staircase window and the wind howling in the grove behind the house. Gradually I grew cold as stone, and my courage sank. My usual state of humiliation, self-doubt, and bleak depression settled like damp ashes on the dying embers of my anger. Everyone said I was wicked, and perhaps I was. What had I just been thinking about? Starving myself to death? That was certainly a crime. And was I fit to die? Was the vault beneath the chancel of Gateshead Church an inviting destination? I had been told that Mr. Reed was buried in such a vault, and that thought led me to picture him, which filled me with growing dread. I couldn't remember him, but I knew he had been my uncle—my mother's brother—and that he had taken me in as a parentless baby. In his final moments, he had made Mrs. Reed promise to raise me as one of her own children. Mrs. Reed probably believed she had kept that promise, and I suppose she had, as well as her nature allowed. But how could she truly care for an outsider, not of her blood, with no connection to her after her husband's death? It must have been deeply irksome to find herself bound by a grudging promise to act as mother to a strange child she couldn't love, and to see an unwelcome stranger permanently embedded in her own family.

A strange idea occurred to me. I had never doubted that if Mr. Reed had been alive, he would have treated me kindly. And now, as I sat staring at the white bed and shadowed walls—glancing now and then at the dimly glinting mirror—I began to recall what I'd heard about dead men, disturbed in their graves when their last wishes were violated, returning to earth to punish oath-breakers and protect the wronged. I imagined Mr. Reed's spirit, troubled by the suffering of his sister's child, might leave its resting place—whether in the church vault or wherever the dead go—and appear before me in this room. I wiped my tears and stifled my sobs, afraid that any sign of violent grief might summon a supernatural voice to comfort me, or draw from the shadows some glowing face bending over me with unearthly pity. This idea, comforting in theory, would have been terrifying in reality, and I tried with all my strength to suppress it. I tried to be brave. Shaking my hair from my eyes, I raised my head and forced myself to look boldly around the dark room. At that moment, a light gleamed on the wall. Was it, I wondered, a ray of moonlight coming through a gap in the blind? No—moonlight would be steady, and this was moving. As I watched, it glided up to the ceiling and flickered above my head. I can easily guess now that the light was probably from a lantern carried by someone crossing the lawn. But at the time, with my mind primed for horror and my nerves shattered, I thought the darting beam was a sign of some approaching vision from another world. My heart pounded, my head burned. A sound filled my ears that I took for the rushing of wings. Something seemed near me. I felt crushed, suffocated. My endurance broke. I rushed to the door and shook the lock in desperate effort. Footsteps came running along the hallway outside. The key turned. Bessie and Abbot entered.
"Miss Eyre, are you ill?" said Bessie.
"What a dreadful noise! It went right through me!" exclaimed Abbot.
"Take me out! Let me go to the nursery!" I cried.
"Why? Are you hurt? Did you see something?" Bessie asked again.
"Oh! I saw a light, and I thought a ghost was going to come." I had grabbed hold of Bessie's hand, and she didn't pull it away.
"She screamed on purpose," Abbot declared with disgust. "And what a scream! If she'd been in real pain, you could excuse it, but she just wanted to bring us all running. I know her tricks."

"What is all this?" demanded another voice sharply. Mrs. Reed came down the corridor, her cap flying wide, her gown rustling furiously. "Abbot and Bessie, I believe I gave orders that Jane Eyre was to be left in the red room until I came for her myself."
"Miss Jane screamed so loudly, ma'am," Bessie pleaded.

"Let her go," was the only answer. "Let go of Bessie's hand, child. You will not succeed in getting out this way, I assure you. I despise manipulation, especially in children. It is my duty to show you that tricks will not work. You will stay here an hour longer, and only on the condition of complete silence and obedience will I let you out then."
"Oh, Aunt! Have pity! Forgive me! I can't bear it—let me be punished some other way! I'll be killed if—"

"Silence! This behavior is utterly revolting." And no doubt she believed it. In her eyes, I was a dramatic little actress. She genuinely saw me as a bundle of violent passions, petty spirit, and dangerous deceit.

After Bessie and Abbot left, Mrs. Reed, fed up with my frantic anguish and wild sobbing, shoved me back and locked me in without another word. I heard her sweep away. And soon after she was gone, I suppose I had some kind of fit. I lost consciousness, and everything went dark.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: The next thing I remember is waking up with the feeling of having had a terrible nightmare. Before me was a frightening red glow, crossed with thick black bars. I heard voices too, speaking with a hollow sound, as if muffled by rushing wind or water. Confusion, uncertainty, and an overwhelming sense of terror scrambled my thoughts. Before long, I became aware that someone was handling me, lifting me up and holding me in a sitting position, more gently than I had ever been held before. I rested my head against a pillow or an arm, and felt at ease.

Within five minutes, the fog of confusion cleared. I knew perfectly well that I was in my own bed, and that the red glow was the nursery fire. It was night. A candle burned on the table. Bessie stood at the foot of the bed with a basin in her hand, and a gentleman sat in a chair by my pillow, leaning over me.

I felt an indescribable relief, a soothing certainty of safety and protection, knowing there was a stranger in the room—someone who didn't belong to Gateshead and wasn't related to Mrs. Reed. Turning away from Bessie (though her presence bothered me far less than Abbot's would have), I studied the gentleman's face. I knew him: it was Mr. Lloyd, the apothecary sometimes called in by Mrs. Reed when the servants were sick. For herself and the children, she used a physician.
"Well, who am I?" he asked.

I said his name and offered him my hand. He took it, smiling, and said, "We'll be just fine before long." Then he laid me down and told Bessie to make sure I wasn't disturbed during the night. After giving some further instructions and saying he would call again the next day, he left—to my grief. I had felt so safe and cared for while he sat by my pillow. And as he closed the door behind him, the whole room darkened and my heart sank again. An inexpressible sadness weighed it down.
"Do you think you could sleep, Miss?" asked Bessie, rather softly.
I barely dared answer her, afraid the next words might be harsh. "I'll try."
"Would you like something to drink, or could you eat anything?"
"No, thank you, Bessie."
"Then I think I'll go to bed, since it's past midnight. But you can call me if you need anything in the night."
Such remarkable kindness! It gave me the courage to ask a question.
"Bessie, what's the matter with me? Am I ill?"
"You fainted, I suppose, in the red room from all the crying. You'll be better soon, I'm sure."
Bessie went into the housemaid's room next door. I heard her say—
"Sarah, come sleep with me in the nursery. I'm terrified to be alone with that poor child tonight. She could die. It's so strange that she had that fit. The Missus was rather too hard on her."

Sarah came back with her. They both went to bed and whispered together for half an hour before falling asleep. I caught scraps of their conversation, from which I could clearly piece together the main topic.
"Something passed her, all dressed in white, and vanished"—"A great black dog behind him"—"Three loud knocks on the bedroom door"—"A light in the churchyard, right over his grave"—and so on.

At last they both slept. The fire and the candle went out. For me, the hours of that long night passed in horrible wakefulness. My ears, my eyes, my mind were all strained with dread—the kind of dread only children can feel.

No serious or lasting physical illness followed the red room incident. It only gave my nerves a shock whose aftershocks I feel to this day. Yes, Mrs. Reed, I owe you some terrible moments of mental anguish. But I should forgive you, because you didn't know what you were doing. While you were tearing my heart apart, you thought you were only correcting my bad tendencies.

The next day, by noon, I was up and dressed and sat wrapped in a shawl by the nursery fire. I felt physically weak and broken, but my worst suffering was an unspeakable misery of the mind—a wretchedness that kept drawing silent tears from me. No sooner had I wiped one salty drop from my cheek than another followed. Yet I thought I should have been happy, since none of the Reeds were there—they had all gone out in the carriage with their mama. Abbot was sewing in another room, and Bessie, as she moved around putting away toys and tidying drawers, spoke to me every now and then with unusual kindness. This should have been paradise for someone used to a life of constant criticism and thankless drudgery. But my shattered nerves were in such a state that no calm could soothe them and no pleasure could reach them.

Bessie had been down to the kitchen and brought back a tart on a certain brightly painted china plate, whose bird of paradise nestled in a wreath of flowers. That plate had always stirred in me a rush of admiration, and I had often begged to be allowed to hold it and examine it up close, but had always been considered unworthy of such a privilege. Now this precious dish was placed on my knee, and I was warmly invited to eat the ring of delicate pastry on it. But it was no use. Like most long-awaited favors, it came too late. I couldn't eat the tart, and the plumage of the bird, the colors of the flowers, seemed strangely faded. I pushed both plate and tart away. Bessie asked if I wanted a book. The word book acted as a brief spark, and I asked her to fetch Gulliver's Travels from the library. I had read that book again and again with delight. I considered it a true account and found in it a deeper interest than fairy tales offered. As for elves, having searched for them in vain among foxglove leaves and bells, under mushrooms, and beneath the ivy on old walls, I had finally accepted the sad truth that they had all left England for some wild country where the forests were thicker and the people fewer. But Lilliput and Brobdingnag, I firmly believed, were real places on the earth's surface, and I had no doubt that someday, by taking a long voyage, I would see with my own eyes the tiny fields, houses, and trees, the miniature people, the little cows, sheep, and birds of one realm, and the towering crops, the enormous dogs, the monstrous cats, and the giant men and women of the other. Yet now, when this beloved book was placed in my hands—when I turned its pages and looked for the magic in its wonderful pictures that had never failed me before—everything was eerie and bleak. The giants were gaunt goblins, the little people were sinister imps, and Gulliver was the loneliest wanderer in the most terrifying of lands. I closed the book, afraid to keep reading, and put it on the table beside the untouched tart.

Bessie had finished dusting and tidying the room. Having washed her hands, she opened a small drawer full of beautiful scraps of silk and satin and began making a new bonnet for Georgiana's doll. As she worked, she sang. Her song was—
"In the days when we went gipsying, A long time ago."

I had often heard the song before and always loved it, because Bessie had a sweet voice—at least, I thought so. But now, though her voice was still sweet, I found an indescribable sadness in the melody. Sometimes, absorbed in her work, she sang the refrain very low, very lingeringly. "A long time ago" came out like the saddest note of a funeral hymn. She moved on to another song, this one truly sorrowful.
"My feet they are sore, and my limbs they are weary; Long is the way, and the mountains are wild; Soon will the twilight close moonless and dreary Over the path of the poor orphan child.
Why did they send me so far and so lonely, Up where the moors spread and grey rocks are piled? Men are hard-hearted, and kind angels only Watch o'er the steps of a poor orphan child.
Yet distant and soft the night breeze is blowing, Clouds there are none, and clear stars beam mild, God, in His mercy, protection is showing, Comfort and hope to the poor orphan child.
Ev'n should I fall o'er the broken bridge passing, Or stray in the marshes, by false lights beguiled, Still will my Father, with promise and blessing, Take to His bosom the poor orphan child.
There is a thought that for strength should avail me, Though both of shelter and kindred despoiled; Heaven is a home, and a rest will not fail me; God is a friend to the poor orphan child."

"Come now, Miss Jane, don't cry," said Bessie when she finished. She might as well have told the fire not to burn. But how could she have known the depth of suffering I was enduring? Later that morning, Mr. Lloyd came again.
"What, up already!" he said as he entered the nursery. "Well, nurse, how is she?"
Bessie said I was doing well enough.
"Then she should look more cheerful. Come here, Miss Jane. Your name is Jane, isn't it?"
"Yes, sir. Jane Eyre."
"Well, you've been crying, Miss Jane Eyre. Can you tell me why? Are you in pain?"
"No, sir."
"Oh, I expect she's crying because she couldn't go with the Missus in the carriage," Bessie put in.
"Surely not! She's too old for that kind of fuss."

I thought so too, and with my pride stung by the false accusation, I answered promptly: "I never cried about anything like that in my life. I hate going out in the carriage. I'm crying because I'm miserable."
"Oh, really, Miss!" said Bessie.

The kind apothecary looked a little puzzled. I was standing before him, and he studied me steadily. His eyes were small and gray, not especially bright, but I think now they were quite shrewd. He had a rough-featured but kind-looking face. After considering me for a moment, he said—
"What made you ill yesterday?"
"She had a fall," said Bessie, jumping in again.
"A fall! That's like a baby! Can't she manage to walk at her age? She must be eight or nine."
"I was knocked down," I said bluntly, the words jerked out of me by another pang of wounded pride. "But that didn't make me ill," I added, while Mr. Lloyd helped himself to a pinch of snuff.

As he tucked the box back into his waistcoat pocket, a loud bell rang for the servants' dinner. He knew what it was. "That's for you, nurse," he said. "You can go down. I'll have a talk with Miss Jane while you're gone."
Bessie would rather have stayed, but she had to go—punctuality at meals was strictly enforced at Gateshead Hall.
"The fall didn't make you ill. So what did?" Mr. Lloyd asked once Bessie was gone.
"I was locked in a room where there's a ghost, until after dark."
I saw Mr. Lloyd smile and frown at the same time.
"Ghost! So you are a baby after all! You're afraid of ghosts?"

"I'm afraid of Mr. Reed's ghost. He died in that room and was laid out there. Nobody—not Bessie or anyone else—will go in there at night if they can help it. And it was cruel to shut me up alone without a candle—so cruel that I think I'll never forget it."
"Nonsense! And is that what makes you so unhappy? Are you afraid now, in the daylight?"
"No. But night will come again before long. And besides—I'm unhappy—very unhappy, for other reasons."
"What other reasons? Can you tell me some of them?"

How desperately I wanted to answer that question fully! And how hard it was to form a reply. Children can feel, but they can't analyze their feelings. And even if they manage to sort through their emotions in their minds, they don't know how to put the result into words. Afraid of losing this first and only chance to relieve my grief by sharing it, I paused, struggled, and managed to piece together a thin but truthful answer.
"For one thing, I have no father or mother, no brothers or sisters."
"You have a kind aunt and cousins."
I paused again, then clumsily went on—
"But John Reed knocked me down, and my aunt locked me in the red room."
Mr. Lloyd took out his snuffbox a second time.
"Don't you think Gateshead Hall is a very beautiful house?" he asked. "Aren't you thankful to have such a fine place to live?"
"It's not my house, sir. And Abbot says I have less right to be here than a servant."
"Come now, you can't be foolish enough to want to leave such a splendid place?"
"If I had somewhere else to go, I'd be glad to leave. But I can never get away from Gateshead until I'm grown."
"Perhaps you could—who knows? Do you have any other relatives besides Mrs. Reed?"
"I don't think so, sir."
"None on your father's side?"
"I don't know. I asked Aunt Reed once, and she said I might have some poor, low-class relatives called Eyre, but she knew nothing about them."
"If you did have such relatives, would you like to go to them?"

I thought about it. Poverty looks harsh to adults and even harsher to children. They don't have much sense of honest, hardworking, respectable poverty. They connect the word only with ragged clothes, not enough food, cold hearths, rough manners, and degrading habits. To me, poverty meant humiliation.
"No, I wouldn't want to belong to poor people," I answered.
"Not even if they were kind to you?"

I shook my head. I couldn't see how poor people had the means to be kind. And then to learn to talk like them, to adopt their habits, to go uneducated, to grow up like the poor women I sometimes saw nursing their children or washing their clothes at the cottage doors of Gateshead village—no, I wasn't brave enough to buy my freedom at the cost of my social standing.
"But are your relatives really so poor? Are they working people?"
"I can't say. Aunt Reed says if I have any, they must be a wretched lot. I wouldn't want to go begging."
"Would you like to go to school?"

I thought again. I barely knew what school was. Bessie sometimes described it as a place where young ladies sat on hard benches, wore stiff boards strapped to their backs for posture, and were expected to be extremely refined and proper. John Reed hated his school and complained about his teachers—but John Reed's tastes were no guide for mine. And if Bessie's accounts of school discipline (gathered from the young ladies of a family where she had worked before Gateshead) were somewhat alarming, her descriptions of the skills those same young ladies had acquired were, I thought, equally appealing. She boasted of beautiful landscape and flower paintings they had done, songs they could sing and pieces they could play, purses they could knit, French books they could translate. My spirit stirred with ambition as I listened. Besides, school would be a complete change. It would mean a long journey, a total separation from Gateshead, and entry into a new life.
"I would indeed like to go to school," I said, speaking my thoughts aloud.
"Well, well! Who knows what may happen?" said Mr. Lloyd, getting to his feet. "The child needs a change of air and scenery," he added to himself. "Her nerves are in a bad state."
Bessie returned just then, and at the same moment the carriage was heard rolling up the gravel drive.
"Is that your mistress, nurse?" asked Mr. Lloyd. "I'd like to speak with her before I go."

Bessie invited him into the breakfast room and led the way out. In the conversation that followed between him and Mrs. Reed, I gathered from what happened afterward that the apothecary suggested I be sent to school. The suggestion was no doubt eagerly accepted, because as Abbot said when discussing it with Bessie one night while they sewed in the nursery—after I was in bed and, they assumed, asleep—"The Missus was glad enough to get rid of such a tiresome, ill-natured child, who was always watching everybody and scheming behind their backs." Abbot, I think, gave me credit for being a sort of infant Guy Fawkes.

On that same occasion, I learned for the first time, from Miss Abbot's conversation with Bessie, that my father had been a poor clergyman. My mother had married him against the wishes of her family, who considered the match beneath her. My grandfather Reed was so angry at her disobedience that he cut her off without a penny. After my parents had been married a year, my father caught typhus while visiting the poor of a large manufacturing town where he served as curate, and where the disease was widespread at the time. My mother caught the infection from him, and both died within a month of each other.
Bessie, when she heard this story, sighed and said, "Poor Miss Jane deserves some pity too, Abbot."
"Yes," Abbot replied. "If she were a nice, pretty child, you might feel sorry for her being alone in the world. But you really can't care much about such an ugly little creature."
"Not a great deal, I suppose," Bessie agreed. "At any rate, a beauty like Miss Georgiana would stir more sympathy in the same situation."

"Yes, I adore Miss Georgiana!" cried the passionate Abbot. "Little darling! With her long curls and blue eyes, and such lovely color—as if she were painted! Bessie, I could go for a Welsh rarebit for supper."
"Me too—with a roasted onion. Come, let's go down." They went.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: From my conversation with Mr. Lloyd and from the discussion between Bessie and Abbot that I overheard, I gathered enough hope to keep me going while I waited to get well. A change seemed near, and I longed for it in silence. But it was slow in coming. Days and weeks passed. I regained my normal health, but no one mentioned the subject I was constantly thinking about. Mrs. Reed watched me sometimes with a stern eye but rarely spoke to me. Since my illness, she had drawn an even sharper line between me and her own children, giving me a small closet to sleep in alone, making me eat my meals by myself, and spending all my time in the nursery while my cousins stayed in the drawing room. She dropped no hint about sending me to school, yet I felt instinctively certain she wouldn't keep me under her roof much longer. Her glance, more than ever, expressed a deep and fixed aversion when it fell on me.

Eliza and Georgiana, clearly following orders, spoke to me as little as possible. John stuck his tongue in his cheek whenever he saw me and once tried to hit me. But when I instantly turned on him, driven by the same deep fury and desperate defiance that had flared up before, he decided it was better to back off. He ran from me, cursing and swearing I had broken his nose. I had indeed aimed the hardest blow my fist could deliver right at that prominent feature, and when I saw that either the punch or my expression scared him, I was strongly tempted to press my advantage. But he was already running to his mama. I heard him blubbering out the tale of how "that awful Jane Eyre" had attacked him like a wild cat. He was cut off rather sharply—
"Don't talk to me about her, John. I told you not to go near her. She is not worth your notice. I don't want you or your sisters associating with her."
Leaning over the banister, I suddenly cried out, without thinking at all about my words—
"They are not fit to associate with me."

Mrs. Reed was a fairly stout woman, but on hearing this brazen declaration, she ran nimbly up the stairs, swept me like a whirlwind into the nursery, and, crushing me down on the edge of my crib, dared me in a fierce voice to get up or say one more word for the rest of the day.

"What would Uncle Reed say to you if he were alive?" The words came out of me almost involuntarily. It felt as if my tongue was speaking without my permission—something inside me that I had no control over.

"What?" said Mrs. Reed under her breath. Her usually cold, composed gray eyes filled with something like fear. She took her hand off my arm and stared at me as if she truly didn't know whether I was a child or a demon. I was in for it now.
"My Uncle Reed is in heaven, and he can see everything you do and think. So can my papa and mama. They know how you lock me up all day, and how you wish I were dead."

Mrs. Reed quickly recovered herself. She shook me hard, boxed both my ears, and left without a word. Bessie filled the gap with an hour-long lecture, proving beyond doubt that I was the most wicked and abandoned child ever raised under a roof. I half believed her, because all I could feel were dark emotions surging inside me.

November, December, and half of January passed. Christmas and New Year had been celebrated at Gateshead with the usual festivities—presents exchanged, dinners and parties given. I was excluded from all of it, of course. My share of the celebrations consisted of watching Eliza and Georgiana get dressed in their thin muslin frocks and red sashes, their hair elaborately curled, and seeing them go down to the drawing room. After that, I listened to the sounds of piano or harp playing below, to the footsteps of the butler and footman, to the clinking of glass and china as refreshments were served, and to the muffled hum of conversation whenever the drawing room door opened and closed. When I tired of this, I retreated from the top of the stairs to the lonely, silent nursery. There, though somewhat sad, I wasn't miserable. To tell the truth, I had no desire to join the company—when I was among people, I was almost never noticed. If Bessie had only been kind and companionable, I would have considered it a treat to spend the evenings quietly with her instead of enduring the formidable gaze of Mrs. Reed in a room full of guests. But as soon as Bessie had dressed the young ladies, she took herself off to the lively kitchen and housekeeper's room, usually taking the candle with her. I would sit with my doll on my knee until the fire burned low, glancing around now and then to make sure nothing worse than myself haunted the shadowy room. When the embers faded to a dull red, I undressed quickly, struggling with knots and buttons as best I could, and sought shelter from the cold and darkness in my crib. I always took my doll to bed with me. Human beings need to love something, and with nothing worthier to love, I managed to find pleasure in loving and cherishing a faded little figure, shabby as a miniature scarecrow. It puzzles me now to remember with what absurd devotion I doted on this toy, half-imagining it was alive and could feel. I couldn't sleep unless it was tucked inside my nightgown, and when it lay there safe and warm, I was relatively happy, believing it was happy too.

The hours dragged while I waited for the guests to leave, listening for Bessie's step on the stairs. Sometimes she would come up between events to fetch her thimble or scissors, or perhaps to bring me something for supper—a bun or a small cake. Then she would sit on the bed while I ate, and when I finished, she would tuck the covers around me. Twice she kissed me and said, "Good night, Miss Jane." When she was gentle like this, Bessie seemed to me the best, prettiest, kindest person in the world, and I desperately wished she would always be so pleasant and never push me around or scold me or make unreasonable demands, as she too often did. Bessie Lee must have been a girl of real natural ability, because she was sharp in everything she did and had a remarkable gift for storytelling—at least, that's how I judge it from the impression her nursery tales made on me. She was pretty too, if I remember her face and figure correctly. I recall her as a slim young woman with black hair, dark eyes, very nice features, and a clear complexion. But she had a changeable and hasty temper, and vague ideas about fairness or justice. Still, such as she was, I preferred her to anyone else at Gateshead Hall.

It was the fifteenth of January, about nine in the morning. Bessie had gone down to breakfast. My cousins hadn't yet been called to their mama. Eliza was putting on her bonnet and warm coat to go feed her chickens, an activity she loved—and she loved selling the eggs to the housekeeper and hoarding the money just as much. She had a knack for business and a marked talent for saving, shown not only in selling eggs and chickens but also in driving hard bargains with the gardener over flower roots, seeds, and plant cuttings. The gardener had orders from Mrs. Reed to buy whatever his young lady wished to sell from her garden plot, and Eliza would have sold the hair off her head if she could have turned a handsome profit. As for her money, she first hid it in odd corners, wrapped in rags or old curl papers. But after the housemaid discovered some of these stashes, Eliza, terrified of losing her treasure, agreed to deposit it with her mother—at an outrageous interest rate of fifty or sixty percent, which she collected every quarter, keeping careful accounts in a little notebook.

Georgiana sat on a high stool at the mirror, doing her hair and weaving in artificial flowers and faded feathers she'd found in an attic drawer. I was making my bed, under strict orders from Bessie to have it done before she came back (for Bessie now often used me as a sort of assistant nursemaid, to tidy the room, dust the furniture, and so on). After spreading the quilt and folding my nightgown, I went to the window seat to straighten some picture books and dollhouse furniture scattered there. An abrupt command from Georgiana to leave her things alone (the tiny chairs and mirrors, the fairy plates and cups were hers) stopped me. With nothing else to do, I breathed on the frost patterns on the window, melting enough of the silvery-white designs to clear a space through which I could look out at the grounds, where everything lay still and frozen under a hard frost.

From this window I could see the porter's lodge and the carriage road. Just as I had melted enough frost to peer through, I saw the gates thrown open and a carriage roll through. I watched it come up the drive without much interest—carriages often came to Gateshead, but none ever brought visitors who mattered to me. It stopped in front of the house. The doorbell rang loudly. The newcomer was let in. Since none of this concerned me, my idle attention soon found a livelier attraction in a little hungry robin that came chirping on the bare branches of a cherry tree nailed against the wall near my window. The remains of my bread and milk breakfast sat on the table. I crumbled a bit of roll and was tugging at the window sash to put the crumbs on the sill when Bessie came rushing upstairs into the nursery.

"Miss Jane, take off your pinafore! What are you doing there? Have you washed your hands and face this morning?" I gave another tug before answering, because I wanted the bird to get its bread. The sash gave way. I scattered the crumbs, some on the stone sill, some on the cherry tree branch. Then, closing the window, I replied—
"No, Bessie. I've only just finished dusting."
"Troublesome, careless child! And what are you doing now? You look quite red, as if you've been up to something. Why were you opening the window?"

I was spared having to answer, because Bessie seemed in too much of a hurry to listen to explanations. She hauled me to the washstand, gave my face and hands a rough but thankfully brief scrubbing with soap, water, and a coarse towel, attacked my hair with a stiff brush, stripped off my pinafore, and then hurried me to the top of the stairs, telling me to go down at once—I was wanted in the breakfast room.

I would have asked who wanted me. I would have demanded to know if Mrs. Reed was there. But Bessie was already gone, shutting the nursery door behind her. I went down slowly. For nearly three months, I had never been called to Mrs. Reed's presence. Confined to the nursery for so long, the breakfast room, dining room, and drawing room had become terrifying territories that I dreaded entering.

I now stood in the empty hall. Before me was the breakfast room door, and I stopped, intimidated and trembling. What a miserable little coward fear and unjust punishment had made of me in those days! I was afraid to go back to the nursery and afraid to go forward to the parlor. For ten minutes I stood in anxious indecision. The fierce ringing of the breakfast room bell decided it—I had to go in.

"Who could want me?" I asked myself, as I turned the stiff door handle with both hands. It resisted for a second or two. "What will I see besides Aunt Reed in there? A man or a woman?" The handle turned, the door opened, and passing through with a low curtsy, I looked up at—a black pillar! That, at least, was what it looked like at first glance: a straight, narrow, black-clad shape standing stiffly on the rug. The grim face at the top was like a carved mask placed above a column.
Mrs. Reed sat in her usual place by the fire. She signaled me to come closer, and introduced me to the stony stranger with the words: "This is the little girl I wrote to you about."
He—for it was a man—turned his head slowly toward me. Having examined me with two curious gray eyes twinkling under bushy brows, he said solemnly in a deep voice, "She's small. What is her age?"
"Ten years old."
"That much?" he said doubtfully, and studied me for several minutes more. Then he spoke to me. "Your name, little girl?"
"Jane Eyre, sir."
I looked up as I said it. He seemed to me a tall gentleman, but then I was very small. His features were large, and everything about his face and figure was equally harsh and rigid.
"Well, Jane Eyre, and are you a good child?"

It was impossible to say yes. My little world held the opposite opinion. I stayed silent. Mrs. Reed answered for me with an expressive shake of her head, adding, "Perhaps the less said about that, the better, Mr. Brocklehurst."
"Sorry to hear it! She and I must have a talk." And bending from his towering height, he settled himself into the armchair opposite Mrs. Reed. "Come here," he said.
I crossed the rug. He positioned me squarely in front of him. What a face he had, now that it was almost level with mine! What a great nose! What a mouth! And what large, prominent teeth!
"No sight is sadder than that of a naughty child," he began, "especially a naughty little girl. Do you know where the wicked go after death?"
"They go to hell," was my ready, textbook answer.
"And what is hell? Can you tell me that?"
"A pit full of fire."
"And would you like to fall into that pit and burn there forever?"
"No, sir."
"What must you do to avoid it?"
I thought for a moment. My answer, when it came, was unacceptable: "I must stay healthy and not die."

"How can you stay healthy? Children younger than you die every day. I buried a little child of five just a day or two ago—a good little child, whose soul is now in heaven. I fear the same could not be said of you if you were called away."
Unable to reassure him on that point, I just looked down at his two large feet planted on the rug and sighed, wishing myself far away.
"I hope that sigh comes from the heart, and that you repent of ever having caused distress to your excellent benefactress."
"Benefactress! Benefactress!" I said to myself. "They all call Mrs. Reed my benefactress. If so, a benefactress is a disagreeable thing."
"Do you say your prayers morning and night?" my interrogator continued.
"Yes, sir."
"Do you read your Bible?"
"Sometimes."
"With pleasure? Are you fond of it?"
"I like Revelation, and the Book of Daniel, and Genesis, and Samuel, and a little bit of Exodus, and some parts of Kings and Chronicles, and Job and Jonah."
"And the Psalms? I hope you like them?"
"No, sir."

"No? Oh, shocking! I have a little boy, younger than you, who knows six Psalms by heart. And when you ask him which he'd rather have, a gingerbread biscuit to eat or a verse of a Psalm to learn, he says: 'Oh, the verse of a Psalm! Angels sing Psalms,' says he. 'I wish to be a little angel here below.' And then he gets two biscuits as a reward for his goodness."
"Psalms are not interesting," I observed.
"That proves you have a wicked heart. You must pray to God to change it—to give you a new and clean one, to take away your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh."
I was about to ask exactly how this operation of changing my heart was to be done, when Mrs. Reed cut in, telling me to sit down. She then proceeded to take over the conversation.

"Mr. Brocklehurst, I believe I mentioned in my letter three weeks ago that this little girl does not have quite the character and temperament I would wish. If you accept her at Lowood school, I would be grateful if the superintendent and teachers were asked to keep a strict eye on her and, above all, to guard against her worst fault—a tendency toward deceit. I mention this in your hearing, Jane, so that you won't try to deceive Mr. Brocklehurst."

I had every right to dread Mrs. Reed and every reason to dislike her, because it was in her nature to wound me cruelly. I was never happy in her presence. No matter how carefully I obeyed or how hard I tried to please her, my efforts were always rejected and repaid with words like these. Now, spoken in front of a stranger, the accusation cut me to the heart. I dimly sensed that she was already destroying hope in the new life she was sending me to. I felt, though I couldn't have put it into words, that she was planting hatred and suspicion along my future path. I could see myself being transformed in Mr. Brocklehurst's eyes into a cunning, dangerous child. And what could I do to undo the damage?
"Nothing," I thought, as I struggled to hold back a sob and quickly wiped away tears—the helpless proof of my anguish.

"Deceit is indeed a terrible fault in a child," said Mr. Brocklehurst. "It is close to lying, and all liars will have their place in the lake of burning fire and brimstone. She will be watched, Mrs. Reed. I will speak to Miss Temple and the teachers."

"I would like her to be raised in a manner suited to her prospects," my benefactress continued. "To be made useful, to be kept humble. As for the holidays, she will, with your permission, spend them all at Lowood."

"Your decisions are perfectly sound, madam," replied Mr. Brocklehurst. "Humility is a Christian virtue, and one especially suited to the pupils of Lowood. I direct that special attention be given to cultivating it among them. I have studied how best to crush worldly pride in these girls, and just the other day I had a pleasing proof of my success. My second daughter, Augusta, went with her mama to visit the school, and when she came back she exclaimed: 'Oh, dear Papa, how plain and quiet all the girls at Lowood look, with their hair combed behind their ears and their long pinafores and those little linen pockets on the front of their dresses—they look almost like poor people's children! And,' she said, 'they stared at my dress and Mama's as if they'd never seen a silk gown before.'"

"That is exactly the state of things I approve," said Mrs. Reed. "If I had searched all of England, I could hardly have found a system more perfectly suited to a child like Jane Eyre. Consistency, my dear Mr. Brocklehurst—I believe in consistency in all things."

"Consistency, madam, is the first of Christian duties, and it has been observed in every aspect of Lowood: plain food, simple clothing, modest accommodations, and vigorous, active habits. Such is the order of the day in the house and among its residents."
"Quite right, sir. May I depend on this child being accepted as a pupil at Lowood, and being trained in a manner suited to her position and prospects?"
"You may, madam. She shall be placed in that nursery of chosen plants, and I trust she will show herself grateful for the precious privilege of being admitted."
"I will send her as soon as possible, then, Mr. Brocklehurst. I assure you, I'm anxious to be relieved of a responsibility that was becoming too burdensome."

"No doubt, no doubt, madam. And now I wish you good morning. I shall return to Brocklehurst Hall within a week or two—my good friend the Archdeacon won't let me leave sooner. I will send Miss Temple notice to expect a new girl, so there will be no difficulty receiving her. Good-bye."
"Good-bye, Mr. Brocklehurst. Please give my regards to Mrs. and Miss Brocklehurst, and to Augusta and Theodore, and Master Broughton Brocklehurst."

"I will, madam. Little girl, here is a book called the Child's Guide. Read it with prayer, especially the part about the terribly sudden death of Martha G——, a naughty child addicted to lying and deceit."
With these words, Mr. Brocklehurst put a thin pamphlet into my hand, rang for his carriage, and left.

Mrs. Reed and I were left alone. Several minutes passed in silence. She was sewing; I was watching her. Mrs. Reed must have been about thirty-six or thirty-seven at the time. She was a solidly built woman—square-shouldered and strong-limbed, not tall, and though heavy, not fat. She had a somewhat large face with a very developed and solid jaw. Her brow was low, her chin large and prominent, her mouth and nose ordinary enough. Beneath her light eyebrows gleamed eyes devoid of compassion. Her skin was dark and dull, her hair nearly blond. Her constitution was rock-solid—illness never touched her. She was a precise, capable manager. Her household and tenants were thoroughly under her control; only her children occasionally defied her authority and laughed at it. She dressed well and had a bearing calculated to show off fine clothes.

Sitting on a low stool a few yards from her armchair, I studied her figure and examined her features. In my hand I held the pamphlet about the sudden death of the Liar, to which my attention had been directed as an appropriate warning. What had just happened—what Mrs. Reed had said about me to Mr. Brocklehurst, the whole tone of their conversation—was fresh, raw, and stinging in my mind. I had felt every word as sharply as I had heard it clearly, and a passionate resentment now burned inside me.
Mrs. Reed looked up from her work. Her eye settled on mine, and at the same time her fingers stopped their nimble movements.

"Leave the room. Go back to the nursery," she ordered. My expression or something else must have struck her as offensive, because she spoke with extreme though controlled irritation. I got up. I went to the door. I came back. I walked to the window, then across the room, then right up close to her.
I had to speak. I had been trampled on too hard and had to fight back. But how? What power did I have to strike at my enemy? I gathered my energy and launched it in this blunt sentence—

"I am not deceitful. If I were, I would say I loved you. But I declare I do not love you. I dislike you more than anyone in the world except John Reed. And this book about the liar—you can give it to your daughter Georgiana, because she's the one who tells lies, not me."
Mrs. Reed's hands still lay idle on her work. Her icy eyes continued to bore into mine.
"What else do you have to say?" she asked, in a tone one might use with an adult opponent rather than a child.
That stare of hers, that voice, roused every hostile feeling in me. Shaking from head to foot, thrilling with uncontrollable emotion, I continued—

"I'm glad you're no relation of mine. I will never call you Aunt again as long as I live. I will never come to visit you when I'm grown up. And if anyone asks me how I liked you and how you treated me, I will say the very thought of you makes me sick, and that you treated me with miserable cruelty."
"How dare you say that, Jane Eyre?"

"How dare I, Mrs. Reed? How dare I? Because it is the truth. You think I have no feelings and that I can survive without a single bit of love or kindness. But I cannot live like that, and you have no pity. I will remember how you shoved me back—roughly and violently shoved me back—into the red room and locked me in there, until my dying day. Even though I was in agony. Even though I cried out, while choking with distress, 'Have mercy! Have mercy, Aunt Reed!' And that punishment you gave me because your wicked boy hit me—knocked me down for nothing. I will tell anyone who asks the exact truth. People think you're a good woman, but you are bad and hard-hearted. You are the deceitful one!"
How dare I, Mrs. Reed? How dare I? Because it is the truth.

Before I had even finished, my soul began to expand and soar with the strangest sense of freedom and triumph I had ever felt. It was as if an invisible chain had snapped and I had broken through into an undreamed-of liberty. Mrs. Reed looked frightened. Her sewing had slipped from her lap. She was lifting her hands, rocking back and forth, and even twisting her face as if she might cry.
"Jane, you're mistaken. What's the matter with you? Why are you trembling so violently? Would you like a glass of water?"
"No, Mrs. Reed."
"Is there anything else you want, Jane? I assure you, I want to be your friend."
"Not you. You told Mr. Brocklehurst I had a bad character, a deceitful nature. And I'll let everyone at Lowood know what you are and what you've done."
"Jane, you don't understand these things. Children must be corrected for their faults."
"Deceit is not my fault!" I cried out in a fierce, high voice.
"But you are passionate, Jane—you must admit that. Now go back to the nursery—there's a dear—and lie down for a bit."
"I am not your dear. I cannot lie down. Send me to school soon, Mrs. Reed, because I hate living here."
"I will indeed send her to school soon," murmured Mrs. Reed under her breath. And gathering up her work, she abruptly left the room.

I was left alone—the winner of the battle. It was the hardest fight I had ever fought and the first victory I had ever won. I stood for a while on the rug where Mr. Brocklehurst had stood, savoring my triumph. First I smiled to myself and felt elated. But this fierce pleasure faded as quickly as my racing pulse slowed. A child cannot fight with her elders as I had done, cannot let her furious feelings run wild as I had let mine, without suffering the sting of remorse and the chill of reaction afterward. A line of burning heath, alive with leaping, devouring flame, would have been the right image for my mind when I accused and threatened Mrs. Reed. That same line, blackened and dead after the fire burns out, would have perfectly captured my state half an hour later, when silence and reflection had shown me the madness of what I'd done and the bleakness of my hated, hating situation.

I had tasted revenge for the first time. Going down, it felt like rich wine—warm and heady. But the aftertaste was metallic and corrosive, as if I'd swallowed poison. I would gladly have gone and begged Mrs. Reed's forgiveness now, but I knew, partly from experience and partly from instinct, that this would only make her reject me with doubled scorn, reigniting every turbulent impulse in my nature.

I wished I could use some better ability than savage speaking, and find nourishment for some less dark feeling than bitter resentment. I picked up a book—some Arabian tales—and sat down, trying to read. But the words made no sense; my own thoughts kept swimming between me and the page. I opened the glass door to the breakfast room. The shrubbery was perfectly still, gripped by black frost with no sun or breeze to break it. I wrapped my head and arms in the skirt of my dress and went out to walk in a secluded part of the grounds. But I found no pleasure in the silent trees, the falling pine cones, or the frozen relics of autumn—russet leaves swept into piles by past winds, now stiff and stuck together. I leaned against a gate and looked into an empty field where no sheep grazed, where the short grass was bitten down and bleached. It was a very gray day, the sky completely overcast and threatening snow. Flakes fell now and then, settling on the hard path and the frosty meadow without melting. I stood there, wretched child that I was, whispering to myself over and over, "What shall I do? What shall I do?"
Suddenly I heard a clear voice call, "Miss Jane! Where are you? Come to lunch!"
It was Bessie—I knew her voice well—but I didn't move. Her light step came tripping down the path.
"You naughty little thing!" she said. "Why don't you come when you're called?"

Bessie's presence, compared with the dark thoughts I'd been brooding over, seemed cheerful—even though, as usual, she was a bit cross. The fact is, after my battle with and victory over Mrs. Reed, I wasn't inclined to worry about the nursemaid's passing irritation. And I was inclined to enjoy her youthful lightness of spirit. I just wrapped my arms around her and said, "Come on, Bessie, don't scold."
This was a bolder and more open gesture than I usually allowed myself, and it seemed to please her.
"You are a strange child, Miss Jane," she said, looking down at me. "A little wandering, solitary thing. And you're going to school, I suppose?"
I nodded.
"And won't you be sorry to leave poor Bessie?"
"What does Bessie care about me? She's always scolding me."
"Because you're such a strange, frightened, shy little thing. You should be bolder."
"What, so I can get knocked around more?"

"Nonsense! But you do get pushed around, that's for certain. My mother said, when she came to see me last week, that she wouldn't want one of her own children in your position. Now come inside—I have some good news for you."
"I don't think you do, Bessie."

"Child! What do you mean? What sad eyes you're fixing on me! Well, the Missus and the young ladies and Master John are going out for tea this afternoon, and you can have tea with me. I'll ask the cook to bake you a little cake, and then you can help me go through your drawers—I'll need to pack your trunk soon. The Missus plans to send you away from Gateshead in a day or two, and you can choose which toys you'd like to take with you."
"Bessie, you must promise not to scold me anymore before I go."
"All right, I will. But you must be very good, and don't be afraid of me. Don't flinch when I happen to speak a bit sharply—it's so annoying."
"I don't think I'll ever be afraid of you again, Bessie, because I've gotten used to you, and I'll soon have a whole new set of people to fear."
"If you fear them, they'll dislike you."
"Like you do, Bessie?"
"I don't dislike you, Miss. I think I'm fonder of you than of any of the others."
"You don't show it."
"You sharp little thing! You've got a whole new way of talking. What's made you so bold?"
"Well, I'll be leaving soon, and besides—" I was about to say something about what had passed between me and Mrs. Reed, but on second thought I decided it was better to keep quiet about that.
"So you're glad to leave me?"
"Not at all, Bessie. Actually, right now I'm rather sorry."
"Right now! And rather! How coolly my little lady says it! I bet if I asked you for a kiss, you wouldn't give me one—you'd say you'd rather not."

"I'll kiss you gladly—bend your head down." Bessie stooped. We hugged each other, and I followed her into the house feeling quite comforted. That afternoon passed in peace and harmony, and in the evening Bessie told me some of her most enchanting stories and sang some of her sweetest songs. Even for me, life had its moments of sunshine.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: It was barely five o'clock on the morning of January nineteenth when Bessie brought a candle into my closet and found me already up and nearly dressed. I had risen half an hour before she came in and had washed my face and put on my clothes by the light of a half-moon just setting, its rays streaming through the narrow window near my crib. I was to leave Gateshead that day on a coach that passed the lodge gates at six in the morning. Bessie was the only person up yet. She had lit a fire in the nursery and now set about making my breakfast. Few children can eat when excited about a journey, and I was no exception. After Bessie pressed me in vain to take a few spoonfuls of the boiled milk and bread she'd prepared, she wrapped some biscuits in paper and put them in my bag. Then she helped me into my coat and bonnet, wrapped herself in a shawl, and together we left the nursery. As we passed Mrs. Reed's bedroom, she asked, "Will you go in and say good-bye to the Missus?"

"No, Bessie. She came to my crib last night when you were down at supper and said I needn't disturb her in the morning, or my cousins either. She told me to remember that she had always been my best friend and to speak well of her and be grateful to her."
"What did you say, Miss?"
"Nothing. I pulled the bedcovers over my face and turned to the wall."
"That was wrong, Miss Jane."
"It was perfectly right, Bessie. Your Missus has not been my friend. She has been my enemy."
"Oh, Miss Jane! Don't say that!"
"Good-bye, Gateshead!" I cried as we passed through the hall and out the front door.

The moon had set and it was very dark. Bessie carried a lantern whose light glinted on the wet steps and the gravel road, soaked by a recent thaw. The winter morning was raw and cold. My teeth chattered as I hurried down the drive. A light burned in the porter's lodge. When we reached it, we found the porter's wife just lighting her fire. My trunk, brought down the evening before, stood strapped and ready at the door. It was almost six, and shortly after the hour struck, the distant rumble of wheels announced the approaching coach. I went to the door and watched its lamps coming rapidly through the darkness.
"Is she going by herself?" asked the porter's wife.
"Yes."
"And how far is it?"
"Fifty miles."
"What a long way! I wonder Mrs. Reed isn't afraid to send her so far alone."

The coach pulled up—there it was at the gates with its four horses and its roof loaded with passengers. The guard and coachman called out urgently to hurry. My trunk was hoisted up. I was torn from Bessie's neck, where I clung with kisses.
"Make sure you take good care of her," she called to the guard as he lifted me inside.

"Will do!" was the answer. The door slammed shut, a voice cried "All right!" and we drove off. And so I was separated from Bessie and Gateshead, carried away to unknown and, as I then believed, distant and mysterious places.

I remember little of the journey. I only know the day seemed supernaturally long, and that we appeared to travel over hundreds of miles. We passed through several towns. In one very large one, the coach stopped. The horses were changed and the passengers got out to eat. I was carried into an inn where the guard wanted me to have some dinner, but since I had no appetite, he left me in an enormous room with a fireplace at each end, a chandelier hanging from the ceiling, and a small red gallery high on the wall filled with musical instruments. I wandered around this room for a long time, feeling very strange and desperately afraid someone might come in and kidnap me—for I believed in kidnappers, whose exploits featured regularly in Bessie's fireside stories. At last the guard returned. I was packed back into the coach, my protector climbed to his seat, sounded his horn, and off we rattled.

The afternoon turned wet and somewhat misty. As it faded toward dusk, I began to feel we were getting very far from Gateshead indeed. We stopped passing through towns. The landscape changed. Great gray hills rose up around the horizon. As twilight deepened, we descended into a valley, dark with woods. Long after night had blotted out the view, I heard a wild wind rushing through the trees.

Lulled by the sound, I finally fell asleep. I hadn't slept long when the sudden stop of the coach woke me. The door was open, and someone who looked like a servant stood beside it. I could see her face and dress by the light of the lamps.
"Is there a little girl called Jane Eyre here?" she asked. I said yes and was lifted out. My trunk was handed down, and the coach drove off immediately.

I was stiff from sitting so long and dazed by the noise and motion. Gathering my senses, I looked around. Rain, wind, and darkness filled the air. But I could dimly make out a wall and an open door. I passed through it with my new guide, and she shut and locked it behind us. Now I could see a house—or houses, for the building spread far—with many windows, some lit. We went up a broad, pebbly path, splashing through puddles, and were let in at a door. The servant led me through a hallway to a room with a fire, where she left me alone.

I stood warming my numb fingers over the flames, then looked around. There was no candle, but the flickering firelight revealed wallpapered walls, carpet, curtains, and gleaming mahogany furniture. It was a parlor, not as large or grand as the drawing room at Gateshead, but comfortable enough. I was trying to make out the subject of a painting on the wall when the door opened and someone came in carrying a light. Another person followed close behind.
The first was a tall lady with dark hair, dark eyes, and a pale, broad forehead. She was partly wrapped in a shawl, her expression was serious, and she carried herself very upright.
"The child is very young to be sent alone," she said, setting her candle on the table. She studied me attentively for a minute or two, then added—
"She should be put to bed soon. She looks tired. Are you tired?" she asked, placing her hand on my shoulder.
"A little, ma'am."
"And hungry too, I'm sure. Let her have some supper before bed, Miss Miller. Is this the first time you've left your parents to come to school, my little girl?"

I explained that I had no parents. She asked how long they had been dead, then how old I was, what my name was, whether I could read, write, and sew a little. Then she gently touched my cheek with her finger and said she hoped I would be a good child, and sent me off with Miss Miller.

The lady I had just left was perhaps twenty-nine. The one who now accompanied me seemed some years younger. The first had impressed me with her voice, manner, and bearing. Miss Miller was more ordinary: ruddy-complexioned though careworn-looking, hurried in her movements, like someone who always had too many tasks at hand. She looked, and I later found she truly was, an assistant teacher. Led by her, I passed from room to room, corridor to corridor, through a large, rambling building, until we emerged from the total and rather gloomy silence of the section we'd been crossing and heard the hum of many voices. We entered a wide, long room with large plain tables, two at each end, each lit by a pair of candles. Seated all around on benches was a gathering of girls of every age from nine or ten to twenty. In the dim candlelight, they seemed countless to me, though there were really no more than eighty. They were all dressed alike in brown wool dresses of an old-fashioned cut and long linen pinafores. It was study hour. They were memorizing their lessons for the next day, and the hum I'd heard was the combined sound of their whispered recitations.
Miss Miller pointed me to a bench near the door, then walked to the far end of the long room and called out—
"Monitors, collect the lesson books and put them away!"
Four tall girls rose from different tables, went around gathering the books, and removed them. Miss Miller gave another order—
"Monitors, bring the supper trays!"

The tall girls went out and came back, each carrying a tray with portions of something—I couldn't tell what—and a pitcher of water with a mug in the middle. The food was handed around. Those who wanted water drank from the shared mug. When my turn came, I drank because I was thirsty, but I couldn't touch the food—excitement and exhaustion had killed my appetite. I could see now that it was a thin oat cake, broken into pieces.

After the meal, Miss Miller read prayers, and the classes filed off two by two upstairs.
