By now I was overwhelmed with tiredness and barely noticed what the bedroom looked like, except that, like the schoolroom, it was very long. That night I shared Miss Miller's bed. She helped me undress. Once in bed, I glanced down the long rows of beds, each quickly filled by two girls. Within ten minutes the single candle was blown out, and in the silence and complete darkness, I fell asleep.

The night passed quickly. I was too tired even to dream. I woke only once, to hear the wind howling in fierce gusts and rain pouring down, and to feel Miss Miller settle into bed beside me. When I opened my eyes again, a loud bell was ringing. The girls were up and dressing. Dawn hadn't broken yet, and one or two rush-lights burned in the room. I got up reluctantly. It was bitterly cold, and I dressed as well as I could while shivering. I washed when a basin was free, which took a while since there was only one basin for every six girls on the stands down the middle of the room. The bell rang again. We all formed a line, two by two, and marched downstairs into the cold, dimly lit schoolroom. Miss Miller read prayers, then called out—
"Form classes!"

A great commotion followed for several minutes, during which Miss Miller kept shouting "Silence!" and "Order!" When it settled, I saw all the girls arranged in four half-circles in front of four chairs placed at four tables. Each girl held a book, and a large book like a Bible lay on each table before the empty seat. A pause followed, filled by the low, vague murmur of many voices. Miss Miller walked from class to class, quieting the sound.

A distant bell tinkled. Three ladies entered the room at once, each going to a table and taking a seat. Miss Miller took the fourth vacant chair, nearest the door, surrounded by the smallest children. I was assigned to this lowest class and placed at the bottom.

Lessons began. The day's prayer was recited, then certain Bible verses, followed by a long reading of Scripture chapters that lasted an hour. By the time that was over, full daylight had come. The tireless bell rang for the fourth time. The classes formed up and marched to another room for breakfast. How glad I was at the prospect of eating! I was nearly faint with hunger, having eaten so little the day before.

The dining hall was a large, low-ceilinged, gloomy room. On two long tables, basins of something hot were steaming—but to my dismay, the smell was anything but appetizing. I saw a wave of displeasure ripple through the girls as the fumes hit their nostrils. From the front of the line, the tallest girls of the first class whispered—
"Disgusting! The porridge is burned again!"

"Silence!" called a voice—not Miss Miller's, but one of the senior teachers, a small, dark woman, smartly dressed but somewhat severe-looking. She seated herself at the head of one table, while a more robust lady presided at the other. I looked in vain for the woman I'd met the night before—she was nowhere to be seen. Miss Miller sat at the foot of my table, and a strange, foreign-looking elderly lady, whom I later learned was the French teacher, took the corresponding seat at the other table. A long grace was said and a hymn sung. Then a servant brought tea for the teachers, and the meal began.

Starving and now very faint, I shoveled down a spoonful or two without tasting it. But once the worst edge of hunger was blunted, I realized I was eating something revolting. Burned porridge is almost as bad as rotten potatoes—even starvation quickly gives up on it. The spoons moved slowly. I watched each girl taste her food and try to swallow it, but most soon gave up. Breakfast was over and no one had eaten. After we gave thanks for what we hadn't received and sang a second hymn, the dining hall emptied into the schoolroom. I was one of the last to leave, and passing the tables, I saw one teacher taste a basin of the porridge. She looked at the others. All their faces showed disgust, and one of them, the heavyset one, whispered—
"Abominable stuff! How disgraceful!"

A quarter of an hour passed before lessons resumed, during which the schoolroom erupted in a glorious uproar. For that stretch of time, talking loudly and freely seemed to be allowed, and the girls took full advantage. Every conversation was about the breakfast, which everyone condemned fiercely. Poor things—it was their only comfort. Miss Miller was now the only teacher in the room. A group of older girls stood around her, speaking with serious, angry gestures. I heard the name of Mr. Brocklehurst on several lips. Miss Miller shook her head in disapproval but made no real effort to curb the general outrage—no doubt she shared it.
A clock in the schoolroom struck nine. Miss Miller left her group and, standing in the middle of the room, called out—
"Silence! To your seats!"

Order was restored. Within five minutes the confused crowd had arranged itself, and relative quiet replaced the chaos. The senior teachers promptly returned to their posts, but still, everyone seemed to be waiting. Sitting on benches along the sides of the room, the eighty girls sat motionless and upright—a quaint sight, all with plain hair combed back from their faces, not a curl in sight, wearing brown dresses buttoned high with a narrow band at the throat, and small linen pockets (shaped something like a Highland sporran) pinned to the front of their frocks to hold their sewing things. They all wore woolen stockings and country-made shoes with brass buckles. More than twenty of them were full-grown young women, and the uniform suited them badly, giving an air of oddness even to the prettiest.

I was still studying them, and also glancing at the teachers—none of whom particularly appealed to me: the stout one was a bit rough, the dark one rather fierce, the foreigner harsh and peculiar, and Miss Miller, poor thing, looked purple-faced, weather-beaten, and overworked—when, as my eye wandered from face to face, the whole school rose as one, as if pulled by a single spring.

What was happening? I had heard no command given and was confused. Before I could gather my wits, the classes had sat down again. But since all eyes were now turned in one direction, mine followed, and I saw the woman who had received me the night before. She stood at the far end of the long room by the fireplace (there was one at each end) and surveyed the two rows of girls in silence. Miss Miller went up to her, seemed to ask a question, received an answer, returned to her place, and announced—
"Monitor of the first class, fetch the globes!"

While this was carried out, the lady moved slowly up the room. I must have a strong instinct for reverence, because I still remember the admiring awe with which I watched her. Seen now in full daylight, she was tall, fair, and well-proportioned. Brown eyes with a kindly light and a fine fringe of long lashes softened the whiteness of her broad forehead. Her hair, very dark brown, was arranged in round curls at each temple, in the fashion of the time, when neither smooth bands nor long ringlets were in style. Her dress, also fashionable, was purple cloth trimmed with a sort of Spanish pattern in black velvet. A gold watch (watches were less common then) shone at her waist. Add to this picture refined features, a complexion pale but clear, and a stately bearing, and you will have a fair idea of the appearance of Miss Temple—Maria Temple, as I later saw the name written in a prayer book I was given to carry to church.

The superintendent of Lowood (for that was what she was) took her seat before a pair of globes on one of the tables and called the first class around her to begin a geography lesson. The lower classes were taken by the other teachers. Recitations in history, grammar, and other subjects went on for an hour, followed by writing and arithmetic. Miss Temple gave music lessons to some of the older girls. The length of each lesson was marked by the clock, which at last struck twelve. The superintendent stood—
"I have something to say to the pupils," she said.
The noise of lessons ending was already breaking out, but it quieted at her voice. She went on—
"You had a breakfast this morning that you could not eat. You must be hungry. I have ordered that bread and cheese be served to everyone for lunch."
The teachers looked at her with a kind of surprise.
"It will be on my responsibility," she added, explaining to them, and immediately left the room.

The bread and cheese arrived promptly and was distributed, to the great delight and refreshment of the entire school. The order was given: "To the garden!" Each girl put on a coarse straw bonnet with colored calico strings and a gray wool cloak. I was dressed the same way, and following the stream, I made my way outside.

The garden was a wide enclosure surrounded by walls so high they blocked every view beyond. A covered walkway ran along one side, and broad paths bordered a central space divided into dozens of little beds, each assigned to a pupil to tend. When full of flowers they would doubtless look pretty, but now, at the end of January, everything was winter-blighted and brown. I shivered as I looked around. It was a miserable day for outdoor exercise—not actually raining, but dark with a drizzling yellow fog. The ground was still soaked from yesterday's downpour. The stronger girls ran about playing active games, but a number of pale, thin ones huddled together for shelter under the covered walkway. Among them, as the thick mist soaked through to their shivering bodies, I frequently heard the sound of a hollow cough.

No one had spoken to me yet, and no one seemed to notice me. I stood quite alone, but I was used to that feeling—it didn't bother me much. I leaned against a pillar of the walkway, pulled my gray cloak tight around me, and tried to ignore the cold biting at me from outside and the hunger gnawing at me from within. I gave myself over to watching and thinking. My thoughts were too vague and fragmentary to record. I barely knew where I was yet. Gateshead and my old life seemed to have drifted away to an immeasurable distance. The present was strange and unfamiliar, and of the future I couldn't form any picture. I looked around the convent-like garden, then up at the building—large, half of it seeming old and gray, the other half quite new. The newer section, containing the schoolroom and dormitory, had mullioned and latticed windows that gave it a church-like appearance. A stone plaque over the door read—
LOWOOD INSTITUTION.
This portion was rebuilt A.D. ——, by Naomi Brocklehurst, of Brocklehurst Hall, in this county.
"Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." —St. Matt. v. 16.

I read these words over and over. I felt they must mean something, but I couldn't fully grasp it. I was still puzzling over the word "Institution" and trying to make a connection between the building's name and the Bible verse when a cough close behind me made me turn. I saw a girl sitting on a stone bench nearby, bent over a book she seemed deeply absorbed in. From where I stood I could see the title—Rasselas—a name that struck me as strange and therefore interesting. As she turned a page, she happened to look up, and I spoke to her directly—
"Is your book interesting?" I had already decided to ask her to lend it to me someday.
"I like it," she answered, after a second or two during which she examined me.

"What is it about?" I went on. I hardly know where I found the nerve to start a conversation with a stranger—it was completely unlike me. But I think her reading struck a chord of sympathy, because I too loved books, though mine were of a lighter, more childish kind. I couldn't digest anything serious or substantial.
"You can look at it," the girl said, handing me the book.

I did. A quick look convinced me the contents were less appealing than the title. Rasselas looked dull to my trivial taste—I saw nothing about fairies, nothing about genies, no bright variety on the densely printed pages. I gave it back. She took it quietly, and without a word she was about to return to her reading when I interrupted her again—
"Can you tell me what the writing on that stone over the door means? What is Lowood Institution?"
"It's the house where you've come to live."
"And why do they call it an Institution? Is it different from other schools?"
"It's partly a charity school. You and I, and all the rest of us, are charity children. I assume you're an orphan—isn't at least one of your parents dead?"
"Both died before I can remember."
"Well, all the girls here have lost one or both parents. That's why it's called an institution for educating orphans."
"Do we pay nothing? Do they keep us for free?"
"We pay, or our friends pay, fifteen pounds a year for each of us."
"Then why do they call us charity children?"
"Because fifteen pounds isn't enough to cover room, board, and teaching, and the rest is made up by donations."
"Who donates?"
"Various generous ladies and gentlemen from the area and from London."
"Who was Naomi Brocklehurst?"
"The lady who built the new part of the building, as that plaque records. Her son oversees and runs everything here."
"Why?"
"Because he is the treasurer and manager of the school."
"Then the building doesn't belong to the tall lady who wears a watch and said we should have bread and cheese?"
"You mean Miss Temple? Oh, no! I wish it did. She has to answer to Mr. Brocklehurst for everything she does. Mr. Brocklehurst buys all our food and all our clothes."
"Does he live here?"
"No—two miles away, at a large estate."
"Is he a good man?"
"He's a clergyman, and people say he does a great deal of good."
"Did you say that tall lady is called Miss Temple?"
"Yes."
"And what are the other teachers called?"

"The one with red cheeks is Miss Smith. She oversees the needlework and cutting-out—we make our own clothes, our dresses and coats and everything. The small one with black hair is Miss Scatcherd. She teaches history and grammar and hears the second class recitations. And the one who wears a shawl with a handkerchief tied to her side with a yellow ribbon is Madame Pierrot. She comes from Lille in France and teaches French."
"Do you like the teachers?"
"Well enough."
"Do you like the little dark one, and the Madame—? I can't pronounce her name the way you do."
"Miss Scatcherd is sharp-tempered—you have to be careful not to offend her. Madame Pierrot isn't bad."
"But Miss Temple is the best—isn't she?"
"Miss Temple is very good and very clever. She's above the rest because she knows far more than they do."
"Have you been here long?"
"Two years."
"Are you an orphan?"
"My mother is dead."
"Are you happy here?"
"You ask too many questions. I've given you enough answers for now. I want to read."

But at that moment the bell rang for dinner. Everyone went back inside. The smell that now filled the dining hall was scarcely more appetizing than what had greeted us at breakfast. Dinner was served in two huge tin-plated vessels, from which rose a strong steam reeking of rancid fat. The food turned out to be mediocre potatoes and strange shreds of gristly meat, mixed and cooked together. Each girl received a fairly generous plate of it. I ate what I could and wondered if every day's food would be like this.
After dinner, we went straight back to the schoolroom. Lessons resumed and continued until five o'clock.

The only notable event of the afternoon was seeing the girl I'd talked to in the garden dismissed in disgrace by Miss Scatcherd from a history class and sent to stand in the middle of the large schoolroom. The punishment struck me as deeply humiliating, especially for such a grown-up girl—she looked thirteen or older. I expected her to show signs of great distress and shame. But to my surprise, she neither cried nor blushed. Calm though serious, she stood there, the focus of every eye. "How can she bear it so quietly, so firmly?" I asked myself. "If I were in her place, I think I'd want the earth to swallow me up. She looks as if she's thinking about something beyond her punishment, beyond her situation—something not around her or in front of her. I've heard of daydreams. Is she in one now? Her eyes are fixed on the floor, but I'm sure she doesn't see it. Her gaze seems turned inward, gone down into her heart. She's seeing what she remembers, I think, not what's actually here. I wonder what kind of girl she is—whether good or bad."

Shortly after five we had another meal: a small mug of coffee and half a slice of brown bread. I devoured my bread and drank my coffee eagerly but would gladly have had twice as much—I was still hungry. Half an hour of free time followed, then study, then a glass of water and a piece of oat cake, prayers, and bed. Such was my first day at Lowood.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: The next day began like the one before—getting up and dressing by rush-light. But this morning we had to skip washing. The water in the pitchers had frozen solid. An overnight change in the weather had brought a biting northeast wind that whistled through the cracks in our bedroom windows all night, making us shiver in our beds and turning the water in the jugs to ice.

By the time the hour and a half of prayers and Bible reading was over, I felt ready to collapse from the cold. Breakfast finally came, and this morning the porridge wasn't burned. It was edible, but there wasn't much of it. How tiny my portion seemed! I wished it had been twice as large.

During the course of the day I was enrolled in the fourth class and given regular lessons and tasks. Until now I had only been a spectator at Lowood; I was about to become a participant. At first, being unaccustomed to learning things by heart, the lessons seemed both long and difficult. The constant switching from one subject to another bewildered me, and I was glad when, around three in the afternoon, Miss Smith put a two-yard strip of muslin into my hands along with a needle and thimble and sent me to sit in a quiet corner of the schoolroom to hem it. At that hour most of the others were sewing too. But one class still stood around Miss Scatcherd's chair, reading aloud. Since everything was quiet, I could hear the subject of their lesson and how each girl performed, along with Miss Scatcherd's criticisms or occasional praise. It was English history. Among the readers I noticed my new acquaintance from the garden. At the start of the lesson, she'd been at the top of the class, but for some error of pronunciation or lapse in attention, she was suddenly sent to the very bottom. Even in that lowly position, Miss Scatcherd continued to single her out, constantly directing remarks at her such as—

"Burns" (that was apparently her name—here the girls were all called by their surnames, like boys elsewhere), "Burns, you're standing on the side of your shoe. Turn your toes out immediately." "Burns, you're poking your chin out most unpleasantly. Pull it in." "Burns, I insist you hold your head up. I will not have you standing before me like that." And so on.

After the chapter had been read through twice, the books were closed and the girls were tested. The lesson had covered part of the reign of Charles I, and there were various questions about tonnage and poundage and ship-money that most of them couldn't answer. But every difficulty was solved the moment it reached Burns. Her memory seemed to have absorbed the entire lesson, and she had ready answers on every point. I kept expecting Miss Scatcherd to praise her. Instead, she suddenly burst out—
"You dirty, disagreeable girl! You haven't cleaned your nails this morning!"
Burns made no reply. I was puzzled by her silence.
"Why," I thought, "doesn't she explain that she couldn't clean her nails or wash her face because the water was frozen?"

My attention was then diverted by Miss Smith, who asked me to hold a skein of thread while she wound it. As she worked, she chatted with me, asking whether I'd been to school before, whether I could do marking, stitching, knitting, and so on. By the time she dismissed me, I had lost track of Miss Scatcherd. When I returned to my seat, that teacher was just giving an order I didn't catch. But Burns immediately left the class, went into the small inner room where the books were kept, and came back carrying a bundle of twigs tied together at one end. She presented this ominous tool to Miss Scatcherd with a respectful curtsy. Then quietly, without being told, she loosened her pinafore, and the teacher instantly struck her a dozen sharp blows on the neck with the bunch of twigs. Not a tear rose to Burns's eye. And while I froze in my sewing, my fingers trembling with helpless, impotent anger at the spectacle, not a feature of her thoughtful face changed its ordinary expression.
"Hardened girl!" exclaimed Miss Scatcherd. "Nothing can cure your slovenly habits. Take the rod away."
Burns obeyed. I watched her closely as she came out of the book closet. She was just putting her handkerchief back in her pocket, and the trace of a tear glistened on her thin cheek.

The evening recreation hour was the pleasantest part of the day at Lowood. The bit of bread and the sip of coffee at five o'clock had revived our energy, if not satisfied our hunger. The long restraint of the day was loosened. The schoolroom felt warmer than in the morning—the fires were allowed to burn a bit brighter, partly substituting for candles, which hadn't been lit yet. The warm glow, the permitted noise, the jumble of many voices gave a welcome feeling of freedom.

On the evening of the day I'd seen Miss Scatcherd beat Burns, I wandered as usual among the benches and tables and laughing groups, without a companion but not feeling lonely. As I passed the windows, I now and then lifted a blind and looked out. It was snowing hard. Drifts were already forming against the lower panes. Pressing my ear to the glass, I could make out, above the happy noise inside, the desolate moan of the wind outside.

If I had recently left a good home and kind parents, this would probably have been the hour when I missed them most. That wind would have saddened my heart, and this murky chaos would have disturbed my peace. As it was, I drew a strange excitement from both, and feeling reckless and feverish, I wished the wind would howl more wildly, the darkness would deepen further, and the noise would rise to uproar.

Jumping over benches and creeping under tables, I made my way to one of the fireplaces. There, kneeling by the tall wire fire-guard, I found Burns—absorbed, silent, cut off from everything around her by a book she was reading in the dim glow of the embers.
"Is it still Rasselas?" I asked, coming up behind her.
"Yes," she said, "and I've just finished it."
Five minutes later she closed it. I was glad.
"Now," I thought, "maybe I can get her to talk." I sat down beside her on the floor.
"What is your name besides Burns?"
"Helen."
"Do you come from far away?"
"From a place farther north, right on the border of Scotland."
"Will you ever go back?"
"I hope so, but nobody can be sure of the future."
"You must want to leave Lowood."
"No! Why should I? I was sent here to get an education, and there would be no point in leaving until I've done that."
"But that teacher, Miss Scatcherd—she's so cruel to you."
"Cruel? Not at all. She's strict. She dislikes my faults."
"If I were in your place, I'd hate her. I'd fight back. If she hit me with that rod, I'd grab it out of her hand. I'd break it right in front of her."

"You probably wouldn't do anything of the sort. But if you did, Mr. Brocklehurst would expel you from the school, and that would be a great grief to your family. It's far better to endure a pain that only you feel than to do something rash whose consequences would hurt everyone connected to you. Besides, the Bible tells us to return good for evil."
"But it seems so humiliating to be beaten and sent to stand in the middle of a room full of people. And you're such a big girl—I'm much younger than you, and I couldn't bear it."
"Yet it would be your duty to bear it if you couldn't avoid it. It's weak and foolish to say you can't bear what fate requires you to bear."

I listened with wonder. I couldn't grasp this philosophy of endurance, and even less could I understand or share the forgiveness she showed toward her tormentor. Yet I sensed that Helen Burns saw things by a light invisible to my eyes. I suspected she might be right and I might be wrong. But I wasn't ready to think it through deeply. Like Felix in the Bible, I put it off to a more convenient time.
"You say you have faults, Helen. What are they? To me you seem very good."

"Then learn from me not to judge by appearances. I am, as Miss Scatcherd says, untidy. I rarely organize things and never keep them in order. I'm careless. I forget rules. I read when I should be studying my lessons. I have no method. And sometimes, like you, I feel I can't stand being forced into systematic routines. All of this is very annoying to Miss Scatcherd, who is naturally neat, punctual, and precise."
"And harsh and cruel," I added. But Helen Burns wouldn't accept my addition and stayed silent.
"Is Miss Temple as strict with you as Miss Scatcherd?"
At the mention of Miss Temple's name, a soft smile flickered across her serious face.

"Miss Temple is full of goodness. It pains her to be harsh with anyone, even the worst girl in the school. She sees my mistakes and points them out gently. And if I do anything praiseworthy, she's generous with her praise. One strong proof of how hopelessly flawed I am is that even her gentle, reasonable corrections can't cure me of my faults, and even her praise, though I value it highly, can't motivate me to be consistently careful and attentive."
"That's strange," I said. "It's so easy to be careful."

"For you, I'm sure it is. I watched you in class this morning and saw how closely you paid attention. Your mind never seemed to wander while Miss Miller explained the lesson and questioned you. But mine constantly drifts. When I should be listening to Miss Scatcherd and absorbing every word, I often lose the very sound of her voice. I fall into a kind of dream. Sometimes I imagine I'm back in Northumberland, and the noises around me are the bubbling of a little brook that runs through Deepden, near our house. Then when it's my turn to answer, I have to be woken up, and having heard nothing of what was read, I have nothing to say."
"Yet you answered so well this afternoon."

"That was pure chance. The subject we were reading about had caught my interest. This afternoon, instead of dreaming about Deepden, I was wondering how a man who wanted to do right could sometimes act as unjustly and unwisely as Charles the First did. I thought what a pity it was that, with all his integrity and conscience, he couldn't see past the privileges of the crown. If only he'd been able to look ahead and see which way the spirit of the age was moving! Still, I like Charles—I respect him—I pity him, poor murdered king! Yes, his enemies were worse. They spilled blood they had no right to spill. How dared they kill him!"
Helen was talking to herself now. She'd forgotten I couldn't really follow her—that I knew little about the subject she was discussing. I brought her back to my level.
"And when Miss Temple teaches you, does your mind wander then?"

"No, certainly not often. Miss Temple usually has something to say that's newer than my own thoughts. Her way of speaking appeals to me, and the information she shares is often exactly what I'd been wanting to know."
"So with Miss Temple, you're good?"
"Yes, in a passive way. I don't try. I just follow wherever my interest leads. There's no virtue in that kind of goodness."

"There's a great deal of it. You're good to those who are good to you. That's all I ever want to be. If people were always kind and obedient to those who are cruel and unjust, the wicked would have everything their way. They'd never feel afraid, so they'd never change—they'd just get worse and worse. When someone hits us for no reason, we should hit back, and hard—hard enough to teach them never to do it again."
"You'll change your mind when you're older, I hope. You're still just a young, untaught girl."

"But I feel this, Helen: I have to dislike people who keep disliking me no matter what I do. I have to resist people who punish me unjustly. It's as natural as loving those who are kind to me, or accepting punishment when I know I deserve it."
"That's what heathens and savages believe. Christians and civilized people reject it."
"How? I don't understand."
"It's not violence that best overcomes hatred—nor revenge that most surely heals injury."
"What, then?"
"Read the New Testament and pay attention to what Christ says and how He acts. Make His words your rule and His conduct your example."
"What does He say?"
"Love your enemies. Bless those who curse you. Do good to those who hate you and mistreat you."
"Then I should love Mrs. Reed, which I cannot do. I should bless her son John, which is impossible."

Helen in turn asked me to explain, and I launched into a full account of my sufferings and resentments, told my own way. Bitter and fierce when roused, I spoke exactly as I felt, without holding back or softening anything.
Helen listened patiently to the end. I expected some comment, but she said nothing.
"Well," I asked impatiently, "isn't Mrs. Reed a hard-hearted, bad woman?"

"She has been unkind to you, no doubt, because she dislikes your personality—just as Miss Scatcherd dislikes mine. But how precisely you remember everything she has done and said to you! What a remarkably deep impression her injustice has made on your heart! No ill-treatment leaves such a record on my feelings. Wouldn't you be happier if you tried to forget her cruelty, along with the angry emotions it stirred up? Life seems too short to me to be spent nursing grudges or cataloguing wrongs. We are all burdened with faults in this world, every one of us. But the time will come, I trust, when we shed those faults along with our perishable bodies—when sin and degradation fall away with this heavy frame of flesh, and only the spark of the spirit remains, the intangible essence of light and thought, as pure as when it left the Creator to give life to the creature. Where it came from, it will return—perhaps to be given to some being higher than us, perhaps to pass through levels of glory, from the pale human soul brightening to the radiance of an angel! Surely it will never be allowed to degrade from human to demon? No, I cannot believe that. I hold a different belief, one no one ever taught me, one I rarely speak of, but which gives me joy and which I cling to—because it offers hope to everyone. It makes Eternity a place of rest, a great home, not a terror and an abyss. And with this belief, I can clearly separate the wrongdoer from the wrong. I can sincerely forgive the person while hating the act. With this belief, revenge never torments my heart, degradation never crushes me too deeply, injustice never brings me too low. I live in peace, looking toward the end."

Helen's head, always drooping a little, sank lower as she finished. I could see she no longer wished to talk to me but would rather be alone with her own thoughts. She wasn't given much time to reflect, though. A monitor—a big, rough girl—came up and exclaimed in a strong northern accent—
"Helen Burns, if you don't go and sort out your drawer and fold your sewing this minute, I'll tell Miss Scatcherd to come look at it!"
Helen sighed as her reverie dissolved. She got up and obeyed the monitor without a word and without delay.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: My first term at Lowood felt like an eternity—and not a golden age, either. It was a grueling struggle to adapt to new rules and unfamiliar tasks. The fear of failure haunted me worse than the physical hardships, though those were no small matter.

During January, February, and part of March, deep snow and then nearly impassable roads kept us trapped within the garden walls, except for church. But even within those boundaries, we had to spend an hour outdoors every day. Our clothing was nowhere near warm enough for the bitter cold. We had no boots, and the snow got into our shoes and melted there. Our bare hands became numb and covered with chilblains, as were our feet. I vividly remember the maddening itching I suffered every evening when my feet swelled, and the torture of forcing my raw, stiff toes into my shoes each morning. Then there was the food—or lack of it. With the fierce appetites of growing children, we were barely given enough to keep a frail invalid alive. This shortage led to an abuse that fell hardest on the younger girls: whenever the starving older girls got the chance, they would beg or bully the little ones out of their portions. Many times I shared my precious bit of brown bread between two claimants at teatime, and after surrendering half my mug of coffee to a third, I swallowed the rest with secret tears, wrung from me by raw hunger.

Sundays were bleak days in that wintry season. We had to walk two miles to Brocklebridge Church, where our patron led the service. We set out cold and arrived even colder. During the morning service, we were practically frozen. It was too far to go back for dinner, so cold meat and bread, in the same stingy portions as our regular meals, were distributed between services.
After the afternoon service, we returned by an exposed, hilly road where the bitter winter wind, blowing across a range of snow-covered peaks to the north, nearly flayed the skin from our faces.

I remember Miss Temple walking quickly and lightly along our drooping line, her plaid cloak fluttering in the frosty wind, wrapped tight around her, encouraging us by word and example to keep our spirits up and march forward, as she put it, "like brave soldiers." The other teachers, poor things, were generally too defeated themselves to attempt to cheer anyone.

How we longed for the light and warmth of a blazing fire when we got back! But for the little ones, at least, this was denied. Each fireplace in the schoolroom was immediately surrounded by a double ring of older girls, and behind them the younger children crouched in clusters, wrapping their frozen arms in their pinafores.

A small consolation came at teatime: a double ration of bread—a whole slice instead of half—with the glorious addition of a thin scraping of butter. This was the weekly treat we all looked forward to from one Sunday to the next. I usually managed to save some of this feast for myself, but the rest I was invariably forced to give away.

Sunday evenings were spent reciting the Church Catechism and chapters five, six, and seven of St. Matthew by heart, and listening to a long sermon read by Miss Miller, whose irrepressible yawns revealed her boredom. A frequent interruption was the spectacle of half a dozen small girls, overwhelmed by sleep, toppling off the fourth bench like so many Eutychuses. The remedy was to push them into the center of the schoolroom and make them stand until the sermon was done. Sometimes their legs gave out and they collapsed in a heap. Then they were propped up with the monitors' tall stools.

I haven't mentioned the visits of Mr. Brocklehurst yet. In fact, that gentleman was away from home for most of the first month after my arrival, presumably lingering with his friend the Archdeacon. His absence was a relief to me. I need not explain that I had my own reasons for dreading his appearance. But appear he did, at last.

One afternoon (I had been at Lowood three weeks by then), as I sat with a slate in my hand, struggling with a long division problem, I happened to glance up at the window and caught sight of a figure just passing. I recognized that gaunt outline almost instantly. And when, two minutes later, the entire school, teachers included, rose as one, I didn't need to look up to know whose entrance they were acknowledging. A long stride crossed the schoolroom, and soon there beside Miss Temple, who had also risen, stood the same black column that had loomed so ominously over me on the hearthrug at Gateshead. I glanced sideways at this pillar of a man. Yes, I was right: it was Mr. Brocklehurst, buttoned into a topcoat, looking taller, thinner, and more rigid than ever.

I had my own reasons to be alarmed by this appearance. I remembered all too well Mrs. Reed's treacherous hints about my character, and Mr. Brocklehurst's promise to warn Miss Temple and the teachers about my wicked nature. All along, I had been dreading the fulfillment of that promise—watching daily for the arrival of this man, whose report about my past was going to brand me as a bad child forever. And now here he was.

He stood at Miss Temple's side, speaking low in her ear. I had no doubt he was revealing my supposed wickedness, and I watched her face with painful anxiety, expecting at any moment to see her dark eyes turn on me with disgust and contempt. I listened too, and since I happened to be sitting near the front of the room, I caught most of what he said. Its content relieved me of immediate fear.

"I suppose, Miss Temple, the thread I bought at Lowton will do. It struck me as just the right quality for the calico chemises, and I selected needles to match. You may tell Miss Smith I forgot to note down the darning needles, but she'll have some sent next week. And she must not, under any circumstances, give out more than one at a time to each pupil—if they have more, they get careless and lose them. And, oh, ma'am! I wish the woolen stockings were better looked after! When I was here last, I went into the kitchen garden and examined the clothes on the line. There were a great many black stockings in a terrible state of repair. From the size of the holes, I was sure they hadn't been properly mended."
He paused.
"Your instructions will be followed, sir," said Miss Temple.
"And, ma'am," he continued, "the laundress tells me some girls have had two clean collars in one week. That's too many. The rules allow only one."
"I believe I can explain that, sir. Agnes and Catherine Johnstone were invited to tea with friends at Lowton last Thursday, and I gave them permission to put on clean collars for the occasion."
Mr. Brocklehurst nodded.

"Well, for once it may pass. But please don't let it happen too often. And there's something else that surprised me. In settling accounts with the housekeeper, I find that a lunch of bread and cheese was served to the girls twice in the past two weeks. How is this? I checked the regulations and found no such meal as lunch mentioned. Who introduced this innovation, and by what authority?"

"I must take responsibility for that, sir," Miss Temple replied. "The breakfast was so badly prepared that the pupils couldn't possibly eat it, and I couldn't allow them to go hungry until dinnertime."

"Madam, allow me a moment. You are aware that my purpose in educating these girls is not to accustom them to luxury and indulgence, but to make them hardy, patient, and self-denying. If some small disappointment of appetite occurs, such as a spoiled meal or an under- or over-cooked dish, the proper response is not to replace it with something finer, thereby pampering the body and undermining the purpose of this institution. Rather, the incident should be used for the spiritual improvement of the pupils, by encouraging them to show courage in the face of temporary deprivation. A brief talk on such occasions would be perfectly appropriate, in which a wise teacher might refer to the sufferings of the early Christians, to the torments of martyrs, to the exhortations of our blessed Lord Himself, calling upon His disciples to take up their cross and follow Him—to His warnings that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God—to His divine comfort: 'If you suffer hunger or thirst for My sake, blessed are you.' Oh, madam, when you put bread and cheese instead of burned porridge into these children's mouths, you may indeed feed their worthless bodies, but you little realize how you starve their immortal souls!"

Mr. Brocklehurst paused again—perhaps overcome by his own feelings. Miss Temple had looked down when he first began speaking to her, but now she gazed straight ahead. Her face, naturally pale as marble, seemed to be taking on the coldness and rigidity of that same stone—especially her mouth, closed as if it would have taken a chisel to open it, and her brow, which settled gradually into petrified severity.

Meanwhile, Mr. Brocklehurst stood by the fire with his hands behind his back, majestically surveying the whole school. Suddenly his eye blinked, as if it had met something that either dazzled or shocked it. Turning, he said in a sharper, faster voice than he'd used before—
"Miss Temple, Miss Temple, what—what is that girl with curled hair? Red hair, ma'am, curled—curled all over?" And extending his cane, he pointed at the offending sight, his hand shaking as he did so.
"It is Julia Severn," replied Miss Temple very calmly.

"Julia Severn, ma'am! And why has she, or any other girl, curled hair? Why, in defiance of every rule and principle of this house, does she conform to worldly fashion so openly—here in an evangelical, charitable institution—by wearing her hair in a mass of curls?"
"Julia's hair curls naturally," Miss Temple returned, even more quietly.

"Naturally! Yes, but we are not to follow nature. I want these girls to be children of Grace. And why so much of it? I have said again and again that I want their hair arranged simply, modestly, plainly. Miss Temple, that girl's hair must be cut off entirely. I'll send a barber tomorrow. And I see others with far too much of it—that tall girl, tell her to turn around. Tell the entire first class to stand up and face the wall."

Miss Temple passed her handkerchief across her lips, as if smoothing away an involuntary smile. She gave the order, though, and when the first class understood what was being asked, they obeyed. Leaning back on my bench a little, I could see the looks and grimaces they exchanged. It was a pity Mr. Brocklehurst couldn't see them too—he might have realized that however much he controlled the outside of the cup, the inside was far beyond his reach.
He examined the backs of their heads for about five minutes, then delivered his verdict. The words fell like a death sentence—
"All those topknots must be cut off."
Miss Temple seemed to protest.

"Madam," he pressed on, "I serve a Master whose kingdom is not of this world. My mission is to crush the desires of the flesh in these girls, to teach them to dress with modesty and restraint, not with braided hair and fine clothes. Each of these young persons has braids that vanity itself might have woven. They must be cut off, I repeat. Think of the time wasted, of—"

Mr. Brocklehurst was interrupted at this point. Three more visitors, all women, now entered the room. They should have arrived a little sooner to hear his lecture on dress, for they were magnificently attired in velvet, silk, and furs. The two younger ones (elegant girls of sixteen and seventeen) wore fashionable gray beaver hats with ostrich plumes, and beneath the brims fell a profusion of carefully curled light-colored hair. The older lady was wrapped in an expensive velvet shawl trimmed with ermine, and she wore a wig of French curls on her forehead.

These ladies were received with great deference by Miss Temple as Mrs. and the Misses Brocklehurst, and shown to seats of honor at the front of the room. It seemed they had come in the carriage with their reverend relative and had been inspecting the rooms upstairs while he dealt with the housekeeper, questioned the laundress, and lectured the superintendent. They now proceeded to direct various remarks and criticisms at Miss Smith, who was in charge of the linen and dormitories. But I had no time to listen—other matters had seized my attention.

While following the conversation between Mr. Brocklehurst and Miss Temple, I had not neglected precautions for my own safety, which I thought could be secured if I simply avoided being noticed. To that end, I had sat well back on my bench and held my slate up to hide my face, pretending to work on my sum. I might have escaped notice entirely if my treacherous slate hadn't somehow slipped from my hand, falling with a loud crash that drew every eye in the room to me. I knew it was all over. As I stooped to pick up the two broken pieces, I braced myself for the worst. It came.

"A careless girl!" said Mr. Brocklehurst, and immediately after: "It's the new pupil, I see." Then, before I could draw breath: "I must not forget I have something to say about her." Then loudly—how horribly loud it sounded to me: "Let the child who broke her slate come forward!"

I couldn't have moved on my own—I was paralyzed. But the two tall girls on either side of me stood me up and pushed me toward the dread judge. Then Miss Temple gently guided me to his very feet, and I caught her whispered words—
"Don't be afraid, Jane. I saw it was an accident. You won't be punished."
Those kind words stabbed my heart like a dagger.
"Any moment now she'll despise me for a fraud," I thought, and a surge of fury against Reed, Brocklehurst, and company pulsed through me. I was no Helen Burns.
"Fetch that stool," said Mr. Brocklehurst, pointing to a very tall one from which a monitor had just risen. It was brought.
"Place the child upon it."

And I was placed there—by whom, I don't know. I was in no state to notice details. I was only aware that they had hoisted me up to the level of Mr. Brocklehurst's nose, that he was within a yard of me, and that below me spread a display of orange and purple silk coats and a cloud of silvery feathers.
Mr. Brocklehurst cleared his throat.
"Ladies," he said, turning to his family, "Miss Temple, teachers, and children—you all see this girl?"
Of course they did. I felt their eyes aimed at my burning skin like magnifying glasses in the sun.

"You see she is still young. You observe she has the ordinary appearance of a child. God has graciously given her the same form He has given to us all. No visible defect marks her out as unusual. Who would think that the Evil One had already found a servant and agent in her? Yet that, I grieve to say, is the case."
A pause—during which I began to steady my shaking nerves and felt that the worst had happened and could no longer be avoided. It must be faced.

"My dear children," continued the black marble clergyman with great emotion, "this is a sad, a melancholy occasion. It becomes my duty to warn you that this girl, who might have been one of God's own lambs, is instead a little outcast—not a member of the true flock, but clearly an interloper and a stranger. You must be on your guard against her. You must avoid her example. If necessary, stay away from her company, exclude her from your games, and shut her out of your conversations. Teachers, you must watch her. Keep your eyes on her movements, weigh her words carefully, examine her actions, discipline her body to save her soul—if indeed such salvation is possible. For, and my tongue falters as I say it, this girl, this child, born in a Christian land, worse than many a little pagan who prays to Brahma and kneels before Juggernaut—this girl is—a liar!"

A ten-minute pause followed, during which I—by now in full command of my senses—observed the female Brocklehursts pull out their handkerchiefs and press them to their eyes, while the older lady swayed back and forth, and the two younger ones whispered, "How shocking!"
Mr. Brocklehurst resumed.

"This I learned from her benefactress, the pious and charitable lady who took her in as an orphan, raised her as her own daughter, and whose kindness and generosity the ungrateful girl repaid with ingratitude so terrible that her excellent patroness was finally forced to separate her from her own young ones, for fear the girl's wicked example would corrupt them. She has been sent here to be healed, even as the Jews of old sent their sick to the troubled pool of Bethesda. Teachers, superintendent, I beg you not to let the waters grow stagnant around her."

With this magnificent conclusion, Mr. Brocklehurst adjusted the top button of his coat, muttered something to his family, who rose, bowed to Miss Temple, and then the whole grand party swept out of the room. Turning at the door, my judge declared—
"Let her stand on that stool for half an hour longer, and let no one speak to her for the rest of the day."

There I was, raised up high—I, who had said I couldn't bear the shame of standing on my own feet in the middle of the room, was now displayed on a pedestal of disgrace for everyone to see. What I felt, no words can describe. But just as all those feelings rose, choking me and closing my throat, a girl walked past. As she passed, she raised her eyes. What a strange light filled them! What an extraordinary feeling that glance sent through me! How it lifted me up! It was as if a hero had walked past a slave and passed on strength just by being near. I mastered the rising hysteria, raised my head, and stood firm on the stool. Helen Burns asked Miss Smith some trivial question about her work, was scolded for bothering her, returned to her place, and smiled at me as she went by. What a smile! I remember it now, and I know it was the expression of a fine mind and real courage. It lit up her plain features, her thin face, her sunken gray eyes, like the reflection of an angel. Yet at that very moment, Helen Burns wore the "untidy" badge on her arm. Barely an hour ago, I had heard Miss Scatcherd sentence her to a dinner of bread and water the next day for blotting a copying exercise. Such is the imperfect nature of humanity! Such spots exist on the surface of the brightest star—and eyes like Miss Scatcherd's can only see those tiny flaws, blind to the full brilliance of the whole.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Before the half hour was up, five o'clock struck. School was dismissed and everyone went to the dining hall for tea. I dared to climb down from the stool. It was deep dusk. I retreated to a corner and sat on the floor. The spell that had sustained me began to dissolve. Reaction set in, and soon the grief that seized me was so overwhelming that I collapsed face-down on the floor. Now I cried. Helen Burns wasn't there. Nothing held me up. Left to myself, I gave in completely, and my tears soaked the floorboards. I had meant to be so good, and to do so much at Lowood—to make friends, earn respect, and win affection. That very morning I had already made real progress: I'd reached the head of my class. Miss Miller had praised me warmly. Miss Temple had smiled with approval and promised to teach me drawing and let me start French if I kept improving for another two months. I had been welcomed by my fellow students—treated as an equal by those my age, and left alone by everyone else. And now here I was, crushed and trampled again. Would I ever be able to rise?

"Never," I thought, and passionately wished I could die. While I sobbed out this wish in broken words, someone approached. I looked up—Helen Burns was near me again. The dying fires just showed her coming up the long, empty room. She brought my coffee and bread.

"Come, eat something," she said. But I pushed both away, feeling as if a single drop or crumb would choke me. Helen studied me, probably with surprise. I couldn't calm down despite my best efforts, and I kept weeping loudly. She sat down on the floor near me, hugged her knees, and rested her head on them. In that position she stayed, silent as a statue. I was the first to speak—
"Helen, why do you stay with a girl everyone thinks is a liar?"
"Everyone, Jane? There are only eighty people who heard you called that. The world has hundreds of millions."
"But what do millions matter to me? The eighty I know despise me."
"Jane, you're wrong. Probably not one person in this school despises or dislikes you. Many of them, I'm sure, feel very sorry for you."
"How can they feel sorry for me after what Mr. Brocklehurst said?"

"Mr. Brocklehurst is not God, nor is he even a great or admired man. He's not well liked here. He's never made an effort to be liked. If he had singled you out as a favorite, you would have found enemies all around you, open or secret. As it is, most of the girls would offer you their sympathy if they dared. Teachers and students may treat you coldly for a day or two, but kind feelings are hidden in their hearts, and if you keep doing well, those feelings will show themselves all the more clearly for having been suppressed. Besides, Jane—" She paused.
"Yes, Helen?" I said, putting my hand in hers. She rubbed my fingers gently to warm them and went on—
"If the whole world hated you and believed you wicked, but your own conscience approved you and knew you were innocent, you would not be without friends."

"No, I know I'd think well of myself. But that isn't enough. If others don't love me, I'd rather die than live. I can't bear to be lonely and hated, Helen. Look—to earn real affection from you, or Miss Temple, or anyone I truly love, I would gladly let someone break my arm, or let a bull toss me, or stand behind a kicking horse and let it strike my chest—"

"Hush, Jane! You care too much about human love. You are too passionate, too intense. The hand that made you and gave you life has provided you with other resources besides your own frail self, or other frail creatures like you. Beyond this earth and the human race, there is an invisible world and a kingdom of spirits. That world surrounds us, for it is everywhere. Those spirits watch over us, for they are charged with guarding us. And if we were dying in pain and shame, if scorn attacked us from all sides and hatred crushed us, angels would see our suffering, recognize our innocence (if innocent we are, as I know you are of this charge Mr. Brocklehurst has pompously repeated secondhand from Mrs. Reed—for I read a sincere nature in your passionate eyes and clear face), and God waits only for the spirit to leave the body to crown us with a full reward. Why, then, should we ever sink into despair, when life is so soon over and death is so certain a gateway to happiness—to glory?"

I was silent. Helen had calmed me, but in the peace she gave there was an undertone of unspeakable sadness. I felt the shadow of sorrow as she spoke, though I couldn't tell where it came from. And when she finished and breathed a little fast, followed by a short cough, I briefly forgot my own troubles in a vague concern for her.

Resting my head on Helen's shoulder, I put my arms around her waist. She drew me close, and we sat in silence. We hadn't been there long when someone else came in. Heavy clouds, swept from the sky by a rising wind, had left the moon exposed, and its light, streaming through a nearby window, shone full on both of us and on the approaching figure, which we immediately recognized as Miss Temple.
"I came looking for you, Jane Eyre," she said. "I want you in my room. And since Helen Burns is with you, she may come too."

We followed her. Guided by the superintendent, we threaded through winding passages and climbed a staircase before reaching her room. It had a good fire and looked warm and cheerful. Miss Temple told Helen Burns to sit in a low armchair on one side of the hearth. She took another herself and called me to her side.
"Is it all over?" she asked, looking down at my face. "Have you cried all your grief away?"
"I'm afraid I never will."
"Why?"
"Because I've been wrongly accused, and now you, ma'am, and everyone else will think I'm wicked."
"We will think of you as you prove yourself to be, my child. Keep acting like a good girl, and you'll satisfy us."
"Will I, Miss Temple?"
"You will," she said, putting her arm around me. "Now tell me, who is the lady Mr. Brocklehurst called your benefactress?"
"Mrs. Reed, my uncle's wife. My uncle is dead, and he left me in her care."
"She didn't adopt you of her own accord, then?"
"No, ma'am. She resented having to do it. But my uncle, as I often heard the servants say, made her promise before he died that she would always keep me."

"Well now, Jane—you know, or at least I'll tell you, that when someone is accused of a crime, they are always allowed to speak in their own defense. You have been accused of being a liar. Defend yourself to me as best you can. Say whatever you honestly remember as true, but add nothing and exaggerate nothing."

I resolved with all my heart to be careful and fair. After thinking for a few minutes to organize what I had to say, I told her the whole story of my unhappy childhood. Drained by emotion, my language was calmer than it usually was when I talked about that sad subject. And remembering Helen's warnings against giving in to resentment, I put far less bitterness into the account than usual. Restrained and simplified like this, it sounded more believable. I could feel as I went on that Miss Temple fully believed me.

In telling the story, I had mentioned Mr. Lloyd visiting me after my fit, because I could never forget the terrifying episode of the red room. When I described it, my emotions inevitably broke through to some degree—nothing could soften in my memory the spasm of agony when Mrs. Reed rejected my desperate plea for mercy and locked me back in that dark, haunted room.
I finished. Miss Temple looked at me silently for a few moments, then said—
"I know something of Mr. Lloyd. I will write to him. If his reply matches your account, you will be publicly cleared of every charge. To me, Jane, you are already cleared."

She kissed me and, still keeping me at her side (where I was happy to stand, because I took a child's delight in studying her face, her dress, her few pieces of jewelry, her white forehead, her clustered shining curls, and her bright dark eyes), she turned to address Helen Burns.
"How are you tonight, Helen? Have you coughed much today?"
"Not quite as much, I think, ma'am."
"And the pain in your chest?"
"It's a little better."

Miss Temple rose, took her hand, and checked her pulse. Then she returned to her chair. As she sat down, I heard her sigh quietly. She looked thoughtful for a moment, then brightened and said cheerfully—
"But you two are my guests tonight. I must treat you properly." She rang her bell.
"Barbara," she said to the servant who came, "I haven't had tea yet. Bring the tray, and set out cups for these two young ladies."

A tray soon arrived. How lovely the china cups and bright teapot looked, set on the little round table by the fire! How fragrant the steam from the tea, and the scent of the toast! Though of the toast, I noticed with dismay (for I was getting hungry again), there was very little. Miss Temple noticed it too.
"Barbara," she said, "could you bring a bit more bread and butter? There isn't enough for three."
Barbara went out and came back shortly—
"Ma'am, Mrs. Harden says she sent up the usual amount."
Mrs. Harden, it should be noted, was the housekeeper—a woman after Mr. Brocklehurst's own heart, made of equal parts whalebone and iron.

"Oh, very well!" said Miss Temple. "We'll have to make do, Barbara, I suppose." And as the girl left, she added with a smile, "Fortunately, I happen to have the means to fill the gap, just this once."

Having invited Helen and me to the table, and placed before each of us a cup of tea with one delicious but thin piece of toast, she got up, unlocked a drawer, and took out a parcel wrapped in paper. It turned out to be a good-sized seed cake.
"I meant to give each of you some of this to take with you," she said, "but since there's so little toast, you'd better have it now." And she began cutting generous slices.

We feasted that evening like gods. And the greatest pleasure of the meal was the smile of satisfaction on our hostess's face as she watched us satisfy our starving appetites with the fine food she so generously provided.
After tea, when the tray was cleared, she called us to the fire again. We sat one on each side of her, and a conversation followed between her and Helen that it was truly a privilege to witness.

Miss Temple always carried an air of calm dignity, of refined propriety in her speech, that kept any conversation from becoming too heated or emotional. There was something about her that tempered the pleasure of watching and listening with a restraining sense of awe—and that was what I felt now. But as for Helen Burns, I was struck with amazement.

The good food, the warm fire, the presence and kindness of her beloved teacher, or perhaps more than all of these, something in her own extraordinary mind, had awakened her powers. They stirred, they caught fire: first glowing in the bright flush of her cheek, which until this hour I had only ever seen pale and bloodless; then shining in the liquid brilliance of her eyes, which had suddenly acquired a beauty more striking than Miss Temple's—a beauty not of fine color or long lashes or sculpted brows, but of meaning, of animation, of radiance. Then her soul sat on her lips, and words flowed from a source I cannot name. Does a fourteen-year-old girl have a heart large enough, strong enough, to hold the swelling spring of pure, passionate eloquence? That was the nature of Helen's speech on that memorable evening. Her spirit seemed to be racing to live as much in a brief span as many live in a long lifetime.

They talked about subjects I'd never heard of—nations and ages past, distant countries, secrets of nature discovered or guessed at. They spoke of books—how many they had read! What stores of knowledge they possessed! They seemed so familiar with French names and French authors. But my amazement reached its peak when Miss Temple asked Helen if she sometimes found a moment to review the Latin her father had taught her, and taking a book from a shelf, asked her to read and translate a page of Virgil. Helen obeyed, and my sense of awe grew with every sonorous line. She had barely finished when the bell rang for bed. No delay was allowed. Miss Temple embraced us both, and as she drew us to her heart, she said—
"God bless you, my children!"

She held Helen a little longer than me. She let her go more reluctantly. It was Helen her eye followed to the door. It was for her she breathed a second sad sigh. For her she wiped a tear from her cheek.

When we reached the dormitory, we heard Miss Scatcherd's voice. She was inspecting drawers. She had just pulled open Helen Burns's, and when we entered, Helen was met with a sharp scolding and told that the next day she would have half a dozen untidily folded garments pinned to her shoulder.
"My things really were in terrible disorder," Helen whispered to me. "I meant to have sorted them, but I forgot."

The next morning, Miss Scatcherd wrote the word "SLATTERN" in large letters on a piece of cardboard and tied it like a crown of thorns around Helen's large, gentle, intelligent, kind-looking forehead. She wore it all day, patient and uncomplaining, accepting it as a deserved punishment. The moment Miss Scatcherd left after afternoon classes, I ran to Helen, tore it off, and threw it in the fire. The fury that Helen was incapable of feeling had been burning in my soul all day, and tears—hot, large tears—had been scalding my cheeks continuously, because the sight of her quiet resignation caused me unbearable pain.

About a week after these events, Miss Temple, who had written to Mr. Lloyd, received his reply. What he said apparently confirmed my account. Miss Temple gathered the whole school together and announced that an investigation had been made into the charges against Jane Eyre, and that she was most happy to be able to declare me completely cleared of every accusation. The teachers shook my hand and kissed me, and a murmur of pleasure ran through the ranks of my classmates.

Freed from that crushing weight, I set to work again from that hour, determined to push through every difficulty. I worked hard, and my success matched my effort. My memory, not naturally strong, improved with practice. Exercise sharpened my mind. Within a few weeks I was promoted to a higher class. In less than two months I was allowed to start French and drawing. I learned the first two tenses of the verb etre and sketched my first cottage (whose walls, I should mention, rivaled the leaning tower of Pisa in their slope) on the same day. That night, going to bed, I forgot to fantasize about the imaginary feast of hot roast potatoes or fresh bread and milk that I usually conjured to comfort my hunger. Instead I feasted on visions of ideal drawings, all created by my own hands—freely sketched houses and trees, picturesque rocks and ruins, groups of cattle like something from a Dutch painting, lovely paintings of butterflies hovering over rosebuds, birds picking ripe cherries, wren's nests holding pearl-like eggs wreathed in young ivy. I also pondered whether I would ever be able to translate a certain little French story that Madame Pierrot had shown me that day. That problem was not solved to my satisfaction before I fell sweetly asleep.
Solomon was right: "Better a dinner of herbs where love is, than a fattened calf with hatred."
I would not now have traded Lowood, with all its hardships, for Gateshead and its daily comforts.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: But the hardships of Lowood eased. Spring arrived—she was already here, in fact. The frosts of winter had ended, the snows had melted, the cutting winds had softened. My wretched feet, raw and swollen to the point of lameness from the sharp January air, began to heal and recover under the gentler breath of April. The nights and mornings no longer froze the blood in our veins with their arctic cold. We could now enjoy the play hour in the garden. Sometimes on a sunny day it even began to feel pleasant, and a green tinge spread over those brown beds, freshening daily, suggesting that Hope had walked through them in the night and left brighter traces of her steps each morning. Flowers peeked out among the leaves: snowdrops, crocuses, purple auriculas, and golden-eyed pansies. On Thursday afternoons, which were half-holidays, we now went on walks and found still sweeter flowers opening along the roadsides and under the hedges.

I also discovered that a great pleasure—a joy bounded only by the horizon—lay beyond the high, spike-topped walls of our garden. This pleasure was the view: noble summits encircling a great green valley, and a bright stream full of dark stones and sparkling eddies. How different this scene had looked when I first saw it under the iron winter sky, frozen stiff, shrouded in snow! When mists as cold as death drifted along those purple peaks and rolled down into the hollows until they merged with the frozen fog of the stream! That stream had been a torrent then, muddy and wild, tearing through the woods and sending a roaring sound through the air, often thickened with driving rain or whirling sleet. And the forest on its banks had shown only ranks of bare skeletons.

April gave way to May—a bright, clear May of blue skies, calm sunshine, and soft western breezes that filled its days from start to finish. The greenery surged with new life. Lowood shook out its foliage. It became all green, all flowers. Its great elms, ashes, and oaks, which had been mere skeletons, were restored to majestic life. Woodland plants sprang up thickly in every hollow. Countless varieties of moss filled the shadowy places, and the wild primroses made a strange ground-level sunshine with their pale gold gleam. I have seen them shining in overshadowed spots like scatterings of the gentlest light. All this I enjoyed often and freely, unwatched and nearly alone. For this unusual freedom, there was a cause, which I must now explain.
Haven't I described a pleasant spot for a home—nestled among hills and woods, rising from the bank of a stream? Pleasant enough, certainly. But whether it was healthy is another question.

That forest hollow where Lowood sat was a breeding ground for fog and fog-born disease. As spring quickened, so did the sickness, creeping into the orphan school, breathing typhus through its crowded schoolroom and dormitory. Before May arrived, it had transformed the school into a hospital.

Chronic hunger and untreated colds had left most of the girls vulnerable to infection. Forty-five of the eighty were sick at the same time. Classes collapsed, rules dissolved. The few who stayed well were given nearly unlimited freedom, because the doctor insisted they needed regular exercise to stay healthy. And even without his orders, no one had time to watch them. Miss Temple was completely absorbed by the patients. She lived in the sickroom, leaving only to steal a few hours of sleep at night. The other teachers were busy preparing for the departure of girls lucky enough to have family willing and able to take them away from the contagion. Many who were already sick went home only to die. Some died at the school and were buried quickly and quietly, the nature of the disease making delay impossible.

While disease had moved into Lowood and death was its frequent visitor, while fear and gloom hung within its walls, while its rooms and corridors reeked of hospital smells that medicines and disinfectants tried in vain to mask, that bright May shone cloudless over the bold hills and beautiful woods outside. The garden glowed with flowers too—hollyhocks had shot up tall as trees, lilies had opened, tulips and roses were blooming. The borders of the little beds were bright with pink thrift and crimson double daisies. The wild roses gave off their scent of spice and apple morning and evening. And all these fragrant treasures were useless to most of Lowood's residents, except to provide the occasional handful of herbs and blossoms to lay in a coffin.

But I, and the rest who stayed well, fully enjoyed the beauty of the season. They let us roam the woods like free spirits, from morning until night. We did what we liked and went where we pleased. We ate better too. Mr. Brocklehurst and his family never came near Lowood now. Household matters went unscrutinized. The stern housekeeper was gone, driven away by fear of infection. Her replacement, who had been matron at the Lowton Dispensary, was unfamiliar with the ways of the place and provided food with relative generosity. Besides, there were fewer mouths to feed—the sick could eat little. Our breakfast bowls were better filled. When there wasn't time to prepare a proper dinner, which happened often, she would give us a large piece of cold pie or a thick slice of bread and cheese, and we carried it into the woods, where each of us chose our favorite spot and dined royally.

My favorite seat was a smooth, broad stone rising white and dry from the very middle of the stream, reachable only by wading through the water—a feat I accomplished barefoot. The stone was just wide enough for me and one other girl, my chosen companion at that time: Mary Ann Wilson. She was a shrewd, observant person whose company I enjoyed, partly because she was witty and original, and partly because she had a manner that put me at ease. Several years older than me, she knew more of the world and could tell me many things I liked hearing. She satisfied my curiosity. She was also tolerant of my faults, never curbing or censoring anything I said. She had a talent for telling stories; I had a talent for asking questions. So we got along wonderfully together, drawing much entertainment, if not much improvement, from each other's company.

And where, meanwhile, was Helen Burns? Why didn't I spend these sweet, free days with her? Had I forgotten her? Or was I so fickle that I'd grown tired of her pure company? Surely the Mary Ann Wilson I've mentioned was inferior to my first friend. She could only tell me amusing stories and trade sharp gossip with me, while Helen, if I've spoken truly of her, was able to give anyone who shared her conversation a taste of far higher things.

True, reader, and I knew it and felt it. And though I'm a flawed person with many faults and few virtues, I never grew tired of Helen Burns. I never stopped cherishing for her a feeling of love as strong, tender, and reverent as any that has ever filled my heart. How could it have been otherwise, when Helen, at all times and in all circumstances, showed me a quiet, faithful friendship that bad moods never soured and irritation never disturbed? But Helen was ill. For some weeks she had been removed from my sight to some room upstairs. She was not, I was told, in the hospital wing with the typhus patients. Her illness was consumption—tuberculosis—and in my ignorance, I took that to be something mild that time and care would certainly cure.

I was encouraged in this belief by the fact that she had once or twice come downstairs on very warm, sunny afternoons and been taken by Miss Temple into the garden. But on these occasions, I wasn't allowed to speak to her. I only saw her from the schoolroom window, and not clearly—she was bundled up and sat at a distance under the covered walkway.

One evening, in early June, I had stayed out very late with Mary Ann in the woods. We had separated from the others as usual and wandered so far that we got lost and had to ask directions at a lonely cottage where a man and woman lived, tending a herd of half-wild pigs that fed on acorns in the forest. When we got back, the moon had risen. A pony we recognized as the surgeon's was standing at the garden door. Mary Ann remarked that someone must be very ill if Mr. Bates had been sent for at that hour. She went inside. I stayed behind a few minutes to plant some roots I'd dug up in the forest and was afraid would wilt if I left them until morning. That done, I lingered a little longer. The flowers smelled so sweet as the dew fell. It was such a pleasant evening—so calm, so warm. The still-glowing west promised another fine day tomorrow. The moon rose with such majesty in the solemn east. I was noticing all these things and enjoying them as a child does, when a thought entered my mind that had never come before—
"How sad to be lying on a sickbed right now, in danger of dying! This world is lovely—it would be terrible to be called away from it, to go who knows where."

And then my mind made its first real effort to understand what it had been taught about heaven and hell. For the first time, it recoiled in confusion. For the first time, looking behind, beside, and ahead, it saw nothing but a vast, unfathomable gulf all around. It felt the one solid point where it stood—the present. Everything else was formless cloud and empty depth. It shuddered at the thought of losing its footing and plunging into that chaos. While I was turning this over, I heard the front door open. Mr. Bates came out, and with him a nurse. After she watched him mount his horse and ride away, she was about to close the door, but I ran up to her.
"How is Helen Burns?"
"Very poorly," was the answer.
"Is she the one Mr. Bates came to see?"
"Yes."
"And what does he say about her?"
"He says she won't be here long."

If I had heard this phrase yesterday, I would have thought it simply meant she was about to be sent home to Northumberland. I wouldn't have guessed it meant she was dying. But I understood instantly now. It hit me with blinding clarity that Helen Burns was counting her final days in this world, and that she was going to the realm of spirits, if such a realm existed. I felt a shock of horror, then a powerful surge of grief, then a need—a compulsion—to see her. I asked which room she was in.
"She's in Miss Temple's room," said the nurse.
"May I go up and speak to her?"
"Oh no, child! Not likely. And it's time you came inside. You'll catch the fever if you stay out in the dew."
The nurse closed the front door. I went in through a side entrance that led to the schoolroom. I was just in time—it was nine o'clock and Miss Miller was calling the girls to bed.

It might have been two hours later, probably near eleven, when I—having been unable to fall asleep, and judging from the perfect silence of the dormitory that everyone else was deeply asleep—rose quietly, put my dress on over my nightgown, and without shoes, crept from the room and set off to find Miss Temple's room. It was at the far end of the building, but I knew the way, and the light of the cloudless summer moon, shining here and there through hallway windows, helped me find it easily. A smell of camphor and burnt vinegar warned me when I neared the fever room, and I hurried past its door, afraid the night nurse might hear me. I dreaded being caught and sent back—I had to see Helen, I had to hold her before she died, I had to give her one last kiss and exchange one last word.

Down a staircase, through part of the ground floor, opening and closing two doors without a sound, I reached another flight of steps. I climbed them, and directly opposite was Miss Temple's room. A light shone through the keyhole and under the door. A profound stillness filled the hallway. Drawing near, I found the door slightly ajar—probably to let fresh air into the close, sickly room. Unwilling to hesitate, full of urgent impulse, my soul and senses trembling with sharp feeling, I pushed the door open and looked in. My eyes searched for Helen, afraid of what they might find.

By Miss Temple's bed, half-hidden by its white curtains, stood a small crib. I could see the outline of a figure under the covers, but the face was hidden by the bed hangings. The nurse I'd spoken to in the garden was asleep in an armchair. An untrimmed candle flickered dimly on the table. Miss Temple was nowhere to be seen—I learned later that she had been called to a delirious patient in the fever room. I came closer, then paused at the side of the crib. My hand was on the curtain, but I wanted to speak before pulling it back. I still shrank from the fear of seeing a corpse.
"Helen!" I whispered softly. "Are you awake?"
She stirred and pushed back the curtain. I saw her face—pale, wasted, but perfectly calm. She looked so little changed that my fear dissolved instantly.
"Can it be you, Jane?" she asked in her own gentle voice.
"Oh!" I thought, "she's not going to die. They're wrong. She couldn't speak and look so peacefully if she were."
I climbed onto the crib and kissed her. Her forehead was cold, and her cheek was both cold and thin. So were her hand and wrist. But she smiled just as she always had.
"Why have you come here, Jane? It's past eleven. I heard the clock strike a few minutes ago."
"I came to see you, Helen. I heard you were very ill, and I couldn't sleep until I'd spoken to you."
"You came to say good-bye, then. You're probably just in time."
"Are you going somewhere, Helen? Are you going home?"
"Yes—to my final home. My last home."

"No, no, Helen!" I stopped, distressed. While I tried to swallow my tears, a fit of coughing seized Helen. It didn't wake the nurse, though. When it passed, she lay exhausted for a few minutes, then whispered—
"Jane, your little feet are bare. Lie down and cover yourself with my blanket."
I did. She put her arm over me, and I nestled close to her. After a long silence, she spoke again, still whispering—

"I am very happy, Jane. And when you hear that I'm dead, you must promise not to grieve. There is nothing to grieve about. We all must die someday, and the illness that is taking me away is not painful. It's gentle and gradual. My mind is at peace. I leave no one who will miss me much.
