I have only a father, and he has recently remarried. He won't miss me. By dying young, I'll be spared great suffering. I didn't have the qualities or talents to do well in the world. I would always have been making mistakes."
"But where are you going, Helen? Can you see? Do you know?"
"I believe. I have faith. I am going to God."
"Where is God? What is God?"

"My Maker and yours. He will never destroy what He created. I trust completely in His power and wholly in His goodness. I count the hours until that momentous one arrives that will bring me back to Him and reveal Him to me."
"You are sure, then, Helen, that there is such a place as heaven? And that our souls can reach it when we die?"
"I am sure there is a life after death. I believe God is good. I can surrender my soul to Him without fear. God is my father. God is my friend. I love Him. I believe He loves me."
"And will I see you again, Helen, when I die?"
"You will come to the same place of happiness, received by the same mighty, universal Parent—I have no doubt of it, dear Jane."

Again I questioned, but this time only in thought. "Where is that place? Does it exist?" And I held Helen tighter. She seemed dearer to me than ever. I felt as if I couldn't let her go. I lay with my face hidden against her neck. After a while, she said in the sweetest tone—
"How comfortable I am! That last coughing fit tired me a little. I feel as if I could sleep. But don't leave me, Jane. I like having you near."
"I'll stay with you, dear Helen. No one will take me away."
"Are you warm, darling?"
"Yes."
"Good night, Jane."
"Good night, Helen."
She kissed me, and I kissed her, and we both soon fell asleep.

When I woke, it was daylight. An unusual movement roused me. I looked up. I was in someone's arms—the nurse was carrying me through the corridor back to the dormitory. I was not scolded for leaving my bed; people had other things on their minds. No one answered my many questions at the time. But a day or two later I learned that Miss Temple, returning to her room at dawn, had found me in the little crib, my face against Helen Burns's shoulder, my arms around her neck. I was asleep, and Helen was dead.

Her grave is in Brocklebridge churchyard. For fifteen years after her death, it was marked only by a grassy mound. But now a gray marble tablet stands there, inscribed with her name and the single word: Resurgam.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Until now I have recorded the events of my insignificant life in detail, devoting almost as many chapters to the first ten years as they deserve. But this is not meant to be a full autobiography. I need only call on memory where her answers will hold some interest. So I now skip over a space of eight years almost in silence. A few lines will suffice to keep the thread connected.

When the typhus had finished its devastation at Lowood, it gradually disappeared. But not before its violence and its death toll had drawn public attention to the school. An investigation was launched into the origins of the epidemic, and gradually various facts emerged that provoked widespread outrage. The unhealthy location, the quantity and quality of the children's food, the brackish, foul water used to prepare it, the students' wretched clothing and living conditions—all of this came to light, and the discovery proved humiliating for Mr. Brocklehurst but beneficial for the school.

Several wealthy and generous individuals in the county contributed large sums to build a more suitable building in a better location. New rules were established. Improvements in food and clothing were introduced. The school's funds were placed under the management of a committee. Mr. Brocklehurst, whose wealth and social connections made him impossible to ignore, kept his post as treasurer, but he was now aided by men of broader and more compassionate minds. His role as inspector was likewise shared with people who knew how to combine reason with discipline, comfort with economy, and compassion with integrity. The school, thus reformed, became in time a truly valuable and admirable institution. I remained within its walls for eight years after its transformation: six as a student and two as a teacher. In both roles, I can testify to its worth.

During those eight years my life was routine but not unhappy, because it was not idle. I had access to an excellent education. A love for some of my subjects, a desire to excel in all, and a deep pleasure in pleasing my teachers—especially those I loved—drove me forward. I made full use of every opportunity. In time I rose to become the top student in the top class. Then I was appointed teacher, a role I filled with enthusiasm for two years. But at the end of that time, something changed.

Miss Temple had remained superintendent through all the school's changes. I owed the best part of my education to her teaching. Her friendship and company had been my constant comfort. She had served as my mother, my governess, and eventually my companion. Then she married, and moved with her husband (a clergyman—an excellent man, almost worthy of such a wife) to a distant county. She was lost to me.

From the day she left, I was no longer the same person. With her went every settled feeling, every connection that had made Lowood something of a home. I had absorbed much from her nature and her habits: more balanced thoughts, more regulated emotions had taken up residence in my mind. I had pledged myself to duty and order. I was quiet. I believed I was content. To others, and usually even to myself, I appeared disciplined and subdued.

But fate, in the form of the Reverend Mr. Nasmyth, came between me and Miss Temple. I watched her step into a carriage in her traveling clothes, shortly after the wedding ceremony. I watched the carriage climb the hill and disappear over the top. Then I returned to my room and spent most of the half-day holiday alone.

I paced the room for most of it. I thought I was simply mourning my loss and wondering how to fill the gap. But when my reflections ended and I looked up to find that the afternoon was gone and evening was well advanced, another discovery dawned on me: during that time, I had undergone a transformation. My mind had shed everything it had borrowed from Miss Temple—or rather, she had taken with her the calm atmosphere I had been breathing in her presence. Now I was left in my natural element, beginning to feel the stirring of old emotions. It didn't feel as though a support had been removed, but rather as though a purpose had vanished. It wasn't the ability to be calm that had failed me—it was the reason for calmness that was gone. For years, my world had been Lowood, my experience limited to its rules and routines. Now I remembered that the real world was vast, and that a varied landscape of hopes and fears, sensations and excitements, awaited anyone brave enough to venture out into it and seek real knowledge of life among its dangers.

I went to my window, opened it, and looked out. There were the two wings of the building. There was the garden. There were the edges of Lowood. There was the hilly horizon. My eye passed over everything else to rest on the most distant objects—the blue peaks. Those were what I longed to reach. Everything within their boundary of rock and heath felt like a prison. I traced the white road winding around the base of one mountain and vanishing into a pass between two others. How I longed to follow it! I remembered the time I had traveled that very road in a coach, descending that hill at twilight. It felt like a lifetime ago since the day that first brought me to Lowood, and I had never left since. All my holidays had been spent at school. Mrs. Reed had never sent for me. Neither she nor any of her family had ever visited. I had had no contact with the outside world—no letters, no messages. School rules, school duties, school habits and ideas, and voices and faces and phrases and uniforms and preferences and grudges—that was all I knew of existence. And now I felt it wasn't enough. I grew tired of eight years of routine in a single afternoon. I wanted freedom. I gasped for freedom. I said a prayer for freedom, and it seemed to scatter on the faint breeze. I gave that up and made a humbler plea—for change, for stimulus. That prayer too seemed to dissolve into emptiness. "Then," I cried, half-desperate, "grant me at least a new servitude!"
A bell ringing for supper called me downstairs.

I couldn't resume my broken chain of thoughts until bedtime, and even then a teacher who shared my room kept me from the subject I wanted to return to with a long stream of small talk. How I wished sleep would silence her! It seemed that if I could just get back to the idea I'd had while standing at the window, some useful solution would come to me.

Miss Gryce finally snored. She was a heavyset Welsh woman, and until now I had never regarded her habitual snoring as anything but a nuisance. Tonight I welcomed the first deep rumbles with satisfaction. I was free of interruption. My half-forgotten thought instantly revived.

"A new servitude! There's something in that," I said to myself (silently, of course—I didn't speak aloud). "I know there is, because it doesn't sound too sweet. It's not like words such as Liberty, Excitement, Enjoyment—delightful sounds, certainly, but nothing more than sounds for me, so hollow and fleeting that listening to them is a waste of time. But Servitude! That's something practical. Anyone can serve. I've served here for eight years. Now all I want is to serve somewhere else. Can I not have that much of my own way? Is the thing doable? Yes—yes—the goal isn't so hard. If only I had a brain active enough to figure out how to reach it."
I sat up in bed to get my brain working. It was a cold night. I wrapped a shawl around my shoulders and then proceeded to think with all my might.

"What do I want? A new position, in a new house, among new faces, in new circumstances. I want this because there's no point wanting anything better. How do people find new positions? They ask friends, I suppose. I have no friends. There are many others without friends who must fend for themselves. What is their solution?"

I couldn't answer. Nothing came to me. I ordered my brain to find a response, and quickly. It churned and churned faster. I felt my pulse throb in my head and temples. But for nearly an hour it worked in chaos, producing nothing. Feverish with the useless effort, I got up and paced the room, pulled back the curtain, noted a star or two, shivered with cold, and crept back to bed.

Some kind fairy must have dropped the answer on my pillow while I was gone, because as I lay down, the thought came to me, quietly and naturally: "People who want positions advertise. You must advertise in the ——shire Herald."
"How? I know nothing about advertising."
Answers came smoothly now—

"You must put the advertisement and the payment in an envelope addressed to the editor of the Herald. You must mail it at the Lowton post office at the first chance. Replies should be sent to J.E., care of the post office there. You can go and check for answers about a week later, and act accordingly."
I went over this plan twice, three times. Then it was clear and solid in my mind. I felt satisfied and fell asleep.
At first light I was up. I had my advertisement written, sealed, and addressed before the bell rang to wake the school. It read:

"A young lady experienced in teaching" (hadn't I been a teacher for two years?) "seeks a position in a private family where the children are under fourteen" (since I was barely eighteen, I thought it unwise to take on pupils near my own age). "She is qualified to teach the standard subjects of a good English education, along with French, Drawing, and Music" (in those days, reader, this now-modest list would have been considered reasonably comprehensive). "Address: J.E., Post Office, Lowton, ——shire."

This document stayed locked in my drawer all day. After tea, I asked the new superintendent for permission to go to Lowton, saying I had some errands for myself and a couple of fellow teachers. Permission was readily given, and I went. It was a two-mile walk and the evening was wet, but the days were still long. I visited a shop or two, slipped the letter into the post office, and came back through heavy rain, my clothes soaked but my heart lighter.

The next week seemed endless. But it finally ended, like everything on this earth, and once more, toward the close of a pleasant autumn day, I found myself walking the road to Lowton. It was a lovely route, following the stream through the sweetest curves of the valley. But that day I thought more about the letters that might or might not be waiting for me than about the beauty of the landscape.

My excuse for the trip was to get measured for shoes, so I took care of that first. Then I crossed the quiet little street from the shoemaker's to the post office, run by an old woman who wore horn-rimmed spectacles and black mittens.
"Are there any letters for J.E.?" I asked.

She peered at me over her spectacles, then opened a drawer and rummaged through it for a long time—so long that my hopes started to sink. At last, after holding a document up to her glasses for nearly five minutes, she slid it across the counter with another curious, suspicious look. It was for J.E.
"Is there only one?" I asked.
"There are no more," she said. I put it in my pocket and headed home. I couldn't open it yet—I had to be back by eight, and it was already half past seven.

Various duties awaited me when I arrived. I had to sit with the girls during their study hour, then it was my turn to read prayers, then see them to bed. After that, I had supper with the other teachers. Even when we finally retired, the inevitable Miss Gryce was still my roommate. We had only a short stub of candle, and I was terrified she would talk until it burned out. Fortunately, the heavy supper she'd eaten had a sedative effect—she was snoring before I'd finished undressing. There was still an inch of candle left. I took out my letter. The seal bore the initial F. I broke it open. The contents were brief.

"If J.E., who advertised in the ——shire Herald of last Thursday, possesses the qualifications mentioned, and if she is able to provide satisfactory references as to character and ability, a position can be offered where there is only one pupil, a girl under ten years of age, and where the salary is thirty pounds per year. J.E. is requested to send references, name, address, and full particulars to:
"Mrs. Fairfax, Thornfield, near Millcote, ——shire."

I studied the letter for a long time. The handwriting was old-fashioned and a bit shaky, like an elderly lady's. This was reassuring. A private fear had nagged me that in acting on my own, without guidance, I might get into some kind of trouble. Above all, I wanted the outcome to be respectable and proper. Now I felt that an elderly lady was a comforting element. Mrs. Fairfax! I pictured her in a black dress and widow's cap—perhaps a bit stiff, but perfectly civil. A model of elderly English respectability. Thornfield! That was obviously the name of her house. I imagined a neat, orderly place, though I couldn't form a clear picture of it. Millcote, ——shire—I refreshed my memory of the map of England. Yes, I found it. The county was seventy miles closer to London than the remote region where I lived now. That appealed to me. I longed to go somewhere with life and movement. Millcote was a large manufacturing town on the banks of a river—a busy place, no doubt. All the better. It would be a complete change, at least. Not that I was particularly attracted to the idea of factory chimneys and smoke—"but," I told myself, "Thornfield is probably a good distance from the town."
At that point the candle guttered and went out.

The next day, new steps had to be taken. My plans could no longer stay private—I had to share them to make them work. Having requested and been granted a meeting with the superintendent during the midday break, I told her I had a prospect of a new position at double my current salary (at Lowood I earned only fifteen pounds a year), and asked if she would raise the matter with Mr. Brocklehurst or the committee and find out whether they would let me use them as references. She kindly agreed to act as go-between. The next day she put the matter to Mr. Brocklehurst, who said that Mrs. Reed must be written to, as she was my legal guardian. A letter was sent accordingly. The reply came back that "I could do as I pleased—she had long since given up any involvement in my affairs." This note was circulated among the committee, and at last, after what seemed an agonizing delay, I was formally given permission to improve my situation if I could. They also assured me that since I had always conducted myself well, both as teacher and student, a testimonial of character and ability, signed by the school's inspectors, would be provided right away.

I received this testimonial about a month later, forwarded a copy to Mrs. Fairfax, and received that lady's reply confirming she was satisfied and setting a date two weeks hence for me to begin as governess in her household.

I now threw myself into preparations. The two weeks flew by. I didn't have a large wardrobe, though it was enough for my needs, and the last day was enough to pack my trunk—the same one I had brought from Gateshead eight years earlier.

The trunk was strapped and labeled. In half an hour the carrier was coming to take it to Lowton, where I myself would go early the next morning to catch the coach. I had brushed my black traveling dress, prepared my bonnet, gloves, and muff, and searched every drawer to make sure nothing was left behind. Now, with nothing left to do, I sat down and tried to rest. I couldn't. Though I'd been on my feet all day, I couldn't sit still for a moment. I was too excited. One phase of my life was ending tonight and another beginning tomorrow. Sleep in the interval was impossible. I had to watch, feverish with anticipation, while the change took place.
"Miss," said a servant I met in the hallway, where I was pacing like a restless ghost, "someone downstairs wants to see you."
"The carrier, I suppose," I thought, and ran down without asking. I was passing the teachers' sitting room, whose door was half open, on my way to the kitchen, when someone rushed out—
"It's her! I'm sure of it! I'd have known her anywhere!" cried the person who stopped me and grabbed my hand.
I looked. I saw a woman dressed like a respectable servant—mature but still young, very pretty, with black hair and eyes and a lively complexion.
"Well, who is it?" she asked, in a voice and with a smile I half recognized. "You haven't quite forgotten me, I think, Miss Jane?"

In another second I was hugging and kissing her with wild joy. "Bessie! Bessie! Bessie!" That was all I could say. She half laughed, half cried, and we both went into the sitting room. By the fire stood a little boy of about three, wearing a plaid outfit.
"That's my little boy," said Bessie proudly.
"Then you're married, Bessie?"
"Yes, nearly five years now, to Robert Leaven, the coachman. And I have a little girl besides Bobby there—I've named her Jane."
"And you don't live at Gateshead?"
"I live at the lodge. The old porter has left."
"Well, and how is everyone? Tell me everything about them, Bessie—but sit down first. And Bobby, come sit on my knee, will you?" But Bobby preferred to sidle over to his mother.

"You haven't grown very tall, Miss Jane, nor very stout," continued Mrs. Leaven. "I expect they haven't fed you too well at school. Miss Reed is a head and shoulders taller than you, and Miss Georgiana is twice your width."
"Georgiana is pretty, I suppose, Bessie?"

"Very. She went to London last winter with her mama, and everyone admired her. A young lord fell in love with her, but his family was against the match. And—can you believe it?—he and Miss Georgiana planned to elope. But they were found out and stopped. It was Miss Reed who discovered them. I think she was jealous. Now the two sisters fight like cats—always quarreling."
"And what about John Reed?"

"Oh, he's not doing as well as his mama hoped. He went to university and failed—got expelled, I think they call it. Then his uncles wanted him to become a lawyer, but he's such a wild young man that I don't think they'll make much of him."
"What does he look like?"
"He's very tall. Some people call him handsome, but he has very thick lips."
"And Mrs. Reed?"
"The Missus looks healthy enough, but I don't think she's easy in her mind. Mr. John's behavior doesn't please her—he spends a lot of money."
"Did she send you here, Bessie?"

"Oh, no. But I've wanted to see you for ages, and when I heard there had been a letter from you, and that you were going to another part of the country, I thought I'd come and get a look at you before you were completely out of reach."
"I'm afraid you're disappointed in me, Bessie." I said this laughing—I could see that Bessie's look, while showing fondness, showed no admiration.
"No, Miss Jane, not exactly. You look genteel enough—like a lady, and that's as much as I ever expected of you. You were no beauty as a child."

I smiled at Bessie's blunt honesty. I knew it was accurate, but I admit I wasn't entirely indifferent to what it implied. At eighteen, most people want to be attractive, and the realization that your appearance won't help is far from welcome.
"I expect you're clever, though," Bessie continued, by way of consolation. "What can you do? Can you play the piano?"
"A little."
There was one in the room. Bessie went and opened it, then asked me to sit down and play. I played a waltz or two, and she was delighted.
"The Miss Reeds couldn't play as well!" she said triumphantly. "I always said you'd outshine them in learning. Can you draw?"
"That's one of my paintings above the fireplace." It was a watercolor landscape I had given to the superintendent as thanks for her help with the committee. She had framed and glazed it.
"Well, that's beautiful, Miss Jane! It's as fine as anything Miss Reed's drawing teacher could paint, let alone the young ladies themselves, who couldn't come close. And have you learned French?"
"Yes, Bessie—I can both read and speak it."
"And you can do embroidery and needlework?"
"I can."

"Oh, you're quite a lady, Miss Jane! I knew you would be. You'll do well whether your relatives notice you or not. There was something I wanted to ask you. Have you ever heard anything from your father's family, the Eyres?"
"Never in my life."

"Well, you know the Missus always said they were poor and low-class—and they may be poor, but I believe they're as much gentry as the Reeds. About seven years ago, a Mr. Eyre came to Gateshead wanting to see you. The Missus told him you were at school fifty miles away. He seemed very disappointed, because he couldn't stay—he was about to leave on a voyage overseas, and his ship was sailing from London in a day or two. He looked quite like a gentleman, and I believe he was your father's brother."
"What country was he going to, Bessie?"
"An island thousands of miles away, where they make wine—the butler told me the name—"
"Madeira?" I suggested.
"Yes, that's it—that's the very word."
"So he went?"
"Yes. He only stayed a few minutes. The Missus was very cold to him. Afterward she called him a 'sneaky tradesman.' My Robert thinks he was a wine merchant."
"Very likely," I said, "or perhaps a clerk or agent for a wine merchant."

Bessie and I talked about old times for another hour, then she had to leave. I saw her again briefly the next morning at Lowton while I waited for the coach. We parted for good at the door of the Brocklehurst Arms inn. Each went her separate way—she headed back toward Lowood Fell to catch her ride home to Gateshead, and I climbed aboard the coach that would carry me to new duties and a new life in the unknown surroundings of Millcote.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: A new chapter in a novel is something like a new scene in a play. And when I raise the curtain this time, reader, you must imagine yourself in a room at the George Inn in Millcote, with the sort of large patterned wallpaper that inn rooms have, that kind of carpet, that kind of furniture, those kinds of ornaments on the mantelpiece, and those kinds of prints—including a portrait of George III, another of the Prince of Wales, and a painting of the death of Wolfe. All this is visible by the light of an oil lamp hanging from the ceiling and an excellent fire, near which I sit in my cloak and bonnet. My muff and umbrella lie on the table, and I am warming away the numbness and chill from sixteen hours of exposure to a raw October day. I left Lowton at four in the morning, and the Millcote town clock is now striking eight.

Reader, though I look comfortably settled, my mind is far from calm. I expected someone to meet me when the coach stopped here. I looked around anxiously as I stepped down, expecting to hear my name called and to see a carriage waiting to take me to Thornfield. There was nothing. When I asked a waiter if anyone had inquired for a Miss Eyre, the answer was no. So I had no choice but to ask for a private room, and here I sit waiting, while all kinds of doubts and fears trouble my thoughts.

It is a very strange sensation for inexperienced youth to feel completely alone in the world, cut off from every connection, uncertain whether your destination can be reached, and unable to go back to what you've left. The thrill of adventure sweetens the feeling and the glow of pride warms it, but then the pulse of fear disturbs it. Fear became the dominant emotion when half an hour passed and I was still alone. I decided to ring the bell.
"Is there a place near here called Thornfield?" I asked the waiter who came.
"Thornfield? I don't know, ma'am. I'll ask at the bar." He vanished, but reappeared immediately—
"Is your name Eyre, Miss?"
"Yes."
"Someone's here waiting for you."
I jumped up, grabbed my muff and umbrella, and hurried into the passage. A man stood by the open door, and in the lamp-lit street I could dimly see a one-horse carriage.
"This'll be your luggage, I suppose?" said the man rather abruptly when he saw me, pointing to my trunk in the hallway.
"Yes." He hoisted it onto the vehicle—a sort of small carriage—and I climbed in. Before he closed the door, I asked how far it was to Thornfield.
"About six miles."
"How long will it take?"
"Maybe an hour and a half."

He fastened the door, climbed to his seat outside, and we set off. We moved at a leisurely pace, which gave me plenty of time to think. I was glad to be so close to the end of my journey. Leaning back in the comfortable if not elegant carriage, I reflected at my ease.

"I suppose," I thought, judging from the plainness of the servant and carriage, "Mrs. Fairfax is not a very grand person. So much the better—I've only once lived among fine people, and I was miserable. I wonder if she lives alone apart from this little girl. If so, and if she's at all friendly, I should be able to get along with her. I'll do my best—though doing one's best doesn't always work. At Lowood I made that resolution, kept it, and succeeded in pleasing. But with Mrs. Reed, my best was always thrown back in my face. God grant that Mrs. Fairfax doesn't turn out to be a second Mrs. Reed. But if she does, I'm not obliged to stay. If the worst comes to the worst, I can advertise again. How far along are we now, I wonder?"

I lowered the window and looked out. Millcote was behind us. Judging by the number of lights, it seemed a place of considerable size—much larger than Lowton. We appeared to be crossing some kind of common land, with houses scattered across the area. I sensed we were in a different region from Lowood—more populated, less picturesque, more bustling, less romantic.
The roads were heavy and the night misty. The driver let his horse walk the entire way, and the hour and a half stretched, I'm quite sure, to two hours. At last he turned in his seat and said—
"You're not far from Thornfield now."

I looked out again. We were passing a church—I could see its low, broad tower against the sky, and its bell was tolling the quarter hour. I also spotted a narrow cluster of lights on a hillside, marking a village or hamlet. About ten minutes later, the driver got down and opened a pair of gates. We passed through, and they clanged shut behind us. We slowly climbed a drive and came upon the long front of a house. Candlelight gleamed from one curtained bow window; all the rest were dark. The carriage stopped at the front door. A maid opened it, and I stepped down and went in.

"This way, ma'am," said the girl, and I followed her across a square hall with tall doors all around. She showed me into a room whose double glow of firelight and candlelight dazzled me at first, coming out of two hours of darkness. But when my eyes adjusted, a cozy and inviting scene presented itself.

A snug little room. A round table by a cheerful fire. A high-backed, old-fashioned armchair, and in it sat the neatest imaginable little elderly lady, wearing a widow's cap, a black silk dress, and a snowy white apron—exactly as I had pictured Mrs. Fairfax, only less imposing and gentler-looking. She was knitting. A large cat sat primly at her feet. Nothing was missing from the perfect image of domestic comfort. A more reassuring welcome for a new governess could hardly be imagined. There was no grandeur to overwhelm, no formality to intimidate. And as I entered, the old lady stood up and came forward promptly and warmly to greet me.
"How do you do, my dear? I'm afraid you've had a tedious ride—John drives so slowly. You must be cold. Come to the fire."
"Mrs. Fairfax, I presume?" I said.
"Yes, that's right. Do sit down."
She led me to her own chair and began to remove my shawl and untie my bonnet strings. I begged her not to trouble herself.
"Oh, it's no trouble. I'm sure your hands are nearly frozen. Leah, make a little hot toddy and cut a sandwich or two. Here are the keys to the storeroom."
And she produced from her pocket a thoroughly housewifely bunch of keys and handed them to the servant.
"Now, then, come closer to the fire," she continued. "You've brought your luggage, haven't you, my dear?"
"Yes, ma'am."
"I'll have it taken to your room," she said, and bustled out.

"She treats me like a guest," I thought. "I hadn't expected such a reception. I anticipated only coldness and formality. This isn't what I've heard about how governesses are treated. But I mustn't get my hopes up too soon."

She returned, cleared her knitting and a book or two from the table to make room for the tray Leah now brought in, and then served me the refreshments herself. I felt rather flustered at receiving more attention than I'd ever experienced before—and from my employer and superior, no less. But since she didn't seem to think she was doing anything unusual, I thought it best to accept her hospitality gracefully.
"Will I have the pleasure of meeting Miss Fairfax tonight?" I asked, after eating what she offered.
"What did you say, my dear? I'm a little deaf," said the kind lady, putting her ear closer to my mouth.
I repeated the question more clearly.
"Miss Fairfax? Oh, you mean Miss Varens! Varens is your future pupil's name."
"Really! Then she isn't your daughter?"
"No—I have no family."
I should have followed up by asking how Miss Varens was connected to her, but I remembered it wasn't polite to ask too many questions. Besides, I would certainly find out in time.

"I'm so glad," she continued, sitting down opposite me and taking the cat on her lap. "I'm so glad you've come. It will be quite pleasant living here now with a companion. Of course it's pleasant at any time—Thornfield is a fine old house, a bit neglected in recent years perhaps, but still a respectable place. Yet in winter one feels terribly alone, even in the best rooms. I say alone—Leah is a nice girl, and John and his wife are very decent people, but they're servants, and you can't talk to them as equals. You have to keep your distance, or you lose your authority. Last winter—it was very harsh, you may recall, and when it wasn't snowing it was raining and blowing—not a soul came to the house between November and February except the butcher and the postman. I really got quite depressed sitting night after night by myself. I had Leah read to me sometimes, but I don't think the poor girl enjoyed it much—she found it confining. Spring and summer are better—sunshine and long days make such a difference. And then, just at the start of this autumn, little Adela Varens arrived with her nurse. A child brings a house alive immediately. And now that you're here, things will be quite lively."
My heart genuinely warmed to this kind woman as I listened. I pulled my chair a little closer and told her sincerely that I hoped she would find my company as pleasant as she expected.

"But I won't keep you up late tonight," she said. "It's nearly midnight, and you've been traveling all day. You must be exhausted. Once your feet are properly warmed, I'll show you your room. I've had the room next to mine prepared for you. It's only a small room, but I thought you'd prefer it to one of the large front bedrooms. They have finer furniture, but they're so gloomy and lonely—I never sleep in them myself."

I thanked her for the thoughtful choice, and since I truly was worn out from the journey, I said I was ready to go up. She took her candle, and I followed her out of the room. First she checked that the front door was locked, then she led me upstairs. The steps and banisters were oak. The staircase window was tall and latticed. Both the window and the long gallery where the bedroom doors opened looked as though they belonged in a church rather than a house. A cold, vault-like air filled the stairs and gallery, creating a bleak sense of space and solitude. I was glad, when finally shown into my room, to find it small and furnished in a plain, modern style.

After Mrs. Fairfax bid me a kind good night, I locked my door and looked around the room at a leisurely pace. The cheerful appearance of my little room gradually erased the eerie impression left by that wide hall, that dark and cavernous staircase, and that long, cold gallery. I remembered that after a day of physical exhaustion and mental worry, I was at last in a safe harbor. Gratitude swelled my heart. I knelt by the bedside and gave thanks where thanks were due, not forgetting to ask for guidance on the road ahead, and for the strength to deserve the kindness so freely offered before I had earned it. My bed held no thorns that night, and my solitary room held no fears. Weary and content at once, I slept quickly and deeply. When I woke, it was broad daylight.

How bright my room looked as the sun streamed in through the cheerful blue chintz curtains, revealing papered walls and a carpeted floor—so unlike the bare planks and stained plaster of Lowood. My spirits lifted at the sight. Surroundings have a powerful effect on the young. I thought a happier era of life was beginning for me, one that would have its flowers and pleasures as well as its thorns and toils. My mind, stimulated by the change of scene and the new prospects it offered, seemed fully awake. I can't say exactly what I expected, but it was something pleasant—if not that day or that month, then at some point in the future.

I got up and dressed with care. I was obliged to dress plainly—every article of clothing I owned was made with extreme simplicity—but I was by nature careful about my appearance. It wasn't my habit to be careless about how I looked or the impression I made. On the contrary, I always wanted to look as well as I could, and to please as much as my lack of beauty would allow. I sometimes regretted that I wasn't prettier. I sometimes wished for rosy cheeks, a straight nose, and a small, shapely mouth. I wished I were tall, stately, and well-proportioned. I felt it was a misfortune to be so small, so pale, and to have such irregular, striking features. And why did I have these wishes and regrets? It would be hard to say—I couldn't clearly explain it to myself at the time, though I had a reason, a logical, natural one. In any case, once I had brushed my hair very smooth and put on my black dress—which, Quaker-like as it was, at least had the virtue of fitting perfectly—and straightened my clean white collar, I thought I would look respectable enough for Mrs. Fairfax, and that my new pupil wouldn't shrink from me in horror. Having opened my window and checked that everything on the dressing table was neat and tidy, I ventured out.

Walking down the long, matted gallery, I descended the slippery oak stairs to the entrance hall. I paused there a moment to look at some paintings on the walls (one showed a stern man in armor, another a lady with powdered hair and a pearl necklace), a bronze lamp hanging from the ceiling, and a great clock in an oak case, elaborately carved and blackened with age and polishing. Everything struck me as very grand and impressive—but then I was unused to grandeur. The front door, which was half glass, stood open. I stepped outside. It was a fine autumn morning. The early sun shone calmly on the russet groves and still-green fields. Walking onto the lawn, I looked up and surveyed the front of the house. It was three stories high, of considerable though not vast proportions—a gentleman's manor house, not a nobleman's palace. Battlements around the roofline gave it a picturesque look. Its gray facade stood out against the background of a rookery, whose cawing inhabitants were now in flight, swooping over the lawn and grounds to land in a great meadow separated from the garden by a sunken fence. There an array of mighty old thorn trees, as strong, gnarled, and broad as oaks, immediately explained the origin of the mansion's name. Beyond were hills—not as lofty as those around Lowood, nor as craggy, nor as much like barriers shutting out the living world, but still quiet and lonely enough, and seeming to wrap Thornfield in a seclusion I hadn't expected to find so close to a bustling place like Millcote. A small hamlet, its rooftops mingled with trees, straggled up the side of one of these hills. The local church stood nearer to Thornfield—its old tower top peeked over a knoll between the house and the gates.

I was still enjoying the calm view and the pleasant fresh air, still listening with delight to the cawing of the rooks, still studying the wide, weathered front of the hall and thinking what a grand place it was for one little old lady like Mrs. Fairfax to live in alone, when that lady appeared at the door.
"What! Out already?" she said. "I see you're an early riser." I went up to her and was received with a friendly kiss and handshake.
"How do you like Thornfield?" she asked. I told her I liked it very much.

"Yes," she said, "it's a pretty place. But I'm afraid it will fall into disrepair unless Mr. Rochester decides to come and live here permanently—or at least visit more often. Grand houses and fine grounds need the presence of the owner."
"Mr. Rochester!" I exclaimed. "Who is he?"
"The owner of Thornfield," she answered calmly. "Didn't you know his name was Rochester?"
Of course I didn't—I had never heard of him. But the old lady seemed to regard his existence as a universally known fact that everyone would naturally be aware of.
"I thought," I continued, "Thornfield belonged to you."

"To me? Bless you, child—what an idea! To me! I'm only the housekeeper, the manager. I'm distantly related to the Rochesters on his mother's side—or rather, my husband was. He was a clergyman, the rector of Hay, that little village on the hill up there. The church near the gates was his. The current Mr. Rochester's mother was a Fairfax, and second cousin to my husband. But I never presume on the connection—it means nothing to me, really. I think of myself as an ordinary housekeeper. My employer is always civil to me, and I ask for nothing more."
"And the little girl—my pupil?"

"She's Mr. Rochester's ward. He asked me to find a governess for her. He wants her raised in ——shire, I believe. Here she comes now, with her 'bonne,' as she calls her nurse." So the mystery was solved. This friendly, kind little widow was no great lady but a dependent like me. I didn't think less of her for it—quite the opposite. I was more pleased than ever. The equality between us was genuine, not just the result of politeness on her part. So much the better—my position was all the freer.

As I was reflecting on this, a little girl came running up the lawn, followed by her attendant. I looked at my pupil, who didn't seem to notice me at first. She was quite small—perhaps seven or eight years old—slightly built, with a pale, fine-featured face and a mass of hair falling in curls to her waist.
"Good morning, Miss Adela," said Mrs. Fairfax. "Come and say hello to the lady who is going to be your teacher and make you a clever woman someday." She came forward.
"C'est la ma gouvernante!" she said, pointing at me and speaking to her nurse, who answered—
"Mais oui, certainement."
"Are they foreign?" I asked, surprised to hear French.

"The nurse is foreign, and Adela was born on the Continent. I believe she never left it until about six months ago. When she first came, she couldn't speak a word of English. Now she can manage a little, but I can't understand her—she mixes it so much with French. But I'm sure you'll make sense of her."

Fortunately, I had been taught French by a Frenchwoman. I had always made a point of speaking French with Madame Pierrot as often as possible, and had spent the last seven years memorizing a portion of French daily, working hard on my accent and imitating my teacher's pronunciation as closely as I could. I had developed a reasonable fluency and accuracy in the language and was unlikely to struggle much with Mademoiselle Adela. She came and shook hands when she heard I was her governess. As I led her in to breakfast, I spoke to her in French. She answered briefly at first, but after we were seated at the table and she had studied me for about ten minutes with her large hazel eyes, she suddenly began chattering away.

"Ah!" she cried in French, "you speak my language as well as Mr. Rochester does! I can talk to you the way I talk to him, and so can Sophie. She'll be glad—nobody here understands her. Madame Fairfax is all English. Sophie is my nurse. She came with me across the sea in a great ship with a chimney that smoked—how it smoked!—and I was sick, and so was Sophie, and so was Mr. Rochester. Mr. Rochester lay on a sofa in a pretty room called the salon, and Sophie and I had little beds in another part of the ship. I nearly fell out of mine—it was like a shelf. And Mademoiselle—what is your name?"
"Eyre—Jane Eyre."

"Aire? Bah! I can't say that. Well, our ship stopped in the morning, before it was quite light, at a great city—a huge city with very dark, smoky houses, nothing like the pretty, clean town I came from. Mr. Rochester carried me in his arms across a plank to the shore, and Sophie came after us, and we all got into a coach that took us to a beautiful large house, much bigger and finer than this one, called a hotel. We stayed there nearly a week. Sophie and I used to walk every day in a great green place full of trees, called the Park. There were many other children there, and a pond with beautiful birds that I fed with crumbs."
"Can you understand her when she goes on so fast?" asked Mrs. Fairfax.
I understood perfectly, having grown accustomed to Madame Pierrot's rapid speech.
"I wish," continued Mrs. Fairfax, "you'd ask her something about her parents. I wonder if she remembers them."
"Adele," I asked, "who did you live with when you were in that pretty, clean town you mentioned?"

"I lived with Mama for a long time, but she has gone to be with the Holy Virgin. Mama used to teach me to dance and sing and recite poetry. Many ladies and gentlemen came to see Mama, and I would dance for them, or sit on their knees and sing. I liked it. Shall I sing for you now?"

She had finished her breakfast, so I let her demonstrate her talents. She slipped off her chair, came and settled on my knee, then, folding her little hands primly before her, shaking back her curls and lifting her eyes to the ceiling, she began singing a song from some opera. It was the lament of an abandoned woman who, after bewailing her lover's betrayal, summons her pride, orders her maid to dress her in her finest jewels and richest gowns, and resolves to meet the faithless man at a ball that night and prove by her gaiety how little his desertion has affected her.
The subject seemed strangely chosen for a child singer. But I suppose the point was to hear notes of love and jealousy warbled in a child's lisp—and in very poor taste that was, to my mind.
Adele sang the little song tunefully enough, with the innocence of her age. When she finished, she hopped off my knee and said, "Now, Mademoiselle, I will recite some poetry for you."

Striking a pose, she began: "La Ligue des Rats: a fable by La Fontaine." She then delivered the piece with an attention to punctuation and emphasis, a flexibility of voice, and an appropriateness of gesture very unusual for her age, proving she had been carefully trained.
"Was it your mama who taught you that piece?" I asked.

"Yes, and she used to say it just like this: 'Qu'avez vous donc? lui dit un de ces rats; parlez!' She made me raise my hand—like this—to remind me to raise my voice for the question. Now shall I dance for you?"
"No, that's enough. But after your mama went to the Holy Virgin, as you say, who did you live with then?"

"With Madame Frederic and her husband. She looked after me, but she's no relation. I think she's poor, because her house wasn't as nice as Mama's. I wasn't there long. Mr. Rochester asked if I'd like to go and live with him in England, and I said yes, because I knew Mr. Rochester from before I knew Madame Frederic, and he was always kind to me and gave me pretty dresses and toys. But he hasn't kept his word—he brought me to England and then went away again, and I never see him."

After breakfast, Adele and I went to the library, which Mr. Rochester had designated as the schoolroom. Most of the books were locked behind glass doors, but one bookcase stood open, containing all the elementary works needed, plus several volumes of lighter reading—poetry, biography, travel books, a few novels, and so on. He had probably decided that these were all a governess would need for her own reading, and indeed they more than satisfied me for now. Compared to the meager pickings I had occasionally managed at Lowood, they seemed a rich harvest of entertainment and knowledge. The room also held a cabinet piano, brand new and of excellent quality, as well as an easel for painting and a pair of globes.

I found my pupil cooperative enough, though reluctant to concentrate. She hadn't been accustomed to any kind of regular work. I felt it would be unwise to push her too hard at first. So after talking to her a great deal and getting her to learn a little, when mid-morning came I let her go back to her nurse. I then planned to spend the time before dinner making some sketches for her to use.

As I was going upstairs to fetch my portfolio and pencils, Mrs. Fairfax called to me. "Your morning lessons are finished now, I suppose?" She was in a room whose folding doors stood open. I stepped in when she spoke. It was a large, stately room with purple chairs and curtains, a Turkish carpet, walnut-paneled walls, one magnificent window rich in stained glass, and a high, beautifully molded ceiling. Mrs. Fairfax was dusting some vases of fine purple stone that stood on a sideboard.
"What a beautiful room!" I exclaimed, looking around. I had never seen anything half so grand.
"Yes, this is the dining room. I've just opened the window to let in some air and sunshine. Everything gets so damp in rooms that aren't used. The drawing room through there feels like a vault."

She pointed to a wide arch matching the window, hung with a curtain dyed deep purple, now looped up. Climbing two broad steps and looking through, I thought I glimpsed a fairy-tale room, so dazzling it appeared to my inexperienced eyes. Yet it was simply a very pretty drawing room, and beyond it a sitting room—both carpeted in white, on which seemed scattered brilliant garlands of flowers. Both had ceilings molded with white grapes and vine leaves, beneath which glowed crimson sofas and ottomans in rich contrast. The ornaments on the pale marble mantelpiece were of sparkling Bohemian glass, ruby red. Between the windows, large mirrors reflected the blending of snow and flame throughout.
"What beautiful order you keep these rooms in, Mrs. Fairfax!" I said. "No dust, no covers. If it weren't for the chill in the air, you'd think they were used every day."

"Well, Miss Eyre, though Mr. Rochester visits rarely, he always comes suddenly and without warning. I noticed it annoyed him to find everything covered up, with a fuss of arranging when he arrived, so I decided to keep the rooms ready at all times."
"Is Mr. Rochester a demanding, fussy sort of man?"
"Not particularly. But he has a gentleman's tastes and habits, and he expects things managed to suit them."
"Do you like him? Is he generally liked?"
"Oh, yes. The family has always been respected here. Almost all the land in this area, as far as you can see, has belonged to the Rochesters for as long as anyone can remember."
"Well, but setting his land aside, do you like him? Is he liked for himself?"
"I have no reason not to like him, and I believe his tenants consider him a fair and generous landlord. But he's never spent much time among them."
"But does he have any peculiarities? What, in short, is his character?"

"Oh, his character is perfectly respectable, I suppose. He is rather unusual, perhaps. He's traveled extensively and seen a great deal of the world, I imagine. I expect he's clever, but I've never had much conversation with him."
"In what way is he unusual?"

"I can't quite say—it's hard to describe. Nothing obvious, but you feel it when he speaks to you. You can never be sure whether he's joking or serious, whether he's pleased or not. You don't fully understand him—at least, I don't. But it doesn't matter. He's a very good employer."

This was all the information I could extract from Mrs. Fairfax about her employer and mine. Some people have no talent for sketching a character or noting the distinctive features of a person or thing. The good lady clearly belonged to this category. My questions puzzled her but drew nothing further out. Mr. Rochester was Mr. Rochester in her eyes—a gentleman, a landowner, nothing more. She probed no deeper and plainly wondered at my desire to form a clearer picture of him.

When we left the dining room, she offered to show me the rest of the house. I followed her up and down, admiring everything. It was all well arranged and handsome. The large front bedrooms struck me as especially grand. And some of the third-floor rooms, though dark and low-ceilinged, were fascinating in their antiquity. Furniture once used in the main rooms had been moved up here as fashions changed. In the dim light coming through narrow windows, I saw bedsteads a hundred years old, oak and walnut chests carved with palm branches and cherubs' heads that looked like miniature arks, rows of venerable high-backed chairs, and even older stools whose cushions still showed traces of half-faded embroidery, worked by hands that had been dust for two generations. These relics gave the third floor of Thornfield Hall the feel of a museum of the past—a shrine of memory. I liked the hush, the gloom, the quaintness of these rooms in daylight. But I certainly didn't want to sleep in one of those wide, heavy beds—some enclosed behind oak doors, others curtained with ancient English tapestries crusted with thick needlework depicting strange flowers, even stranger birds, and the strangest human figures. All of which would have looked eerie indeed in pale moonlight.
"Do the servants sleep in these rooms?" I asked.
"No, they have a row of smaller rooms at the back. No one ever sleeps here. You'd almost think that if Thornfield had a ghost, this would be where it lived."
"I agree. You don't have a ghost, then?"
"None that I've ever heard of," said Mrs. Fairfax with a smile.
"No traditions of one? No legends or ghost stories?"
"I don't think so. Though they say the Rochesters were a rather violent family in their day. Perhaps that's why they rest peacefully in their graves now."
"Yes—'after life's fitful fever, they sleep well,'" I murmured. "Where are you going now, Mrs. Fairfax?" She was moving away.

"Up to the roof—would you like to come and see the view?" I followed her up a very narrow staircase to the attics, then up a ladder and through a trapdoor to the roof. I was now level with the rooks' colony and could peer into their nests. Leaning over the battlements and looking far down, I surveyed the grounds spread out like a map: the bright, velvety lawn closely circling the gray base of the house; the park-like field dotted with ancient trees; the woods, brown and dry, divided by a path more green with moss than the trees were with leaves; the church at the gates; the road; the peaceful hills—all basking in the autumn sunshine. The horizon was bounded by a clear sky, blue marbled with pearly white. Nothing in the scene was extraordinary, but everything was lovely. When I turned away and went back through the trapdoor, I could barely see my way down the ladder. The attic seemed pitch-black compared to the arch of blue sky I'd been gazing at, and the sunlit scene of grove, meadow, and green hills over which the hall presided.

Mrs. Fairfax stayed behind a moment to secure the trapdoor. I groped my way to the exit from the attic and began descending the narrow staircase. I lingered in the long corridor at the bottom, which separated the front and back rooms of the third floor. It was narrow, low, and dim, with only one small window at the far end. With its two rows of little black doors, all shut, it looked like a passage in some Bluebeard's castle.

As I walked softly along, I heard the last sound I would have expected in such a still place—a laugh. It was a peculiar laugh: distinct, deliberate, joyless. I stopped. The sound ceased, but only for a moment. It started again, louder than before—though at first it had been quite low. It built into a loud peal that seemed to echo in every lonely room, though it came from only one, and I could have pointed to the door it came from.
"Mrs. Fairfax!" I called out—I could hear her coming down the main stairs. "Did you hear that loud laugh? Who is it?"
"One of the servants, most likely," she answered. "Probably Grace Poole."
"Did you hear it?" I asked again.
"Yes, clearly. I hear her often. She sews in one of these rooms. Sometimes Leah is with her. They're frequently noisy together."
The laugh came again—low, measured, syllabic—and ended in a strange murmur.
"Grace!" called Mrs. Fairfax.

I truly hadn't expected anyone called Grace to appear, because the laugh had been as eerie and unnatural as any I'd ever heard. If it hadn't been broad noon, with nothing ghostly about the circumstances—if neither the place nor the time encouraged fear—I would have been superstitious enough to be frightened. But what happened next showed me I was foolish to feel even surprise.

The nearest door opened and a servant came out—a woman of about thirty-five, with a stocky, square build, red hair, and a hard, plain face. A less romantic or less ghostly apparition could hardly be imagined.
"Too much noise, Grace," said Mrs. Fairfax. "Remember what I've told you." Grace curtsied silently and went back in.

"She's employed to sew and help Leah with the housework," the widow continued. "Not entirely satisfactory in some ways, but she does well enough. By the way, how did you get on with your new pupil this morning?"
The conversation turned to Adele and continued until we reached the bright, cheerful lower floor. Adele came running to meet us in the hall, calling out—
"Mesdames, vous etes servies!" adding, "J'ai bien faim, moi!"
We found dinner ready and waiting in Mrs. Fairfax's room.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: The promise of a smooth career that my calm introduction to Thornfield Hall seemed to make was not broken by longer acquaintance with the place and its people. Mrs. Fairfax turned out to be exactly what she appeared: a mild-tempered, kind-natured woman of decent education and average intelligence. My pupil was a lively child who had been spoiled and indulged and was therefore sometimes willful. But since she was entirely in my care, with no meddling from anyone else to undermine my plans for her improvement, she soon dropped her little tantrums and became obedient and teachable. She had no great talents, no remarkable traits, no unusual depth of feeling or taste that raised her above the ordinary level of childhood. But neither did she have any deficiency or fault that lowered her below it. She made reasonable progress and felt a lively, if perhaps not very deep, affection for me. Her simplicity, cheerful chatter, and eagerness to please inspired in return enough attachment to keep us both content in each other's company.

This, as an aside, will strike some as cold language—people who hold solemn beliefs about the angelic nature of children and the duty of their teachers to worship them with blind devotion. But I am not writing to flatter parental vanity, to echo platitudes, or to prop up pretense. I am simply telling the truth. I felt a genuine concern for Adele's welfare and progress, and a quiet liking for the child herself—just as I felt toward Mrs. Fairfax a gratitude for her kindness and a pleasure in her company proportional to the calm regard she had for me and the moderation of her mind and character.

Anyone who wants to can blame me when I add that, now and then, when I walked alone in the grounds, or went down to the gates and looked along the road, or when, while Adele played with her nurse and Mrs. Fairfax made preserves in the storeroom, I climbed the three staircases, pushed open the attic trapdoor, and stood on the roof looking out over the secluded fields, the hills, and the dim horizon—that then I longed for a power of vision that could reach beyond that boundary, that could see the busy world, the towns, the regions full of life I had heard of but never witnessed. That then I craved more practical experience than I possessed, more contact with my fellow human beings, more acquaintance with the variety of human character than was within my reach here. I valued what was good in Mrs. Fairfax and in Adele, but I believed in the existence of other, more vivid kinds of goodness, and I wanted to see what I believed in.

Who blames me? Many, no doubt, and I'll be called discontented. I couldn't help it. The restlessness was in my nature; it sometimes tormented me. Then my only relief was to pace the third-floor corridor, back and forth, safe in the silence and solitude, and let my mind's eye dwell on whatever bright visions rose before it—and there were many, vivid and glowing. To let my heart swell with an exultant surge that, even as it troubled me, expanded me with life. And best of all, to open my inner ear to a tale that never ended—a tale my imagination created and narrated continuously, rich with all the adventure, life, fire, and feeling that I wanted and didn't have in my actual existence.

It is useless to tell people they should be satisfied with calm. They need action, and they will create it if they can't find it. Millions are condemned to a stiller fate than mine, and millions are in silent rebellion against their lot. Nobody knows how many uprisings besides political ones are fermenting in the vast populations of this earth. Women are supposed to be very calm, as a rule. But women feel exactly as men feel. They need exercise for their minds, and a field for their efforts, just as much as their brothers do. They suffer from too rigid a confinement, too total a stagnation, exactly as men would suffer. And it is narrow-minded of their more privileged fellow creatures to say they should limit themselves to making puddings and knitting stockings, to playing the piano and embroidering bags. It is thoughtless to condemn them, or laugh at them, if they seek to do more or learn more than custom has declared necessary for their sex.

When alone like this, I often heard Grace Poole's laugh—the same peal, the same low, slow "Ha! Ha!" that had startled me the first time. I also heard her strange murmurs, even odder than the laugh. Some days she was perfectly quiet, but on others I couldn't account for the sounds she made. I occasionally saw her: she would come out of her room with a basin or a plate or a tray, go down to the kitchen, and shortly return—generally (oh, romantic reader, forgive me for stating the plain truth!) carrying a pot of beer. Her appearance always dampened whatever curiosity her odd noises had aroused. Hard-featured and stolid, she had nothing about her to spark interest. I tried a few times to draw her into conversation, but she was a woman of few words. A one-syllable answer usually ended every such attempt.

The other members of the household—John and his wife, Leah the housemaid, and Sophie the French nurse—were decent enough people, but unremarkable in every way. I used to speak French with Sophie and sometimes asked her about her native country, but she had no gift for description or storytelling, and generally gave answers so dull and muddled they discouraged further questions.

October, November, and December passed. One afternoon in January, Mrs. Fairfax had requested a holiday for Adele because she had a cold. Since Adele backed the request with an enthusiasm that reminded me how precious holidays had been in my own childhood, I agreed, thinking it right to be flexible. It was a fine, calm day, though very cold. I was tired of sitting still in the library all morning. Mrs. Fairfax had just written a letter that needed posting, so I put on my bonnet and cloak and volunteered to carry it to Hay—a pleasant two-mile walk on a winter afternoon. After settling Adele comfortably in her little chair by Mrs. Fairfax's fire, giving her the best wax doll (which I usually kept wrapped in silver paper in a drawer) and a storybook for variety, and answering her "Come back soon, my dear friend, my darling Mademoiselle Jeannette" with a kiss, I set out.

The ground was hard, the air was still, the road was deserted. I walked fast until I was warm, then slowed to enjoy and savor the particular pleasure the hour and the setting offered me. It was three o'clock. The church bell tolled as I passed beneath the tower. The charm of the hour lay in the approaching dusk, in the low, pale sun sliding down the sky. I was a mile from Thornfield, in a lane known for wild roses in summer, for nuts and blackberries in autumn, and even now adorned with a few bright red hips and haws. But its greatest winter beauty was its total solitude and bare stillness. If any breeze stirred, it made no sound here—there was no holly, no evergreen to rustle. The stripped hawthorn and hazel bushes were as motionless as the white, worn stones that paved the middle of the path. On either side, far and wide, there were only fields with no grazing cattle, and the small brown birds that occasionally stirred in the hedge looked like single russet leaves that had forgotten to fall.

The lane climbed steadily toward Hay. Halfway up, I sat down on a stile that led into a field. Wrapping my cloak around me and sheltering my hands in my muff, I didn't feel the cold, though it was freezing hard—as proved by a sheet of ice covering the path where a small brook, now frozen, had overflowed after a sudden thaw some days earlier. From my seat I could look down on Thornfield: the gray, battlemented hall was the main landmark in the valley below, its woods and dark rookery rising against the western sky. I sat there until the sun sank among the trees and dropped crimson and clear behind them. Then I turned east.

On the hilltop above me sat the rising moon, pale as a cloud but brightening by the minute. She looked down on Hay, half-hidden in trees, which sent a thin blue smoke from its few chimneys. The village was still a mile away, but in the absolute hush I could clearly hear its faint murmurs of life. My ear also caught the sound of running water from valleys and depths I couldn't identify—there were many hills beyond Hay, and doubtless many streams winding through them. That evening calm carried equally the tinkle of the nearest brook and the whisper of the most distant.

A harsh noise broke through these delicate sounds—suddenly, clearly: a definite tramp, tramp, a metallic clattering that drowned out the soft whispering, the way a solid crag or the rough trunk of a great oak in the foreground of a painting blots out the pale distance of blue hills, sunlit horizon, and melting clouds.

The noise was on the path: a horse was approaching. The bends of the lane still hid it, but it was coming closer. I was just leaving the stile, but since the path was narrow, I sat back down to let it pass. In those days I was young, and all kinds of bright and dark fancies filled my mind. Among them were memories of nursery tales, and now that I was older, they had a force and vividness that childhood could never have given them. As this horse drew near and I watched for it to appear through the dusk, I remembered certain of Bessie's stories featuring a North of England spirit called a Gytrash—which, in the form of a horse, mule, or large dog, haunted lonely roads and sometimes appeared to travelers caught out after dark, as this horse was now appearing to me.

It was very near but not yet visible when, along with the tramp, tramp, I heard a rush under the hedge. Close by the hazel stems, a great dog glided past—its black and white coloring standing out sharply against the trees. It was exactly one form of Bessie's Gytrash: a lion-like beast with long hair and a massive head. It passed me quietly enough, though, without stopping to fix me with any strange, supernatural eyes, as I half expected. The horse followed—a tall animal, and on its back a rider. The man, the human being, broke the spell immediately. Nothing ever rode the Gytrash; it was always alone. And goblins, to my way of thinking, though they might inhabit the bodies of animals, would hardly take shelter in an ordinary human form. This was no Gytrash—just a traveler taking the shortcut to Millcote. He passed, and I walked on. A few steps later, I turned back: a sliding sound, an exclamation of "What the devil is going on now?" and a clattering crash caught my attention. Man and horse were down. They had slipped on the sheet of ice covering the path. The dog came bounding back, and seeing his master in trouble and hearing the horse groan, barked until the evening hills echoed—a deep sound, matching his size. He sniffed around the fallen pair, then ran to me. It was all he could do—there was no other help to summon. I obeyed his silent appeal and walked down to the traveler, who was by now struggling free of his horse. His efforts were so vigorous that I thought he couldn't be badly hurt, but I asked—
"Are you injured, sir?"
I think he was swearing, but I'm not certain. In any case, he was muttering something that prevented him from answering me directly.
"Can I do anything?" I asked again.

"Just stand to one side," he answered as he rose, first to his knees, then to his feet. I did. What followed was a heaving, stamping, clattering commotion, accompanied by barking and howling that drove me back several yards. But I refused to leave entirely until I saw the outcome. This turned out well—the horse was back on its feet and the dog was silenced with a "Down, Pilot!" The traveler then stooped and felt his foot and leg, as if checking whether they were sound. Apparently something was wrong, because he limped to the stile I had just left and sat down.
I was in a helpful mood—or perhaps an officious one—so I approached him again.
"If you're hurt and need help, sir, I can fetch someone from Thornfield Hall or from Hay."
"Thank you, I'll manage. No broken bones—just a sprain." He stood up again and tested his foot, but the effort wrung an involuntary "Ugh!" from him.

Some daylight still lingered, and the moon was growing bright. I could see him clearly. His figure was wrapped in a riding cloak with a fur collar and steel clasp. The details weren't clear, but I could make out a man of medium height with a broad chest. He had a dark face with stern features and a heavy brow. His eyes and drawn eyebrows looked angry and frustrated. He was past youth but hadn't reached middle age—perhaps thirty-five. I felt no fear of him, and very little shyness. If he had been a handsome, heroic-looking young gentleman, I wouldn't have dared stand there questioning him against his will and offering unsolicited help. I had hardly ever seen a handsome young man, and had never in my life spoken to one. I had a theoretical admiration for beauty, elegance, charm, and fascination, but if I had met those qualities in masculine form, I would have known instinctively that they could have no sympathy with anything in me, and I would have avoided them as one avoids fire, lightning, or anything else that is bright but hostile.

Even if this stranger had smiled and been good-natured when I spoke to him, if he had cheerfully waved off my offer of help with thanks, I would have gone on my way without a second thought. But the frown, the gruffness of the traveler, put me at ease. I stayed when he waved me away, and announced—
"I can't think of leaving you, sir, at this late hour, on this lonely road, until I see you're fit to ride your horse."
He looked at me when I said this—he had hardly glanced in my direction before.
"I should think you ought to be home yourself," he said, "if you have a home in this area. Where do you come from?"
"From just below. And I'm not at all afraid of being out late when there's moonlight. I'll happily run to Hay for you if you like—in fact, I'm on my way there to post a letter."

"You live just below—do you mean at that house with the battlements?" He pointed to Thornfield Hall, on which the moon cast a pale gleam, picking it out distinct and silvery from the woods, which against the western sky now seemed a solid mass of shadow.
"Yes, sir."
"Whose house is it?"
"Mr. Rochester's."
"Do you know Mr. Rochester?"
"No, I've never met him."
"He's not in residence, then?"
"No."
"Can you tell me where he is?"
"I cannot."

"You're not a servant at the hall, obviously. You are—" He stopped, running his eye over my clothes, which as usual were plain: a black wool cloak, a black bonnet—neither fine enough for a lady's maid. He seemed puzzled about what I was. I helped him.
"I'm the governess."

"Ah, the governess!" he repeated. "Good lord, I'd forgotten! The governess!" And again my outfit came under scrutiny. After two minutes he stood up from the stile. His face showed pain when he tried to move.
"I can't send you to fetch help," he said, "but you can help me a little yourself, if you'd be so kind."
"Yes, sir."
"You don't have an umbrella I could use as a walking stick?"
"No."
"Try to grab my horse's bridle and lead him to me. You're not afraid?"

I would have been afraid to approach a horse on my own, but when told to do it, I was ready to obey. I set my muff on the stile and went up to the tall animal. I tried to catch the bridle, but it was a spirited horse and wouldn't let me near its head. I tried again and again, without success, terrified all the while of its stamping front hooves. The traveler watched for some time, then finally laughed.
I was terrified of its stamping front hooves.
"I see," he said, "the mountain won't come to Mohammed, so all you can do is help Mohammed get to the mountain. I'll have to ask you to come here."

I came. "Excuse me," he went on, "necessity forces me to make use of you." He laid a heavy hand on my shoulder, and leaning on me with considerable weight, limped to his horse. Once he had the bridle, he mastered the animal immediately and swung up into the saddle, grimacing at the pain it caused his sprain.
"Now," he said, releasing his lip from a hard bite, "just hand me my riding crop. It's there under the hedge."
I found it and brought it to him.
"Thank you. Now hurry with that letter to Hay, and get back as fast as you can."
A touch of his spurred heel made the horse start, rear, and then bound away. The dog raced after them. All three vanished—
"Like heath that, in the wilderness, the wild wind whirls away."

I picked up my muff and walked on. The incident had happened and was gone. It was nothing special, really—no drama, no romance, no particular interest. Yet it marked a change in one single hour of a monotonous life. My help had been needed and asked for. I had given it. I was pleased to have done something—trivial and fleeting as it was, it had been an act, and I was tired of a purely passive existence. The new face, too, was like a new picture added to the gallery of my memory, and it was unlike any of the others hanging there. First, because it was male. And second, because it was dark, strong, and stern. I still had it before me when I reached Hay and slipped the letter into the post office. I saw it as I walked fast downhill all the way home. When I reached the stile, I paused, looked around, and listened, half-expecting to hear a horse's hooves ring on the path again, and to see a cloaked rider and a Gytrash-like Newfoundland dog appear once more. I saw only the hedge and a pollard willow before me, standing still and straight against the moonlight. I heard only the faintest breath of wind stirring fitfully among the trees around Thornfield, a mile away. And when I glanced toward the sound, my eye caught a light kindling in a window of the hall. It reminded me I was late, and I hurried on.

I didn't want to go back inside Thornfield. To cross its threshold was to return to stagnation. To pass through the silent hall, climb the dark staircase, find my lonely little room, and then sit with tranquil Mrs. Fairfax through the long winter evening—hers the only company—was to completely extinguish the faint excitement my walk had kindled. To slip back into the invisible chains of a routine too still and too unchanging—a life whose very privileges of safety and ease I was becoming unable to appreciate. What good it would have done me then to be tossed in the storms of an uncertain, struggling life, to learn from rough and bitter experience to long for the calm I now found stifling! Yes—exactly as much good as it does a man tired of sitting in a too-comfortable chair to take a long walk. And the wish to move was just as natural in my circumstances as it would be in his.

I lingered at the gates. I lingered on the lawn. I paced back and forth on the path. The shutters of the glass door were closed; I couldn't see inside. Both my eyes and my spirit seemed pulled away from the gloomy house—from the gray hollow of dark, lifeless rooms it seemed to be—toward the sky spread before me: a blue sea without a cloud. The moon climbing in solemn procession, her globe seeming to look upward as she left the hilltops far below and aspired to the zenith, midnight-dark in its fathomless depth and limitless distance. And the trembling stars that followed in her path—they made my heart tremble and my blood glow when I gazed at them. Small things call us back to earth. The clock struck in the hall. That was enough. I turned from moon and stars, opened a side door, and went in.

The hall was neither dark nor fully lit—only the high-hung bronze lamp illuminated it, plus a warm glow that suffused both the hall and the lower steps of the oak staircase. This ruddy light came from the great dining room, whose double doors stood open, showing a cheerful fire in the grate gleaming on the marble hearth and brass fire tools and casting the most pleasant radiance over the purple curtains and polished furniture. It also revealed a group near the mantelpiece. I had barely glimpsed them, and barely registered a cheerful mix of voices among which I thought I heard Adele's, when the door was closed.

I hurried to Mrs. Fairfax's room. There was a fire there too, but no candle and no Mrs. Fairfax. Instead, sitting bolt upright on the rug and gazing solemnly at the flames, I saw a great black and white long-haired dog—exactly like the Gytrash from the lane. It was so like it that I walked up and said "Pilot." The creature got up, came to me, and sniffed my hand. I petted him and he wagged his huge tail. But he looked like an eerie companion to be left alone with, and I couldn't figure out where he'd come from. I rang the bell, wanting a candle and wanting an explanation for this visitor. Leah came in.
"What dog is this?"
"He came with the master."
"With whom?"
"With the master—Mr. Rochester. He's just arrived."
"Really! And is Mrs. Fairfax with him?"
"Yes, and Miss Adele. They're in the dining room. John has gone for the surgeon—the master has had an accident. His horse fell and his ankle is sprained."
"Did the horse fall on Hay Lane?"
"Yes, coming downhill. It slipped on the ice."
"Ah! Bring me a candle, will you, Leah?"

Leah brought it. She came in followed by Mrs. Fairfax, who repeated the news, adding that Mr. Carter the surgeon had arrived and was now with Mr. Rochester. Then she hurried out to arrange tea, and I went upstairs to take off my outdoor things.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Mr. Rochester, on the surgeon's orders it seemed, went to bed early that night, and didn't rise early the next morning either. When he did come down, it was to deal with business: his agent and some of his tenants had arrived and were waiting to speak with him.

Adèle and I now had to give up the library: it would be needed daily as a reception room for visitors. A fire was lit in a room upstairs, and I carried our books there, arranging it as our future schoolroom. Over the course of the morning, I noticed that Thornfield Hall was a changed place: no longer silent as a church, it echoed every hour or two with a knock at the door or a clang of the bell. Footsteps crossed the hall frequently, and new voices spoke in different tones below. A stream from the outer world was flowing through the house; it had a master. For my part, I liked it better.

Adèle was not easy to teach that day. She couldn't concentrate: she kept running to the door and peering over the banisters for a glimpse of Mr. Rochester, then inventing excuses to go downstairs—to visit the library, I shrewdly suspected, where I knew she was not wanted. When I grew a little angry and made her sit still, she talked incessantly about her "ami, Monsieur Edouard Fairfax de Rochester," as she called him (I hadn't before heard his first names), and speculated about what presents he had brought her. Apparently he had hinted the night before that when his luggage came from Millcote, there would be a little box among it whose contents would interest her.

"Et cela doit signifier," said she, "qu'il y aura là dedans un cadeau pour moi, et peut-être pour vous aussi, mademoiselle.
