Monsieur a parlé de vous: il m'a demandé le nom de ma gouvernante, et si elle n'était pas une petite personne, assez mince et un peu pâle. J'ai dit qu'oui: car c'est vrai, n'est-ce pas, mademoiselle?"

My pupil and I dined as usual in Mrs. Fairfax's parlour. The afternoon was wild and snowy, and we spent it in the schoolroom. At dark, I let Adèle put away her books and work and run downstairs, since from the relative silence below and the absence of appeals to the doorbell, I guessed that Mr. Rochester was now free. Left alone, I walked to the window, but there was nothing to see: twilight and snowflakes together thickened the air and hid even the shrubs on the lawn. I let down the curtain and went back to the fireside.

In the clear embers I was tracing a view, not unlike a picture I remembered seeing of the castle of Heidelberg on the Rhine, when Mrs. Fairfax came in, breaking up the fiery mosaic I had been piecing together, and scattering some heavy, unwelcome thoughts that were beginning to crowd into my solitude.
"Mr. Rochester would be glad if you and your pupil would take tea with him in the drawing room this evening," she said. "He has been so busy all day that he couldn't ask to see you before."
"When is his tea time?" I asked.
"Oh, at six o'clock: he keeps early hours in the country. You'd better change your dress now; I'll go with you and fasten it. Here's a candle."
"Is it necessary to change my dress?"
"Yes, you'd better. I always dress for the evening when Mr. Rochester is here."

This additional ceremony seemed rather formal. Still, I went to my room and, with Mrs. Fairfax's help, replaced my plain black dress with one of black silk—the best and only extra one I had, aside from a light grey that, in my Lowood notions of fashion, I thought too fine to wear except on first-rate occasions.

"You need a brooch," said Mrs. Fairfax. I had a single little pearl ornament that Miss Temple had given me as a parting gift. I put it on, and then we went downstairs. Unaccustomed as I was to strangers, it was something of a trial to appear so formally summoned into Mr. Rochester's presence. I let Mrs. Fairfax go ahead of me into the dining room and kept in her shadow as we crossed the room, passing through the arch—its curtain now drawn—into the elegant alcove beyond.

Two wax candles stood lit on the table and two on the mantelpiece. Basking in the light and heat of a magnificent fire lay Pilot, with Adèle kneeling beside him. Half reclined on a couch was Mr. Rochester, his foot propped on a cushion. He was watching Adèle and the dog, the firelight full on his face. I recognized my traveller with his broad, dark eyebrows, his square forehead made squarer by the straight sweep of his black hair. I recognized his decisive nose, more notable for character than beauty, his full nostrils suggesting a quick temper, his stern mouth, chin, and jaw—yes, all three were very stern, no mistake about it. His build, now free of its cloak, matched the squareness of his features. I suppose it was a good figure in the athletic sense—broad-chested and lean-flanked, though neither tall nor graceful.
Mr. Rochester must have noticed Mrs. Fairfax and me come in, but he was apparently not in the mood to acknowledge us, for he never lifted his head as we approached.
"Here is Miss Eyre, sir," said Mrs. Fairfax in her quiet way. He bowed, still not taking his eyes from the dog and child.

"Let Miss Eyre be seated," he said. There was something in the forced, stiff bow and the impatient yet formal tone that seemed to say, "What the deuce is it to me whether Miss Eyre is here or not? At this moment I have no wish to speak to her."

I sat down quite at ease. A reception of polished courtesy would probably have flustered me. I couldn't have matched it with equal grace and elegance. But harsh whims placed me under no obligation. On the contrary, maintaining a calm composure under his odd manner gave me the advantage. Besides, the eccentricity of it all was intriguing: I was curious to see what he would do next.

He carried on as a statue would—that is, he neither spoke nor moved. Mrs. Fairfax seemed to feel someone should be pleasant, and she began to talk. Kindly as always—and as always, rather dull—she sympathized with him about the pressure of business he'd had all day, about the annoyance it must have been with that painful sprain, then praised his patience and perseverance in getting through it all.

"Madam, I should like some tea," was the only reply she got. She hurried to ring the bell, and when the tray came, she busied herself arranging the cups and spoons with efficient speed. Adèle and I went to the table, but the master didn't leave his couch.
"Will you hand Mr. Rochester his cup?" Mrs. Fairfax said to me. "Adèle might spill it."
I did as she asked. As he took the cup from my hand, Adèle, thinking the moment right for making a request on my behalf, cried out—
"N'est-ce pas, monsieur, qu'il y a un cadeau pour Mademoiselle Eyre dans votre petit coffre?"
"Who talks of cadeaux?" he said gruffly. "Did you expect a present, Miss Eyre? Are you fond of presents?" He searched my face with eyes that I saw were dark, angry, and piercing.
"I hardly know, sir. I have little experience of them. They are generally thought to be pleasant things."
"Generally thought? But what do you think?"
"I would need a moment, sir, before I could give you an answer worthy of your acceptance. A present has many sides to it, hasn't it? One should consider all of them before pronouncing an opinion."
"Miss Eyre, you are not as unsophisticated as Adèle: she demands a 'cadeau' loudly the moment she sees me. You beat around the bush."

"Because I have less confidence in my merits than Adèle has in hers. She can claim the right of old acquaintance and custom, since she says you have always given her toys. But if I had to make a case for myself, I would be at a loss, since I am a stranger and have done nothing to earn such a gift."
"Oh, don't retreat into false modesty! I have examined Adèle and find you have taken great pains with her. She is not bright, she has no talents; yet in a short time she has made real improvement."
"Sir, you have now given me my 'cadeau.' I am grateful: it is the reward teachers prize most—praise of their pupils' progress."
"Humph!" said Mr. Rochester, and he drank his tea in silence.

"Come to the fire," said the master, when the tray was taken away and Mrs. Fairfax had settled into a corner with her knitting. Adèle had been leading me by the hand around the room, showing me the beautiful books and ornaments on the side tables and cabinets. We obeyed, as duty required. Adèle wanted to sit on my knee, but she was told to amuse herself with Pilot.
"You have been living in my house for three months?"
"Yes, sir."
"And you came from—?"
"From Lowood school, in ——shire."
"Ah! A charity school. How long were you there?"
"Eight years."

"Eight years! You must have a fierce grip on life. I would have thought half that time in such a place would have destroyed anyone's health! No wonder you look as if you belong to another world. I couldn't figure out where you'd gotten that sort of face. When you appeared before me in Hay Lane last night, I thought, quite inexplicably, of fairy tales and half wanted to ask whether you had bewitched my horse. I'm still not sure. Who are your parents?"
"I have none."
"Nor ever had, I suppose? Do you remember them?"
"No."
"I thought not. And so you were waiting for your people when you sat on that stile?"
"For whom, sir?"
"For the fairies. It was a perfect moonlit evening for them. Did I break through one of your rings, and you spread that cursed ice on the road?"

I shook my head. "The fairies all left England a hundred years ago," I said, speaking as seriously as he had. "And not even in Hay Lane, or the fields around it, could you find a trace of them. I don't think summer, harvest, or winter moon will ever shine on their revels again."
Mrs. Fairfax had dropped her knitting and, with raised eyebrows, seemed to wonder what sort of conversation this was.
"Well," Mr. Rochester resumed, "if you deny having parents, you must have some sort of relatives—uncles and aunts?"
"No. None that I ever saw."
"And your home?"
"I have none."
"Where do your brothers and sisters live?"
"I have no brothers or sisters."
"Who recommended you to come here?"
"I advertised, and Mrs. Fairfax answered my advertisement."

"Yes," said the good lady, who now understood what ground we were on, "and I am daily thankful for the choice Providence led me to make. Miss Eyre has been an invaluable companion to me, and a kind and careful teacher to Adèle."
"Don't trouble yourself to give her a character reference," Mr. Rochester returned. "Praise won't sway me; I shall judge for myself. She began by bringing down my horse."
"Sir?" said Mrs. Fairfax.
"I have her to thank for this sprain."
The widow looked baffled.
"Miss Eyre, have you ever lived in a town?"
"No, sir."
"Have you seen much of society?"
"None but the pupils and teachers of Lowood, and now the people of Thornfield."
"Have you read much?"
"Only the books that came my way, and they haven't been many or very scholarly."
"You have lived the life of a nun. No doubt you are well drilled in religious observances. Brocklehurst, who I understand runs Lowood, is a clergyman, isn't he?"
"Yes, sir."
"And you girls probably worshipped him, as a convent of nuns would worship their director."
"Oh, no."
"How cool you are! No? A novice not worship her priest? That sounds blasphemous."

"I disliked Mr. Brocklehurst, and I was not alone in feeling that way. He is a harsh man, both pompous and meddling. He cut off our hair, and to save money bought us bad needles and thread that we could barely sew with."
"That was very false economy," remarked Mrs. Fairfax, who had again caught the drift of the conversation.
"And was that the worst of his offences?" demanded Mr. Rochester.

"He starved us when he had sole charge of provisions, before the committee was appointed. And he bored us with long lectures once a week, and evening readings from books he wrote himself, about sudden deaths and divine judgments, which made us afraid to go to bed."
"How old were you when you went to Lowood?"
"About ten."
"And you stayed there eight years—so you are now eighteen?"
I agreed.

"Arithmetic, you see, is useful. Without it, I could hardly have guessed your age. It's a difficult point to fix when the features and the expression are so at odds, as in your case. And now, what did you learn at Lowood? Can you play?"
"A little."

"Of course—that is the standard answer. Go into the library—I mean, if you please. (Excuse my commanding tone; I am used to saying, 'Do this,' and it's done. I can't change my habits for one new arrival.) Go, then, into the library; take a candle with you; leave the door open; sit down at the piano and play something."
I left, following his directions.
"Enough!" he called out after a few minutes. "You play a little, I see—like any other English schoolgirl. Perhaps rather better than some, but not well."
I closed the piano and came back. Mr. Rochester continued—
"Adèle showed me some sketches this morning that she said were yours. I don't know whether they were entirely your work. A master probably helped you?"
"No, indeed!" I cut in.
"Ah! That stings your pride. Well, fetch me your portfolio, if you can vouch that its contents are original. But don't give your word unless you're certain—I can recognize borrowed work."
"Then I will say nothing, and you shall judge for yourself, sir."
I brought the portfolio from the library.
"Bring it to the table," he said, and I wheeled it to his couch. Adèle and Mrs. Fairfax came closer to see the pictures.
"No crowding," said Mr. Rochester. "Take the drawings from my hand as I finish with them, but don't push your faces into mine."
He studied each sketch and painting carefully. Three he set aside; the others, once examined, he pushed away.

"Take those to the other table, Mrs. Fairfax," he said, "and look at them with Adèle. You"—he glanced at me—"sit back down and answer my questions. I can see these pictures were done by one hand. Was it yours?"
"Yes."
"And when did you find time to do them? They must have taken considerable time and thought."
"I did them during the last two vacations I spent at Lowood, when I had nothing else to do."
"Where did you get your subjects?"
"Out of my head."
"That head I see now on your shoulders?"
"Yes, sir."
"Does it have other work of the same kind inside?"
"I should think so. I should hope—better."
He spread the pictures before him and studied them again.

While he does so, I will tell you, reader, what they are—and first I should say they are nothing remarkable. The subjects had indeed risen vividly in my mind. As I saw them with my mind's eye before attempting to give them form, they were striking. But my hand couldn't match my imagination, and in each case it had produced only a pale echo of what I had conceived.

The pictures were watercolours. The first showed clouds, low and dark, rolling over a swollen sea. Everything was in shadow—distance and foreground alike, for there was no land. One gleam of light fell on a half-submerged mast, on which perched a cormorant, dark and large, its wings flecked with foam. Its beak held a gold bracelet set with gems, which I had painted in the most brilliant tints my palette could yield, with as much glittering detail as my brush could manage. Below the bird and mast, a drowned body was visible through the green water—a fair arm the only limb clearly seen, from which the bracelet had been washed or torn.

The second picture showed only the dim peak of a hill in the foreground, with grass and leaves slanting as if blown by a breeze. Beyond and above spread a vast sky, dark blue as at twilight. Rising into the sky was a woman's shape, visible to the bust, painted in tints as dusky and soft as I could blend. The shadowy forehead was crowned with a star; the features below were seen as through a veil of vapour; the eyes shone dark and wild; the hair streamed like a cloud torn by storm or lightning. On the neck lay a pale glow like moonlight; the same faint gleam touched the trail of thin clouds from which this vision of the Evening Star rose and bowed.

The third showed the peak of an iceberg piercing a polar winter sky. A line of northern lights raised their dim lances along the horizon. In the foreground, dwarfing these into distance, rose a colossal head tilted toward the iceberg and resting against it. Two thin hands, clasped beneath the forehead and propping it up, drew a black veil over the lower features. Only a bloodless brow, white as bone, and an eye—hollow and fixed, blank except for the glassiness of despair—were visible. Above the temples, amid folds of black cloth as vague and shapeless as cloud, gleamed a ring of white flame studded with darker, more ominous sparks. This pale crescent was "the likeness of a kingly crown;" what it crowned was "the shape which shape had none."
"Were you happy when you painted these pictures?" Mr. Rochester asked after a moment.
"I was absorbed, sir—yes, and I was happy. To paint them was to experience one of the most intense pleasures I have ever known."

"That is not saying much. Your pleasures, by your own account, have been few. But I imagine you did inhabit a kind of artist's dreamland while you mixed and arranged these strange colours. Did you spend long on them each day?"
"I had nothing else to do, because it was the vacation. I sat at them from morning to noon and from noon to night. The length of the midsummer days favoured my inclination to keep working."
"And you felt satisfied with the result of your passionate efforts?"
"Far from it. I was tormented by the gap between my idea and what I had actually made. In each case I had imagined something I was completely powerless to realize."

"Not completely: you've caught the shadow of your thought, but no more, probably. You lacked enough of the artist's skill and knowledge to give it full life. Yet the drawings are, for a schoolgirl, extraordinary. As for the ideas behind them—they are otherworldly. Those eyes in the Evening Star you must have seen in a dream. How did you make them look so clear yet not at all bright? The planet above dims their light. And what meaning lies in their solemn depth? And who taught you to paint wind? There's a fierce gale in that sky and on that hilltop. Where did you see Latmos? For that is Latmos. There—put the drawings away!"
I had barely tied the strings of the portfolio when, glancing at his watch, he said abruptly—
"It is nine o'clock. What are you thinking, Miss Eyre, letting Adèle stay up so late? Take her to bed."
Adèle went to kiss him before leaving the room. He endured the embrace but barely seemed to enjoy it more than Pilot would have—and perhaps less.

"I wish you all goodnight now," he said, waving his hand toward the door to show he was tired of our company and wished to dismiss us. Mrs. Fairfax folded up her knitting. I took my portfolio. We curtsied to him, received a cold bow in return, and withdrew.
"You said Mr. Rochester was not particularly eccentric, Mrs. Fairfax," I remarked when I rejoined her in her room, after putting Adèle to bed.
"Well, is he?"
"I think so. He is very changeable and abrupt."
"True—no doubt he may seem so to a stranger. But I am so used to his ways that I never think about it. And if he has peculiarities of temperament, allowances should be made."
"Why?"
"Partly because it is his nature—and none of us can help our nature. And partly because he has painful thoughts, no doubt, that trouble him and make his mood uneven."
"What about?"
"Family troubles, for one thing."
"But he has no family."
"Not now, but he has had—or at least, relatives. He lost his elder brother a few years ago."
"His elder brother?"
"Yes. The present Mr. Rochester has not been in possession of the property very long—only about nine years."
"Nine years is a considerable time. Was he so fond of his brother that he's still inconsolable over the loss?"

"Well, no—perhaps not. I believe there were some misunderstandings between them. Mr. Rowland Rochester was not entirely fair to Mr. Edward, and perhaps he turned their father against him. The old gentleman was fond of money and anxious to keep the family estate intact. He didn't want to divide the property, yet he was eager for Mr. Edward to have wealth too, to uphold the family name. Soon after Edward came of age, certain steps were taken that were not quite fair, and caused a great deal of trouble. Old Mr. Rochester and Mr. Rowland conspired to manoeuvre Edward into what he considered a painful position, all for the sake of securing his fortune. What exactly that position was I never clearly understood, but his spirit could not endure what he had to suffer. He is not very forgiving: he broke with his family, and for many years now he has led an unsettled life. I don't think he has stayed at Thornfield for as long as two weeks at a stretch since his brother's death without a will left him master of the estate. And indeed, no wonder he avoids the old place."
"Why should he avoid it?"
"Perhaps he finds it gloomy."

The answer was evasive. I would have liked something clearer, but Mrs. Fairfax either could not or would not give me more definite information about the source and nature of Mr. Rochester's troubles. She insisted they were a mystery to her as well, and that what she knew was mostly guesswork. It was obvious she wanted me to drop the subject, which I did.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: For several days afterward I saw little of Mr. Rochester. In the mornings he seemed busy with business, and in the afternoons, gentlemen from Millcote or the neighbourhood called and sometimes stayed to dine. When his sprain had healed enough for riding, he went out a good deal—probably returning these visits, since he generally didn't come back until late at night.

During this time, even Adèle was rarely sent for. All my contact with him was limited to occasional meetings in the hall, on the stairs, or in the gallery, where he would sometimes pass me haughtily and coldly, acknowledging my presence with only a distant nod or a cool glance, and sometimes bow and smile with gentlemanly friendliness. His changes of mood didn't offend me, because I could see they had nothing to do with me; the ebb and flow depended on causes entirely unconnected with anything I had done.

One day he had had company for dinner and had sent for my portfolio, no doubt to show its contents. The gentlemen left early to attend a public meeting at Millcote, as Mrs. Fairfax told me; but since the night was wet and miserable, Mr. Rochester didn't go with them. Soon after they left, he rang the bell. A message came that Adèle and I were to go downstairs. I brushed Adèle's hair and made her neat, and having confirmed that I was in my usual plain Quaker-like attire—with nothing to adjust, everything too close and simple, braided hair included, to come undone—we went down. Adèle wondered whether the petit coffre had finally arrived, since some mix-up had delayed it. She was gratified: there it stood, a little box, on the table when we entered the dining room. She seemed to recognize it by instinct.
"Ma boîte! ma boîte!" she exclaimed, running toward it.

"Yes, there is your 'boîte' at last. Take it into a corner, you genuine daughter of Paris, and amuse yourself with tearing it apart," said the deep and rather sarcastic voice of Mr. Rochester from the depths of an enormous armchair by the fire. "And mind," he continued, "don't bore me with details of the surgical process, or any report on the state of its insides. Conduct your operation in silence: tiens-toi tranquille, enfant; comprends-tu?"

Adèle hardly needed the warning. She had already retreated to a sofa with her treasure and was busy untying the cord that secured the lid. Having removed this obstacle and lifted several silvery layers of tissue paper, she simply exclaimed—
"Oh ciel! Que c'est beau!" and then remained absorbed in ecstatic contemplation.
"Is Miss Eyre there?" the master now demanded, half rising from his seat to look toward the door, near which I still stood.

"Ah! Well, come forward; sit down here." He drew a chair near his own. "I am not fond of children's chatter," he continued. "As the old bachelor I am, I have no pleasant associations with their prattle. It would be intolerable to spend an entire evening alone with a child. Don't pull that chair farther away, Miss Eyre; sit down exactly where I placed it—if you please, that is. Confound these courtesies! I keep forgetting them. Nor do I particularly enjoy the company of simple-minded elderly ladies. By the way, I must be mindful of mine; it won't do to neglect her. She is a Fairfax, or married to one, and blood is said to be thicker than water."
He rang and sent an invitation to Mrs. Fairfax, who soon arrived, knitting basket in hand.

"Good evening, madam. I sent for you for a charitable purpose. I have forbidden Adèle to talk to me about her presents, and she is bursting with excitement. Be so kind as to serve as her audience and conversational partner; it will be one of the most benevolent acts you have ever performed."

Adèle, the moment she saw Mrs. Fairfax, summoned her to the sofa and quickly filled her lap with the porcelain, ivory, and wax figures from her "boîte," pouring out explanations and exclamations in such broken English as she could manage.

"Now that I have played the good host," Mr. Rochester went on, "and set my guests up to amuse each other, I should be free to attend to my own pleasure. Miss Eyre, draw your chair a little farther forward: you are still too far back. I cannot see you without shifting my position in this comfortable chair, which I have no intention of doing."
I did as he asked, though I would much rather have stayed somewhat in the shadows. But Mr. Rochester had such a direct way of giving orders that it felt natural to obey him promptly.

We were, as I have said, in the dining room. The chandelier, lit for dinner, filled the room with a festive brightness. The large fire blazed red and clear. Purple curtains hung richly before the tall window and taller arch. Everything was still except the quiet chatter of Adèle (she dared not speak loud) and, filling every pause, the beating of winter rain against the panes.

Mr. Rochester, sitting in his damask-covered chair, looked different than I had seen him before—not quite so stern, much less gloomy. There was a smile on his lips and a sparkle in his eyes, whether from wine or not, I couldn't be sure, though I thought it likely. He was, in short, in his after-dinner mood: more relaxed and genial, and also more self-indulgent than the cold, rigid temper of the morning. Still he looked formidably stern, resting his massive head against the high back of his chair, the firelight playing on his granite-hewn features and his great dark eyes—for he had great dark eyes, very fine ones too, with a certain shifting in their depths that, if it was not tenderness, at least reminded you of it.
He had been staring at the fire for two minutes, and I had been watching him for the same length of time, when he turned suddenly and caught my gaze fixed on his face.
"You are studying me, Miss Eyre," he said. "Do you think me handsome?"
If I had taken time to think, I would have given some conventionally vague and polite reply. But the answer somehow slipped from my tongue before I could stop it—"No, sir."

"Ah! My word! There is something unusual about you," he said. "You have the air of a little nun—quaint, quiet, serious, and simple, sitting there with your hands folded and your eyes generally cast down to the carpet (except, that is, when they are aimed piercingly at my face, as just now). And when someone asks you a question or makes a remark you must reply to, you come out with a blunt answer that is, if not exactly rude, at least brusque. What do you mean by it?"

"Sir, I was too blunt. I beg your pardon. I should have said that it is not easy to give a snap answer to a question about appearances, that tastes differ, and that beauty is of little consequence—or something of that sort."

"You should have said no such thing. Beauty of little consequence, indeed! So under the pretence of softening your earlier offence, of soothing me into peace, you slip a sly penknife under my ear! Go on—what fault do you find with me? I suppose I have all my limbs and features like any other man?"
"Mr. Rochester, let me take back my first answer. I intended no cutting remark—it was only a blunder."
"Exactly—I think so too, and you shall answer for it. Criticize me: does my forehead displease you?"
He lifted the dark waves of hair that lay across his brow, revealing a solid enough mass of intellectual development, but a notable deficiency where the gentle curve of benevolence should have risen.
"Now, ma'am, am I a fool?"
"Far from it, sir. You might think me rude if I asked in return whether you are a philanthropist?"

"There again! Another jab of the penknife when she pretended to pat my head. And that is because I said I did not like the company of children and old women (said quietly!). No, young lady, I am not a general philanthropist; but I do have a conscience"—he pointed to the bumps on his skull said to indicate that quality, which were, fortunately for him, quite prominent, giving a marked breadth to the upper part of his head—"and besides, I once had a kind of rough tenderness of heart. When I was your age, I was a feeling sort of fellow, partial to the young, the unprotected, and the unlucky. But Fortune has knocked me around since then: she has even kneaded me with her knuckles, and now I flatter myself I am hard and tough as a rubber ball—with a crack or two still open, though, and one sensitive point in the middle. Yes—does that leave hope for me?"
"Hope of what, sir?"
"Of my eventual transformation back from rubber to flesh?"
"He's definitely had too much wine," I thought, and I didn't know how to answer his odd question. How could I tell whether he was capable of being transformed?

"You look very puzzled, Miss Eyre. And though you are not pretty any more than I am handsome, a puzzled expression suits you. Besides, it is convenient, for it keeps those searching eyes of yours off my face and busy with the pattern of the rug. So puzzle away. Young lady, I am in the mood to be sociable and talkative tonight."

With this announcement he rose from his chair and stood leaning his arm on the marble mantelpiece. In that posture his build was plainly visible as well as his face—the unusual breadth of his chest, almost out of proportion with the length of his limbs. I am sure most people would have called him an ugly man. Yet there was so much unconscious pride in his bearing, so much ease in his manner, such complete indifference to his own appearance, so haughty a faith in the power of other qualities—inherent or acquired—to make up for the lack of mere good looks, that in watching him, you inevitably shared his indifference and, even in some blind, instinctive way, trusted his confidence.

"I am in the mood to be sociable and talkative tonight," he repeated, "and that is why I sent for you. The fire and the chandelier were not sufficient company, nor would Pilot have been, for none of them can talk. Adèle is a degree better, but still far from adequate; Mrs. Fairfax the same. You, I am convinced, can suit me if you will. You puzzled me the first evening I invited you down here. I have nearly forgotten you since—other thoughts have pushed yours from my mind. But tonight I am determined to be at ease: to dismiss what troubles me and recall what pleases. It would please me now to draw you out—to learn more of you—so speak."
Instead of speaking, I smiled—and not a very agreeable or submissive smile either.
"Speak," he urged.
"About what, sir?"
"Whatever you like. I leave both the choice of subject and the manner of treating it entirely to you."
So I sat and said nothing. "If he expects me to talk for the mere sake of talking and showing off, he will find he has spoken to the wrong person," I thought.
"You are silent, Miss Eyre."
I remained silent. He leaned his head slightly toward me and with a single sharp glance seemed to look straight into my eyes.

"Stubborn?" he said. "And irritated. Ah! That is consistent. I put my request in an absurd, almost rude form. Miss Eyre, I apologize. The fact is, once and for all, I don't wish to treat you as an inferior. That is"—he corrected himself—"I claim only the advantage that must come from twenty years' difference in age and a century's advance in experience. This is fair, et j'y tiens, as Adèle would say. And it is by virtue of this advantage, and this alone, that I ask you to be good enough to talk to me a little now and distract my thoughts, which are raw from dwelling on one point—festering like a rusty nail."
He had offered an explanation, almost an apology, and I did not feel indifferent to his condescension, nor did I wish to appear so.
"I am willing to amuse you, if I can, sir—quite willing. But I cannot introduce a topic, because how do I know what will interest you? Ask me questions, and I will do my best to answer them."

"Then, first of all, do you agree that I have some right to be a little commanding, abrupt, perhaps demanding, on the grounds I stated—namely, that I am old enough to be your father, and that I have fought through a wide experience with many men of many nations and roamed over half the globe, while you have lived quietly with one group of people in one house?"
"Do as you please, sir."
"That is no answer—or rather, it is a very irritating one, because it is evasive. Reply clearly."

"I don't think, sir, that you have a right to command me merely because you are older than I, or because you have seen more of the world. Your claim to authority depends on the use you have made of your time and experience."

"Humph! Bluntly spoken. But I won't accept that, seeing as it would never suit my case—I have made a poor, not to say bad, use of both advantages. Setting authority aside, then, you must still agree to take my orders now and then without being stung or hurt by the commanding tone. Will you?"
I smiled. I thought to myself that Mr. Rochester was peculiar indeed—he seemed to forget that he paid me thirty pounds a year for taking his orders.
"The smile is good," he said, catching my expression instantly, "but speak too."
"I was thinking, sir, that very few employers would trouble themselves to ask whether their paid subordinates were stung or hurt by their orders."
"Paid subordinates! What—you are my paid subordinate, are you? Oh yes, I'd forgotten the salary! Well then, on that mercenary basis, will you let me bully you a little?"
"No, sir, not on that basis. But on the basis that you did forget it, and that you care whether a dependent is comfortable in her dependency, I agree wholeheartedly."
"And will you consent to drop a great many conventional forms and phrases, without thinking the omission arises from rudeness?"
"I am sure, sir, I would never mistake informality for rudeness. One I rather like; the other, no one with any self-respect would endure, even for a salary."

"Nonsense! Most people with self-respect will endure anything for a salary. So keep your opinions to yourself and don't venture into generalizations you are wholly ignorant about. However, I mentally shake your hand for that answer, inaccurate as it is—as much for the way it was said as for its substance. The manner was frank and sincere; one does not often encounter such a manner. No, on the contrary, affectation, or coldness, or stupid, thick-headed misunderstanding of one's meaning are the usual rewards of candour. Not three in three thousand inexperienced school-girl governesses would have answered me as you just did. But I don't mean to flatter you. If you are made from a different mould than the majority, it is no credit to you—Nature did it. And after all, I go too fast in my conclusions. For all I know yet, you may be no better than the rest; you may have intolerable flaws to offset your few good points."
"And so may you," I thought. My eye met his as the idea crossed my mind: he seemed to read the glance, answering as if its meaning had been spoken as well as imagined—

"Yes, yes, you are right," he said. "I have plenty of faults of my own—I know it, and I don't wish to minimize them. God knows I don't need to be harsh about other people when I have so much to answer for myself. I have a past—a series of actions, a pattern of living—that I could contemplate in my own breast, which might well redirect my sneers and judgments from my neighbours to myself. I was set on a wrong course—or rather, like other wrongdoers, I prefer to blame bad luck and circumstances—I was pushed onto a wrong path at the age of twenty-one, and I have never found my way back since. But I might have been very different. I might have been as good as you—wiser—nearly as untainted. I envy you your peace of mind, your clean conscience, your unspoiled memory. Little girl, a memory without stain or corruption must be an exquisite treasure—an inexhaustible source of pure refreshment. Isn't it?"
"How was your memory when you were eighteen, sir?"

"Perfectly clear then—clean and healthy. No flood of foul water had turned it into a poisoned pool. I was your equal at eighteen—quite your equal. Nature meant me to be, on the whole, a good man, Miss Eyre—one of the better kind. And you see I am not. You would say you don't see it; at least I flatter myself I read that much in your eye (beware, by the way, what you express with that eye of yours; I am quick at reading its language). Then take my word for it—I am not a villain. You are not to think that, not to attribute any such deep wickedness to me. But, owing I truly believe to circumstances rather than my natural inclination, I am an ordinary, commonplace sinner, worn out by all the petty vices that the rich and worthless use to pass the time. Does it surprise you that I confess this to you? Know that in the course of your future life you will often find yourself elected the unwilling keeper of other people's secrets. They will instinctively discover, as I have done, that it is not your way to talk about yourself, but to listen while others speak of themselves. They will feel, too, that you listen without malicious scorn at their indiscretion, but with a kind of natural sympathy—all the more comforting because it is so quietly given."
"How do you know? How can you guess all this, sir?"

"I know it well; and so I speak almost as freely as if I were writing my thoughts in a diary. You would say I should have been stronger than my circumstances; and I should have—I should have. But I was not. When fate wronged me, I lacked the wisdom to stay calm. I turned desperate; then I degenerated. Now, when some shallow fool disgusts me with his cheap depravity, I cannot flatter myself that I am better than he is. I am forced to admit that he and I are on the same level. I wish I had stood firm—God knows I do! Dread remorse when you are tempted to stray, Miss Eyre. Remorse is the poison of life."
"Repentance is said to be its cure, sir."

"It is not its cure. Reformation may be its cure; and I could reform—I still have the strength for that—if—but what is the use of thinking about it, hampered, burdened, cursed as I am? Besides, since happiness is permanently denied me, I have a right to get pleasure out of life, and I will get it, whatever the cost."
"Then you will degenerate still more, sir."
"Possibly. Yet why should I, if I can get sweet, fresh pleasure? And I may get it as sweet and fresh as the wild honey the bee gathers on the moor."
"It will sting—it will taste bitter, sir."

"How do you know? You have never tried it. How very serious—how very solemn you look. And you are as ignorant of the matter as this cameo head"—he took one from the mantelpiece. "You have no right to preach to me, you novice, who have not even passed through life's entrance and are completely unacquainted with its depths."
"I only remind you of your own words, sir. You said error brought remorse, and you called remorse the poison of existence."

"And who is talking about error now? I hardly think the notion that just crossed my mind was an error. I believe it was an inspiration rather than a temptation—it was very warm, very soothing—I know that. Here it comes again! It is no devil, I assure you; or if it is, it has put on the robes of an angel of light. I think I must let so fair a guest in when it asks entrance to my heart."
"Distrust it, sir. It is not a true angel."
"Once more, how do you know? By what instinct do you claim to tell the difference between a fallen angel from the abyss and a messenger from the eternal throne—between a guide and a seducer?"
"I judged by your expression, sir, which was troubled when you said the thought had returned. I am sure it will cause you more misery if you listen to it."
"Not at all—it brings the most gracious message in the world. As for the rest, you are not my conscience-keeper, so don't trouble yourself. Here, come in, beautiful wanderer!"
He said this as if speaking to a vision visible only to himself; then, folding his arms—which he had half extended—across his chest, he seemed to embrace an invisible being.
"Now," he continued, turning back to me, "I have welcomed the pilgrim—a disguised god, I truly believe. Already it has done me good: my heart was a kind of tomb; now it will be a shrine."

"To be honest, sir, I don't understand you at all. I cannot keep up with this conversation because it has gone beyond my depth. Only one thing I know: you said you were not as good as you wanted to be, and that you regretted your own flaws. One thing I can grasp: you implied that having a stained memory was a constant curse. It seems to me that if you tried hard, you would in time find it possible to become what you yourself would approve of, and that if from this day you resolved to correct your thoughts and actions, you would in a few years build up a new, clean store of memories that you could look back on with pleasure."
"Well thought; well said, Miss Eyre. And at this very moment, I am paving the road to hell with good intentions."
"Sir?"
"I am laying down intentions I believe to be as solid as flint. My companions and pursuits shall certainly be different than they have been."
"And better?"

"And better—as much better as pure gold is than worthless slag. You seem to doubt me; I don't doubt myself. I know what my aim is, what my motives are; and at this moment I pass a law, as unalterable as the laws of the Medes and Persians, that both are right."
"They cannot be, sir, if they require a new law to make them legitimate."
"They are, Miss Eyre, though they absolutely require a new law. Unprecedented circumstances demand unprecedented rules."
"That sounds like a dangerous principle, sir, because one can see at once how easily it could be abused."
"Wise moralist! So it could. But I swear by my household gods not to abuse it."
"You are human and fallible."
"I am—and so are you. What then?"
"The human and fallible should not claim a power that only the divine and perfect can safely be trusted with."
"What power?"
"The power of declaring any strange, unsanctioned course of action to be right."
"'Let it be right'—the very words. You have spoken them."

"May it be right, then," I said, rising, since it seemed useless to continue a conversation that was all darkness to me. Besides, I sensed that my companion's character was beyond my understanding—at least beyond what I could grasp at present—and I felt the uncertainty, the vague unease that comes with knowing how much you don't know.
"Where are you going?"
"To put Adèle to bed. It is past her bedtime."
"You are afraid of me, because I talk like a Sphinx."
"Your language is mysterious, sir. But though I am bewildered, I am certainly not afraid."
"You are afraid—your pride dreads making a blunder."
"In that sense, yes, I do feel apprehensive. I have no wish to talk nonsense."

"If you did, you would say it in such a grave, quiet way that I'd mistake it for wisdom. Do you never laugh, Miss Eyre? Don't bother answering—I can see you rarely laugh. But you can laugh very merrily: believe me, you are not naturally solemn any more than I am naturally wicked. The Lowood restraint still clings to you, controlling your features, muffling your voice, restricting your movements. In the presence of a man—brother, father, master, whatever you wish to call me—you are afraid to smile too freely, speak too openly, or move too easily. But in time, I think you will learn to be natural with me, as I find it impossible to be conventional with you. And then your looks and movements will have more life and variety than they dare to show now. I see, at intervals, the glance of a strange sort of bird through the bars of a cage: a vivid, restless, resolute captive is in there; if it were free, it would soar to the clouds. You are still set on going?"
"It has struck nine, sir."

"Never mind—wait a moment. Adèle is not ready for bed yet. My position, Miss Eyre, with my back to the fire and my face to the room, gives me a good view. While talking to you, I have also been watching Adèle from time to time (I have my own reasons for finding her a curious study—reasons I may, indeed shall, share with you someday). She pulled from her box, about ten minutes ago, a little pink silk dress. Rapture lit her face as she unfolded it. Vanity runs in her blood, blends with her mind, and seasons her very bones. 'Il faut que je l'essaie!' she cried, 'et à l'instant même!' and she rushed from the room. She is now with Sophie, being dressed up. In a few minutes she will come back, and I know what I shall see—a miniature of Céline Varens, as she used to appear on stage at the rise of—but never mind that. My tenderest feelings are about to receive a shock—such is my feeling. Stay now and see whether it comes true."

Before long, Adèle's little feet were heard tripping across the hall. She entered, transformed as her guardian had predicted. A dress of rose-coloured satin, very short and full in the skirt, had replaced the brown frock she wore before. A wreath of rosebuds circled her forehead; her feet were in silk stockings and small white satin sandals.
"Est-ce que ma robe va bien?" she cried, bounding forward. "Et mes souliers? et mes bas? Tenez, je crois que je vais danser!"
And spreading out her dress, she danced across the room until she reached Mr. Rochester, where she spun lightly on her toes before him, then dropped to one knee at his feet, exclaiming—
"Monsieur, je vous remercie mille fois de votre bonté." Then, rising, she added, "C'est comme cela que maman faisait, n'est-ce pas, monsieur?"

"Pre-cise-ly!" was the answer. "And 'just like that,' she charmed my English gold out of my British pockets. I have been green, too, Miss Eyre—oh, green as grass: no fresher shade colours you now than once coloured me. My Spring is gone, however, but it has left me this French flower on my hands, which, in some moods, I would gladly be rid of. Not valuing now the root it sprang from—having found it was a sort that nothing but gold dust could nourish—I have only half a fondness for the blossom, especially when it looks as artificial as it does just now. I keep it and raise it on the Roman Catholic principle of atoning for many sins, great or small, by one good deed. I'll explain all this someday. Goodnight."

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: Mr. Rochester did, on a later occasion, explain. It was one afternoon when he happened to find me and Adèle in the grounds. While she played with Pilot and her shuttlecock, he asked me to walk up and down a long beech avenue within sight of her.

He told me then that she was the daughter of a French opera dancer named Céline Varens, toward whom he had once felt what he called a "grande passion." Céline had claimed to return the feeling with even greater ardour. He thought himself her idol, ugly as he was—he believed, as he said, that she preferred his "taille d'athlète" to the elegance of the Apollo Belvedere.

"And, Miss Eyre, I was so flattered by this French nymph's preference for her British gnome that I set her up in a hotel, gave her a full household of servants, a carriage, cashmeres, diamonds, lace, and the rest. In short, I began the standard process of ruining myself, like any other lovesick fool. I lacked, it seems, the originality to blaze a new trail to shame and destruction, and walked the old path with stupid precision, never straying an inch from the beaten centre. I had—as I deserved—the fate of all such fools. Happening to call one evening when Céline wasn't expecting me, I found her out. But it was a warm night and I was tired from wandering through Paris, so I sat down in her boudoir, happy to breathe the air she had so recently inhabited. No—I exaggerate. I never believed there was anything sacred about her. It was more like a lingering perfume she had left—a scent of musk and amber rather than the fragrance of holiness. I was just beginning to choke on the fumes of hothouse flowers and sprinkled essences when I thought to open the window and step out onto the balcony. It was moonlit and gaslit besides, and very still and calm. The balcony had a chair or two; I sat down and took out a cigar—I will take one now, if you'll excuse me."
Here came a pause, filled by the producing and lighting of a cigar. Having put it to his lips and breathed a trail of Havana smoke into the freezing, sunless air, he went on—

"I liked sweets too in those days, Miss Eyre, and I was crunching chocolate bonbons and smoking by turns, watching the carriages roll along the fashionable streets toward the nearby opera house, when in an elegant closed carriage drawn by a beautiful pair of English horses, clearly visible in the brilliant city night, I recognized the carriage I had given Céline. She was returning: of course my heart pounded against the iron railing I leaned on. The carriage stopped, as I expected, at the hotel door; my flame (the very word for an opera mistress) stepped out. Though wrapped in a cloak—an unnecessary covering on so warm a June evening—I knew her instantly by her little foot, visible beneath the hem of her dress as she hopped from the carriage step. Leaning over the balcony, I was about to murmur 'Mon ange'—in a tone, naturally, meant only for the ears of love—when a figure jumped from the carriage after her, also cloaked. But that was a spurred heel that rang on the pavement, and that was a hatted head that now passed under the arched entrance of the hotel.

"You have never felt jealousy, have you, Miss Eyre? Of course not—I need not ask; because you have never felt love. Both feelings are still ahead of you. Your soul sleeps; the shock that will wake it has not yet come. You think all of existence flows as quietly as the stream your youth has drifted down so far. Floating along with closed eyes and blocked ears, you see neither the rocks jutting from the riverbed ahead nor hear the breakers crashing at their base. But I tell you—mark my words—you will come someday to a treacherous passage in the channel, where life's whole current will be shattered into whirlpools and turmoil, foam and noise. Either you will be dashed to pieces on the rocks, or lifted up and carried by some great wave into calmer waters—as I am now.

"I like this day. I like that sky of steel. I like the harshness and stillness of the world under this frost. I like Thornfield—its age, its seclusion, its old crow-trees and thorn-trees, its grey face and rows of dark windows reflecting that metallic sky. And yet how long have I despised the very thought of it, avoided it like a plague house? How I still despise—"
He clenched his teeth and stopped. He halted mid-step and struck his boot against the hard ground. Some hated thought seemed to grip him and hold him so tightly he could not move forward.

We were climbing the avenue when he paused like this; the hall was before us. Lifting his eyes to its battlements, he cast over them a look such as I had never seen before or since. Pain, shame, fury, disgust, loathing, seemed to wage a trembling war in the wide pupil beneath his dark eyebrow. Fierce was the struggle for dominance; but another feeling rose and conquered: something hard and cynical, self-willed and resolute. It settled his passion and turned his face to stone. He went on—

"During the moment I was silent, Miss Eyre, I was settling a point with my destiny. She stood there, by that beech trunk—a hag like one of those who appeared to Macbeth on the heath of Forres. 'You like Thornfield?' she said, lifting her finger; and then she wrote in the air a warning, which ran in fiery letters all along the front of the house, between the upper and lower rows of windows: 'Like it if you can! Like it if you dare!'

"'I will like it,' I said. 'I dare like it.' And"—he added moodily—"I will keep my word. I will break through obstacles to happiness, to goodness—yes, goodness. I wish to be a better man than I have been, than I am. As Job's leviathan broke the spear, the javelin, and the coat of mail, I will consider the barriers that others call iron and brass to be nothing but straw and rotten wood."

Adèle ran up to him with her shuttlecock. "Away!" he cried harshly. "Keep your distance, child; or go in to Sophie!" Then, continuing his walk in silence, I ventured to bring him back to the point from which he had abruptly wandered—
"Did you leave the balcony, sir," I asked, "when Mademoiselle Varens came in?"

I half expected a rebuff for this poorly timed question, but on the contrary, shaking off his scowling reverie, he turned his eyes toward me and the shadow seemed to lift from his brow. "Oh, I had forgotten Céline! Well, to continue. When I saw my darling arrive accompanied by a gentleman, I seemed to hear a hiss, and the green snake of jealousy, rising on undulating coils from the moonlit balcony, slid inside my waistcoat and in two minutes had eaten its way to my heart. Strange!" he exclaimed, suddenly starting off on another tangent. "Strange that I should choose you as my confidante for all this, young lady—passing strange that you should sit and listen so calmly, as if it were the most natural thing in the world for a man like me to tell stories of his former mistresses to a quiet, inexperienced girl like you! But the last oddity explains the first, as I hinted before: you, with your gravity, thoughtfulness, and caution, were made to be the keeper of secrets. Besides, I know the kind of mind I have opened a channel to: I know it will not be infected. It is a peculiar mind—a unique one. Luckily I do not mean to harm it; but if I did, it would take no harm from me. The more you and I talk, the better: while I cannot damage you, you may refresh me." After this digression, he went on—

"I stayed on the balcony. 'They will go to her boudoir, no doubt,' I thought. 'Let me set a trap.' So reaching through the open window, I drew the curtain across it, leaving only a gap through which I could observe; then I closed the window, all but a crack just wide enough to catch any whispered endearments; then I crept back to my chair. As I sat down, the pair came in. My eye was quickly at the opening. Céline's maid entered, lit a lamp, left it on the table, and withdrew. The couple were clearly revealed: both removed their cloaks, and there was 'the Varens,' shining in satin and jewels—my gifts, of course—and there was her companion in an officer's uniform. I recognized him as a young rake of a vicomte—a brainless, depraved youth I had sometimes encountered in society and had never bothered to hate because I despised him so completely. The moment I recognized him, jealousy's fang snapped, because in that same instant my love for Céline collapsed like a snuffed candle. A woman who could betray me for such a rival was not worth fighting for; she deserved only contempt—less, though, than I deserved, for having been her fool.

"They began to talk; their conversation cured me entirely. Shallow, mercenary, heartless, and mindless—it was more likely to bore a listener than enrage one. My calling card lay on the table. This was noticed, and brought my name into the discussion. Neither of them had the energy or wit to attack me properly, but they insulted me as crudely as they could in their small way—especially Céline, who even grew rather clever on the subject of my physical defects, or 'deformities' as she called them. Now, she had always made a point of gushing over what she called my 'beauté mâle'—in which she was the exact opposite of you, who told me flat out, at our second meeting, that you did not think me handsome. The contrast struck me at the time, and—"
Adèle came running up again.
"Monsieur, John has just come to say that your agent has called and wishes to see you."

"Ah! In that case I must cut this short. Opening the window, I walked in on them; freed Céline from my protection; gave her notice to vacate the hotel; offered her a purse for immediate expenses; ignored screams, hysterics, prayers, protestations, and convulsions; and made an appointment with the vicomte for a meeting in the Bois de Boulogne. The next morning I had the pleasure of meeting him and left a bullet in one of his sickly arms, as feeble as the wing of a dying chicken, and then thought I was done with the whole lot. But unfortunately, six months earlier, the Varens had presented me with this child, Adèle, who, she swore, was my daughter—and perhaps she is, though I see no proof of it in her face. Pilot looks more like me than she does. Some years after I broke with the mother, she abandoned the child and ran off to Italy with a musician or singer. I acknowledged no claim on Adèle's part to be supported by me, nor do I now, for I am not her father. But hearing that she was utterly destitute, I took the poor creature out of the filth and gutter of Paris and brought her here, to grow up clean in the healthy soil of an English country garden. Mrs. Fairfax found you to educate her. But now you know she is the illegitimate child of a French opera girl, you will perhaps think differently of your position and your charge. You'll come to me someday with notice that you've found another place—that you beg me to find a new governess, and so on. Eh?"

"No. Adèle is not responsible for her mother's faults or yours. I care for her; and now that I know she is, in a sense, without parents—abandoned by her mother and disowned by you, sir—I shall hold closer to her than before. How could I possibly prefer the spoiled pet of a wealthy family, who would resent her governess as a nuisance, to a lonely little orphan who turns to me as a friend?"
"Oh, that is how you see it! Well, I must go in now; and so must you. It's getting dark."

But I stayed out a few minutes longer with Adèle and Pilot—ran a race with her and played a game of battledore and shuttlecock. When we went inside and I had removed her bonnet and coat, I took her on my knee and kept her there for an hour, letting her chatter as she liked, not even correcting some of the small liberties and silly remarks she tended to make when given attention—traits that revealed a shallowness of character probably inherited from her mother, and not quite suited to an English sensibility. Still, she had her merits, and I was inclined to appreciate everything good in her to the fullest. I searched her face for a resemblance to Mr. Rochester but found none: no feature, no expression suggested kinship. It was a pity: if she could have been shown to look like him, he would have thought more of her.

It was not until I had withdrawn to my own room for the night that I steadily reviewed the tale Mr. Rochester had told me. As he had said, there was probably nothing extraordinary in the story itself: a wealthy Englishman's passion for a French dancer, and her betrayal—these were everyday matters in society. But there was something decidedly strange in the storm of emotion that had suddenly seized him just as he was expressing contentment with his present mood, and his renewed pleasure in the old hall and its surroundings. I thought about this puzzling moment; but gradually letting it go, since I could not explain it, I turned to considering my master's manner toward me. The trust he had chosen to place in me seemed like a tribute to my discretion, and I regarded and accepted it as such. His behaviour toward me had been steadier for some weeks now than at first. I never seemed to be in his way; he no longer had spells of chilling haughtiness. When he met me unexpectedly, the encounter seemed welcome; he always had a word and sometimes a smile for me. When formally invited to his presence, I was received with a warmth that made me feel I genuinely had the power to entertain him, and that these evening conversations were sought as much for his pleasure as for my benefit.

I spoke relatively little, it is true, but I listened to him talk with relish. It was his nature to be open, to share with a mind unfamiliar with the world glimpses of its scenes and ways (not its corrupt scenes and wicked ways, but those that drew their interest from the grand scale on which they played out, the strange novelty that marked them). And I took keen delight in absorbing his new ideas, imagining the new pictures he painted, and following him in thought through the new regions he revealed—never startled or troubled by any unwholesome suggestion.

The ease of his manner freed me from painful self-consciousness. The friendly frankness, as proper as it was warm, with which he treated me, drew me to him. At times I felt as though he were a relative rather than my employer. He was still imperious sometimes; but I did not mind—I saw it was his way. I became so happy, so fulfilled by this new interest added to my life, that I stopped longing for family. My once thin, crescent-shaped destiny seemed to grow fuller; the empty spaces of existence were filled in; my health improved; I gained weight and strength.

And was Mr. Rochester ugly in my eyes now? No, reader. Gratitude, and many pleasant associations, made his face the one I most liked to see; his presence in a room was more cheering than the brightest fire. Yet I had not forgotten his faults—I could not, for he constantly put them before me. He was proud, sardonic, harsh toward anything he deemed inferior. In my secret heart I knew that his great kindness to me was balanced by unjust severity to many others. He was moody too, inexplicably so; more than once, when sent for to read to him, I found him in the library alone, head buried in his folded arms, and when he looked up, a sullen, almost malevolent scowl darkened his features. But I believed his moodiness, his harshness, and his past moral failings (I say past, for now he seemed to have corrected them) had their source in some cruel blow of fate. I believed he was by nature a man of better tendencies, higher principles, and purer tastes than those that circumstances had developed, education instilled, or destiny encouraged. I thought there were excellent materials in him, though for the present they were somewhat tangled and spoiled. I cannot deny that I grieved for his grief, whatever it was, and would have given much to ease it.

Though I had now blown out my candle and lay in bed, I could not sleep for thinking of his expression when he paused in the avenue and told how his destiny had risen up before him and dared him to be happy at Thornfield.

"Why not?" I asked myself. "What keeps him away from this house? Will he leave again soon? Mrs. Fairfax said he rarely stays longer than two weeks at a time, and he has now been here eight weeks. If he does go, the change will be bleak. Imagine spring, summer, and autumn without him—how cheerless the sunshine and fine days would be!"

I hardly know whether I had slept or not after these thoughts; at any rate, I was jolted fully awake by a vague murmur, strange and mournful, which seemed to come from just above me. I wished I had kept my candle burning; the night was drearily dark, my spirits low. I sat up in bed and listened. The sound stopped.

I tried to sleep again, but my heart beat with worry; my inner calm was shattered. The clock, far down in the hall, struck two. Just then something seemed to touch my bedroom door, as if fingers had brushed the panels while groping along the dark gallery outside. I said, "Who is there?" No answer. I was chilled with fear.

Then I remembered it might be Pilot, who, when the kitchen door happened to be left open, often found his way up to the threshold of Mr. Rochester's room. I had seen him lying there in the mornings. The thought calmed me somewhat; I lay down. Silence soothes the nerves, and as unbroken quiet now reigned through the whole house, I felt sleep beginning to return. But I was not fated to sleep that night. A dream had barely brushed my ear when it fled, scared off by an incident terrifying enough to freeze the blood.

This was a demonic laugh—low, stifled, and deep—uttered, it seemed, at the very keyhole of my door. My bed was near the door, and I thought at first the goblin-laugher stood at my bedside—or rather crouched by my pillow. But I rose, looked around, and saw nothing; yet as I stared, the unnatural sound came again, and I knew it came from behind the door. My first impulse was to get up and bolt the door; my next, to cry out again, "Who is there?"

Something gurgled and moaned. Soon footsteps retreated along the gallery toward the third-floor staircase. A door that had recently been installed to close off that staircase—I heard it open and close, and then all was still.

"Was that Grace Poole? Is she possessed by a devil?" I thought. It was impossible to stay alone any longer. I had to go to Mrs. Fairfax. I threw on my dress and a shawl, drew back the bolt, and opened my door with a trembling hand. A candle was burning just outside, on the gallery floor. I was surprised by this; but I was even more amazed to find the air thick, as if filled with smoke. Looking left and right to find where these blue wisps came from, I became aware of a strong smell of burning.

Something creaked: it was a door ajar; and that door was Mr. Rochester's. Smoke poured from it in clouds. I forgot Mrs. Fairfax; I forgot Grace Poole and the laugh. In an instant I was inside the room. Tongues of flame darted around the bed; the curtains were on fire. In the middle of the blaze and smoke, Mr. Rochester lay stretched out, motionless, in deep sleep.

"Wake! Wake!" I cried. I shook him, but he only muttered and turned. The smoke had stupefied him. Not a moment could be lost: the very sheets were starting to catch fire. I ran to his basin and pitcher; luckily, one was wide and the other deep, and both were full of water. I heaved them up and drenched the bed and its occupant, flew back to my own room, brought my own water jug, doused the bed again, and, by God's aid, succeeded in putting out the flames that were devouring it.

The hiss of the quenched fire, the crash of the pitcher I flung from my hand once empty, and above all, the thorough drenching I had given him, finally roused Mr. Rochester. Though it was now dark, I knew he was awake, because I heard him cursing furiously at finding himself lying in a pool of water.
"Is there a flood?" he cried.
"No, sir," I answered, "but there has been a fire. Get up—do. You are soaked now; I will fetch you a candle."
"In the name of all the spirits in Christendom, is that Jane Eyre?" he demanded. "What have you done to me, witch? Sorceress? Who is in the room besides you? Have you plotted to drown me?"
"I will fetch you a candle, sir, and in heaven's name, get up. Somebody has plotted something—the sooner you find out who and what, the better."
"There! I am up now. But at your peril, don't fetch a candle yet. Wait two minutes until I get into some dry clothes, if any are dry—yes, here is my dressing gown. Now run!"
I ran. I brought the candle that still sat in the gallery. He took it from my hand, held it up, and surveyed the bed—all blackened and scorched, the sheets drenched, the carpet swimming in water.
"What is it? And who did it?" he asked.

I told him briefly what had happened: the strange laugh I had heard in the gallery, the footsteps ascending to the third floor, the smoke and smell of fire that had led me to his room, the state I had found it in, and how I had doused him with every drop of water I could find.
"What is it and who did it?" he asked.
He listened very seriously. His face, as I went on, showed more concern than surprise. He did not speak right away when I had finished.
"Shall I call Mrs. Fairfax?" I asked.
"Mrs. Fairfax? No—what on earth would you call her for? What can she do? Let her sleep undisturbed."
"Then I will fetch Leah and wake John and his wife."

"Not at all. Just stay still. You have a shawl on. If you're not warm enough, take my cloak over there; wrap it around you and sit in the armchair. There—I will put it on for you. Now put your feet on the stool, to keep them out of the wet. I am going to leave you for a few minutes. I will take the candle. Stay where you are until I return. Be as still as a mouse. I must visit the second floor. Don't move, remember, or call anyone."

He left. I watched the light recede. He passed along the gallery very softly, opened the staircase door with barely a sound, closed it behind him, and the last glow vanished. I was left in total darkness. I listened for any noise but heard nothing. A very long time passed. I grew weary; it was cold despite the cloak; and I could not see the point of staying if I was not to rouse the house. I was on the verge of disobeying Mr. Rochester's orders when the light gleamed dimly on the gallery wall once more, and I heard his stockinged feet on the matting. "I hope it is him," I thought, "and not something worse."
He came back in, pale and very grim. "I have found it all out," he said, setting his candle on the washstand. "It is as I thought."
"How, sir?"
He made no reply but stood with his arms folded, staring at the floor. After a few minutes he asked, in a rather odd tone—
"I forget whether you said you saw anything when you opened your bedroom door."
"No, sir, only the candlestick on the ground."
"But you heard a strange laugh? You have heard that laugh before, I imagine, or something like it?"
"Yes, sir. There is a woman who sews here, called Grace Poole. She laughs like that. She is a very odd person."

"Just so. Grace Poole—you've guessed it. She is, as you say, odd—very. Well, I shall think about it. Meanwhile, I am glad you are the only person besides myself who knows the full details of tonight's incident. You are not a gossip—say nothing about it. I will account for the state of things"—he pointed to the bed—"and now go back to your own room. I shall do well enough on the library sofa for the rest of the night. It is nearly four; in two hours the servants will be up."
"Goodnight then, sir," I said, turning to leave.
He seemed surprised—very oddly so, since he had just told me to go.
"What!" he exclaimed. "Are you leaving me already, and like that?"
"You said I could go, sir."

"But not without a farewell—not without a word or two of thanks and goodwill. Not so quick and cold. Why, you have saved my life! Snatched me from a horrible and agonizing death! And you walk past me as if we were strangers! At least shake hands."
He held out his hand; I gave him mine. He took it first in one, then in both of his.

"You have saved my life. I have a pleasure in owing you so great a debt. I cannot say more. Nothing else in the world would have been bearable to me as a creditor for such an obligation—but you: it is different. I feel your kindness no burden, Jane."
He paused, gazing at me. Words nearly visible trembled on his lips—but his voice was checked.
"Goodnight again, sir. There is no debt, burden, or obligation in the case."

"I knew," he continued, "you would do me good in some way, at some time. I saw it in your eyes when I first looked at you: their expression and smile did not"—he stopped again—"did not"—he rushed on—"strike delight to my very heart for nothing. People talk of natural sympathies; I have heard of guardian spirits. There are grains of truth in the wildest fairy tales. My dear preserver, goodnight!"
Strange energy was in his voice, strange fire in his look.
"I am glad I happened to be awake," I said, and then I was going.
"What! You will go?"
"I am cold, sir."
"Cold? Yes—and standing in a puddle! Go, then, Jane—go!" But he still held my hand, and I could not free it. I thought of an excuse.
"I think I hear Mrs. Fairfax moving, sir," I said.
"Well, leave me." He released his fingers, and I was gone.

I reached my bed but never thought of sleep. Until morning dawned, I was tossed on a buoyant but restless sea, where waves of trouble rolled under swells of joy. Sometimes I thought I glimpsed beyond those wild waters a shore as sweet as the hills of Beulah; now and then a freshening wind, stirred by hope, carried my spirit triumphantly toward that distant land. But I could not reach it, even in fancy—an opposing breeze blew off shore and continually drove me back. Reason would resist delusion; judgment would warn passion. Too feverish to rest, I rose as soon as daylight broke.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: I both wished and feared to see Mr. Rochester on the day that followed this sleepless night. I wanted to hear his voice again, yet dreaded meeting his eye. During the early part of the morning, I kept expecting him to appear. He didn't usually come into the schoolroom, but he sometimes stepped in for a few minutes, and I had a feeling he would certainly visit it today.

But the morning passed as usual: nothing interrupted the quiet course of Adèle's lessons. Soon after breakfast, though, I heard some commotion near Mr. Rochester's room—Mrs. Fairfax's voice, and Leah's, and the cook's (that is, John's wife), and even John's own gruff tones. There were exclamations: "What a mercy the master wasn't burned in his bed!" "It's always dangerous to keep a candle lit at night." "How lucky he had the sense to think of the water jug!" "I wonder he didn't wake anyone!" "Let's hope he won't catch cold from sleeping on the library sofa." And so on.

After much discussion came the sounds of scrubbing and cleaning. When I passed the room on my way down to dinner, I saw through the open door that everything had been restored to complete order, except that the bed had been stripped of its hangings. Leah stood on the window seat, polishing the glass panes that were dimmed with smoke. I was about to speak to her—I wanted to know what account had been given of the affair—but as I came closer, I saw a second person in the room: a woman sitting in a chair by the bedside, sewing rings onto new curtains. That woman was none other than Grace Poole.

There she sat, composed and silent as always, in her brown dress, her checked apron, white handkerchief, and cap. She was intent on her work, her whole mind apparently absorbed in it. On her hard forehead and plain features there was nothing of the pallor or desperation you would expect on the face of a woman who had attempted murder—a woman whose intended victim had followed her last night to her lair and (as I believed) confronted her with the crime she had tried to commit. I was stunned, baffled. She looked up while I still stared at her: no start, no change of colour betrayed emotion, guilt, or fear of discovery. She said "Good morning, Miss," in her usual flat, brief manner, and picking up another ring and more tape, went on with her sewing.
"I will test her," I thought. "Such perfect composure defies understanding."
"Good morning, Grace," I said. "Has anything happened here? I thought I heard the servants all talking together a while ago."

"Only the master had been reading in bed last night; he fell asleep with his candle lit, and the curtains caught fire. But fortunately he woke before the bedclothes or the woodwork caught, and managed to put out the flames with water from the pitcher."
"A strange business!" I said in a low voice; then, looking at her steadily—"Did Mr. Rochester wake nobody? Did no one hear him?"
She raised her eyes to me again, and this time there was something aware in their expression. She seemed to examine me carefully; then she answered—

"The servants sleep so far off, you know, Miss, they wouldn't be likely to hear. Mrs. Fairfax's room and yours are nearest to the master's; but Mrs. Fairfax said she heard nothing. When people get older, they often sleep heavily." She paused, then added, with a sort of forced casualness but in a pointed and meaningful tone—"But you are young, Miss, and I should say a light sleeper. Perhaps you heard a noise?"

"I did," said I, dropping my voice so that Leah, who was still polishing the windows, could not hear. "And at first I thought it was Pilot. But Pilot cannot laugh, and I am certain I heard a laugh—and a strange one."
She took a new length of thread, waxed it carefully, threaded her needle with a steady hand, and then observed, with perfect calm—
"It is hardly likely the master would laugh, I should think, Miss, when he was in such danger. You must have been dreaming."
"I was not dreaming," I said with some heat, for her brazen coolness provoked me. Again she looked at me—with the same scrutinizing, knowing eye.
"Have you told the master that you heard a laugh?" she asked.
"I have not had the chance to speak to him this morning."
"You did not think of opening your door and looking out into the gallery?" she went on.

She seemed to be cross-examining me, trying to draw information from me without my realizing it. The thought struck me that if she discovered I knew or suspected her guilt, she might play some of her dangerous tricks on me. I decided to be on my guard.
"On the contrary," I said, "I bolted my door."
"Then you are not in the habit of bolting your door every night before bed?"

"Fiend! She wants to know my habits, so she can plan accordingly!" Indignation overwhelmed caution. I replied sharply, "Until now I have often forgotten to fasten the bolt. I did not think it necessary. I was not aware there was any danger to be feared at Thornfield Hall. But in future"—and I stressed the words—"I shall take care to make everything secure before I go to sleep."

"That would be wise," was her answer. "This neighbourhood is as quiet as any I know, and I never heard of the hall being broken into since it was a house, though there are hundreds of pounds' worth of silver plate in the closet, as everyone knows. And for such a large house, there are very few servants, because the master has never lived here much; and when he does come, being a bachelor, he needs little waiting on. But I always think it best to err on the side of caution; a door is soon fastened, and it is just as well to have a drawn bolt between yourself and any trouble that may be about. Many people trust entirely to Providence; but I say Providence will not excuse you from taking sensible precautions, though He often blesses them when they are wisely used." Here she concluded her speech—a long one for her, delivered with the primness of a Quaker woman.
I still stood absolutely dumbfounded at what appeared to be her miraculous self-possession and unfathomable hypocrisy, when the cook came in.
"Mrs. Poole," she said, addressing Grace, "the servants' dinner will be ready soon. Will you come down?"
"No; just put my pint of beer and bit of pudding on a tray, and I'll carry it upstairs."
"You'll have some meat?"
"Just a morsel, and a taste of cheese. That's all."
"And the sago?"
"Never mind that now. I'll be coming down before teatime; I'll make it myself."
The cook then turned to me, saying that Mrs. Fairfax was waiting for me, so I left.

I barely heard Mrs. Fairfax's account of the curtain fire over dinner, so preoccupied was I with puzzling over Grace Poole's enigmatic character, and even more with the question of her position at Thornfield and why she had not been handed over to the authorities that morning—or at the very least dismissed from service. Mr. Rochester had practically declared his conviction of her guilt last night. What mysterious reason held him back from accusing her? Why had he ordered me to keep silent too? It was strange: a bold, proud, assertive gentleman seemed somehow in the power of one of the lowliest of his dependents—so much in her power that even when she raised her hand against his life, he dared not openly charge her with it, let alone punish her.

Had Grace been young and attractive, I might have been tempted to think that softer feelings than caution or fear influenced Mr. Rochester in her favour. But plain and matronly as she was, that idea was out of the question. "Yet," I reflected, "she was young once; her youth would overlap with her master's. Mrs. Fairfax told me she had lived here many years. I don't think she was ever pretty; but for all I know, she may have originality and strength of character to make up for the lack of personal charms. Mr. Rochester has a taste for the bold and unusual, and Grace is unusual at least. What if a former whim—quite possible in a nature as impulsive and headstrong as his—has put him in her power, and she now holds a secret influence over his actions, the result of his own recklessness, which he cannot shake off and dare not defy?"
