But having reached this point in my speculation, Mrs. Poole's square, flat figure and her plain, dry, even coarse face came so vividly to my mind that I thought, "No—impossible! My theory cannot be right." Yet the secret voice that speaks in our own hearts whispered, "You are not beautiful either, and perhaps Mr. Rochester likes you. At any rate, you have often felt as if he did; and last night—remember his words; remember his look; remember his voice!"

I remembered all of it well; language, glance, and tone seemed for a moment vividly renewed. I was now in the schoolroom; Adèle was drawing; I leaned over her and guided her pencil. She looked up with a sort of start.
"Qu'avez-vous, mademoiselle?" she said. "Vos doigts tremblent comme la feuille, et vos joues sont rouges: mais, rouges comme des cerises!"
"I am hot, Adèle, from bending over!" She went on sketching; I went on thinking.

I hurried to banish the hateful idea I had been forming about Grace Poole; it disgusted me. I compared myself with her and found we were nothing alike. Bessie Leaven had said I was quite a lady, and she spoke the truth—I was a lady. And now I looked much better than when Bessie last saw me; I had more colour and more flesh, more life, more spirit, because I had brighter hopes and sharper joys.

"Evening is coming," I said, as I looked toward the window. "I have not heard Mr. Rochester's voice or step in the house all day; but surely I will see him before night. I dreaded the meeting this morning; now I want it, because my expectation has been disappointed so long that it has grown impatient."

When dusk actually fell and Adèle left me to play in the nursery with Sophie, I desired the meeting keenly. I listened for the bell to ring below; listened for Leah coming up with a message; sometimes I imagined I heard Mr. Rochester's own step and turned toward the door, expecting it to open and admit him. The door stayed shut; only darkness came in through the window. Still, it was not late; he often sent for me at seven or eight o'clock, and it was only six. Surely I would not be wholly disappointed tonight, when I had so many things to say to him! I wanted to bring up the subject of Grace Poole again and hear what he would say; I wanted to ask him directly whether he truly believed she had made last night's murderous attempt, and if so, why he kept her crime a secret. It hardly mattered whether my curiosity annoyed him; I knew the pleasure of provoking and then soothing him by turns—it was one I particularly enjoyed, and a sure instinct always kept me from going too far. Beyond the brink of real provocation I never ventured; on the very edge of it I liked to test my skill. Always keeping every form of respect, every propriety of my position, I could still meet him in argument without fear or awkward restraint. This suited us both.

At last a footstep creaked on the stairs. Leah appeared—but only to say that tea was ready in Mrs. Fairfax's room. I went there, glad at least to go downstairs, since that brought me, I imagined, nearer to Mr. Rochester.
"You must want your tea," said the good lady as I joined her. "You ate so little at dinner. I'm afraid you are not well today—you look flushed and feverish."
"Oh, quite well! I have never felt better."

"Then you must prove it by showing a good appetite. Will you pour the tea while I finish this row of knitting?" Having completed her task, she rose to lower the blind, which she had kept up so far, I suppose to make the most of the daylight, though dusk was now deepening into full darkness.
"It is a fine night," she said, looking through the panes, "though not starry. Mr. Rochester has, on the whole, had favourable weather for his journey."
"Journey! Is Mr. Rochester gone somewhere? I did not know he was out."

"Oh, he set off the moment he'd had breakfast! He has gone to the Leas, Mr. Eshton's place, ten miles on the other side of Millcote. I believe there is quite a party assembled there: Lord Ingram, Sir George Lynn, Colonel Dent, and others."
"Do you expect him back tonight?"

"No—nor tomorrow either. I should think he is very likely to stay a week or more. When these fine, fashionable people get together, they are so surrounded by elegance and amusement, so well provided with everything that can please and entertain, they are in no hurry to separate. Gentlemen especially are often in demand on such occasions; and Mr. Rochester is so talented and so lively in company that I believe he is a general favourite. The ladies are very fond of him, though you would not think his appearance particularly calculated to recommend him. But I suppose his accomplishments and abilities, perhaps his wealth and good family, make up for any slight flaw in looks."
"Are there ladies at the Leas?"

"There are Mrs. Eshton and her three daughters—very elegant young ladies indeed. And the Honourable Blanche and Mary Ingram, most beautiful women, I believe; indeed, I have seen Blanche, six or seven years ago, when she was a girl of eighteen. She came here for a Christmas ball and party that Mr. Rochester gave. You should have seen the dining room that day—how richly it was decorated, how brilliantly lit! I should think there were fifty ladies and gentlemen present—all from the first families in the county—and Miss Ingram was considered the belle of the evening."
"You saw her, you say, Mrs. Fairfax? What was she like?"

"Yes, I saw her. The dining room doors were thrown open, and since it was Christmas, the servants were allowed to gather in the hall to hear some of the ladies sing and play. Mr. Rochester invited me to come in, and I sat down in a quiet corner and watched. I never saw a more splendid scene: the ladies were magnificently dressed; most of them—at least the younger ones—were handsome. But Miss Ingram was certainly the queen."
"And what did she look like?"

"Tall, with a fine figure, sloping shoulders, a long graceful neck; olive complexion, dark and clear; noble features; eyes rather like Mr. Rochester's—large and black, and as brilliant as her jewels. And then she had such a fine head of hair: raven-black and so beautifully arranged—a crown of thick plaits behind, and in front the longest, glossiest curls I ever saw. She was dressed in pure white; an amber-coloured scarf was draped over her shoulder and across her chest, tied at the side, falling in long fringed ends below her knee. She wore an amber-coloured flower in her hair too, which set off the jet-black mass of her curls."
"She was greatly admired, of course?"
"Yes indeed—and not only for her beauty but for her talents. She was one of the ladies who sang; a gentleman accompanied her on the piano. She and Mr. Rochester sang a duet."
"Mr. Rochester? I did not know he could sing."
"Oh! He has a fine bass voice, and an excellent taste for music."
"And Miss Ingram—what sort of voice did she have?"

"A very rich and powerful one. She sang beautifully; it was a treat to listen to her. And she played the piano afterwards. I am no judge of music, but Mr. Rochester is, and I heard him say her playing was remarkably good."
"And this beautiful and accomplished lady—she is not yet married?"
"It seems not. I fancy neither she nor her sister has a very large fortune. Old Lord Ingram's estates were mostly entailed, and the eldest son inherited almost everything."
"But I wonder that no wealthy nobleman or gentleman has taken a fancy to her. Mr. Rochester, for instance. He is rich, is he not?"
"Oh yes. But there is a considerable difference in age: Mr. Rochester is nearly forty; she is only twenty-five."
"What of that? More unequal matches are made every day."
"True; yet I would hardly expect Mr. Rochester to think along those lines. But you're not eating—you've barely touched your food since we began tea."
"No—I am too thirsty to eat. Will you let me have another cup?"
I was about to return to the subject of a possible match between Mr. Rochester and the beautiful Blanche, but Adèle came in and the conversation turned another way.

When I was alone again, I reviewed the information I had gathered. I looked into my heart, examined its thoughts and feelings, and tried to pull back—with a firm hand—those that had been wandering through imagination's boundless and trackless waste, back into the safe fold of common sense.

Arraigned at my own court—Memory having given her evidence of the hopes, wishes, and sentiments I had been nursing since last night, and of the general state of mind I had indulged for nearly two weeks; Reason having come forward and told, in her calm way, a plain unvarnished tale, showing how I had rejected reality and greedily devoured fantasy—I pronounced this judgment:
That a greater fool than Jane Eyre had never drawn breath; that a more deluded idiot had never gorged herself on sweet lies and swallowed poison as if it were nectar.

"You," I said, "a favourite with Mr. Rochester? You, gifted with the power to please him? You, of importance to him in any way? Go—your folly sickens me. And you have taken pleasure from occasional tokens of preference—ambiguous tokens shown by a gentleman of family and a man of the world to a dependent and a novice. How dared you? Poor stupid dupe! Could not even self-preservation make you wiser? You repeated to yourself this morning the brief scene of last night? Cover your face and be ashamed! He said something flattering about your eyes, did he? Blind puppy! Open your bleary lids and look at your own wretched foolishness! It does no woman good to be flattered by a superior who cannot possibly intend to marry her; and it is madness in all women to let a secret love kindle within them which, if unreturned and unknown, must consume the life that feeds it; and if discovered and returned, must lead, like a will-o'-the-wisp, into swamps from which there is no escape.

"Listen, then, Jane Eyre, to your sentence. Tomorrow, place a mirror before you and draw your own portrait in chalk, faithfully, without softening a single defect. Leave out no harsh line, smooth away no displeasing feature. Write under it: 'Portrait of a Governess, disconnected, poor, and plain.'

"Afterwards, take a piece of smooth ivory—you have one ready in your drawing box. Take your palette, mix your freshest, finest, clearest colours; choose your most delicate camel-hair brushes; and carefully paint the loveliest face you can imagine. Paint it in your softest shades and sweetest lines, following Mrs. Fairfax's description of Blanche Ingram. Remember the raven ringlets, the dark eastern eyes—What! You are thinking of Mr. Rochester as your model! Order! No snivelling! No sentiment! No regret! I will tolerate only sense and resolution. Paint the noble yet harmonious features, the Grecian neck and bust; let the round and dazzling arm be visible, and the delicate hand; forget neither the diamond ring nor the gold bracelet; portray faithfully the dress—airy lace and gleaming satin, graceful scarf and golden rose. Call it 'Blanche, an accomplished lady of rank.'

"Whenever, in future, you should happen to fancy that Mr. Rochester thinks well of you, take out these two pictures and compare them. Say: 'Mr. Rochester might probably win that noble lady's love, if he chose to try. Is it likely he would waste a serious thought on this poor and insignificant nobody?'"
"I'll do it," I resolved. And having made this decision, I grew calm and fell asleep.

I kept my word. An hour or two was enough to sketch my own portrait in chalk, and in less than two weeks I had completed an ivory miniature of an imaginary Blanche Ingram. It was a lovely face, and when set beside the real head in chalk, the contrast was as stark as self-control could wish. I benefited from the exercise: it had kept my head and hands busy, and had driven home the new truths I wished to stamp permanently on my heart.

Before long, I had reason to be glad of the harsh discipline I had forced upon my feelings. Thanks to it, I was able to meet what came next with a composure that, had it caught me unprepared, I probably could not have maintained even on the surface.

chapters.title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: A week passed with no news of Mr. Rochester; ten days, and still he did not come. Mrs. Fairfax said she would not be surprised if he went straight from the Leas to London and from there to the Continent, not showing his face at Thornfield again for a year. He had left just as abruptly and unexpectedly before. When I heard this, I felt a strange chill and sinking at the heart. I was actually letting myself feel a sickening sense of disappointment. But rallying my wits and remembering my principles, I called my emotions to order at once—and it was remarkable how quickly I got over the blunder of supposing Mr. Rochester's movements were something I had any reason to care about. Not that I humbled myself with some slavish sense of inferiority; on the contrary, I simply said—

"You have nothing to do with the master of Thornfield beyond receiving the salary he pays you for teaching his ward, and being grateful for whatever respectful and kind treatment you have a right to expect if you do your duty. That is the only connection he seriously recognizes between you and him. So don't make him the object of your fine feelings, your raptures and agonies. He is not of your class: keep to your own, and be too self-respecting to pour out the love of your whole heart and soul where such a gift is not wanted and would be despised."

I went on with my day's business calmly enough, but now and then vague thoughts kept drifting across my mind about reasons I should leave Thornfield. I kept involuntarily composing advertisements and imagining new positions. I did not try to suppress these thoughts; they could grow and bear fruit if they wished.
Mr. Rochester had been away for more than two weeks when the post brought Mrs. Fairfax a letter.
"It is from the master," she said, looking at the address. "Now I suppose we shall know whether to expect his return or not."

While she broke the seal and read the letter, I went on with my coffee (we were at breakfast); it was hot, and I blamed that for the fiery glow that suddenly rose to my face. Why my hand shook, and why I involuntarily spilled half the contents of my cup into my saucer, I did not choose to examine.
"Well, I sometimes think we are too quiet here; but we may be busy enough now, for a little while at least," said Mrs. Fairfax, still holding the note before her spectacles.
Before I let myself ask for an explanation, I tied the string of Adèle's pinafore, which happened to be loose. Having also given her another roll and refilled her mug with milk, I said casually—
"Mr. Rochester is not likely to return soon, I suppose?"

"On the contrary—in three days, he says. That will be next Thursday. And not alone either. I don't know how many of the fine people at the Leas are coming with him. He sends instructions for all the best bedrooms to be prepared, and the library and drawing rooms are to be cleaned out. I am to hire more kitchen help from the George Inn at Millcote and wherever else I can find them. The ladies will bring their maids and the gentlemen their valets, so we shall have a full house." And Mrs. Fairfax swallowed her breakfast and hurried away to begin preparations.

The three days were, as she had predicted, busy enough. I had thought all the rooms at Thornfield beautifully clean and well arranged, but apparently I was wrong. Three extra women were brought in, and such scrubbing, brushing, and washing of paintwork, such beating of carpets, taking down and putting up of pictures, polishing of mirrors and chandeliers, lighting of fires in bedrooms, and airing of sheets and feather beds before the hearths—I had never seen the like, before or since. Adèle ran wild in the middle of it all. The preparations for company and the prospect of guests seemed to throw her into ecstasy. She had Sophie look over all her "toilettes," as she called her dresses, to freshen up any that were faded and to air and arrange the new ones. For herself, she did nothing but race through the front bedrooms, jump on and off the beds, and lie on the mattresses and stacked pillows before the roaring fires. She was excused from lessons: Mrs. Fairfax had pressed me into service, and I spent all day in the storeroom, helping (or hindering) her and the cook—learning to make custards and cheesecakes and French pastry, to truss game and garnish dessert dishes.

The party was expected to arrive on Thursday afternoon, in time for dinner at six. During the wait, I had no time to nurse fantasies, and I believe I was as active and cheerful as anyone—except Adèle. Still, now and then, something dampened my spirits and threw me back, despite myself, into the territory of doubt and dark speculation. This happened when I chanced to see the third-floor staircase door (which lately had always been kept locked) open slowly and give passage to Grace Poole, in her neat cap, white apron, and handkerchief. I watched her glide along the gallery, her quiet step muffled in a cloth slipper; I saw her look into the busy, upside-down bedrooms, perhaps say a word to the charwoman about the proper way to polish a grate, clean a marble mantelpiece, or remove stains from wallpaper, and then move on. She would descend to the kitchen once a day, eat her dinner, smoke a moderate pipe by the hearth, and go back, carrying her pot of porter for her own private comfort to her gloomy upper rooms. Only one hour out of twenty-four did she spend with the other servants below; the rest of her time was spent in some low-ceilinged, oak-panelled room on the second floor. There she sat and sewed—and probably laughed bleakly to herself—as solitary as a prisoner in a dungeon.

The strangest thing of all was that no one in the house except me noticed her habits or seemed to find them remarkable. No one discussed her position or employment; no one pitied her solitude. Once, indeed, I overheard part of a conversation between Leah and one of the charwomen, in which Grace was the subject. Leah had said something I didn't catch, and the charwoman replied—
"She gets good wages, I expect?"

"Yes," said Leah. "I wish I had as good—not that mine are anything to complain about; there's no stinginess at Thornfield. But they are not one-fifth of what Mrs. Poole receives. And she is saving: she goes every quarter to the bank at Millcote. I wouldn't be surprised if she has saved enough to live independently if she chose. But I suppose she's used to the place; and she's not yet forty, and strong and capable. It's too soon for her to retire."
"She is good at her job, I daresay," said the charwoman.
"Ah—she understands what she has to do, nobody better," replied Leah pointedly. "And not everyone could fill her shoes—not for all the money she gets."
"That's the truth!" was the reply. "I wonder whether the master—"
The charwoman was going on; but here Leah turned and noticed me, and she instantly nudged her companion.
"Doesn't she know?" I heard the woman whisper.
Leah shook her head, and the conversation naturally stopped. All I had gathered from it came to this: that there was a mystery at Thornfield, and that I was deliberately excluded from it.

Thursday came. All the work had been finished the night before: carpets were laid, bed hangings arranged, gleaming white counterpanes spread, dressing tables set up, furniture polished, flowers piled in vases. Both bedrooms and reception rooms looked as fresh and bright as human effort could make them. The hall, too, was scrubbed, and the great carved clock, as well as the staircase steps and banisters, were polished to the brightness of glass. In the dining room, the sideboard blazed with silver plate. In the drawing room and boudoir, vases of exotic flowers bloomed on every side.

Afternoon arrived. Mrs. Fairfax put on her best black satin dress, her gloves, and her gold watch, since it was her role to receive the company and show the ladies to their rooms. Adèle, too, was to be dressed, though I thought she had little chance of being introduced to the party that day. Still, to please her, I let Sophie put her in one of her short, full muslin frocks. For myself, I needed no change; I would not be called from my sanctuary of the schoolroom—for a sanctuary it had now become to me, a most welcome refuge in time of trouble.

It had been a mild, serene spring day—one of those days near the end of March or the beginning of April that rise shining over the earth as heralds of summer. It was drawing to a close now, but the evening was still warm, and I sat working in the schoolroom with the window open.

"It's getting late," said Mrs. Fairfax, entering in rustling grandeur. "I'm glad I ordered dinner an hour after the time Mr. Rochester mentioned, because it's past six now. I've sent John down to the gates to look for them—you can see a long way from there toward Millcote." She went to the window. "Here he is! Well, John"—leaning out—"any news?"
"They're coming, ma'am," was the answer. "They'll be here in ten minutes."
Adèle flew to the window. I followed, taking care to stand to one side so that, screened by the curtain, I could see without being seen.

The ten minutes John had given seemed very long, but at last wheels were heard. Four riders galloped up the drive, and after them came two open carriages. Fluttering veils and waving plumes filled the vehicles. Two of the horsemen were young, dashing-looking gentlemen; the third was Mr. Rochester, on his black horse Mesrour, Pilot bounding before him. At his side rode a lady, and they were the first of the party. Her purple riding habit nearly swept the ground, her veil streamed long in the breeze; mingling with its transparent folds and gleaming through them shone rich raven ringlets.
"Miss Ingram!" exclaimed Mrs. Fairfax, and hurried away to her post below.

The cavalcade, following the curve of the drive, quickly turned the corner of the house, and I lost sight of it. Adèle now begged to go down; but I took her on my knee and made her understand that she must not on any account think of appearing before the ladies, now or at any other time, unless expressly sent for—that Mr. Rochester would be very angry, and so on. She shed a few natural tears at being told this, but as I began to look very stern, she agreed at last to wipe them.

A happy commotion was now audible in the hall: gentlemen's deep voices and ladies' silvery tones blending together, and rising above them all, though not loud, the resonant voice of the master of Thornfield Hall, welcoming his handsome and gallant guests under his roof. Then light steps ascended the stairs, and there was tripping along the gallery, soft cheerful laughter, and opening and closing of doors, and then, for a time, quiet.
"Elles changent de toilettes," said Adèle, who had been listening to every movement, and she sighed.

"Chez maman," she said, "quand il y avait du monde, je le suivais partout, au salon et à leurs chambres; souvent je regardais les femmes de chambre coiffer et habiller les dames, et c'était si amusant: comme cela on apprend."
"Don't you feel hungry, Adèle?"
"Mais oui, mademoiselle: voilà cinq ou six heures que nous n'avons pas mangé."
"Well now, while the ladies are in their rooms, I will venture down and get you something to eat."

And slipping from my refuge with caution, I found a back staircase that led directly to the kitchen. Down there, all was fire and chaos: the soup and fish were in their final stages, and the cook hung over her pots in a state of mind and body threatening spontaneous combustion. In the servants' hall, two coachmen and three gentlemen's valets stood or sat around the fire; the ladies' maids, I supposed, were upstairs with their mistresses; the new servants hired from Millcote bustled everywhere. Threading my way through this confusion, I finally reached the larder, where I took possession of a cold chicken, a roll of bread, some tarts, a plate or two, and a knife and fork. With this haul I made a hasty retreat. I had regained the gallery and was just shutting the back door behind me when an accelerated murmur warned me the ladies were about to emerge from their rooms. I could not reach the schoolroom without passing some of their doors, risking being caught with my cargo of food. So I stood still at this end of the gallery, which, having no window, was dark—quite dark now, for the sun had set and twilight was gathering.

Presently the rooms released their elegant occupants one after another. Each came out gaily, dresses gleaming through the dusk. For a moment they stood in a group at the far end of the gallery, conversing in sweet, subdued tones; then they descended the staircase almost as noiselessly as a bright mist rolling down a hill. Their collective appearance left me with an impression of high-born elegance such as I had never felt before.

I found Adèle peeping through the schoolroom door, which she held ajar. "What beautiful ladies!" she cried in English. "Oh, I wish I could go to them! Do you think Mr. Rochester will send for us after dinner?"
"No, indeed I don't. Mr. Rochester has other things on his mind. Never mind the ladies tonight; perhaps you will see them tomorrow. Here is your dinner."

She was genuinely hungry, so the chicken and tarts held her attention for a while. It was lucky I had secured this food, or she, Sophie, and I—I brought Sophie a share of our meal—would have risked going without dinner entirely. Everyone downstairs was too busy to think of us. Dessert was not cleared until after nine, and at ten, footmen were still running back and forth with trays and coffee cups. I let Adèle stay up much later than usual, since she declared she could not possibly sleep while doors kept opening and closing below and people hurried about. Besides, she added, a message might still come from Mr. Rochester when she was undressed—"et alors quel dommage!"

I told her stories as long as she would listen, and then for a change I took her into the gallery. The hall lamp was now lit, and it amused her to lean over the balustrade and watch the servants passing below. When the evening was far advanced, music drifted from the drawing room, where the piano had been moved. Adèle and I sat on the top step of the stairs to listen. A voice blended with the rich tones of the instrument: it was a lady singing, and very sweet her notes were. After the solo came a duet, then a glee; cheerful murmurs of conversation filled the intervals. I listened for a long time; suddenly I realized my ear was entirely focused on sorting out the mingled sounds, trying to pick out Mr. Rochester's voice from the rest. When I caught it, which I soon did, I found a further task in shaping the tones, made indistinct by distance, into words.

The clock struck eleven. I looked at Adèle, whose head was leaning against my shoulder, her eyes growing heavy. I picked her up in my arms and carried her to bed. It was nearly one before the gentlemen and ladies retired to their rooms.

The next day was as fine as the one before. The party devoted it to an excursion to some nearby site. They set out early in the morning, some on horseback, the rest in carriages. I watched both the departure and the return. Miss Ingram, as before, was the only lady on horseback, and as before, Mr. Rochester galloped at her side; the two rode a little apart from the rest. I pointed this out to Mrs. Fairfax, who was standing at the window with me—
"You said it was unlikely they would think of marrying," I observed, "but you see Mr. Rochester clearly prefers her to any of the other ladies."
"Yes, I daresay: no doubt he admires her."
"And she him," I added. "Look how she leans her head toward him as though speaking confidentially. I wish I could see her face; I haven't caught a glimpse of it yet."

"You will see her this evening," answered Mrs. Fairfax. "I happened to mention to Mr. Rochester how much Adèle wished to be introduced to the ladies, and he said: 'Oh! let her come to the drawing room after dinner; and ask Miss Eyre to come with her.'"
"Yes—he said that out of mere politeness. I need not go, I'm sure," I answered.

"Well, I told him that since you were unused to company, I didn't think you would enjoy appearing before so large and fashionable a group, all strangers; and he replied, in his quick way, 'Nonsense! If she objects, tell her it is my particular wish; and if she resists, say I shall come and fetch her personally.'"
"I won't give him that trouble," I answered. "I will go, if I must; but I don't like it. Will you be there, Mrs. Fairfax?"

"No; I begged off, and he accepted my excuse. I'll tell you how to manage so as to avoid the embarrassment of a formal entrance, which is the worst part. Go into the drawing room while it is empty, before the ladies leave the dinner table; find yourself a seat in any quiet corner you like. You needn't stay long after the gentlemen come in, unless you want to; just let Mr. Rochester see you are there and then slip away. Nobody will notice you."
"Will these people stay long, do you think?"

"Perhaps two or three weeks, certainly not more. After the Easter recess, Sir George Lynn, who was recently elected member for Millcote, will have to go up to London to take his seat. I imagine Mr. Rochester will go with him. It surprises me that he has already stayed so long at Thornfield."

It was with some nervousness that I watched the hour approach when I was to take Adèle down to the drawing room. She had been in a state of ecstasy all day, since hearing she was to be presented to the ladies that evening, and it was only when Sophie began dressing her that she calmed down. Then the importance of the process quickly sobered her, and by the time she had her curls arranged in smooth, drooping clusters, her pink satin frock put on, her long sash tied, and her lace mittens adjusted, she looked as grave as a judge. There was no need to warn her not to disarrange her outfit; once dressed, she sat demurely in her little chair, first carefully lifting up the satin skirt so as not to crease it, and assured me she would not stir until I was ready. I was ready quickly: my best dress (the silver-grey one, bought for Miss Temple's wedding and never worn since) was soon on; my hair was smoothed; my one ornament, the pearl brooch, was pinned in place. We went down.

Fortunately there was another entrance to the drawing room besides the one through the salon where they all sat at dinner. We found the room empty: a large fire burning silently on the marble hearth, and wax candles shining in bright solitude amid the exquisite flowers that adorned the tables. The crimson curtain hung before the arch; slight as this barrier was between us and the party in the adjoining salon, they spoke in such low tones that nothing of their conversation could be made out beyond a soothing murmur.

Adèle, still under the influence of something like awe, sat down without a word on the footstool I pointed out to her. I retreated to a window seat, and taking a book from a nearby table, tried to read. Adèle brought her stool to my feet; before long, she touched my knee.
"What is it, Adèle?"
"Est-ce que je ne puis pas prendre une seule de ces fleurs magnifiques, mademoiselle? Seulement pour compléter ma toilette."

"You think too much about your appearance, Adèle—but you may have a flower." I took a rose from a vase and fastened it in her sash. She sighed with deep satisfaction, as if her cup of happiness were now full. I turned my face away to hide a smile I could not suppress: there was something both funny and touching in the little Parisian girl's earnest, inborn devotion to matters of dress.

A soft sound of movement now became audible; the curtain was swept back from the arch; through it appeared the dining room, with its lit chandelier pouring light down on the silver and glass of a magnificent dessert service covering a long table. A line of ladies stood in the opening; they entered, and the curtain fell behind them.

There were only eight, yet somehow, as they swept in, they gave the impression of a much larger number. Some were very tall; many wore white; and all had a flowing amplitude of dress that seemed to magnify their figures as a mist magnifies the moon. I rose and curtsied to them. One or two bent their heads in return; the rest only stared at me.

They spread about the room, reminding me, by the lightness and buoyancy of their movements, of a flock of white-plumed birds. Some threw themselves in half-reclining positions on the sofas and ottomans; some bent over the tables to examine the flowers and books; the rest gathered in a group around the fire. All spoke in a low but clear tone that seemed habitual. I learned their names afterwards, and may as well give them now.

First, there was Mrs. Eshton and two of her daughters. She had clearly been a handsome woman and was well preserved still. Of her daughters, the eldest, Amy, was rather small—naive and childlike in face and manner, with a pretty figure. Her white muslin dress and blue sash suited her well. The second, Louisa, was taller and more elegant; with a very pretty face, of the kind the French call a cheeky little face. Both sisters were fair as lilies.

Lady Lynn was a large, stout woman of about forty, very upright, very haughty-looking, richly dressed in a satin robe of shimmering colour. Her dark hair shone glossily beneath an azure plume, and within a circlet of gems.

Mrs. Colonel Dent was less showy but, I thought, more ladylike. She had a slight figure, a pale gentle face, and fair hair. Her black satin dress, her scarf of fine foreign lace, and her pearl ornaments pleased me better than the rainbow radiance of the titled dame.

But the three most striking—partly, perhaps, because the tallest of the group—were the Dowager Lady Ingram and her daughters, Blanche and Mary. All three were of the most imposing height for women. The Dowager might have been between forty and fifty; her figure was still fine; her hair (by candlelight at least) still black; her teeth, too, still apparently perfect. Most people would have called her a splendid woman for her age, and physically speaking, she was. But there was an expression of almost unbearable haughtiness in her bearing and face. She had Roman features and a double chin merging into a neck like a pillar—features that seemed to me not merely heavy and dark, but actually furrowed with pride; the chin was held up by the same principle, in a position of almost unnatural erectness. She also had a fierce, hard eye that reminded me of Mrs. Reed's. She mouthed her words when speaking; her voice was deep, her tone pompous, dogmatic—in short, intolerable. A crimson velvet robe and a turban of gold-embroidered Indian fabric gave her (she seemed to think) a truly imperial dignity.

Blanche and Mary were the same height—straight and tall as poplars. Mary was too slender for her stature, but Blanche had the build of a Diana. I studied her, naturally, with particular interest. First, I wanted to see whether her appearance matched Mrs. Fairfax's description; second, whether it resembled the miniature I had painted from imagination; and third—I may as well admit it—whether it was such as I would expect to appeal to Mr. Rochester.

As far as her person went, she matched both my picture and Mrs. Fairfax's description point for point. The noble figure, the sloping shoulders, the graceful neck, the dark eyes and black ringlets were all there. But her face? Her face was like her mother's—a youthful, unwrinkled copy: the same low brow, the same strong features, the same pride. It was not, however, quite so oppressive a pride; she laughed constantly, and her laugh was mocking, as was the habitual expression of her arched and haughty lip.

They say genius is self-aware. I cannot tell whether Miss Ingram was a genius, but she was certainly self-aware—remarkably so. She launched into a discussion of botany with the gentle Mrs. Dent. It seemed Mrs. Dent had not studied the science, though, as she said, she liked flowers, "especially wild ones." Miss Ingram had studied it, and she rattled off its vocabulary with an air. I soon realized she was mocking Mrs. Dent—that is, playing on her ignorance. Her mockery might have been clever, but it was decidedly unkind. She played the piano: her technique was brilliant. She sang: her voice was fine. She spoke French privately with her mother, and spoke it well, with fluency and a good accent.

Mary had a milder and more open face than Blanche, softer features too, and skin a few shades lighter (Miss Ingram was dark as a Spaniard). But Mary was deficient in life: her face lacked expression, her eye lustre; she had nothing to say, and once she had taken her seat, she sat fixed there like a statue in its niche. Both sisters were dressed in spotless white.

And did I now think Miss Ingram a likely choice for Mr. Rochester? I could not tell—I did not know his taste in female beauty. If he admired the majestic, she was majesty itself; and she was accomplished and spirited. Most gentlemen would admire her, I thought, and that he did admire her I already seemed to have proof. To settle the last shade of doubt, I only needed to see them together.

You are not to suppose, reader, that Adèle had been sitting motionless on the stool at my feet all this time. No—when the ladies entered, she had risen, walked up to them, made a stately curtsey, and said with gravity—
"Bon jour, mesdames."
Miss Ingram had looked down at her with a mocking expression and exclaimed, "Oh, what a little puppet!"
Lady Lynn had remarked, "It is Mr. Rochester's ward, I suppose—the little French girl he mentioned."
Mrs. Dent had kindly taken her hand and given her a kiss. Amy and Louisa Eshton had cried out together—
"What a darling child!"

And then they had called her to a sofa, where she now sat, ensconced between them, chattering alternately in French and broken English, absorbing the attention not only of the young ladies but of Mrs. Eshton and Lady Lynn, and getting spoiled to her heart's content.

At last coffee was brought in, and the gentlemen were summoned. I sat in the shadows—if there were any shadows in this brilliantly lit room; the window curtain half hid me. Again the arch opened; they came. The gentlemen's collective appearance, like the ladies', was imposing. They were all in black; most were tall, some young. Henry and Frederick Lynn were very dashing indeed, and Colonel Dent a fine soldierly man. Mr. Eshton, the local magistrate, was gentlemanly: his hair quite white, his eyebrows and whiskers still dark, giving him the air of a distinguished stage father. Lord Ingram, like his sisters, was very tall; like them, he was handsome; but he shared Mary's blank, listless look. He seemed to have more length of limb than energy of blood or vigour of mind.
And where was Mr. Rochester?

He came in last. I was not looking at the arch, yet I saw him enter. I tried to focus on the netting needles, on the meshes of the purse I was making—I wanted to think only of the work in my hands, to see only the silver beads and silk threads in my lap. Yet I saw his figure plainly, and I could not help remembering the last time I had seen it: just after I had done him what he called an essential service, and he, holding my hand and looking down at my face, had gazed at me with eyes that revealed a heart full and ready to overflow—in whose feelings I had a share. How close I had been to him at that moment! What had happened since to change our positions? Yet now, how distant, how far apart we were! So far apart that I did not expect him to come and speak to me. I did not wonder when, without looking my way, he took a seat on the other side of the room and began talking to some of the ladies.

The moment I saw his attention fixed on them, and that I could watch unobserved, my eyes were drawn involuntarily to his face. I could not keep my lids lowered: they would rise, and my gaze would fix on him. I looked, and I took a sharp pleasure in looking—precious yet painful; pure gold, with a steel point of agony. A pleasure like what a man dying of thirst might feel who knows the well he has crawled to is poisoned, yet stoops and drinks the divine water anyway.

It is perfectly true that "beauty is in the eye of the beholder." My master's colourless, olive face, his square, massive brow, broad dark eyebrows, deep eyes, strong features, firm grim mouth—all energy, decision, will—were not beautiful by any rule. But they were more than beautiful to me; they held an interest, an influence that completely mastered me, that seized my feelings from my own control and bound them to his. I had not intended to love him; the reader knows I had fought hard to root out the seeds of love I had found in myself. And now, at the first renewed sight of him, they sprang up green and strong! He made me love him without looking at me.

I compared him with his guests. What was the gallant grace of the Lynns, the languid elegance of Lord Ingram—even the military bearing of Colonel Dent—against his look of native strength and genuine power? I felt no affinity with their appearance or their expression; yet I could imagine that most people would call them handsome, impressive, attractive, while pronouncing Mr. Rochester harsh-featured and melancholy-looking. I watched them smile and laugh—it was nothing; the light of the candles had as much soul in it as their smiles, the tinkle of a bell as much meaning as their laughter. I saw Mr. Rochester smile: his stern features softened; his eye grew both brilliant and gentle, its light both searching and sweet. He was talking at that moment to Louisa and Amy Eshton. I wondered to see them receive calmly a look that seemed to me so piercing. I expected their eyes to drop, their colour to rise; yet I was glad when they showed no such reaction. "He is not to them what he is to me," I thought. "He is not of their kind. I believe he is of mine—I am sure of it—I feel akin to him—I understand the language of his face and movements. Though rank and wealth separate us widely, I have something in my brain and heart, my blood and nerves, that links me to him in spirit. Did I say, a few days ago, that I had nothing to do with him beyond collecting my salary? Did I forbid myself to think of him except as an employer? Blasphemy against nature! Every good, true, strong feeling I have gathers instinctively around him. I know I must hide what I feel; I must smother hope; I must remember that he cannot care much for me. For when I say I am of his kind, I do not mean I have his power to influence or his spell to attract; I mean only that I share certain tastes and feelings with him. I must continually repeat that we are forever separated—and yet, while I breathe and think, I must love him."

Coffee was served. The ladies, since the gentlemen entered, had grown lively as larks; conversation was brisk and merry. Colonel Dent and Mr. Eshton debated politics while their wives listened. The two proud dowagers, Lady Lynn and Lady Ingram, talked together in a corner. Sir George—whom, by the way, I have forgotten to describe: a very large, very ruddy country gentleman—stood before their sofa, coffee cup in hand, occasionally putting in a word. Mr. Frederick Lynn had sat down beside Mary Ingram and was showing her the engravings in a splendid book; she looked, smiled now and then, but said little. The tall, phlegmatic Lord Ingram leaned with folded arms on the back of little, lively Amy Eshton's chair; she glanced up at him and chattered like a wren—she liked him better than Mr. Rochester. Henry Lynn had claimed an ottoman at Louisa's feet; Adèle shared it with him, and he was trying to speak French with her while Louisa laughed at his blunders. With whom would Blanche Ingram pair? She stood alone at a table, bending gracefully over an album. She seemed to be waiting to be approached; but she would not wait long—she would choose her own partner.
Mr. Rochester, having left the Eshtons, stood on the hearth as solitary as she stood by the table. She confronted him, taking her position on the opposite side of the mantelpiece.
"Mr. Rochester, I thought you were not fond of children?"
"Nor am I."
"Then what made you take charge of such a little doll as that?"—pointing to Adèle. "Where did you pick her up?"
"I did not pick her up; she was left on my hands."
"You should have sent her to school."
"I could not afford it: schools are so expensive."

"Why, I suppose you have a governess for her. I saw someone with her just now—is she gone? Oh no! There she is still, behind the window curtain. You pay her, of course; I should think that is just as expensive—more so, since you have to keep both of them."
I feared—or should I say, hoped?—the reference to me would make Mr. Rochester glance my way. I involuntarily shrank further into the shadows. But he never turned his eyes.
"I have not thought about it," he said indifferently, looking straight ahead.

"No, you men never do think about economy and common sense. You should hear mama on the subject of governesses. Mary and I have had, I should think, at least a dozen in our day; half of them detestable and the rest ridiculous, and all of them a plague—weren't they, mama?"
"Did you say something, my dear?"
The young lady, thus claimed as the dowager's special property, repeated her question with an explanation.
"My dearest, don't mention governesses; the word makes me nervous. I have suffered a martyrdom from their incompetence and their whims. I thank heaven I have done with them now!"
Mrs. Dent here leaned over to the pious lady and whispered something in her ear; I suppose, from the answer it drew, it was a reminder that a member of the hated tribe was present.

"So much the worse!" said her ladyship. "I hope it may do her good!" Then, in a lower tone, but still loud enough for me to hear: "I noticed her; I am a judge of faces, and in hers I see all the faults of her class."
"What are they, madam?" Mr. Rochester asked aloud.
"I will tell you privately," she replied, wagging her turban three times with great significance.
"But my curiosity will have lost its appetite by then; it craves food now."
"Ask Blanche; she is nearer you than I."

"Oh, don't refer him to me, mama! I have just one word for the whole tribe: they are a plague. Not that I ever suffered much from them—I took care to turn the tables. The tricks Theodore and I used to play on our Miss Wilsons and Mrs. Greys and Madame Jouberts! Mary was always too sleepy to join a plot with any spirit. The best fun was with Madame Joubert: Miss Wilson was a poor sickly creature, tearful and low-spirited—not worth the trouble of conquering, really—and Mrs. Grey was coarse and thick-skinned; nothing bothered her. But poor Madame Joubert! I can still see her in her towering rages, when we had pushed her to the limit—spilling our tea, crumbling our bread and butter, flinging our books at the ceiling, and making a racket with the ruler and desk, the fender and fire-irons. Theodore, do you remember those merry days?"

"Yeeees, of course I do," drawled Lord Ingram. "And the poor old stick used to cry, 'Oh you villains children!'—and then we lectured her on the presumption of trying to teach clever ones like us, when she was so ignorant herself."

"We did; and Tedo, you know, I helped you persecute your tutor too—pasty-faced Mr. Vining, 'the parson in the pip' as we called him. He and Miss Wilson took the liberty of falling in love with each other—at least Tedo and I thought so; we caught various tender glances and sighs which we interpreted as tokens of passion, and I assure you the public soon benefited from our discovery. We used it as a lever to hoist those dead weights out of the house. Dear mama, the moment she got wind of it, decided the whole business was immoral. Didn't you, my lady-mother?"

"Certainly, my dear. And I was quite right—depend on it. There are a thousand reasons why romances between governesses and tutors should never be tolerated for a moment in any well-regulated house. First—"

"Oh, mercy, mama! Spare us the list! We all know them: danger of setting a bad example for innocent children; distraction and consequent neglect of duty on the part of those involved; the mutual alliance and dependence; the familiarity that follows; the insolence that accompanies it; the rebellion and the general explosion. Am I right, Baroness Ingram of Ingram Park?"
"My lily-flower, you are right now, as always."
"Then nothing more need be said: change the subject."

Amy Eshton, either not hearing or not heeding this command, joined in with her soft, childlike voice: "Louisa and I used to tease our governess too; but she was such a good soul, she would bear anything. Nothing upset her. She was never cross with us—was she, Louisa?"
"No, never. We could do whatever we pleased—ransack her desk and workbox, turn her drawers inside out—and she was so good-natured she would give us anything we asked for."

"I suppose," said Miss Ingram, curling her lip sarcastically, "we are now to hear the memoirs of every governess in existence. To prevent such a calamity, I propose a new topic. Mr. Rochester, do you second my motion?"
"Madam, I support you on this, as on every point."
"Then the responsibility of introducing it falls on me. Signior Eduardo, are you in voice tonight?"
"Donna Bianca, if you command it, I shall be."
"Then, signior, I lay upon you my royal command to warm up your lungs and vocal apparatus, as they will be needed in my service."
"Who would not be the Rizzio of so divine a Mary?"

"A fig for Rizzio!" she cried, tossing her head with all its curls, as she moved to the piano. "In my opinion the fiddler David must have been an insipid sort of fellow. I prefer black Bothwell: to my mind a man is nothing without a dash of the devil in him; and whatever history may say about James Hepburn, I have a feeling he was just the sort of wild, fierce, outlaw hero I could have consented to give my hand to."
"Gentlemen, you hear! Now which of you most resembles Bothwell?" cried Mr. Rochester.
"I should say the honour falls to you," Colonel Dent replied.
"On my word, I am much obliged to you," was the answer.

Miss Ingram, who had now seated herself with proud grace at the piano, spreading out her white skirts in queenly abundance, launched into a brilliant prelude, talking all the while. She was clearly riding high tonight; both her words and her manner seemed designed to strike her audience as something very dashing and daring indeed.

"Oh, I am so sick of the young men of today!" she exclaimed, rattling away at the keys. "Poor, feeble things, not fit to take a step beyond papa's park gates—or even that far without mama's permission and chaperoning! Creatures so obsessed with their pretty faces and their white hands and their small feet, as if a man had anything to do with beauty! As if loveliness were not the special right of women—our rightful inheritance! I grant that an ugly woman is a stain on creation; but as for men, let them have only strength and courage; let their motto be: Hunt, shoot, and fight—the rest is not worth a snap of the fingers. That would be my motto, were I a man."

"Whenever I marry," she continued after a pause which no one interrupted, "I am resolved my husband shall not be my rival but my foil. I will tolerate no competitor near the throne; I shall demand undivided devotion. His worship shall not be split between me and the face he sees in his mirror. Mr. Rochester, now sing, and I will play for you."
"I am all obedience," he replied.
"Here, then, is a Corsair song. You should know that I adore Corsairs; so sing it con spirito."
"Commands from Miss Ingram's lips would put spirit into a glass of water."
"Be careful, then: if you don't please me, I shall shame you by showing how it should be done."
"That is offering a prize for incompetence: I shall now try to fail."
"Don't you dare! If you fail on purpose, I shall devise a fitting punishment."
"Miss Ingram should be merciful, since she has the power to inflict a punishment beyond human endurance."
"Ha! Explain!" she commanded.
"Pardon me, madam: no explanation needed. Your own fine judgment must tell you that one of your frowns would be punishment enough to replace the death sentence."
"Sing!" she said, and touching the piano again, she struck up an accompaniment in spirited style.

"Now is my chance to slip away," I thought. But the tones that then filled the air stopped me. Mrs. Fairfax had said Mr. Rochester possessed a fine voice, and he did—a mellow, powerful bass into which he poured his own feeling and force, finding a path through the ear to the heart and there stirring something strange and deep. I waited until the last full, resonant vibration had died away—until the tide of talk, briefly checked, had resumed its flow. Then I left my sheltered corner and made my exit by the side door, which was fortunately close. From there a narrow passage led to the hall. Crossing it, I noticed my shoe was loose; I stopped to tie it, kneeling on the mat at the foot of the staircase. I heard the dining room door open; a gentleman came out. Rising quickly, I stood face to face with him: it was Mr. Rochester.
"How do you do?" he asked.
"I am very well, sir."
"Why did you not come and speak to me in the room?"
I thought I might have turned the question back on him, but I would not take that liberty. I answered—
"I did not wish to disturb you, as you seemed busy, sir."
"What have you been doing while I was away?"
"Nothing special; teaching Adèle as usual."
"And getting a good deal paler than you were—as I saw at once. What is the matter?"
"Nothing at all, sir."
"Did you catch cold that night you half drowned me?"
"Not in the least."
"Return to the drawing room: you are leaving too early."
"I am tired, sir."
He looked at me for a moment.
"And a little depressed," he said. "What about? Tell me."
"Nothing—nothing, sir. I am not depressed."

"But I say you are: so much depressed that a few more words would bring tears to your eyes—indeed, they are there now, shining and swimming; and a drop has slipped from your lashes and fallen to the floor. If I had time, and were not in mortal dread of some chattering servant walking past, I would find out what all this means. Well, tonight I excuse you; but understand that as long as my guests are here, I expect you to appear in the drawing room every evening. It is my wish; don't neglect it. Now go, and send Sophie for Adèle. Goodnight, my—" He stopped, bit his lip, and abruptly left me.

chapters.title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Those were merry days at Thornfield Hall, and busy ones too—how different from the first three months of stillness, monotony, and solitude I had spent under its roof! All sadness seemed driven from the house now, all gloomy associations forgotten. There was life everywhere, movement all day long. You could not walk the gallery, once so hushed, or enter the front bedrooms, once so empty, without running into a smart lady's maid or a fashionable valet.

The kitchen, the butler's pantry, the servants' hall, the entrance hall were equally alive; and the drawing rooms stood empty and still only when the blue sky and golden sunshine of the fine spring weather drew their occupants outdoors. Even when the weather broke and steady rain set in for several days, it did not dampen anyone's enjoyment: the indoor amusements only grew livelier and more varied to compensate for the lost outdoor fun.

I wondered what they would do the first evening a change of entertainment was proposed. They spoke of "playing charades," but in my ignorance I did not know what that meant. The servants were called in, the dining room tables wheeled away, the lights rearranged, and chairs placed in a semicircle facing the arch. While Mr. Rochester and the other gentlemen directed these changes, the ladies ran up and down stairs ringing for their maids. Mrs. Fairfax was called upon to report what the house could supply in the way of shawls, dresses, and draperies of any kind. Certain wardrobes on the third floor were ransacked, and their contents—brocaded and hooped petticoats, satin capes, black silk gowns, lace caps, and the like—were brought down in armloads by the maids. A selection was made, and the chosen items were carried to the boudoir off the drawing room.

Meanwhile, Mr. Rochester had again gathered the ladies around him and was choosing certain ones for his team. "Miss Ingram is mine, of course," he said. He then named the two Misses Eshton and Mrs. Dent. He looked at me: I happened to be near him, as I had been fastening the clasp of Mrs. Dent's bracelet, which had come loose.
"Will you play?" he asked. I shook my head. He did not press the point, which I rather feared he would; he let me return quietly to my usual seat.

He and his team now withdrew behind the curtain; the other group, led by Colonel Dent, sat down on the crescent of chairs. One of the gentlemen, Mr. Eshton, noticed me and seemed about to suggest I join them; but Lady Ingram instantly vetoed the idea.
"No," I heard her say. "She looks too stupid for any game of the sort."

Before long a bell tinkled and the curtain rose. Within the arch, the bulky figure of Sir George Lynn, whom Mr. Rochester had also chosen, stood wrapped in a white sheet. Before him on a table lay an open book, and beside him stood Amy Eshton, draped in Mr. Rochester's cloak and holding a book in her hand. Someone unseen rang the bell merrily; then Adèle (who had insisted on joining her guardian's team) bounded forward, scattering flowers from a basket on her arm. Then appeared the magnificent figure of Miss Ingram, dressed in white, a long veil on her head and a wreath of roses around her brow; beside her walked Mr. Rochester, and together they approached the table. They knelt, while Mrs. Dent and Louisa Eshton, also in white, took their places behind them. A ceremony followed in pantomime, easily recognizable as a wedding. When it was over, Colonel Dent and his group whispered together for two minutes, then the Colonel called out—
"Bride!" Mr. Rochester bowed, and the curtain fell.

A considerable pause followed before it rose again. The second scene was more elaborately staged than the first. The drawing room, as I have mentioned, was raised two steps above the dining room, and on the top step, set a yard or two back, stood a large marble basin—I recognized it as an ornament from the conservatory, where it usually stood surrounded by exotic plants and occupied by goldfish. It must have been moved with some difficulty, given its size and weight.

Seated on the carpet beside this basin was Mr. Rochester, wrapped in shawls, with a turban on his head. His dark eyes, swarthy skin, and exotic features suited the costume perfectly: he looked like an Eastern ruler, an agent or victim of the sultan's justice. Presently Miss Ingram advanced into view. She too was dressed in oriental fashion: a crimson scarf tied like a sash around her waist, an embroidered handkerchief knotted about her temples, her beautifully shaped arms bare, one raised in the act of balancing a pitcher on her head. Her figure and features, her complexion and general air all suggested an Israelite princess from the days of the patriarchs—and that was clearly the character she intended to portray.

She approached the basin and bent over it as if filling her pitcher, then lifted it to her head again. The figure at the well's edge seemed to address her, to make some request. "She hurried, let down her pitcher on her hand, and gave him to drink." From his robe he then produced a casket, opened it, and revealed magnificent bracelets and earrings. She acted out astonishment and admiration; kneeling, he laid the treasure at her feet. Disbelief and delight showed in her looks and gestures; the stranger fastened the bracelets on her arms and the rings in her ears. It was Eliezer and Rebecca: only the camels were missing.

The guessing party put their heads together again: apparently they could not agree on the word or syllable the scene illustrated. Colonel Dent, their spokesman, asked for "the full tableau," and the curtain descended once more.

When it rose a third time, only part of the drawing room was visible; the rest was hidden behind a screen hung with some dark, coarse material. The marble basin was gone; in its place stood a plain table and a kitchen chair, lit only by the dim glow of a lantern, all the wax candles having been put out.

In this squalid setting sat a man with clenched fists resting on his knees and his eyes fixed on the ground. I recognized Mr. Rochester, though the grimy face, the disordered clothes (his coat hanging from one arm as if nearly torn off in a struggle), the desperate, scowling expression, and the rough, bristling hair might well have disguised him. As he moved, a chain clanked: his wrists were shackled.
"Bridewell!" exclaimed Colonel Dent, and the charade was solved.
After enough time for the performers to change back into their regular clothes, they returned to the dining room. Mr. Rochester led in Miss Ingram; she was praising his acting.
"Do you know," she said, "that of the three characters, I liked you best in the last? Oh, if only you had lived a few years earlier, what a gallant highwayman you would have made!"
"Is all the soot washed from my face?" he asked, turning it toward her.
"Alas, yes—the worse for it! Nothing could suit your complexion better than that ruffian's grime."
"You would like a highwayman, then?"
"An English highwayman would be next best to an Italian bandit—and that could only be surpassed by a Mediterranean pirate."
"Well, whatever I am, remember you are my wife; we were married an hour ago, before all these witnesses." She giggled, and her colour rose.

"Now, Dent," Mr. Rochester continued, "it's your turn." And as the other group withdrew, he and his team took the empty chairs. Miss Ingram placed herself at her leader's right hand; the other guessers filled the chairs on either side. I no longer watched the actors; I no longer waited with interest for the curtain to rise. My attention was absorbed by the audience; my eyes, previously fixed on the arch, were now irresistibly drawn to the semicircle of chairs. What charade Colonel Dent's group performed, what word they chose, how they managed it—I no longer remember. But I still see the consultation that followed each scene: I see Mr. Rochester turn to Miss Ingram, and Miss Ingram to him; I see her lean her head toward his, until the jet-black curls almost touch his shoulder and brush against his cheek; I hear their murmured exchanges; I recall their exchanged glances; and something of the feeling that spectacle aroused returns to me even now.

I have told you, reader, that I had learned to love Mr. Rochester: I could not stop loving him now merely because I found he had ceased to notice me—because I might spend hours in his presence and he would never once look my way—because I saw all his attention claimed by a great lady who scorned to let the hem of her robe touch me as she passed, and who, if her dark imperious eye happened to fall on me, would withdraw it instantly, as from an object too worthless to deserve notice. I could not stop loving him because I felt sure he would soon marry this very lady—because I read daily in her a proud confidence in his intentions—because I witnessed hourly a style of courtship from him which, if careless and content to be pursued rather than to pursue, was yet, in its very carelessness, captivating, and in its very pride, irresistible.

There was nothing in these circumstances to cool or extinguish love, though much to create despair. Much too, you might think, reader, to breed jealousy—if a woman in my position could presume to be jealous of a woman in Miss Ingram's. But I was not jealous, or very rarely. The nature of my pain could not be captured by that word. Miss Ingram was beneath jealousy: she was too inferior to provoke it. Forgive the apparent contradiction—I mean what I say. She was very showy, but she was not genuine. She had a fine figure and many brilliant accomplishments, but her mind was poor and her heart barren by nature: nothing bloomed spontaneously in that soil; no natural, unforced fruit delighted by its freshness. She was not good; she was not original. She repeated grand-sounding phrases from books; she never offered, nor had, an opinion of her own. She championed lofty sentiments, but she did not know sympathy or pity; tenderness and truth were not in her. Too often she revealed this through the disproportionate spite she directed at little Adèle—pushing her away with some insulting remark if the child came near, sometimes ordering her from the room, always treating her with coldness and hostility. Other eyes besides mine observed these glimpses of her character—watched them closely, keenly, shrewdly. Yes: the prospective bridegroom, Mr. Rochester himself, maintained a ceaseless watch over his intended; and it was from this very perceptiveness of his—this wariness—this clear-eyed awareness of his beauty's flaws—this obvious absence of passion in his feelings toward her—that my ever-present torment arose.

I saw he was going to marry her for family, perhaps political reasons, because her rank and connections suited him. I felt he had not given her his love, and that her qualities were poorly suited to win it. This was the point—this was where the nerve was touched and teased—this was where the fever was kept alive: she could not charm him.

If she had won the victory outright, and he had yielded and sincerely laid his heart at her feet, I would have covered my face, turned to the wall, and (in a manner of speaking) died. If Miss Ingram had been a good and noble woman, gifted with strength, warmth, kindness, and sense, I would have fought one desperate battle with two enemies—jealousy and despair. Then, my heart torn out and devoured, I would have admired her, acknowledged her excellence, and been still for the rest of my days; and the more complete her superiority, the deeper my admiration, the more genuine my peace. But as things actually stood, to watch Miss Ingram's efforts at captivating Mr. Rochester, to see them fail again and again—while she remained blind to her failure, imagining each arrow struck home, preening herself on success while her pride and vanity drove further and further away the very thing she wanted to attract—to witness this was to be under constant excitement and ruthless restraint at the same time.

Because when she failed, I saw how she might have succeeded. Arrows that continually bounced off Mr. Rochester's chest and fell harmless at his feet could, I knew, if shot by a surer hand, have pierced deep into his proud heart—could have drawn love into his stern eye and softness into his sardonic face. Or, better still, without any weapon at all, a silent conquest might have been won.

"Why can she not influence him more, when she has the privilege of being so close to him?" I asked myself. "Surely she cannot truly like him, or not with real affection! If she did, she would not need to manufacture smiles so lavishly, flash her eyes so relentlessly, or contrive such elaborate airs and graces. It seems to me that by merely sitting quietly at his side, saying little and looking less, she could get nearer his heart. I have seen in his face a very different expression from the one that hardens it now while she accosts him so vigorously; but that expression came of itself, not summoned by artificial charm and calculated manoeuvre. One had only to accept it—to answer his questions without pretension, to speak to him when needed without affectation—and it grew warmer and kinder, and enveloped you like nurturing sunlight. How will she manage to please him when they are married? I do not think she will; and yet it could be done, and his wife might, I truly believe, be the happiest woman the sun shines on."

I have not yet said anything critical of Mr. Rochester's plan to marry for status and connections. It surprised me when I first realized that was his intention: I had thought him a man unlikely to be guided by such ordinary motives in choosing a wife. But the longer I considered the position, education, and circumstances of both parties, the less justified I felt in judging or blaming either him or Miss Ingram for acting on ideas and principles drilled into them since childhood. Their entire class held these principles. I supposed they must have reasons I could not grasp. It seemed to me that if I were a gentleman like him, I would take to my heart only a wife I could love; but the very obviousness of how much better this would serve the husband's own happiness convinced me there must be arguments against it that I was quite ignorant of—otherwise surely everyone would act as I wished to act.

But in this and other respects, I was growing very lenient toward my master. I was forgetting all his faults, which I had once been so careful to track. It had formerly been my practice to study every side of his character, to weigh the bad against the good, and form a balanced judgment. Now I saw no bad. The sarcasm that had once repelled me, the harshness that had once startled me, were now only like sharp seasoning in a fine dish: their presence added bite, but their absence would have felt bland. And as for that vague something—was it sinister or sorrowful, calculating or despairing?—that showed itself now and then to a careful observer in his eye, and vanished again before one could plumb the strange depth briefly revealed; that something which used to make me afraid, as if I had been walking among volcanic hills and suddenly felt the earth tremble and saw it crack open: I still saw that something from time to time; and it made my heart pound, but no longer paralyzed my nerves. Instead of wanting to flee, I longed only to dare—to understand it. And I thought Miss Ingram fortunate, because one day she would be free to look into that abyss at her leisure, explore its secrets, and analyze what they meant.

Meanwhile, while I thought only of my master and his future bride—saw only them, heard only their talk, and cared only about their movements—the rest of the party were busy with their own interests and pleasures. Ladies Lynn and Ingram continued their solemn conferences, nodding their turbaned heads at each other and raising their hands in gestures of surprise, mystery, or horror according to their gossip's theme, like a pair of oversized puppets. Gentle Mrs. Dent chatted with good-natured Mrs. Eshton, and the two sometimes gave me a kind word or smile. Sir George Lynn, Colonel Dent, and Mr. Eshton discussed politics, county business, or matters of justice. Lord Ingram flirted with Amy Eshton; Louisa played and sang with one of the Lynn brothers; and Mary Ingram listened languidly to the flattery of the other. Sometimes all of them, as if by common consent, paused their own pursuits to watch the main players—for after all, Mr. Rochester and (because so closely connected with him) Miss Ingram were the life and soul of the party. If he was absent from the room for an hour, a noticeable dullness settled over his guests; his return always gave fresh energy to the conversation.

The lack of his animating presence was especially felt one day when he had been called to Millcote on business and was not expected back until late. The afternoon was wet: a walk the party had planned to a gypsy camp, recently pitched on a common beyond Hay, had to be postponed. Some of the gentlemen had gone to the stables; the younger ones, with the younger ladies, were playing billiards upstairs. The dowagers Ingram and Lynn consoled themselves with a quiet game of cards. Blanche Ingram, after rebuffing with haughty silence some attempts by Mrs. Dent and Mrs. Eshton to draw her into conversation, had first played some sentimental tunes on the piano, then fetched a novel from the library and flung herself in proud boredom on a sofa, prepared to use fiction to kill the tedious hours of Mr. Rochester's absence. The room and the house were quiet; only now and then the laughter of the billiard players could be heard from above.
It was nearing dusk, and the dressing bell had already sounded, when little Adèle, who was kneeling beside me in the drawing room window seat, suddenly exclaimed—
"Voilà Monsieur Rochester, qui revient!"

I turned, and Miss Ingram sprang from her sofa. The others, too, looked up from what they were doing, because at the same time the crunch of wheels and the splash of hooves became audible on the wet gravel. A post-chaise was approaching.
"What can possess him to come home like that?" said Miss Ingram. "He rode Mesrour, the black horse, when he went out, didn't he? And Pilot was with him. What has he done with them?"

As she said this, she brought her tall figure and ample skirts so close to the window that I had to bend back nearly to the breaking point of my spine. In her eagerness she did not notice me at first; but when she did, she curled her lip and moved to another window. The post-chaise stopped; the driver rang the doorbell, and a gentleman stepped out, dressed for travelling—but it was not Mr. Rochester. It was a tall, fashionable-looking man, a stranger.

"How annoying!" exclaimed Miss Ingram. "You tiresome little monkey!"—directing this at Adèle—"who put you in the window to give us false reports?" And she threw me an angry look, as if I were to blame.
Some discussion was audible in the hall, and soon the newcomer entered. He bowed to Lady Ingram, taking her for the eldest lady present.

"It appears I come at an awkward time, madam," he said, "since my friend Mr. Rochester is away from home. But I have come from a very long journey, and I think I may presume enough on old and close acquaintance to settle in here until he returns."

His manner was polite; his accent, when he spoke, struck me as somewhat unusual—not exactly foreign, but not entirely English either. His age might have been close to Mr. Rochester's, between thirty and forty. His complexion was strangely sallow; otherwise he was a fine-looking man, at first glance especially. On closer study, you noticed something in his face that displeased—or rather failed to please. His features were regular but too slack; his eye was large and well shaped, but the life in it was tame and vacant—at least so I thought.

The dressing bell broke up the company. It was not until after dinner that I saw him again; he then seemed perfectly at ease. But I liked his face even less than before: it struck me as being at once restless and lifeless. His eye wandered without purpose: this gave him a strange look unlike any I had seen before. For a handsome and not unpleasant-looking man, he repelled me strongly. There was no force in that smooth-skinned, oval face; no firmness in that straight nose and small, red mouth; no thought on the low, even forehead; no will in that blank, brown eye.

Sitting in my usual corner and studying him by the light of the candelabra on the mantelpiece, which shone full on him—for he had drawn his chair close to the fire and kept shrinking nearer, as if he were cold—I compared him with Mr. Rochester. The contrast, I thought (with all respect), could not have been greater if you set a sleek gander beside a fierce falcon, or a meek sheep next to the rough-coated, keen-eyed dog that guards it.
He had spoken of Mr. Rochester as an old friend. Theirs must have been a curious friendship—a perfect example of the old saying that opposites attract.

Two or three of the gentlemen sat near him, and I caught scraps of their conversation across the room. At first I could not make much sense of what I heard; the chatter of Louisa Eshton and Mary Ingram, who sat nearer to me, confused the fragments that reached me. These two were discussing the stranger; they both called him "a beautiful man." Louisa said he was "a love of a creature" and she "adored him;" Mary cited his "pretty little mouth and nice nose" as her idea of charming.
"And what a sweet-tempered forehead he has!" cried Louisa. "So smooth—none of those scowling lines I dislike so much—and such a calm eye and smile!"
Then, to my great relief, Mr. Henry Lynn called them to the other side of the room to settle some point about the postponed excursion to Hay Common.

I could now focus on the group by the fire, and I soon gathered that the newcomer was called Mr. Mason; that he had just arrived in England; and that he came from some hot country—which no doubt explained his sallow complexion, his habit of sitting so close to the hearth, and his wearing an overcoat indoors. Presently the words Jamaica, Kingston, Spanish Town indicated the West Indies as his home; and I was quite surprised to learn that he had first met and become acquainted with Mr. Rochester there. He mentioned his friend's dislike of the burning heat, the hurricanes, and the rainy seasons of that region. I knew Mr. Rochester had been a traveller—Mrs. Fairfax had told me so—but I had assumed his wanderings were limited to mainland Europe. Until now I had never heard any hint of visits to more distant shores.

I was pondering these things when a somewhat unexpected incident broke the thread of my thoughts. Mr. Mason, shivering when someone happened to open the door, asked for more coal on the fire, which had burned down to glowing embers. The footman who brought the coal, on his way out, stopped beside Mr. Eshton's chair and said something to him in a low voice, of which I caught only the words "old woman" and "quite troublesome."
"Tell her she'll be put in the stocks if she doesn't take herself off," replied the magistrate.

"No—stop!" Colonel Dent interrupted. "Don't send her away, Eshton; we might make use of this. Better consult the ladies." Speaking louder, he continued, "Ladies, you talked about visiting the gypsy camp at Hay Common. Sam here says one of the old fortune-tellers is in the servants' hall at this very moment, insisting on being brought before 'the quality' to tell their fortunes. Would you like to see her?"
"Surely, Colonel," cried Lady Ingram, "you would not encourage such a low fraud? Send her away at once!"

"But I can't persuade her to go, my lady," said the footman, "nor can any of the servants. Mrs. Fairfax is with her now, begging her to leave; but she has planted herself in a chair by the kitchen fire and says nothing will shift her until she's allowed to come in here."
"What does she want?" asked Mrs. Eshton.
"To tell the gentry their fortunes, she says, ma'am; and she swears she must and will do it."
"What does she look like?" asked the Misses Eshton in unison.
"A shockingly ugly old creature, miss; almost as black as a crock."
"Why, she's a real sorceress!" cried Frederick Lynn. "Let us have her in, of course."
"Absolutely," his brother agreed. "It would be a thousand pities to waste such a chance for fun."
"My dear boys, what are you thinking of?" exclaimed Mrs. Lynn.
"I cannot possibly support any such absurd proceeding," declared the Dowager Ingram.

"Indeed, mama, but you can—and will," pronounced the haughty voice of Blanche, as she turned on the piano stool, where she had sat silent until now, apparently examining some sheets of music. "I am curious to hear my fortune told. Therefore, Sam, bring the old woman in."
"My darling Blanche! Consider—"
"I do—I consider everything you can suggest; and I must have my way. Quick, Sam!"
"Yes—yes—yes!" cried all the young people, ladies and gentlemen alike. "Let her come—it will be excellent sport!"
The footman still hesitated. "She looks very rough," he said.
