"Go!" commanded Miss Ingram, and the man went.
Excitement instantly seized the whole party: a rapid exchange of jokes and teasing was underway when Sam returned.

"She won't come now," he said. "She says it is not her mission to appear before 'the vulgar herd' (her words). I must show her into a room by herself, and then those who wish to consult her must go to her one by one."
"You see now, my queenly Blanche," Lady Ingram began, "she goes too far. Take my advice, my angel girl, and—"

"Show her into the library, of course," cut in the "angel girl." "It is not my mission to listen to her before the vulgar herd either. I mean to have her all to myself. Is there a fire in the library?"
"Yes, ma'am—but she looks like such a vagabond."
"Stop that chatter, blockhead! And do as I say."
Sam vanished again; and mystery, excitement, and anticipation rose to full flood once more.
"She's ready now," said the footman, reappearing. "She wants to know who will be her first visitor."
"I think I had better look in on her before any of the ladies go," said Colonel Dent.
"Tell her, Sam, a gentleman is coming."
Sam went and returned.
"She says, sir, that she'll have no gentlemen; they need not trouble themselves to come near her. Nor," he added, barely suppressing a grin, "any ladies either, except the young and single."
"By Jove, she has taste!" exclaimed Henry Lynn.
Miss Ingram rose with great solemnity. "I go first," she said, in a tone that might have suited the leader of a desperate charge, climbing a breach at the head of his men.
"Oh, my darling! Oh, my dearest! Pause—think!" was her mama's cry; but she swept past her in stately silence, passed through the door that Colonel Dent held open, and we heard her enter the library.

A relative hush followed. Lady Ingram saw fit to wring her hands, and did so accordingly. Miss Mary declared she, for one, would never dare go. Amy and Louisa Eshton giggled under their breath and looked a little frightened.
The minutes passed very slowly: fifteen were counted before the library door opened again. Miss Ingram returned through the arch.

Would she laugh? Would she treat it as a joke? Every eye met her with eager curiosity, and she met every eye with a look of cold rebuff. She looked neither flustered nor amused. She walked stiffly to her seat and sat down in silence.
"Well, Blanche?" said Lord Ingram.
"What did she say, sister?" asked Mary.
"What did you think? How do you feel? Is she a real fortune-teller?" demanded the Misses Eshton.

"Now, now, good people," returned Miss Ingram, "don't crowd me. Really, your sense of wonder is easily excited. You seem, judging by the importance you all—my good mama included—attach to this business, actually to believe we have a genuine witch in the house who is in league with the devil. I have seen a gypsy vagrant; she practised the standard tricks of palm reading and told me the usual things. My whim is satisfied; and now I think Mr. Eshton would do well to put the hag in the stocks tomorrow morning, as he threatened."

Miss Ingram took up a book, leaned back in her chair, and refused further conversation. I watched her for nearly half an hour: during all that time she never turned a page, and her face grew steadily darker, more dissatisfied, and more sour with disappointment. She had clearly not heard anything to her advantage; and it seemed to me, from her prolonged gloom and silence, that despite her professed indifference she took whatever had been revealed to her far more seriously than she wanted anyone to know.
During all that time she never turned a page.

Meanwhile, Mary Ingram, Amy, and Louisa Eshton declared they dared not go alone, yet they all wanted to go. A negotiation was opened through the ambassador Sam; and after much going back and forth—until I think poor Sam's legs must have ached with the exercise—permission was at last, with great difficulty, extracted from the stern sibyl for the three to visit her together.

Their visit was not so quiet as Miss Ingram's had been. We heard hysterical giggling and little shrieks from the library; and after about twenty minutes they burst through the door, running across the hall as if scared half out of their wits.

"I am sure she is something supernatural!" they cried, one and all. "She told us such things! She knows everything about us!" And they sank breathlessly into the various seats the gentlemen hurried to bring them.

Pressed for details, they declared she had told them things they had said and done as mere children, described books and ornaments they had in their rooms at home, and keepsakes that various relatives had given them. They swore she had even read their thoughts, and had whispered in each one's ear the name of the person she liked best in the world, and told them what they most wished for.

The gentlemen pressed with eager requests to hear more about these last two points; but they got only blushes, exclamations, trembling, and giggles in return. The older ladies meanwhile offered smelling salts and waved fans, and again and again lamented that their warnings had not been heeded. The older gentlemen laughed, and the younger ones offered their services to the agitated young women.
In the midst of this commotion, with my eyes and ears fully engaged in the scene before me, I heard a polite cough at my elbow. I turned and saw Sam.

"If you please, miss, the gypsy says there is another young single lady in the room who has not been to see her yet, and she vows she will not leave until she has seen everyone. I thought it must be you: there is no one else. What shall I tell her?"

"Oh, I will certainly go," I answered. I was glad of the unexpected chance to satisfy my considerable curiosity. I slipped out of the room unnoticed by anyone—for the whole company was clustered around the trembling trio who had just returned—and I closed the door quietly behind me.
"If you like, miss," said Sam, "I'll wait in the hall for you; and if she frightens you, just call and I'll come in."
"No, Sam, go back to the kitchen. I am not the least bit afraid." Nor was I; but I was very interested and excited.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: The library looked peaceful enough when I entered it, and the sibyl—if sibyl she was—sat snugly in an armchair by the fireplace. She wore a red cloak and a black bonnet, or rather a broad-brimmed gypsy hat tied down with a striped handkerchief under her chin. A dead candle stood on the table; she was hunched over the fire, apparently reading a little black book, like a prayer book, by the light of the flames. She muttered the words to herself, as old women tend to do, and did not stop immediately when I came in—she seemed to want to finish a paragraph.

I stood on the rug and warmed my hands, which were rather cold from sitting far from the drawing room fire. I felt as composed as I had ever been in my life: there was nothing in the gypsy's appearance to disturb anyone's calm. She closed her book and slowly looked up; her hat-brim partly shaded her face, yet I could see, as she raised it, that it was a strange one. It looked all brown and dark: tangled locks bristled out from beneath a white band that passed under her chin and came half over her cheeks, or rather her jaw. Her eye met mine at once, with a bold and direct stare.
"Well, and you want your fortune told?" she said, in a voice as decisive as her gaze, as harsh as her features.
"I don't much care about it, mother; please yourself. But I should warn you, I have no faith in such things."
"That's just like your impudence: I expected it of you. I heard it in your step as you crossed the threshold."
"Did you? You have a quick ear."
"I have; and a quick eye and a quick brain."
"You need them all in your line of work."
"I do; especially when I have customers like you to deal with. Why don't you tremble?"
"I'm not cold."
"Why don't you turn pale?"
"I'm not sick."
"Why don't you consult my art?"
"I'm not foolish."

The old woman cackled a laugh under her bonnet and bandage; then she drew out a short black pipe and, lighting it, began to smoke. After indulging in this for a while, she straightened her bent body, took the pipe from her lips, and while gazing steadily at the fire, said very deliberately—
"You are cold; you are sick; and you are foolish."
"Prove it," I replied.

"I will, in a few words. You are cold because you are alone: no contact strikes fire from the spark that is in you. You are sick because the best of feelings—the highest and sweetest given to humanity—stays far from you. You are foolish because, suffer as you may, you will not call it to you, nor will you take one step to meet it where it waits for you."
She put the short black pipe to her lips again and smoked with vigour.
"You might say all that to almost anyone who lived as a solitary dependent in a great house."
"I might say it to almost anyone: but would it be true of almost anyone?"
"In my circumstances, yes."
"Yes, exactly: in your circumstances. But find me another person in precisely your position."
"You could easily find thousands."

"You could hardly find one. If you only knew it, you are uniquely situated: very near happiness—yes, within reach of it. The materials are all prepared; there only needs a single movement to bring them together. Chance placed them slightly apart; let them once come close and happiness results."
"I don't understand riddles. I never could solve one in my life."
"If you wish me to speak more plainly, show me your palm."
"And I must cross it with silver, I suppose?"
"Of course."

I gave her a shilling. She tucked it into an old stocking foot that she took from her pocket, tied it up, put it back, and told me to hold out my hand. I did. She brought her face close to my palm and studied it without touching it.
"It is too smooth," she said. "I can make nothing of such a hand; almost without lines. Besides, what is in a palm? Destiny is not written there."
"I agree," I said.
"No," she continued, "it is in the face: on the forehead, around the eyes, in the lines of the mouth. Kneel, and lift your head."
"Ah! Now you are coming to something real," I said, as I obeyed. "I shall begin to believe you soon."
I knelt half a yard from her. She stirred the fire, so that a ripple of light broke from the shifted coals; but the glow, from where she sat, only threw her face into deeper shadow. Mine, it lit up.

"I wonder what feelings you came to me with tonight," she said, after studying me for a while. "I wonder what thoughts are busy in your heart during all the hours you sit in that room with the fine people flitting before you like figures in a magic lantern—as little real feeling passing between you and them as if they were merely shadows of human forms, not the actual substance."
"I feel tired often, sleepy sometimes, but rarely sad."
"Then you have some secret hope that buoys you up and whispers promises of the future?"
"Not at all. The most I hope for is to save enough from my wages to start a little school someday, in a house I rent myself."
"A thin diet for the spirit to live on. And sitting in that window seat (you see I know your habits)—"
"You have learned them from the servants."
"Ah! You think yourself sharp. Well, perhaps I have. To be honest, I have an acquaintance with one of them—Mrs. Poole—"
I jumped to my feet when I heard the name.
"You do? Do you?" I thought. "So there is something sinister in this after all!"

"Don't be alarmed," continued the strange figure. "She is safe enough, Mrs. Poole—discreet and quiet; anyone can trust her. But as I was saying: sitting in that window seat, do you think of nothing but your future school? Do you take no interest in any of the company who fill the sofas and chairs before you? Is there not one face you study? One figure whose movements you follow with at least curiosity?"
"I like to observe all the faces and all the figures."
"But do you never single one out from the rest—or perhaps two?"
"I often do, when a pair's gestures or looks seem to tell a story. It amuses me to watch them."
"What story do you like best?"
"Oh, I don't have much choice! They generally run on the same theme—courtship—and promise to end the same way—marriage."
"And do you enjoy that monotonous theme?"
"Honestly, I don't care about it. It is nothing to me."
"Nothing to you? When a lady, young and full of life and health, charming with beauty and blessed with rank and fortune, sits and smiles into the eyes of a gentleman you—"
"I what?"
"You know—and perhaps think well of."

"I don't know the gentlemen here. I have barely exchanged a word with any of them; and as for thinking well of them, I find some respectable, stately, and middle-aged, and others young, dashing, handsome, and lively. But they are all certainly free to receive whatever smiles they please, without my considering it any concern of mine."
"You don't know the gentlemen here? You haven't exchanged a word with any of them? Will you say that of the master of the house?"
"He is not at home."
"What a clever dodge! He went to Millcote this morning and will be back tonight or tomorrow. Does that remove him from your acquaintance—erase him from existence?"
"No; but I can hardly see what Mr. Rochester has to do with the subject you raised."

"I was speaking of ladies smiling into the eyes of gentlemen; and lately so many smiles have been directed at Mr. Rochester's eyes that they overflow like two cups filled past the brim. Have you never noticed?"
"Mr. Rochester has a right to enjoy the company of his guests."
"No argument there. But have you never observed that, of all the tales of courtship told here, Mr. Rochester has been treated to the most eager and the most persistent?"

"An eager listener quickens the tongue of a storyteller." I said this more to myself than to the gypsy, whose strange talk, voice, and manner had by now wrapped me in a kind of dream. One unexpected sentence came from her lips after another, until I was caught in a web of mystification, wondering what unseen spirit had been sitting beside my heart for weeks, watching its workings and recording every pulse.

"An eager listener!" she repeated. "Yes; Mr. Rochester has sat by the hour, his ear inclined to the fascinating lips that took such delight in their task. And Mr. Rochester was so willing to receive, and looked so grateful for the entertainment. You noticed this?"
"Grateful! I cannot recall detecting gratitude in his face."
"Detecting! So you have been analyzing. And what did you detect, if not gratitude?"
I said nothing.
"You have seen love, have you not? And, looking ahead, you have seen him married, and imagined his bride happy?"
"Hmm! Not exactly. Your witch's skill is sometimes off the mark."
"What the devil have you seen, then?"
"Never mind. I came here to ask questions, not to confess. Is it known that Mr. Rochester is to be married?"
"Yes; and to the beautiful Miss Ingram."
"Soon?"

"Appearances would suggest so. And no doubt (though, with an impudence that deserves correction, you seem to question it) they will make a supremely happy couple. He must love such a handsome, noble, witty, accomplished lady; and she probably loves him—or if not him, at least his purse. I know she considers the Rochester estate highly desirable; though (God forgive me!) I told her something about an hour ago on that subject that made her look very serious: the corners of her mouth dropped half an inch. I would advise her dark-browed suitor to watch out: if another comes along with a larger or clearer income, he is done for—"
"But, mother, I did not come to hear Mr. Rochester's fortune. I came to hear my own; and you have told me nothing of it."

"Your fortune is still uncertain: when I studied your face, one trait contradicted another. Chance has set aside a measure of happiness for you—that I know. I knew it before I came here this evening. She has laid it carefully aside for you. I watched her do it. It depends on you to reach out your hand and take it. But whether you will—that is the question I am studying. Kneel again on the rug."
"Don't keep me long; the fire is scorching me."
She did not lean toward me but only gazed, reclining in her chair.
I knelt. She did not lean toward me but only gazed, reclining in her chair. She began to murmur—

"The flame flickers in the eye; the eye shines like dew; it looks soft and full of feeling; it smiles at my jargon. It is responsive; impression follows impression through its clear depths. Where it stops smiling, it is sad; an unconscious weariness weighs on the lid—that means melancholy born of loneliness. It turns from me; it will not bear further scrutiny; it seems to deny, with a mocking glance, the truth of everything I have already seen—to reject the charge of both tenderness and grief. Its pride and reserve only confirm my opinion. The eye is favourable.

"As for the mouth, it delights at times in laughter; it is ready to express all that the brain conceives, though I daresay it would keep silent about much that the heart experiences. Flexible and expressive, it was never meant to be compressed in the eternal silence of solitude. It is a mouth that should speak often and smile often, and have human warmth for its companion. That feature, too, is promising.

"I see no obstacle to a happy outcome except in the brow; and that brow seems to say: 'I can live alone, if self-respect and circumstances require it. I need not sell my soul to buy happiness. I have an inner treasure born with me, which can sustain me if all outward joys are withheld—or offered only at a price I cannot afford.' The forehead declares: 'Reason sits firmly in control, and she will not let the feelings bolt and drag her into wild abysses. The passions may rage as furiously as they like; desires may imagine all sorts of impossible things; but judgment shall still have the last word in every argument and the deciding vote in every question. Strong wind, earthquake, and fire may pass; but I shall follow the guidance of that still small voice which speaks the dictates of conscience.'

"Well said, forehead; your declaration shall be honoured. I have formed my plans—good plans, I believe them to be—and in them I have respected the claims of conscience and the counsel of reason. I know how quickly youth would fade and joy would perish if, in the cup of happiness offered, a single drop of shame or a single hint of remorse were detected; and I do not want sacrifice, sorrow, ruin—that is not what I seek. I wish to nurture, not to destroy—to earn gratitude, not to wring tears of blood—no, nor of salt. My harvest must be in smiles, in tenderness, in sweet— That will do. I think I am raving in a kind of exquisite delirium. I wish I could stretch this moment out forever; but I dare not. So far I have governed myself completely. I have acted as I inwardly swore I would; but to go further might test me beyond my strength. Rise, Miss Eyre; leave me. 'The play is played out.'"

Where was I? Was I awake or asleep? Had I been dreaming? Was I dreaming still? The old woman's voice had changed: her accent, her gesture, everything was as familiar to me as my own face in a mirror—as the sound of my own voice. I got up but did not go. I looked; I stirred the fire and looked again. But she drew her bonnet and bandage closer around her face and again motioned me to leave. The flame lit up her outstretched hand; alert now and watching for clues, I noticed that hand at once. It was no more the withered limb of old age than my own; it was a firm, supple hand with smooth, well-shaped fingers. A broad ring flashed on the little finger, and bending forward, I looked at it and saw a gem I had seen a hundred times before. Again I looked at the face, which was no longer turned away—on the contrary, the bonnet was thrown off, the bandage removed, the head lifted.
"Well, Jane, do you know me?" asked the familiar voice.
"Just take off the red cloak, sir, and then—"
"But the string is knotted—help me."
"Break it, sir."
"There, then—'Off, ye trappings!'" And Mr. Rochester stepped out of his disguise.
"Now, sir, what a strange idea!"
"But well done, wasn't it? Don't you think so?"
"With the ladies you must have managed well."
"But not with you?"
"You did not play the gypsy with me."
"What character did I play? My own?"
"No—some impossible one. In short, I believe you have been trying to draw me out—or trip me up. You have been talking nonsense to make me talk nonsense. It is hardly fair, sir."
"Do you forgive me, Jane?"
"I cannot say until I have thought it all over. If, on reflection, I find I have not made a great fool of myself, I shall try to forgive you. But it was not right."
"Oh, you were very correct—very careful, very sensible."

I thought about it and decided, on the whole, I had been. That was a comfort. But in truth, I had been on my guard almost from the start of the interview. I had suspected some kind of trick. I knew real gypsies and fortune-tellers did not express themselves the way this seeming old woman had; besides, I had noticed her disguised voice and her anxiety to hide her features. But my mind had been running on Grace Poole—that living riddle, that mystery of mysteries, as I considered her. I had never thought of Mr. Rochester.
"Well," he said, "what are you musing about? What does that thoughtful smile mean?"
"Wonder and self-congratulation, sir. I have your permission to leave now, I suppose?"
"No; stay a moment and tell me what the people in the drawing room are doing."
"Discussing the gypsy, I imagine."
"Sit down! Let me hear what they said about me."
"I had better not stay long, sir; it must be nearly eleven. Oh, are you aware, Mr. Rochester, that a stranger has arrived since you left this morning?"
"A stranger! No—who can it be? I expected no one. Is he gone?"
"No; he said he had known you a long time, and that he could take the liberty of making himself at home here until you returned."
"The devil he did! Did he give his name?"
"His name is Mason, sir; and he comes from the West Indies—from Spanish Town, in Jamaica, I think."
Mr. Rochester was standing near me; he had taken my hand, as if to lead me to a chair. As I spoke, he gripped my wrist convulsively. The smile on his lips froze; apparently a spasm seized his breath.

"Mason!—the West Indies!" he said, in the tone you might imagine a speaking machine would use to pronounce its words. "Mason!—the West Indies!" he repeated, going over the syllables three times, growing whiter than ash between each utterance. He hardly seemed to know what he was doing.
"Do you feel ill, sir?" I asked.
"Jane, I've had a blow—I've had a blow, Jane!" He staggered.
"Oh, lean on me, sir."
"Jane, you offered me your shoulder once before; let me have it now."
"Yes, sir, yes; and my arm."
He sat down and made me sit beside him. Holding my hand in both of his, he rubbed warmth into it, gazing at me all the while with the most troubled and desolate look.
"My little friend!" he said. "I wish I were on a quiet island with only you, and trouble, and danger, and horrible memories removed from me."
"Can I help you, sir? I would give my life to serve you."
"Jane, if I need help, I'll seek it from you. I promise."
"Thank you, sir. Tell me what to do—I'll try, at least."
"Fetch me a glass of wine from the dining room. They will be at supper there. And tell me if Mason is with them, and what he is doing."

I went. I found the entire party in the dining room at supper, as Mr. Rochester had said; they were not seated at the table but had helped themselves from the sideboard and stood about in groups with their plates and glasses. Everyone seemed in high spirits; laughter and conversation were general and lively. Mr. Mason stood near the fire, talking to Colonel and Mrs. Dent, and looked as merry as anyone. I filled a wine glass (I saw Miss Ingram watching me with a frown as I did so—she no doubt thought I was taking liberties) and returned to the library.
Mr. Rochester's extreme pallor had vanished, and he looked firm and stern once more. He took the glass from my hand.
"Here is to your health, guardian spirit!" he said. He drained the glass and gave it back to me. "What are they doing, Jane?"
"Laughing and talking, sir."
"They don't look grave and mysterious, as if they had heard something strange?"
"Not at all: they are full of jokes and good cheer."
"And Mason?"
"He was laughing too."
"If all those people came together and spat at me, what would you do, Jane?"
"Throw them out of the room, sir, if I could."
He half smiled. "But if I went to them and they only looked at me coldly, and whispered sneeringly among themselves, and then drifted away one by one—what then? Would you go with them?"
"I rather think not, sir. I should take more pleasure in staying with you."
"To comfort me?"
"Yes, sir, to comfort you as best I could."
"And if they condemned you for standing by me?"
"I probably would not know of their condemnation; and if I did, I would not care about it."
"Then you could bear criticism for my sake?"
"I could bear it for the sake of any friend who deserved my loyalty—as you, I am sure, do."
"Go back to the room now; walk quietly up to Mason and whisper in his ear that Mr. Rochester has returned and wishes to see him. Bring him here and then leave me."
"Yes, sir."

I did as he asked. The whole company stared at me as I walked straight through them. I found Mr. Mason, delivered the message, and led him out of the room. I showed him into the library and then went upstairs.

Late that night, after I had been in bed some time, I heard the guests making their way to their rooms. I could distinguish Mr. Rochester's voice, and heard him say, "This way, Mason; this is your room."
He spoke cheerfully, and the light tone set my heart at ease. I was soon asleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: I had forgotten to draw my curtain, as I usually did, and also to lower my window blind. The result was that when the moon, full and bright (for the night was clear), reached the part of the sky opposite my window and looked in at me through the bare panes, its glorious gaze woke me. Opening my eyes in the dead of night, I stared at its disc—silver-white and crystal clear. It was beautiful, but too solemn. I half rose and stretched my arm to pull the curtain.
Good God! What a cry!
The night—its silence—its rest—was torn apart by a savage, sharp, shrieking sound that rang from one end of Thornfield Hall to the other.

My pulse stopped; my heart froze; my outstretched arm went rigid. The cry died and was not repeated. Indeed, whatever creature had uttered that terrible shriek could not soon repeat it: not the largest condor in the Andes could send such a yell twice in succession from the cloud surrounding its nest. The thing that had made such a sound needed to rest before it could try again.

It came from the third floor, for it passed overhead. And overhead—yes, in the room directly above my ceiling—I now heard a struggle. A deadly one, it seemed, from the noise. A half-smothered voice shouted—
"Help! Help! Help!" three times, rapidly.
"Will no one come?" it cried; and then, while the staggering and stamping raged overhead, I made out through plank and plaster—
"Rochester! Rochester! For God's sake, come!"
A door opened; someone ran, or rushed, along the gallery. Another step pounded on the floor above, something fell, and there was silence.

I had thrown on some clothes, though horror shook every limb. I came out of my room. The sleepers were all awake: cries of alarm and terrified murmurs sounded in every room. Door after door was flung open; one person looked out, then another; the gallery filled. Gentlemen and ladies alike had left their beds, and "Oh! What is it?" "Who is hurt?" "What has happened?" "Fetch a light!" "Is it fire?" "Are there robbers?" "Where shall we run?" was demanded on all sides. Without the moonlight they would have been in total darkness. They ran back and forth; they crowded together; some sobbed, some stumbled. The confusion was hopeless.
"Where the devil is Rochester?" cried Colonel Dent. "I cannot find him in his bed."
"Here! Here!" came the shout in reply. "Stay calm, all of you: I'm coming."

And the door at the end of the gallery opened, and Mr. Rochester appeared with a candle; he had just come down from the upper floor. One of the ladies ran straight to him; she seized his arm. It was Miss Ingram.
"What terrible thing has happened?" she said. "Speak! Let us know the worst at once!"

"But don't pull me down or strangle me," he replied, for the Misses Eshton were now clinging to him, and the two dowagers, in vast white dressing gowns, were bearing down on him like ships in full sail.
"All's well! All's well!" he cried. "It's a mere rehearsal of Much Ado About Nothing. Ladies, keep back, or I shall turn dangerous."
And dangerous he looked: his dark eyes shot sparks. Calming himself with an effort, he added—

"A servant has had a nightmare, that is all. She is an excitable, nervous person: she turned her dream into a ghost or something of the sort, no doubt, and has had a fit of fright. Now, I must see you all back to your rooms; until the house is quiet, she cannot be attended to. Gentlemen, have the goodness to set the ladies an example. Miss Ingram, I am sure you will not stoop to idle terrors. Amy and Louisa, return to your nests like the pair of doves you are. Mesdames"—to the dowagers—"you will certainly catch cold if you stay in this draughty gallery any longer."

And so, by alternately coaxing and commanding, he managed to get them all enclosed in their separate rooms once more. I did not wait to be told to go back to mine, but retreated unnoticed, as unnoticed I had left it.

Not, however, to go to bed. On the contrary, I began to dress myself carefully. The sounds I had heard after the scream, and the words that had been shouted, had probably been heard only by me, since they came from the room directly above mine. But they assured me it was no servant's nightmare that had sent horror through the house, and that Mr. Rochester's explanation was merely a story invented to calm his guests. I dressed, then, to be ready for anything. Once dressed, I sat a long time by the window, looking out over the silent grounds and the silvered fields, waiting for I knew not what. It seemed to me that some event must follow the strange cry, struggle, and call for help.

No: stillness returned. Every murmur and movement gradually ceased, and within about an hour Thornfield Hall was as hushed as a desert. Sleep and night had resumed their rule. Meanwhile the moon sank; she was about to set. Not wanting to sit in the cold and darkness, I thought I would lie on my bed, dressed as I was. I left the window and crossed the carpet quietly; as I stooped to take off my shoes, a cautious hand tapped softly at the door.
"Am I wanted?" I asked.
"Are you up?" asked the voice I expected—my master's.
"Yes, sir."
"And dressed?"
"Yes."
"Come out, then, quietly."
I obeyed. Mr. Rochester stood in the gallery holding a light.
"I need you," he said. "Come this way. Take your time and make no noise."

My slippers were thin; I could walk the matted floor as softly as a cat. He glided along the gallery and up the stairs, stopping in the dark, low corridor of the fateful third floor. I had followed and stood at his side.
"Have you a sponge in your room?" he asked in a whisper.
"Yes, sir."
"Have you any smelling salts?"
"Yes."
"Go back and fetch both."

I returned, found the sponge on my washstand, the salts in my drawer, and retraced my steps. He was still waiting; he held a key in his hand. Approaching one of the small, black doors, he put the key in the lock; he paused, and spoke to me again.
"You don't feel faint at the sight of blood?"
"I think not—I have never been tested."
I felt a thrill as I answered, but no coldness and no weakness.
"Just give me your hand," he said. "It won't do to risk a fainting spell."
I put my fingers into his. "Warm and steady," he remarked. He turned the key and opened the door.

I saw a room I remembered from the day Mrs. Fairfax had shown me around the house. It was hung with tapestry; but the tapestry was now looped up on one side, revealing a door that had previously been hidden. This door was open; light shone from the room within. I heard a snarling, snapping sound, almost like a dog fighting. Mr. Rochester, setting down his candle, said to me, "Wait a minute," and went forward into the inner room. A shout of laughter greeted his entrance—noisy at first, then dying into Grace Poole's own goblin cackle. She was there, then. He made some arrangement without speaking, though I heard a low voice address him. He came out and closed the door behind him.

"Here, Jane!" he said, and I walked around to the other side of a large bed, whose drawn curtains hid a considerable part of the room. An armchair stood near the head of the bed. A man sat in it, dressed except for his coat; he was motionless, his head thrown back, his eyes closed. Mr. Rochester held the candle over him; I recognized in the pale, seemingly lifeless face the stranger, Mason. I saw too that his shirt on one side, and one arm, were nearly soaked in blood.

"Hold the candle," said Mr. Rochester, and I took it. He fetched a basin of water from the washstand. "Hold that," he said. I obeyed. He took the sponge, dipped it in, and moistened the deathlike face; he asked for my smelling bottle and held it to Mason's nostrils. Mr. Mason soon opened his eyes; he groaned. Mr. Rochester opened the wounded man's shirt—his arm and shoulder were bandaged—and sponged away the blood, which was trickling fast.
"Is there immediate danger?" Mason murmured.
"Nonsense! No—a mere scratch. Don't be so overwhelmed, man: bear up! I'll go and fetch a surgeon for you myself. You'll be able to be moved by morning, I hope. Jane," he continued.
"Sir?"

"I shall have to leave you in this room with this gentleman for an hour, perhaps two hours. You will sponge the blood as I did when it starts flowing again; if he feels faint, put the glass of water on that stand to his lips, and the salts to his nose. You will not speak to him on any account—and, Richard, it will be at the peril of your life if you speak to her. Open your lips—agitate yourself—and I will not answer for the consequences."

Again the poor man groaned; he looked as if he dared not move. Fear—either of death or of something else—seemed almost to paralyze him. Mr. Rochester put the now bloody sponge into my hand, and I began to use it as he had done. He watched me a moment, then said "Remember!—No conversation," and left the room. I felt a strange sensation as the key grated in the lock and his retreating footsteps faded away.

Here, then, I was on the third floor, locked into one of its mysterious rooms; night around me; a pale and bloody spectacle under my eyes and hands; a murderess separated from me by a single door. Yes—that was the truly terrifying part—the rest I could endure. But I shuddered at the thought of Grace Poole bursting in on me.

I had to keep to my post, though. I had to watch this ghastly face—these blue, still lips forbidden to open—these eyes now shut, now opening, now wandering through the room, now fixing on me, always glazed with the dullness of horror. I had to dip my hand again and again into the basin of blood and water and wipe away the trickling gore. I had to watch the light of the guttering candle fade over my task; the shadows darken on the antique tapestry around me, and grow black beneath the hangings of the vast old bed, and quiver strangely over the doors of a great cabinet opposite—whose front, divided into twelve panels, bore, in grim design, the heads of the twelve apostles, each enclosed in its separate panel as in a frame; while above them rose an ebony crucifix and a dying Christ.

As the shifting darkness and flickering light hovered here or gleamed there, it was now the bearded physician Luke that furrowed his brow; now Saint John's long hair that waved; and now the devilish face of Judas that seemed to grow out of the panel, gathering life and threatening to reveal the arch-traitor—Satan himself—in his servant's form.

Through all this, I had to listen as well as watch: listen for any movement from the wild creature—or fiend—in that side room. But since Mr. Rochester's visit it seemed under a spell: all night I heard only three sounds at three long intervals—a creaking step, a brief renewal of the snarling, dog-like noise, and a deep human groan.

Meanwhile, my own thoughts tormented me. What crime was this, living incarnate in this isolated mansion, that could neither be driven out nor subdued by its owner? What mystery broke out now in fire and now in blood, at the deadest hours of night? What creature was it that, hidden behind an ordinary woman's face and figure, spoke now with the voice of a mocking demon and now with the cry of a carrion bird?

And this man I bent over—this commonplace, quiet stranger—how had he become entangled in the web of horror? And why had the Fury attacked him? What brought him to this part of the house at such an hour, when he should have been asleep in bed? I had heard Mr. Rochester assign him a room below—what drew him here? And why, now, was he so meek under the violence done to him? Why did he submit so quietly to the secrecy Mr. Rochester imposed? Why did Mr. Rochester impose it? His guest had been savaged, his own life had been plotted against on a previous occasion; and both attacks he smothered in secrecy and buried in silence! Finally, I could see that Mason was submissive to Mr. Rochester; that the latter's forceful will held complete power over the former's passivity. The few words they had exchanged confirmed this. It was obvious that in their history together, the passive nature of the one had always been ruled by the active energy of the other. Where, then, had Mr. Rochester's terror come from when he heard of Mason's arrival? Why had the mere name of this unresisting man—whom a single word now sufficed to control like a child—struck him, a few hours ago, as a thunderbolt strikes an oak?

Oh! I could not forget his look and his whiteness when he whispered: "Jane, I've had a blow—I've had a blow, Jane." I could not forget how the arm he rested on my shoulder had trembled; and it was no small thing that could bend the iron spirit and shake the powerful frame of Fairfax Rochester.

"When will he come? When will he come?" I cried inwardly, as the night dragged on—as my bleeding patient drooped, moaned, sickened, and neither day nor help arrived. Again and again I held the water to Mason's white lips; again and again I offered him the smelling salts. My efforts seemed useless: either physical or mental suffering, or loss of blood, or all three together, were rapidly draining his strength. He moaned so pitifully, and looked so weak, wild, and lost, that I feared he was dying; and I was not even allowed to speak to him.

The candle, burned down at last, went out; as it died, I saw streaks of grey light edging the window curtains. Dawn, then, was coming. Soon I heard Pilot bark far below, from his kennel in the courtyard: hope revived. And it was not false hope: within five minutes the grating key and yielding lock told me my watch was over. It could not have lasted more than two hours; many a week has seemed shorter.
Mr. Rochester entered, and with him the surgeon he had gone to fetch.
"Now, Carter, be quick," he said to the surgeon. "I give you half an hour for dressing the wound, fastening the bandages, getting the patient downstairs and all."
"But is he fit to move, sir?"
"No question about it; it's nothing serious. He is nervous, his spirits need to be kept up. Come, get to work."

Mr. Rochester drew back the heavy curtain, raised the blind, and let in all the daylight he could; and I was surprised and cheered to see how far dawn had advanced—what rosy streaks were beginning to brighten the east. Then he went to Mason, whom the surgeon was already tending.
"Now, my good fellow, how are you?" he asked.
"She's finished me, I fear," was the faint reply.
"Hardly!—courage! Two weeks from now you'll scarcely be the worse for it. You've lost a little blood, that's all. Carter, tell him there's no danger."

"I can say that honestly," said Carter, who had now removed the bandages. "I only wish I had gotten here sooner—he would not have bled so much. But what is this? The flesh on the shoulder is torn as well as cut. This wound was not made with a knife—there have been teeth here!"
"She bit me," he murmured. "She savaged me like a tigress, when Rochester got the knife from her."
"You should not have given way; you should have fought back at once," said Mr. Rochester.
"But under such circumstances, what could I do?" Mason returned. "Oh, it was frightful!" he added, shuddering. "And I didn't expect it; she looked so quiet at first."

"I warned you," his friend answered. "I said—be on your guard when you go near her. Besides, you might have waited until tomorrow and had me with you. It was sheer foolishness to attempt the visit tonight, and alone."
"I thought I could do some good."

"You thought! You thought! It makes me angry to hear you. But you have suffered, and are likely to suffer enough for not taking my advice; so I'll say no more. Carter—hurry! Hurry! The sun will soon rise, and I must get him away."
"Right away, sir; the shoulder is just bandaged. I must look at this other wound on the arm: she has had her teeth there too, I think."
"She sucked the blood; she said she'd drain my heart," said Mason.
I saw Mr. Rochester shudder. A remarkable expression of disgust, horror, and hatred twisted his features almost to distortion; but he only said—
"Enough—be quiet, Richard, and never mind her raving. Don't repeat it."
"I wish I could forget it," was the answer.
"You will when you are out of the country. When you get back to Spanish Town, you can think of her as dead and buried—or rather, you need not think of her at all."
"Impossible to forget this night!"

"It is not impossible: show some backbone, man. You thought you were as good as dead two hours ago, and here you are, alive and talking. There!—Carter is nearly done with you; I'll make you presentable in a moment. Jane"—he turned to me for the first time since returning—"take this key; go down to my bedroom, walk straight through to my dressing room, open the top drawer of the wardrobe and take out a clean shirt and neckerchief. Bring them here, and be quick."
I went, found the items he'd described, and returned with them.
"Now," he said, "go to the other side of the bed while I see to his clothes. But don't leave the room; you may be needed again."
I withdrew as directed.
"Was anyone stirring downstairs when you went, Jane?" Mr. Rochester asked after a moment.
"No, sir; everything was very still."

"We shall get you away quietly, Dick; and it will be better, both for your sake and for the poor creature in there. I have worked hard to avoid exposure, and I should not like it to come now. Here, Carter, help him on with his waistcoat. Where did you leave your fur cloak? You can't travel a mile without it, I know, in this wretched cold climate. In your room?—Jane, run down to Mr. Mason's room, the one next to mine, and fetch a cloak you'll find there."
Again I ran, and again returned, carrying an enormous mantle lined and edged with fur.

"Now I have another errand for you," said my tireless master. "You must go to my room again. What a mercy you move so silently, Jane!—a heavy-footed messenger would never do at a time like this. Open the middle drawer of my dressing table and take out a small bottle and a small glass you'll find there—quick!"
I flew there and back, bringing the items he wanted.

"Good! Now, doctor, I shall take the liberty of administering a dose myself, on my own authority. I got this tonic in Rome, from an Italian quack—a fellow you would have kicked, Carter. It is not something to use carelessly, but it is useful on the right occasion—as now, for example. Jane, a little water."
He held out the tiny glass, and I half filled it from the water bottle on the washstand.
"That will do; now wet the lip of the bottle."
I did so; he measured twelve drops of a crimson liquid and offered it to Mason.
"Drink, Richard: it will give you the courage you lack, for an hour or so."
"But will it hurt me? Is it stimulating?"
"Drink! Drink! Drink!"

Mr. Mason obeyed, since it was clearly useless to resist. He was dressed now: he still looked pale, but he was no longer bloody and dirty. Mr. Rochester let him sit for three minutes after swallowing the liquid, then took his arm—
"Now I'm sure you can stand," he said. "Try."
The patient rose.
"Carter, take him under the other shoulder. Courage, Richard; step forward—that's it!"
"I do feel better," Mr. Mason said.

"I'm sure you do. Now, Jane, go ahead of us to the back stairs; unbolt the side door, and tell the driver of the post-chaise you'll see in the yard—or just outside, since I told him not to drive his rattling wheels over the stones—to be ready. We are coming. And Jane, if anyone is about, come to the foot of the stairs and give a signal."

It was by now half past five, and the sun was about to rise; but I found the kitchen still dark and quiet. The side door was fastened; I opened it as silently as I could. The yard was empty, but the gates stood wide open, and a post-chaise with horses harnessed and the driver on the box waited just outside. I went to him and said the gentlemen were coming; he nodded. Then I looked carefully around and listened. The stillness of early morning held everything; the curtains were still drawn over the servants' windows; small birds were just beginning to chirp in the blossoming orchard trees, whose branches drooped like white garlands over the wall on one side of the yard; the carriage horses stamped now and then in their stalls. All else was quiet.
The gentlemen now appeared. Mason, supported by Mr. Rochester and the surgeon, walked with tolerable ease. They helped him into the chaise; Carter followed.
"Take care of him," said Mr. Rochester to the surgeon, "and keep him at your house until he is well. I shall ride over in a day or two to see how he does. Richard, how do you feel?"
"The fresh air revives me, Fairfax."
"Leave the window open on his side, Carter; there's no wind. Goodbye, Dick."
"Fairfax—"
"Well, what is it?"
"Let her be taken care of; let her be treated as tenderly as possible; let her—" He broke off and burst into tears.
"I do my best; and have done, and will do," was the answer. He shut the chaise door, and the vehicle drove away.
"Yet would to God there were an end to all this!" Mr. Rochester added, as he closed and barred the heavy yard gates.

This done, he walked slowly and abstractedly toward a door in the wall bordering the orchard. I, thinking he was done with me, turned to go back to the house; but I heard him call "Jane!" He had opened the gate and stood waiting for me.
"Come where there is some freshness, for a few moments," he said. "That house is a dungeon—don't you feel it?"
"It seems a splendid mansion to me, sir."

"The glamour of inexperience is over your eyes," he answered, "and you see it through a charmed lens. You cannot tell that the gilding is slime and the silk draperies cobwebs; that the marble is dirty slate, and the polished wood mere rubbish and bark. Now here"—he pointed to the leafy enclosure we had entered—"everything is real, sweet, and pure."

He wandered down a path bordered with box hedges, with apple, pear, and cherry trees on one side, and a flower bed on the other full of old-fashioned flowers—stocks, sweet williams, primroses, pansies—mingled with southernwood, sweet briar, and fragrant herbs. They were fresh now, as a series of April showers and sunny spells, followed by a lovely spring morning, could make them. The sun was just entering the dappled east, and its light illuminated the dewy, garland-draped orchard trees and shone down the quiet paths beneath them.
"Jane, will you have a flower?"
He picked a half-opened rose, the first on the bush, and offered it to me.
"Thank you, sir."
"Do you like this sunrise, Jane? That sky with its high, light clouds that will surely melt as the day grows warm—this calm and gentle air?"
"I do, very much."
"You have had a strange night, Jane."
"Yes, sir."
"And it has made you pale—were you afraid when I left you alone with Mason?"
"I was afraid of someone coming out of the inner room."
"But I had locked the door—I had the key in my pocket. I would have been a careless shepherd if I had left a lamb—my pet lamb—so near a wolf's den, unprotected. You were safe."
"Will Grace Poole go on living here, sir?"
"Oh yes! Don't trouble yourself about her—put the whole thing out of your mind."
"Yet it seems to me your life is hardly safe while she stays."
"Don't worry—I will take care of myself."
"Is the danger you feared last night over now, sir?"
"I cannot guarantee that until Mason is out of England—nor even then. To live, for me, Jane, is to stand on the crust of a volcano that may crack and erupt any day."
"But Mr. Mason seems an easily led man. Your influence is clearly powerful over him: he will never defy you or deliberately harm you."
"Oh, no! Mason will not defy me; nor will he knowingly hurt me. But unintentionally, in a single moment, with one careless word, he might rob me—if not of my life, then forever of my happiness."
"Tell him to be careful, sir; let him know what you fear, and show him how to avoid the danger."
He laughed bitterly, seized my hand, and just as quickly dropped it.

"If I could do that, foolish girl, where would the danger be? Destroyed in an instant. Ever since I have known Mason, I have only had to say to him, 'Do that,' and the thing was done. But I cannot give him orders in this case. I cannot say, 'Be careful not to harm me, Richard,' because it is essential that he remain ignorant that harming me is even possible. Now you look confused; and I will confuse you further. You are my little friend, are you not?"
"I like to serve you, sir, and to obey you in everything that is right."

"Precisely: I can see that. I see genuine contentment in your step and manner, your eye and face, when you are helping and pleasing me—working for me and with me, in, as you so characteristically put it, 'everything that is right.' Because if I ordered you to do what you thought wrong, there would be no light step, no deft hand, no bright eye and lively face. My friend would turn to me, quiet and pale, and say, 'No, sir; that is impossible. I cannot do it, because it is wrong'—and would become as immovable as a fixed star. Well, you too have power over me, and could hurt me. Yet I dare not show you where I am vulnerable, for fear that, loyal and friendly as you are, you might strike me there at once."
"If you have no more to fear from Mr. Mason than from me, sir, you are very safe."
"God grant it may be so! Here, Jane, is an arbour; sit down."
The arbour was an arch in the wall, draped with ivy; it held a rustic bench. Mr. Rochester sat down, leaving room for me. But I stood before him.
"Sit," he said. "The bench is long enough for two. You don't hesitate to sit beside me, do you? Is that wrong, Jane?"
I answered him by sitting down. To refuse, I felt, would have been foolish.

"Now, my little friend, while the sun drinks the dew—while all the flowers in this old garden wake and open, and the birds fetch their young ones' breakfast from the Thornfield hedges, and the early bees begin their first work—I'll put a case to you, which you must try to imagine as your own. But first, look at me and tell me you are at ease, and not worried that I am wrong to keep you here, or that you are wrong to stay."
"No, sir; I am content."

"Well then, Jane, use your imagination. Suppose you were no longer a well-brought-up, disciplined young woman, but a wild boy spoiled from childhood. Imagine yourself in a remote foreign country. Imagine that there you commit a grave error—never mind what kind or from what motive—but one whose consequences must follow you through life and poison your whole existence. Mind, I don't say a crime; I am not speaking of murder or any guilty act that would bring the law down on you. My word is error. The consequences of what you have done become, in time, utterly unbearable. You take steps to find relief—unusual steps, but neither unlawful nor wicked. Still you are miserable; for hope has left you at the very edge of life. Your noon sun darkens in an eclipse that you feel will last until it sets. Bitter and degrading memories become the only food of your mind. You wander here and there, seeking rest in exile—happiness in pleasure, I mean in mindless, shallow pleasure, the kind that dulls the mind and deadens the heart. Weary in heart and withered in soul, you come home after years of self-imposed exile. You meet someone new—how or where doesn't matter. In this stranger you find the good and bright qualities you have sought for twenty years and never found before; and they are all fresh, healthy, unspoiled and unstained. Such company revives you, regenerates you. You feel better days returning—higher hopes, purer feelings. You want to begin your life again, to spend your remaining days in a way more worthy of an immortal being. To achieve this end, are you justified in leaping over a barrier of custom—a mere conventional obstacle that neither your conscience approves nor your judgment supports?"

He paused for an answer: and what was I to say? Oh, for some good spirit to suggest a wise and fitting response! A vain wish! The west wind whispered in the ivy around me; but no gentle angel borrowed its breath to speak through. The birds sang in the treetops; but their song, however sweet, spoke no words.
Again Mr. Rochester pressed his question:

"Is the wandering, sinful, but now rest-seeking and repentant man justified in braving the world's opinion, in order to bind to himself forever this gentle, gracious, generous stranger, thereby securing his own peace of mind and the renewal of his life?"

"Sir," I answered, "a wanderer's peace or a sinner's reform should never depend on another person. Men and women die; philosophers falter in wisdom, and Christians in goodness. If anyone you know has suffered and strayed, let him look higher than his fellow creatures for strength to change and comfort to heal."

"But the instrument—the instrument! God, who does the work, chooses the instrument. I myself—I tell you plainly—have been a worldly, reckless, restless man; and I believe I have found the instrument for my cure in—"

He paused: the birds went on singing, the leaves softly rustling. I almost expected them to hush and listen for the unfinished revelation; but they would have had to wait many minutes—so long did the silence stretch. At last I looked up at the hesitating speaker: he was looking eagerly at me.

"Little friend," he said, in a completely changed tone—his face changing too, losing all its softness and seriousness, becoming hard and mocking—"you have noticed my tender fondness for Miss Ingram. Don't you think if I married her she would set me right with a vengeance?"
He jumped up at once, walked to the far end of the path, and when he came back he was humming a tune.
"Jane, Jane," he said, stopping in front of me, "you are quite pale from your night watch. Don't you curse me for ruining your rest?"
"Curse you? No, sir."
"Shake hands to seal the word. What cold fingers! They were warmer last night when I touched them at the door of that mysterious room. Jane, when will you keep watch with me again?"
"Whenever I can be useful, sir."

"For instance, the night before I am married! I am sure I shall not be able to sleep. Will you promise to sit up with me to keep me company? I can talk to you about my lovely one—for now you have seen her and know her."
"Yes, sir."
"She's a rare one, isn't she, Jane?"
"Yes, sir."

"A magnificent woman—a real stunner, Jane: tall, dark, and voluptuous, with hair like the women of Carthage must have had. Bless me! There's Dent and Lynn in the stables! Go in through the shrubbery, by that gate."
As I went one way, he went another, and I heard him in the yard, saying cheerfully—
"Mason got a head start on all of you this morning; he was gone before sunrise. I got up at four to see him off."

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Premonitions are strange things! And so are sympathies; and so are signs; and the three combined form one mystery to which humanity has not yet found the key. I never laughed at premonitions in my life, because I have had strange ones of my own. Sympathies, I believe, exist—for instance, between relatives long separated and wholly estranged, who still assert, despite their alienation, the bond of their common origin—and their workings baffle human understanding. And signs, for all we know, may be nothing but Nature's sympathy with humanity.

When I was a little girl, only six years old, I once heard Bessie Leaven say to Martha Abbot that she had been dreaming about a small child, and that to dream of children was a sure sign of trouble, either for yourself or your family. The saying might have faded from my memory had not something happened immediately afterwards to fix it there permanently. The next day Bessie was called home to the deathbed of her little sister.

Lately I had often recalled this saying and this event, because during the past week hardly a night had passed without bringing me a dream of an infant—sometimes hushed in my arms, sometimes bounced on my knee, sometimes watched playing with daisies on a lawn, or again, dabbling its hands in running water. It was a crying child one night and a laughing one the next; now it nestled close to me, now it ran from me. But whatever mood the apparition showed, whatever shape it took, for seven straight nights it appeared to me the moment I fell asleep.

I did not like this constant return of one idea—this strange recurrence of one image, and I grew nervous as bedtime approached and the hour of the vision drew near. It was from the company of this phantom baby that I had been roused on that moonlit night when I heard the scream. And it was on the afternoon of the following day that I was called downstairs by a message that someone wanted to see me in Mrs. Fairfax's room. Going there, I found a man waiting for me, dressed like a gentleman's servant. He wore deep mourning, and the hat in his hand had a black band around it.

"I daresay you hardly remember me, Miss," he said, rising as I entered, "but my name is Leaven. I was coachman at Mrs. Reed's when you were at Gateshead, eight or nine years ago, and I still live there."
"Oh, Robert! How do you do? I remember you very well—you used to give me a ride sometimes on Miss Georgiana's bay pony. And how is Bessie? You are married to Bessie?"
"Yes, Miss; my wife is very well, thank you. She had another little one about two months ago—we have three now—and both mother and child are doing fine."
"And are the family well at the house, Robert?"
"I'm sorry I can't give you better news of them, Miss. They are very badly off at present—in great trouble."
"I hope no one is dead," I said, glancing at his black clothes. He too looked down at the mourning band on his hat and replied—
"Mr. John died a week ago yesterday, at his rooms in London."
"Mr. John?"
"Yes."
"And how does his mother bear it?"
"Well, you see, Miss Eyre, it is not a common misfortune: his life has been very wild. These last three years he gave himself up to terrible ways, and his death was shocking."
"I heard from Bessie he was not doing well."

"Doing well! He could not have done worse. He ruined his health and his estate among the worst men and the worst women. He got into debt and into prison; his mother bailed him out twice, but as soon as he was free he went straight back to his old companions and habits. He was not strong-minded; the crooks he lived among cheated him worse than anything I ever heard. He came down to Gateshead about three weeks ago and demanded his mother give him everything. She refused—her own resources have long been drained by his spending. So he went back again, and the next news was that he was dead. How he died, God knows!—they say he killed himself."
I was silent: the news was terrible. Robert Leaven went on—

"Mrs. Reed herself has been in poor health for some time. She had grown very heavy, but was not strong with it; and the loss of money and fear of poverty were breaking her down. The news about Mr. John's death, and the way he died, came too suddenly: it brought on a stroke. She went three days without speaking; but last Tuesday she seemed somewhat better. She appeared to be trying to say something, and kept making signs to my wife and mumbling. It was only yesterday morning, though, that Bessie understood she was saying your name; and at last she made out the words: 'Bring Jane—fetch Jane Eyre. I want to speak to her.' Bessie is not sure whether she is in her right mind, or means anything by it; but she told Miss Reed and Miss Georgiana, and advised them to send for you. The young ladies put it off at first; but their mother grew so restless, and said 'Jane, Jane' so many times, that at last they agreed. I left Gateshead yesterday; and if you can get ready, Miss, I should like to take you back with me early tomorrow morning."
"Yes, Robert, I shall be ready. It seems to me that I ought to go."
"I think so too, Miss. Bessie said she was sure you would not refuse. But I suppose you will have to ask permission before you can leave?"
"Yes; and I will do it now." Having directed him to the servants' hall and recommended him to the care of John's wife and John himself, I went to find Mr. Rochester.

He was not in any of the downstairs rooms; he was not in the yard, the stables, or the grounds. I asked Mrs. Fairfax if she had seen him; yes, she believed he was playing billiards with Miss Ingram. To the billiard room I hurried: the click of balls and the hum of voices came from within. Mr. Rochester, Miss Ingram, the two Misses Eshton, and their admirers were all absorbed in the game. It took some courage to interrupt so lively a party; my errand, however, could not wait, so I approached the master where he stood at Miss Ingram's side. She turned as I drew near and looked at me haughtily; her eyes seemed to demand, "What can the creeping creature want now?" and when I said quietly, "Mr. Rochester," she made a movement as if tempted to wave me away. I remember her appearance at that moment—it was very graceful and very striking: she wore a morning gown of sky-blue crêpe, with a gauzy blue scarf twisted in her hair. She had been all animation over the game, and irritated pride did nothing to soften her haughty expression.

"Does that person want you?" she asked Mr. Rochester; and Mr. Rochester turned to see who the "person" was. He made a curious face—one of his strange, ambiguous expressions—threw down his cue, and followed me from the room.
"Well, Jane?" he said, leaning his back against the schoolroom door, which he had shut.
"If you please, sir, I would like leave of absence for a week or two."
"What for? Where are you going?"
"To see a sick lady who has sent for me."
"What sick lady? Where does she live?"
"At Gateshead, in ——shire."
"——shire? That is a hundred miles away! Who is she, that sends for people from that distance?"
"Her name is Reed, sir—Mrs. Reed."
"Reed of Gateshead? There was a Reed of Gateshead, a magistrate."
"It is his widow, sir."
"And what have you to do with her? How do you know her?"
"Mr. Reed was my uncle—my mother's brother."
"The deuce he was! You never told me that before; you always said you had no relatives."
"None that would claim me, sir. Mr. Reed is dead, and his wife cast me off."
"Why?"
"Because I was poor, and a burden, and she disliked me."

"But Reed left children? You must have cousins? Sir George Lynn was talking yesterday about a Reed of Gateshead who, he said, was one of the worst scoundrels in London; and Ingram mentioned a Georgiana Reed from the same place, who was much admired for her beauty a season or two ago."
"John Reed is dead too, sir. He ruined himself and half ruined his family, and is believed to have killed himself. The news shocked his mother so badly it brought on a stroke."
"And what good can you do her? Nonsense, Jane! I would never think of travelling a hundred miles to see an old lady who will perhaps be dead before you arrive—and besides, you say she threw you out."
"Yes, sir, but that was long ago, and circumstances were very different then. I could not rest easy if I ignored her wishes now."
"How long will you be gone?"
"As briefly as possible, sir."
"Promise me you'll stay only a week—"
"I had better not give my word. I might have to break it."
"But you will come back? You won't be persuaded, under any excuse, to take up permanent residence with her?"
"Oh no! I shall certainly return, if all is well."
"And who goes with you? You don't travel a hundred miles alone."
"No, sir, she has sent her coachman."
"Can he be trusted?"
"Yes, sir, he has been with the family ten years."
Mr. Rochester thought for a moment. "When do you want to leave?"
"Early tomorrow morning, sir."
"Well, you must have some money; you can't travel without money, and I daresay you haven't much. I have given you no salary yet. How much have you in the world, Jane?" he asked, smiling.

I took out my purse—a thin thing. "Five shillings, sir." He took the purse, poured the contents into his palm, and chuckled over it as if its meagreness amused him. Then he produced his pocketbook. "Here," he said, offering me a note. It was fifty pounds, and he owed me only fifteen. I told him I had no change.
"I don't want change; you know that. Take your wages."
I refused to accept more than was owed to me. He scowled at first; then, as if remembering something, he said—
"Right, right! Better not give you the whole sum now—you would perhaps stay away three months if you had fifty pounds. Here are ten; is that not plenty?"
"Yes, sir, but now you owe me five."
"Come back for it, then. I am your banker for forty pounds."
"Mr. Rochester, I may as well mention another matter of business while I have the chance."
"A matter of business? I am curious to hear it."
"You have as good as told me, sir, that you are shortly to be married?"
"Yes; what then?"
"In that case, sir, Adèle ought to go to school. I am sure you will see the necessity of it."

"To get her out of my bride's path, who might otherwise trample her rather too thoroughly? There's sense in the suggestion, no question about it. Adèle, as you say, must go to school; and you, of course, must march straight to—the devil?"
"I hope not, sir; but I must find another position somewhere."
"Of course!" he exclaimed, with a peculiar twist of voice and face, equally absurd and comical. He studied me for some minutes.
"And old Madam Reed, or the Misses, her daughters, will be asked by you to help find you a place, I suppose?"
"No, sir; I am not on terms with my relatives that would justify asking them for favours. I shall advertise."
"You shall climb the pyramids of Egypt!" he growled. "At your peril you advertise! I wish I had offered you a sovereign instead of ten pounds. Give me back nine pounds, Jane; I have a use for it."
"And so have I, sir," I returned, putting my hands and my purse behind my back. "I could not spare the money on any account."
"Little miser!" he said. "Refusing me a financial request! Give me five pounds, Jane."
"Not five shillings, sir; nor five pence."
"Just let me look at the money."
"No, sir; you are not to be trusted."
"Jane!"
"Sir?"
"Promise me one thing."
"I'll promise you anything, sir, that I think I am likely to keep."
"Not to advertise: and to trust this search for a position to me. I'll find you one in time."
"I shall be glad to, sir, if you in turn will promise that Adèle and I shall both be safely out of the house before your bride enters it."
"Very well! Very well! I pledge my word on it. You go tomorrow, then?"
"Yes, sir; early."
"Shall you come down to the drawing room after dinner?"
"No, sir, I must prepare for the journey."
"Then you and I must say goodbye for a little while?"
"I suppose so, sir."
"And how do people perform the ceremony of parting, Jane? Teach me; I'm not quite up to it."
"They say, Farewell, or whatever form they prefer."
"Then say it."
"Farewell, Mr. Rochester, for the present."
"What must I say?"
"The same, if you like, sir."
"Farewell, Miss Eyre, for the present. Is that all?"
"Yes."

"It seems meagre, to my way of thinking, and dry, and unfriendly. I should like something else—a little addition to the ritual. If one shook hands, for instance—but no, that would not satisfy me either. So you'll do no more than say Farewell, Jane?"
"It is enough, sir: as much goodwill may be conveyed in one heartfelt word as in many."
"Very likely; but it is blank and cold—'Farewell.'"

"How long is he going to stand with his back against that door?" I asked myself. "I want to start packing." The dinner bell rang, and suddenly he bolted, without another word. I saw no more of him that day, and was gone before he had risen the next morning.

I reached the lodge at Gateshead about five o'clock on the afternoon of May the first. I stopped in there before going up to the hall. It was very clean and neat: the decorative windows hung with little white curtains; the floor spotless; the grate and fire-irons polished bright; the fire burning clear. Bessie sat by the hearth, nursing her youngest child, and Robert and his sister played quietly in a corner.
"Bless you! I knew you would come!" exclaimed Mrs. Leaven, as I entered.
"Yes, Bessie," I said, after I had kissed her. "And I trust I am not too late. How is Mrs. Reed? Alive still, I hope."
"Yes, she is alive, and more lucid and coherent than she was. The doctor says she may last a week or two yet; but he does not expect her to recover."
"Has she mentioned me lately?"

"She was talking about you only this morning, wishing you would come; but she is sleeping now, or was ten minutes ago when I was up at the house. She generally lies in a sort of stupor all afternoon and wakes about six or seven. Will you rest here an hour, Miss, and then I will go up with you?"

Robert came in, and Bessie laid her sleeping baby in the cradle and went to greet him. Afterwards she insisted on my removing my bonnet and having some tea, saying I looked pale and tired. I was glad to accept her kindness, and I let her relieve me of my travelling clothes just as passively as I used to let her undress me as a child.

Old times came flooding back as I watched her bustling about—setting out the tea tray with her best china, cutting bread and butter, toasting a teacake, and between tasks, giving little Robert or Jane an occasional tap or push, just as she used to give me in those earlier days. Bessie had kept her quick temper as well as her light step and good looks.

When tea was ready I was going to the table, but she told me to sit still, in exactly her old commanding way. I must be served by the fire, she said; and she placed before me a little round stand with my cup and a plate of toast, exactly as she used to set out a secretly obtained treat for me on a nursery chair. I smiled and obeyed her as in the old days.

She wanted to know if I was happy at Thornfield Hall, and what sort of person the mistress was; when I told her there was only a master, whether he was a nice gentleman, and if I liked him. I told her he was rather an ugly man, but quite a gentleman, and that he treated me kindly and I was content. Then I described the fashionable company that had lately been staying at the house; and Bessie listened with interest—these were exactly the kind of details she enjoyed.

In such conversation an hour soon passed. Bessie gave me back my bonnet and coat, and, accompanied by her, I left the lodge for the hall. It was also with her that, nearly nine years ago, I had walked down the path I was now climbing. On a dark, misty, raw morning in January, I had left a hostile roof with a desperate and bitter heart—a sense of being cast out and almost damned—to seek the cold shelter of Lowood, that destination so far away and unknown. The same hostile roof now rose before me again: my prospects were still uncertain, and I still had an aching heart. I still felt like a wanderer on the face of the earth; but I had firmer trust in myself and my own powers now, and less cringing dread of oppression. The raw wound of my wrongs was healed, and the flame of resentment was out.
"You'll go to the breakfast room first," said Bessie, leading the way through the hall. "The young ladies will be there."

A moment later I was in that room. Every piece of furniture looked exactly as it did on the morning I was first introduced to Mr. Brocklehurst: the very rug he had stood on still covered the hearth. Glancing at the bookcases, I thought I could make out the two volumes of Bewick's British Birds in their old place on the third shelf, and Gulliver's Travels and the Arabian Nights just above. The inanimate objects had not changed; but the living things had altered beyond recognition.

Two young women stood before me. One was very tall, almost as tall as Miss Ingram, and very thin, with a sallow face and a severe expression. There was something ascetic in her look, heightened by the extreme plainness of a straight-skirted black dress, a starched linen collar, hair combed back from the temples, and the nun-like adornment of a string of ebony beads and a crucifix. This I felt sure was Eliza, though I could find little resemblance to her former self in that elongated and colourless face.

The other was certainly Georgiana—but not the Georgiana I remembered, the slender, fairy-like girl of eleven. This was a full-blown, very plump young woman, fair as wax, with handsome regular features, dreamy blue eyes, and ringleted golden hair. Her dress was also black, but its style was so different from her sister's—so much more flowing and flattering—that it looked fashionable where the other's looked puritanical.

In each sister there was one trait of the mother, and only one: the thin, pale elder daughter had her parent's hard eye; the blooming, ample younger girl had her contour of jaw and chin—perhaps slightly softened, but still giving an indefinable hardness to a face otherwise so full and handsome.

Both ladies rose to greet me as I came forward, and both addressed me as "Miss Eyre." Eliza's greeting was delivered in a short, abrupt voice, without a smile; then she sat down again, fixed her eyes on the fire, and seemed to forget me. Georgiana added to her "How do you do" several commonplaces about my journey, the weather, and so on, in rather a drawling tone, accompanied by sidelong glances that measured me from head to foot—now scanning the folds of my plain grey coat, now lingering on the simple trim of my modest bonnet. Young ladies have a remarkable way of letting you know they think you dowdy without actually saying the word. A certain superior look, a cool manner, a careless tone express their feelings on the point perfectly, without committing them to any outright rudeness.

A sneer, however, whether hidden or open, no longer had the power over me it once possessed. As I sat between my cousins, I was surprised to find how little I cared about the total neglect of the one and the half-mocking attention of the other. Eliza did not wound me, nor did Georgiana ruffle me. The fact was, I had other things on my mind. Within the last few months, feelings had been stirred in me far more powerful than any they could raise—pleasures and pains far more acute and exquisite than anything they could inflict or give—and their manner was of no consequence to me.
"How is Mrs. Reed?" I asked soon, looking calmly at Georgiana, who seemed affronted by the direct question, as if it were an unexpected liberty.
"Mrs. Reed? Ah—mama, you mean. She is extremely poorly. I doubt you can see her tonight."
"If," I said, "you would just go upstairs and tell her I have come, I would be very grateful."

Georgiana nearly jumped, and opened her blue eyes wide. "I know she had a particular wish to see me," I added, "and I would not want to put off attending to her desire longer than absolutely necessary."

"Mama dislikes being disturbed in the evening," Eliza remarked. I soon rose, quietly removed my bonnet and gloves, uninvited, and said I would just step out to Bessie—who was, I imagined, in the kitchen—and ask her to find out whether Mrs. Reed was willing to see me tonight. I went, and having found Bessie and sent her on my errand, I took further steps. It had always been my habit to shrink from rudeness; received as I had been today, a year ago I would have resolved to leave Gateshead the very next morning. Now, it suddenly became clear to me that this would be foolish. I had come a hundred miles to see my aunt, and I must stay until she was better—or dead. As for her daughters' pride or folly, I must set it aside and make myself independent of it. So I spoke to the housekeeper, asked her to show me a room, told her I should probably be a visitor for a week or two, had my trunk taken to my room, and followed it there myself. I met Bessie on the landing.
"Mrs. Reed is awake," she said. "I've told her you're here. Come and let us see if she recognizes you."

I did not need to be shown to that well-known room, to which I had so often been summoned for punishment or scolding in the old days. I hurried ahead of Bessie; I softly opened the door. A shaded lamp stood on the table, for it was growing dark. There was the great four-poster bed with amber hangings, as before; there the dressing table, the armchair, and the footstool where I had been made to kneel a hundred times to beg pardon for sins I had not committed. I glanced into a certain corner nearby, half expecting to see the thin outline of a cane that used to lurk there, ready to spring out and sting my trembling palm or shrinking neck. I approached the bed; I drew back the curtains and leaned over the high-piled pillows.

I remembered Mrs. Reed's face well, and I eagerly looked for the familiar image. It is a good thing that time dampens the thirst for revenge and silences the voice of hatred. I had left this woman in bitterness and anger, and I came back to her now with no feeling except a kind of pity for her great suffering, and a strong desire to forget and forgive all wrongs—to be reconciled and join hands in friendship.

The well-known face was there: stern, unyielding as ever—there was that flint-like eye that nothing could melt, and the slightly raised, commanding, tyrannical eyebrow. How often had it lowered on me with menace and hatred! And how the memories of childhood terrors and sorrows revived as I traced its harsh line now! And yet I bent down and kissed her. She looked at me.
"Is this Jane Eyre?" she said.
"Yes, Aunt Reed. How are you, dear aunt?"

I had once vowed never to call her aunt again; but I thought it no sin to forget and break that vow now. My fingers had found her hand where it lay outside the sheet. If she had pressed mine kindly, I would at that moment have felt real joy. But cold natures are not so easily softened, nor natural hatreds so quickly erased. Mrs. Reed pulled her hand away, and turning her face from me, remarked that the night was warm. Again she looked at me so icily that I knew at once her opinion of me—her feeling toward me—was unchanged and unchangeable.
