I could see by her stony eye—impervious to tenderness, unreachable by tears—that she was determined to consider me bad to the last; because to believe me good would give her no pleasure, only a sense of humiliation.

I felt hurt, then anger; then a determination to master her—to be her mistress despite both her nature and her will. Tears had risen, as in childhood; I ordered them back. I brought a chair to the bedside, sat down, and leaned over the pillow.
"You sent for me," I said, "and I am here; and I intend to stay until I see how you do."
"Oh, of course! You have seen my daughters?"
"Yes."

"Well, you may tell them I wish you to stay until I can discuss some things with you that are on my mind. Tonight it is too late, and I have difficulty remembering them. But there was something I wanted to say—let me see—"

The wandering look and changed speech told what ruin had occurred in her once vigorous frame. Turning restlessly, she pulled the bedclothes around her; my elbow, resting on a corner of the quilt, pinned it down. She was instantly irritated.
"Sit up!" she said. "Don't annoy me by holding down the covers. Are you Jane Eyre?"
"I am Jane Eyre."

"I have had more trouble with that child than anyone would believe. Such a burden to be left on my hands—and the daily annoyance she caused me with her incomprehensible temperament, and her sudden bursts of fury, and her constant, unnatural watching of everything I did! I declare she once spoke to me like something mad, or like a fiend—no child ever spoke or looked as she did. I was glad to get her out of the house. What did they do with her at Lowood? The fever broke out there, and many of the pupils died. She, however, did not die—but I said she did. I wish she had!"
"A strange wish, Mrs. Reed; why do you hate her so?"

"I had a dislike for her mother always; she was my husband's only sister, and a great favourite of his. He opposed the family's disowning her when she made her low marriage; and when news came of her death, he wept like a fool. He would send for the baby, though I begged him to put it out to nurse and pay for its care. I hated it the first time I laid eyes on it—a sickly, whining, pining thing! It would wail in its cradle all night—not screaming heartily like any other child, but whimpering and moaning. Reed pitied it; he used to hold it and fuss over it as if it were his own—more, indeed, than he ever noticed his own children at that age. He tried to make my children friendly to the little beggar; the darlings couldn't stand it, and he was angry with them when they showed their dislike. In his last illness he had it brought constantly to his bedside; and barely an hour before he died, he bound me with a vow to keep the creature. I would as soon have been charged with a pauper's brat from the workhouse—but he was weak, naturally weak. John does not resemble his father at all, and I am glad of it: John is like me and like my brothers—he is a true Gibson. Oh, I wish he would stop tormenting me with letters begging for money! I have no more money to give him: we are growing poor. I must dismiss half the servants and shut up part of the house, or let it. I can never submit to that—yet how are we to manage? Two thirds of my income goes to pay mortgage interest. John gambles terribly, and always loses—poor boy! He is surrounded by swindlers. John is ruined and degraded—his appearance is frightful—I feel ashamed for him when I see him."
She was becoming very agitated. "I think I had better leave her now," I said to Bessie, who stood on the other side of the bed.
"Perhaps you should, Miss; but she often talks this way toward night. In the morning she is calmer."

I rose. "Stop!" exclaimed Mrs. Reed. "There is another thing I wished to say. He threatens me—he constantly threatens me with his own death, or mine; and I sometimes dream that I see him laid out with a great wound in his throat, or with a swollen and blackened face. I have come to a terrible pass: I have heavy troubles. What is to be done? How is the money to be found?"
Bessie now tried to persuade her to take a sedative; she succeeded with difficulty. Soon after, Mrs. Reed grew calmer and sank into a drowsy state. I left her then.

More than ten days passed before I had another conversation with her. She continued either delirious or stupefied, and the doctor forbade anything that might painfully excite her. Meanwhile, I got on as well as I could with Georgiana and Eliza. They were very cold at first. Eliza would spend half the day sewing, reading, or writing, and barely speak a word to me or her sister. Georgiana would chatter nonsense to her canary bird for hours and ignore me completely. But I was determined not to appear lost for occupation or entertainment: I had brought my drawing materials, and they served me well.

With a case of pencils and some sheets of paper, I would take a seat apart from them, near the window, and busy myself sketching whatever happened to form itself momentarily in the shifting kaleidoscope of my imagination: a glimpse of sea between two rocks; the rising moon with a ship crossing its face; a cluster of reeds and water plants with a water nymph's head, crowned with lotus flowers, rising from among them; an elf sitting in a hedge sparrow's nest, under a canopy of hawthorn blossoms.

One morning I began to sketch a face—what kind of face, I did not know or care. I took a soft black pencil, sharpened it to a broad point, and set to work. Soon I had traced a broad, prominent forehead and a square lower outline of jaw; that shape pleased me, and my fingers went busily on to fill in the features. Strongly marked horizontal eyebrows must go under that brow; then naturally followed a well-defined nose, with a straight ridge and full nostrils; then a flexible-looking mouth, by no means narrow; then a firm chin with a decided cleft. Of course some dark side-whiskers were needed, and some jet-black hair, thick at the temples and waved above the forehead. Now for the eyes: I had saved them for last, because they needed the most careful work. I drew them large; I shaped them well; the lashes I made long and dark; the irises lustrous and deep. "Good! But not quite right," I thought, studying the result. "They need more force and spirit." I darkened the shadows so the highlights would flash more brilliantly—a happy touch or two, and it was done. There I had a friend's face before me; and what did it matter that those young ladies had their backs turned? I looked at it; I smiled at the speaking likeness. I was absorbed and content.

"Is that a portrait of someone you know?" asked Eliza, who had come up behind me unnoticed. I said it was merely an imaginary head, and quickly slipped it beneath my other sheets. Of course I was lying: it was, in fact, a very faithful likeness of Mr. Rochester. But what was that to her, or to anyone but me? Georgiana also came to look. My other drawings pleased her greatly, but she called that one "an ugly man." They were both surprised by my skill. I offered to sketch their portraits; and each sat in turn for a pencil outline. Then Georgiana produced her album. I promised a watercolour, which put her instantly in good spirits. She proposed a walk in the grounds. Before we had been out two hours, we were deep in confidential conversation: she had treated me to an account of the brilliant winter she had spent in London two seasons ago—the admiration she had attracted, the attention she had received—and I even got hints of the titled conquest she had made. Over the course of the afternoon and evening these hints expanded: various tender conversations were reported, and romantic scenes described; in short, a volume of a fashionable novel was improvised that day for my benefit. The stories continued daily: they always ran on the same theme—herself, her loves, and her sorrows. It was remarkable that she never once mentioned her mother's illness, her brother's death, or the present gloomy state of the family's fortunes. Her mind seemed wholly occupied with memories of past glamour and dreams of future amusement. She spent about five minutes each day in her mother's sickroom, no more.

Eliza still said little: she clearly had no time for talk. I never saw a busier person, yet it was hard to say what she accomplished. She had an alarm clock to wake her early. What she did before breakfast I never discovered, but after that meal she divided her day into precise portions, each hour assigned its task. Three times a day she studied a little book which, on inspection, I found was a Book of Common Prayer. I asked her once what she found so compelling in it, and she said, "The Rubric." Three hours she spent stitching a gold-thread border on a square of crimson cloth, nearly large enough for a carpet. When I asked what it was for, she told me it was a covering for the altar of a new church recently built near Gateshead. Two hours she gave to her diary; two to working alone in the kitchen garden; and one to managing her accounts. She seemed to want no company and no conversation. I believe she was happy in her way: this routine was enough for her, and nothing annoyed her more than any event that forced her to break its clockwork regularity.

She told me one evening, in a more communicative mood than usual, that John's behaviour and the threatened ruin of the family had been a source of deep distress to her; but she had now, she said, settled her mind and formed her resolution. Her own fortune she had taken care to protect; and when her mother died—and it was very unlikely, she remarked calmly, that she would either recover or linger long—she would carry out a long-cherished plan: enter a religious retreat where strict habits would be permanently safe from disturbance, and place firm barriers between herself and the frivolous world. I asked if Georgiana would go with her.

"Of course not. Georgiana and she had nothing in common; they never had. She would not be burdened with her company for any consideration. Georgiana should go her own way; and she, Eliza, would go hers."

Georgiana, when not pouring out her heart to me, spent most of her time lying on the sofa, complaining about the dullness of the house, and wishing again and again that her aunt Gibson would invite her to London. "It would be so much better," she said, "if she could just get away for a month or two, until all was over." I did not ask what she meant by "all being over," but I suppose she referred to her mother's expected death and the gloomy business of the funeral. Eliza generally took no more notice of her sister's laziness and complaints than if no such whining, lounging figure were there at all. One day, however, as she put away her account book and unfolded her embroidery, she suddenly rounded on her—

"Georgiana, a more vain and absurd creature than you was certainly never allowed to walk the earth. You had no right to be born, for you make no use of life. Instead of living for, in, and by yourself, as a reasonable being ought, you try only to hang your weakness on someone else's strength. If no one can be found willing to carry such a fat, weak, puffy, useless thing, you cry out that you are ill-treated, neglected, miserable. Then, too, life must be a constant whirl of change and excitement, or else the world is a prison: you must be admired, you must be courted, you must be flattered—you must have music, dancing, and society—or you wither and die. Have you no sense to build a system that will make you independent of all efforts and all wills but your own? Take one day; divide it into portions; assign each portion its task; leave no spare quarter of an hour, no ten minutes, no five minutes unaccounted for—fill them all; do each piece of work in its turn with method and rigid regularity. The day will end almost before you realize it has begun; and you will owe no one thanks for helping you use up a single empty moment. You will not have needed anyone's company, conversation, sympathy, or patience; you will have lived, in short, as an independent being should. Take this advice—the first and last I shall ever give you—and then you will not need me or anyone else, come what may. Ignore it—go on as before, craving, whining, and idling—and suffer the consequences, however bad and intolerable they may be. I tell you this plainly; and listen: though I shall never repeat what I am now saying, I shall act on it steadily. After my mother's death, I wash my hands of you. From the day her coffin is carried to the vault in Gateshead Church, you and I will be as separate as if we had never known each other. Do not think that because we happened to be born of the same parents, I shall let you bind me with even the feeblest claim. I can tell you this: if every other human being were swept away and we two stood alone on the earth, I would leave you in the old world and take myself to the new."
She closed her lips.

"You might have saved yourself the trouble of that speech," Georgiana answered. "Everyone knows you are the most selfish, heartless creature alive, and I know your spiteful hatred of me: I had proof of it before, in the trick you played me over Lord Edwin Vere. You could not bear to see me raised above you, to have a title, to be received in circles where you dare not show your face, and so you acted the spy and informer and ruined my prospects forever." Georgiana took out her handkerchief and blew her nose for the next hour; Eliza sat cold, unmoved, and busily industrious.

True, generous feeling counts for little with some people; but here were two natures made, the one unbearably bitter and the other contemptibly bland, for the lack of it. Feeling without judgment is a watery drink indeed; but judgment without feeling is too harsh and dry a morsel for anyone to swallow.

It was a wet and windy afternoon: Georgiana had fallen asleep on the sofa over a novel; Eliza had gone to attend a saints' day service at the new church—for in matters of religion she was a rigid formalist: no weather ever prevented her from what she considered her devotional duties; rain or shine, she went to church three times every Sunday and as often on weekdays as there were services.

I thought I would go upstairs and see how the dying woman fared, lying there almost unheeded: even the servants only checked on her intermittently, and the hired nurse, being little supervised, would slip from the room whenever she could. Bessie was loyal, but she had her own family to attend to and could only come to the hall occasionally. I found the sickroom unwatched, as I expected: no nurse was there; the patient lay still and apparently unconscious, her livid face sunk in the pillows; the fire dying in the grate. I added fuel, straightened the bedclothes, gazed for a while at her who could no longer gaze at me, and then moved to the window.

The rain beat hard against the glass, the wind blew fiercely. "One lies there," I thought, "who will soon be beyond the storms of this world. Where will that spirit—now struggling to quit its physical dwelling—go when at last released?"

Pondering this great mystery, I thought of Helen Burns, recalled her dying words—her faith—her belief in the equality of disembodied souls. I was still hearing her remembered voice in my thoughts—still picturing her pale and spiritual face, her wasted features and sublime gaze, as she lay on her peaceful deathbed and whispered her longing to be gathered to her divine Father's bosom—when a feeble voice murmured from the bed behind me: "Who is that?"
I knew Mrs. Reed had not spoken for days: was she coming round? I went to her.
"It is I, Aunt Reed."
"Who—I?" was her answer. "Who are you?" looking at me with surprise and a kind of alarm, but not wildly. "You are a complete stranger to me—where is Bessie?"
"She is at the lodge, aunt."
"Aunt," she repeated. "Who calls me aunt? You are not one of the Gibsons; and yet I know you—that face, and the eyes and forehead are strangely familiar. You look like—why, you look like Jane Eyre!"
I said nothing: I was afraid of shocking her by declaring who I was.

"Yet," she said, "I am afraid it is a mistake: my thoughts deceive me. I wished to see Jane Eyre, and I imagine a likeness where none exists; besides, in eight years she must be so changed." I now gently assured her that I was the person she supposed and wished me to be, and seeing that I was understood and that her mind was clear, I explained how Bessie had sent her husband to fetch me from Thornfield.

"I am very ill, I know," she said before long. "I was trying to turn myself a few minutes ago and find I cannot move a limb. It is just as well I should ease my mind before I die: what we think nothing of in health weighs on us at an hour like this. Is the nurse here? Or is there no one in the room but you?"
I assured her we were alone.

"Well, I have twice done you a wrong which I now regret. One was in breaking the promise I gave my husband to raise you as my own child; the other—" she stopped. "After all, it is perhaps of no great importance," she murmured to herself, "and I may get better yet; and to humble myself to her is painful."
She tried to shift her position but could not: her face changed; she seemed to feel some inward sensation—the forerunner, perhaps, of the last agony.
"Well, I must get it over. Eternity is before me: I had better tell her. Go to my dressing case, open it, and take out a letter you will find there."
I obeyed her instructions. "Read the letter," she said.
It was short, and read as follows:

"MADAM,—Will you have the goodness to send me the address of my niece, Jane Eyre, and to tell me how she is? It is my intention to write shortly and ask her to come to me in Madeira. Providence has blessed my efforts to secure a comfortable income; and as I am unmarried and childless, I wish to adopt her during my life, and bequeath her at my death whatever I may have to leave.
I am, Madam, &c., &c., JOHN EYRE, Madeira."
It was dated three years earlier.
"Why did I never hear of this?" I asked.

"Because I disliked you too deeply and thoroughly ever to help lift you to prosperity. I could not forget your behaviour to me, Jane—the fury with which you once turned on me; the tone in which you declared you hated me worst of anyone in the world; the unchildlike look and voice with which you said the very thought of me made you sick, and accused me of treating you with miserable cruelty. I could not forget my own feelings when you started up and poured out the venom of your mind. I felt fear, as if an animal I had struck or kicked had looked up at me with human eyes and cursed me in a man's voice. Bring me some water! Oh, hurry!"

"Dear Mrs. Reed," I said, offering her the drink she needed, "think no more of all that. Let it pass from your mind. Forgive me for my passionate words: I was a child then; eight, nine years have gone by since that day."
She paid no attention to what I said; but when she had drunk the water and caught her breath, she went on—

"I tell you I could not forget it; and I took my revenge. For you to be adopted by your uncle and placed in a state of ease and comfort—that was what I could not bear. I wrote to him; I said I was sorry for his disappointment, but Jane Eyre was dead: she had died of typhus fever at Lowood. Now do as you please: write and contradict my lie—expose my falsehood whenever you like. You were born, I think, to be my torment: my last hour is racked by the memory of a deed which, but for you, I would never have been tempted to commit."
"If you could only be persuaded to think no more of it, aunt, and to regard me with kindness and forgiveness—"

"You have a very bad disposition," she said, "and one to this day I find impossible to understand: how for nine years you could be patient and quiet under any treatment, and in the tenth explode in fire and fury, I can never comprehend."

"My nature is not so bad as you think. I am passionate, but not vengeful. Many a time, as a little child, I would have been glad to love you if you had let me; and I long earnestly to be reconciled to you now. Kiss me, aunt."

I brought my cheek to her lips: she would not touch it. She said I was smothering her by leaning over the bed, and asked again for water. As I laid her down—for I had raised her and supported her on my arm while she drank—I covered her ice-cold, clammy hand with mine. The feeble fingers shrank from my touch; the glazing eyes turned from my gaze.
"Love me, then, or hate me, as you will," I said at last. "You have my full and free forgiveness. Ask now for God's, and be at peace."
Poor, suffering woman! It was too late for her to change the habits of a lifetime. Living, she had always hated me—dying, she must hate me still.

The nurse came in, and Bessie followed. I stayed another half hour, hoping to see some sign of softening; but she gave none. She was sinking rapidly into stupor; her mind did not rally again. At midnight she died. I was not there to close her eyes, nor were either of her daughters. They came to tell us the next morning that it was over. By then she had been laid out. Eliza and I went to see her; Georgiana, who had burst into loud weeping, said she dared not go. There lay Sarah Reed's once robust and active body, rigid and still: her flint-like eye was shut beneath its cold lid; her brow and strong features still bore the stamp of her unyielding soul. A strange and solemn sight she was to me. I gazed at her with gloom and pain: nothing soft, nothing sweet, nothing merciful or hopeful did the spectacle inspire—only a grating anguish for her woes, not my loss, and a sombre, tearless dread at the fearfulness of death in such a form.
Eliza surveyed her mother calmly. After a silence of some minutes she observed—

"With her constitution she should have lived to a good old age: her life was shortened by trouble." And then a spasm constricted her mouth for an instant; as it passed she turned and left the room, and so did I. Neither of us had shed a tear.

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Mr. Rochester had given me only one week's leave of absence; yet a month passed before I left Gateshead. I had wanted to go immediately after the funeral, but Georgiana begged me to stay until she could get away to London, where she was now finally invited by her uncle, Mr. Gibson, who had come down to oversee his sister's burial and settle the family's affairs. Georgiana said she dreaded being left alone with Eliza; from her she got neither sympathy for her sadness, support for her fears, nor help with her preparations. So I endured her feeble-minded laments and selfish complaints as best I could, and did my part sewing and packing her dresses. It is true that while I worked, she sat idle; and I thought to myself, "If you and I were meant to live together always, cousin, we would start things on a different footing. I should not tamely settle into being the patient one; I should assign you your share of the work and make you do it, or else it would go undone. I should also insist that you keep some of those drawling, half-insincere complaints to yourself. It is only because our connection is so brief, and comes at such a sorrowful time, that I consent to be so patient and obliging."

At last I saw Georgiana off; but now it was Eliza's turn to ask me to stay another week. Her plans required all her time and attention, she said; she was about to depart for some unknown destination; and all day she stayed in her own room, the door bolted from inside, filling trunks, emptying drawers, burning papers, and communicating with no one. She wanted me to look after the house, receive visitors, and answer letters of condolence.

One morning she told me I was free to go. "And," she added, "I am grateful for your valuable help and your discretion. There is quite a difference between living with someone like you and with Georgiana: you carry your own weight and burden no one. Tomorrow," she continued, "I leave for the Continent. I shall take up residence in a religious house near Lille—a convent, as you would call it—where I shall be quiet and undisturbed. I shall devote myself for a time to studying Roman Catholic doctrine, and to a careful examination of how their system works. If I find it to be, as I half suspect, the one best designed to ensure that all things are done decently and in order, I shall embrace the faith of Rome and probably take the veil."
I neither expressed surprise at this decision nor tried to dissuade her from it. "The calling will suit you perfectly," I thought. "Much good may it do you!"
When we parted, she said: "Goodbye, cousin Jane Eyre; I wish you well. You have some sense."

I replied: "You are not without sense yourself, cousin Eliza; but what you have, I suppose, will within another year be walled up alive in a French convent. However, it is not my business, and as long as it suits you, I don't much care."

"You are quite right," she said; and with those words we went our separate ways. As I shall have no further occasion to mention either her or her sister, I may as well note here that Georgiana made a good match with a wealthy, worn-out man of fashion, and that Eliza did take the veil, and is to this day the Mother Superior of the convent where she served her novitiate, which she endowed with her fortune.

How people feel when they return home after an absence, long or short, I did not know: I had never experienced the sensation. I knew what it was, as a child, to come back to Gateshead after a long walk and be scolded for looking cold or gloomy. I knew, later, what it was to return from church to Lowood and long for a good meal and a warm fire, unable to get either. Neither of those homecomings was pleasant or desirable: no magnet drew me to a fixed point, growing stronger as I came nearer. The return to Thornfield was yet to be tested.

My journey seemed tedious—very tedious. Fifty miles one day, a night at an inn, fifty miles the next. During the first twelve hours I thought of Mrs. Reed in her last moments; I saw her disfigured and discoloured face, and heard her strangely altered voice. I thought of the funeral day, the coffin, the hearse, the black procession of tenants and servants—how few the relatives—the open vault, the silent church, the solemn service. Then I thought of Eliza and Georgiana; I pictured one the star of a ballroom, the other the occupant of a convent cell; and I dwelt on their separate peculiarities of person and character. The evening arrival in the large town of —— scattered these thoughts; nightfall gave them a different direction entirely. Lying down on my traveller's bed, I left memory behind and turned to anticipation.

I was going back to Thornfield: but how long would I stay? Not long; of that I was sure. I had heard from Mrs. Fairfax during my absence: the house party had broken up; Mr. Rochester had left for London three weeks ago, but was expected back within a fortnight. Mrs. Fairfax guessed he had gone to arrange his wedding, as he had talked of buying a new carriage. She said the idea of his marrying Miss Ingram still struck her as strange; but from what everyone said, and what she herself had seen, she could no longer doubt it would happen soon. "You would be strangely stubborn if you did doubt it," was my silent comment. "I don't doubt it."

The question followed: "Where was I to go?" I dreamed of Miss Ingram all night. In a vivid dream at dawn, I saw her closing the gates of Thornfield against me and pointing me down another road; and Mr. Rochester looked on with folded arms, smiling sardonically, it seemed, at both her and me.

I had not told Mrs. Fairfax the exact day of my return, since I did not want a carriage sent to meet me at Millcote. I planned to walk the distance quietly by myself; and very quietly, after leaving my trunk in the ostler's care, I slipped away from the George Inn about six o'clock on a June evening and took the old road to Thornfield—a road that ran mostly through fields, and was now little used.

It was not a bright or splendid summer evening, though fair and soft: the hay-makers were at work all along the road, and the sky, though far from cloudless, promised well for tomorrow. Its blue—where blue was visible—was mild and calm, and its clouds high and thin. The west, too, was warm: no watery gleam chilled it—it seemed as if a fire were lit, an altar burning behind its screen of marbled vapour, and through openings in it shone a golden red.

I felt glad as the road shortened before me—so glad that I stopped once to ask myself what this joy meant, and to remind reason that I was not going to my home, or to a permanent resting place, or to a place where loving friends waited for me. "Mrs. Fairfax will give you a calm welcome, to be sure," I said, "and little Adèle will clap her hands and jump to see you. But you know perfectly well you are thinking of someone else, and that he is not thinking of you."

But what is as headstrong as youth? What as blind as inexperience? These insisted it was pleasure enough to have the privilege of seeing Mr. Rochester again, whether he saw me or not; and they added, "Hurry! Hurry! Be with him while you may—only a few more days or weeks, at most, and you are parted from him forever!" And then I strangled a newborn agony—a deformed thing I could not bring myself to own or nurture—and ran on.

They are making hay, too, in the Thornfield meadows; or rather, the labourers are just finishing their work, heading home with rakes on their shoulders, now, at the hour I arrive. I have only a field or two to cross, and then I shall reach the road and the gates. How full of roses the hedges are! But I have no time to gather any; I want to reach the house. I passed a tall briar shooting leafy, flowering branches across the path; I see the narrow stile with stone steps; and I see—Mr. Rochester sitting there, a book and a pencil in his hand. He is writing.

Well, he is not a ghost; yet every nerve in my body has come unstrung. For a moment I am beyond my own control. What does this mean? I did not think I would tremble like this when I saw him, or lose my voice or the power of movement in his presence. I will go back as soon as I can move; I need not make an absolute fool of myself. I know another way to the house. It doesn't matter if I knew twenty ways; for he has seen me.
"Hello!" he cries, and puts down his book and pencil. "There you are! Come here, if you please."

I suppose I do go; though in what manner I cannot tell, since I am barely conscious of my movements, concerned only with appearing calm and, above all, with controlling the muscles of my face—which I feel rebelling against my will, struggling to express what I had resolved to hide. But I have a veil—it is down. I may still manage to behave with some composure.

"And this is Jane Eyre? Are you coming from Millcote, and on foot? Yes—just like you: not to send for a carriage and come rattling along the road like an ordinary person, but to steal into the neighbourhood of your home at twilight, just as if you were a dream or a ghost. What on earth have you been doing with yourself this past month?"
"I have been with my aunt, sir, who is dead."

"A classic Jane answer! Heaven protect me! She comes from the other world—from the realm of the dead—and tells me so when she finds me alone here in the dusk! If I dared, I'd touch you, to see if you are flesh or shadow, you elf! But I'd as soon try to catch a will-o'-the-wisp in a swamp. Truant! Truant!" he added, after a moment's pause. "Away from me a whole month, and forgetting me completely, I'll wager!"

I knew there would be pleasure in seeing my master again, even though it was shadowed by the fear that he would soon cease to be my master, and by the knowledge that I was nothing to him. But there was always in Mr. Rochester (or so it seemed to me) such an abundance of the power to communicate happiness that to taste even the crumbs he scattered to stray birds like me was to feast richly. His last words were balm: they seemed to imply that it mattered to him whether I forgot him or not. And he had spoken of Thornfield as my home—if only it were!
He did not move from the stile, and I hardly liked to ask him to let me pass. I soon asked if he had been to London.
"Yes; I suppose you found that out by second sight."
"Mrs. Fairfax told me in a letter."
"And did she tell you what I went to do?"
"Oh yes, sir! Everyone knew your errand."

"You must see the carriage, Jane, and tell me if you don't think it will suit Mrs. Rochester perfectly—and whether she won't look like Queen Boadicea, reclining against those purple cushions. I wish, Jane, I were a little better matched with her outwardly. Tell me now, fairy that you are—can't you give me a charm, or a potion, or something of the sort, to make me handsome?"

"It would be beyond the power of magic, sir." And in my thoughts I added, "A loving eye is all the charm needed: to such an eye you are handsome enough; or rather, your sternness has a power beyond beauty."

Mr. Rochester had sometimes read my unspoken thoughts with an insight I could not understand. In this instance he took no notice of my blunt spoken reply; but he smiled at me with a certain smile of his own, which he used only on rare occasions. He seemed to think it too precious for everyday use: it was the true sunshine of feeling—and he shed it over me now.
"Pass, Janet," he said, making room for me to cross the stile. "Go on home, and rest your weary little wandering feet at a friend's threshold."

All I had to do now was obey him in silence: no need for further conversation. I climbed over the stile without a word, and meant to walk calmly away. An impulse held me fast—a force turned me round. I said—or something in me said for me, and in spite of me—
"Thank you, Mr. Rochester, for your great kindness. I am strangely glad to get back to you; and wherever you are is my home—my only home."

I walked on so fast that even he could hardly have overtaken me had he tried. Little Adèle was half wild with delight when she saw me. Mrs. Fairfax received me with her usual straightforward friendliness. Leah smiled, and even Sophie wished me "bon soir" with pleasure. This was very agreeable; there is no happiness like being loved by the people around you and feeling that your presence adds to their comfort.

That evening I firmly closed my eyes against the future. I stopped my ears against the voice that kept warning me of approaching separation and coming grief. When tea was over and Mrs. Fairfax had taken up her knitting, and I had settled in a low chair near her, and Adèle, kneeling on the carpet, had nestled close to me, and a sense of shared affection seemed to surround us with a ring of golden peace, I offered a silent prayer that we might not be parted far or soon. But when, as we sat like this, Mr. Rochester entered unannounced, and looking at us seemed to take pleasure in the sight of so harmonious a group—when he said he supposed the old lady was all right now that she had her adopted daughter back again, and added that he could see Adèle was "ready to devour her little English mama"—I half dared to hope that even after his marriage he might keep us together somewhere under the shelter of his protection, not entirely banished from the sunshine of his presence.

A fortnight of uncertain calm followed my return to Thornfield Hall. Nothing was said of the master's marriage, and I saw no preparations underway for such an event. Almost every day I asked Mrs. Fairfax whether she had heard anything definite; her answer was always no. Once she said she had actually put the question to Mr. Rochester directly—when was he going to bring his bride home?—but he had answered only with a joke and one of his odd looks, and she could not tell what to make of him.

One thing particularly surprised me: there were no trips back and forth, no visits to Ingram Park. True, it was twenty miles away, on the border of another county; but what was that distance to an eager lover? To so practised and tireless a horseman as Mr. Rochester, it would be merely a morning's ride. I began to nurture hopes I had no right to hold: that the match was off; that rumour had been wrong; that one or both parties had changed their minds. I used to study my master's face for signs of sadness or anger; but I could not recall a time when it had been so consistently free of clouds or dark feelings. If, in the moments I and my pupil spent with him, my spirits flagged and I sank into inevitable gloom, he grew positively cheerful. Never had he called me to his side so often; never been kinder to me when I was there—and, alas, never had I loved him so much.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: A splendid midsummer blazed over England: skies so pure, sunshine so radiant as we saw day after day, seldom blessed our wave-bordered island even once in a season. It was as if a procession of Italian days had come from the south, like a flock of glorious migrating birds, and settled to rest on the cliffs of Britain. The hay was all gathered in; the fields around Thornfield were green and shorn; the roads white and baked; the trees in their dark prime; hedge and wood, full-leaved and deeply coloured, contrasted richly with the sun-bright stretches of the cleared meadows between them.
On Midsummer Eve, Adèle, worn out from gathering wild strawberries in Hay Lane half the day, had gone to bed with the sun. I watched her fall asleep, and when I left her, I went out to the garden.

It was now the sweetest hour of the twenty-four: "Day its burning fires had spent," and dew fell cool on parched plains and scorched hilltops. Where the sun had gone down in simple grandeur—free of any pomp of clouds—a solemn purple spread, burning with the light of rubies and furnace flame at one point, on one hilltop, and stretching high and wide, softer and softer still, over half the sky. The east had its own beauty of fine deep blue and its own modest jewel, a solitary rising star: soon it would boast the moon, but she was still below the horizon.

I walked for a while on the paved path; but a subtle, familiar scent—cigar smoke—drifted from a window. I saw the library casement open a few inches; I knew I might be watched from there, so I went apart into the orchard. No corner of the grounds was more sheltered or more like Eden: it was full of trees and blooming with flowers. A very high wall shut it off from the courtyard on one side; on the other, a beech avenue screened it from the lawn. At the far end was a sunken fence—its only boundary with the open fields beyond. A winding path bordered with laurels and ending at a giant horse-chestnut tree, ringed at the base by a bench, led down to the fence. Here one could wander unseen. While such sweet dew fell, such silence reigned, such twilight gathered, I felt as if I could haunt this shade forever. But as I threaded the flower beds at the upper end of the enclosure, drawn there by the light the now-rising moon cast on this more open area, my step was checked—not by any sound or sight, but once again by a warning fragrance.

Sweet briar and southernwood, jasmine, pink, and rose had long been offering their evening incense; this new scent was neither shrub nor flower. It was—I knew it well—Mr. Rochester's cigar. I looked around and listened. I saw trees heavy with ripening fruit. I heard a nightingale singing in a wood half a mile away; no figure was visible, no approaching footstep audible; but the fragrance grew stronger. I must get away. I headed for the gate leading to the shrubbery, and I saw Mr. Rochester entering. I stepped aside into the ivy recess; he would not stay long; he would soon turn back, and if I kept still he would never see me.

But no—the evening was as pleasant to him as to me, and this old garden as inviting. He strolled on, now lifting gooseberry branches to examine the plum-sized fruit, now plucking a ripe cherry from the wall, now bending over a cluster of flowers to breathe their scent or admire the dewdrops on their petals. A great moth hummed past me; it landed on a plant at Mr. Rochester's feet. He noticed it and stooped to look.
"Now his back is turned," I thought, "and he is occupied. Perhaps if I walk softly I can slip away unnoticed."

I stepped on a strip of turf so the crunch of the gravel would not betray me. He was standing among the flower beds, a yard or two from where I had to pass; the moth apparently held his attention. "I shall get by easily," I thought. But as I crossed his shadow, thrown long over the garden by the moon, not yet risen high, he said quietly, without turning—
"Jane, come and look at this fellow."
I had made no sound: he had no eyes behind him—could his shadow feel? I started at first, then went to him.
"Look at his wings," he said. "He reminds me of a West Indian insect; you don't often see so large and brilliant a night-flier in England. There—he's gone."
The moth flew away. I was meekly retreating too; but Mr. Rochester followed me, and when we reached the gate, he said—
"Turn back: on so lovely a night it is a shame to sit indoors; and surely no one can want to go to bed while sunset is meeting moonrise like this."

It is one of my flaws that though my tongue can sometimes produce a ready answer, there are times when it fails me badly in framing an excuse—and always at some crisis, when a smooth word or plausible pretext is most needed to save me from painful awkwardness. I did not like walking alone with Mr. Rochester in the shadowy orchard at this hour; but I could not think of a reason to leave him. I followed with dragging steps, my thoughts busy searching for an escape. But he himself looked so composed and so serious that I grew ashamed of my confusion: the danger—if any existed—seemed to be entirely in my own mind; his was calm and undisturbed.
"Jane," he began again, as we entered the laurel walk and slowly drifted toward the sunken fence and the horse-chestnut, "Thornfield is a pleasant place in summer, is it not?"
"Yes, sir."
"You must have grown somewhat attached to the house—you, with your eye for natural beauty and your strong capacity for attachment?"
"I am attached to it, indeed."
"And though I can't quite understand how, I notice you have developed some fondness for that silly little child Adèle, and even for plain Mrs. Fairfax?"
"Yes, sir; in different ways, I have affection for both."
"And would be sorry to leave them?"
"Yes."

"A pity!" he said, and sighed and paused. "It is always the way of things in this life," he continued after a moment. "No sooner have you settled into a pleasant resting place than a voice calls out to you to get up and move on, because the hour of rest is over."
"Must I move on, sir?" I asked. "Must I leave Thornfield?"
"I believe you must, Jane. I am sorry, Janet, but I believe indeed you must."
This was a blow; but I did not let it flatten me.
"Well, sir, I shall be ready when the marching orders come."
"They have come now—I must give them tonight."
"Then you are going to be married, sir?"
"Ex-act-ly—pre-cise-ly: with your usual sharpness you have hit the nail on the head."
"Soon, sir?"

"Very soon, my—that is, Miss Eyre. And you'll remember, Jane, that the first time I, or rumour, plainly hinted to you that I meant to put my old bachelor's neck into the sacred noose, to enter the holy state of matrimony—to take Miss Ingram to my bosom, in short (she is quite an armful; but that's beside the point—one can't have too much of such an excellent thing as my beautiful Blanche)—well, as I was saying—listen to me, Jane! You're not turning your head to look for more moths, are you? That was only a ladybird, child, 'flying away home.' I wish to remind you that it was you who first said to me, with that discretion I respect in you—with that foresight, prudence, and humility proper to your responsible and dependent position—that if I married Miss Ingram, you and little Adèle had better leave at once. I pass over the sort of insult this suggestion implies against my beloved's character; indeed, when you are far away, Janet, I'll try to forget it. I shall note only its wisdom, which is such that I have made it my rule of action. Adèle must go to school; and you, Miss Eyre, must find a new position."

"Yes, sir, I will advertise immediately: and meanwhile, I suppose—" I was going to say, "I suppose I may stay here until I find somewhere else to go"—but I stopped, feeling it would be risky to attempt a long sentence, as my voice was not quite under control.
"In about a month I hope to be a bridegroom," Mr. Rochester continued, "and in the meantime, I shall myself look out for employment and a home for you."
"Thank you, sir; I am sorry to give—"

"Oh, no need to apologize! I consider that when a dependent has done her duty as well as you have done yours, she has a sort of claim on her employer for whatever small help he can give. Indeed I have already, through my future mother-in-law, heard of a place that I think will suit you: it is to educate the five daughters of Mrs. Dionysius O'Gall of Bitternutt Lodge, Connaught, Ireland. You'll like Ireland, I think—they say the people there are so warm-hearted."
"It is a long way off, sir."
"No matter—a girl of your sense will not mind the voyage or the distance."
"Not the voyage, but the distance; and then the sea is a barrier—"
"From what, Jane?"
"From England and from Thornfield: and—"
"Well?"
"From you, sir."

I said this almost involuntarily, and, with as little exercise of free will, my tears broke free. I did not cry loudly, though; I avoided sobbing. The thought of Mrs. O'Gall and Bitternutt Lodge struck cold to my heart; colder still the thought of all the ocean destined, it seemed, to rush between me and the master at whose side I now walked; and coldest of all the awareness of the wider ocean—wealth, class, custom—that lay between me and the one I naturally and inevitably loved.
"It is a long way," I said again.

"It is, certainly; and when you reach Bitternutt Lodge, Connaught, Ireland, I shall never see you again, Jane—that's as good as certain. I never go to Ireland, having no particular fondness for the country. We have been good friends, Jane; haven't we?"
"Yes, sir."

"And when friends are on the eve of separation, they like to spend the little time that remains close to each other. Come! We'll talk over the voyage and the parting quietly for half an hour or so, while the stars come out up in heaven. Here is the chestnut tree: here is the bench at its old roots. Come, we will sit here in peace tonight, though we may never again be destined to sit here together." He sat down, and I with him.
"It is a long way to Ireland, Janet, and I am sorry to send my little friend on such a weary journey. But if I can't do better, what is to be done? Are you anything to me, do you think, Jane?"
I could risk no sort of answer now: my heart was full to breaking.

"Because," he said, "I sometimes have a strange feeling about you—especially when you are near me, as now. It is as if I had a string somewhere under my left ribs, tightly and inextricably knotted to a matching string in the same place in your small frame. And if that rough Channel, and two hundred miles of land, came between us, I am afraid that cord of connection would snap; and then I have a nervous feeling I should start bleeding inside. As for you—you'd forget me."
"That I never would, sir: you know—" Impossible to go on.
"Jane, do you hear that nightingale singing in the wood? Listen!"

In listening, I sobbed convulsively; for I could no longer suppress what I was enduring. I was shaken from head to foot with raw distress. When I did speak, it was only to utter a passionate wish that I had never been born, or never come to Thornfield.
"Because you are sorry to leave it?"

The force of emotion—stirred by grief and love within me—was claiming control, fighting for dominance, insisting on its right to prevail, to overcome, to live, rise, and reign at last. Yes—and to speak.

"I grieve to leave Thornfield. I love Thornfield—I love it because I have lived here a full and wonderful life, even if only briefly. I have not been trampled on. I have not been turned to stone. I have not been buried among inferior minds, shut out from every glimpse of what is bright and vital and high. I have talked, face to face, with what I revere, with what I delight in—with an original, a powerful, an expansive mind. I have known you, Mr. Rochester; and it strikes me with terror and anguish to feel I absolutely must be torn from you forever. I see the necessity of going; and it is like staring at the necessity of death."
"Where do you see the necessity?" he asked suddenly.
"Where? You, sir, have placed it before me."
"In what shape?"
"In the shape of Miss Ingram; a noble and beautiful woman—your bride."
"My bride! What bride? I have no bride!"
"But you will have."
"Yes—I will! I will!" He clenched his teeth.
"Then I must go—you have said so yourself."
"No: you must stay! I swear it—and the oath shall be kept."

"I tell you I must go!" I cried, roused now to something like passion. "Do you think I can stay to become nothing to you? Do you think I am a machine—an automaton without feelings—and can bear to have my crust of bread snatched from my lips and my drop of living water dashed from my cup? Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and small, I am soulless and heartless? You think wrong! I have as much soul as you—and fully as much heart! And if God had given me some beauty and great wealth, I should have made it as hard for you to leave me as it is now for me to leave you. I am not speaking to you through convention, or custom, or even mortal flesh: it is my spirit that addresses your spirit, just as if both had passed through the grave, and we stood at God's feet, equal—as we are!"
"As we are!" Mr. Rochester repeated—"so," he added, enclosing me in his arms, gathering me to his chest, pressing his lips on mine: "so, Jane!"

"Yes, so, sir," I answered, "and yet not so; for you are a married man—or as good as married, and wed to someone beneath you—someone with whom you have no sympathy—whom I do not believe you truly love; for I have seen and heard you mock her. I would scorn such a union: therefore I am better than you—let me go!"
"Where, Jane? To Ireland?"
"Yes—to Ireland. I have spoken my mind, and can go anywhere now."
"Jane, be still; don't struggle so, like a wild, frantic bird tearing its own feathers in desperation."
"I am no bird; and no net ensnares me. I am a free human being with an independent will, which I now exert to leave you."
Another effort set me free, and I stood upright before him.
"And your will shall decide your destiny," he said. "I offer you my hand, my heart, and a share of all I possess."
"You are playing a joke, which I merely laugh at."
"I ask you to walk through life at my side—to be my second self, and best earthly companion."
"For that role you have already chosen, and must stand by your choice."
"Jane, be still a moment: you are over-excited. I will be still too."

A gust of wind came sweeping down the laurel walk and trembled through the branches of the chestnut; it wandered away—away—to a measureless distance—it died. The nightingale's song was then the only voice of the hour; listening to it, I wept again. Mr. Rochester sat quiet, looking at me gently and seriously. Some time passed before he spoke; at last he said—
"Come to my side, Jane, and let us explain and understand one another."
"I will never again come to your side: I am torn away now, and cannot return."
"But, Jane, I summon you as my wife: it is you only I intend to marry."
I was silent: I thought he was mocking me.
"Come, Jane—come here."
"Your bride stands between us."
He rose, and in a single stride reached me.
"My bride is here," he said, drawing me to him again, "because my equal is here, and my likeness. Jane, will you marry me?"
Still I did not answer, and still I pulled away from his arms; for I was still incredulous.
"Do you doubt me, Jane?"
"Entirely."
"You have no faith in me?"
"Not a shred."

"Am I a liar in your eyes?" he asked passionately. "Little sceptic, you shall be convinced. What love have I for Miss Ingram? None—and you know it. What love has she for me? None—as I have taken care to prove. I started a rumour that my fortune was not a third of what people supposed, and then I presented myself to see the result; it was coldness, both from her and her mother. I would not—I could not—marry Miss Ingram. You—you strange, you almost unearthly thing!—I love as my own flesh. You—poor and obscure, and small and plain as you are—I beg to accept me as a husband."

"What, me!" I exclaimed, beginning—from his earnestness, and especially from his rudeness—to believe he was sincere. "Me, who have not a friend in the world but you—if you are my friend—not a penny but what you have given me?"
"You, Jane. I must have you for my own—entirely my own. Will you be mine? Say yes, quickly."
"Mr. Rochester, let me look at your face: turn to the moonlight."
"Why?"
"Because I want to read your expression—turn!"
"There! You will find it scarcely more legible than a crumpled, scratched page. Read on: only be quick, for I am in agony."
His face was deeply agitated and deeply flushed, with powerful emotions working in his features and strange light in his eyes.
"Oh, Jane, you torture me!" he cried. "With that searching yet faithful and generous look, you torture me!"
"How can I? If you are telling the truth, and your offer is real, my only feelings toward you must be gratitude and devotion—those cannot torture."
"Gratitude!" he exclaimed, and added wildly—"Jane, accept me quickly. Say, Edward—give me my name—Edward—I will marry you."
"Are you in earnest? Do you truly love me? Do you sincerely wish me to be your wife?"
"I do; and if an oath is needed to convince you, I swear it."
"Then, sir, I will marry you."
"Edward—my little wife!"
"Dear Edward!"
"Come to me—come to me entirely now," he said; and added, in his deepest voice, speaking in my ear as his cheek lay against mine, "Make my happiness—I will make yours."
"God pardon me!" he murmured soon after. "And let no one interfere: I have her, and I will hold her."
"There is no one to interfere, sir. I have no family to object."

"No—that is the best of it," he said. And if I had loved him less, I might have thought his tone and look of triumph savage. But sitting beside him, woken from the nightmare of separation, called to the paradise of union, I thought only of the bliss given me to drink in such abundant measure. Again and again he asked, "Are you happy, Jane?" And again and again I answered, "Yes." After which he murmured, "It will atone—it will atone. Did I not find her friendless, cold, and comfortless? Will I not guard and cherish and comfort her? Is there not love in my heart, and constancy in my resolve? It will stand justified before God's tribunal. I know my Maker approves what I do. For the world's judgment—I wash my hands of it. For human opinion—I defy it."

But what had happened to the night? The moon had not yet set, and we were all in shadow; I could barely see my master's face, near as I was. And what was wrong with the chestnut tree? It writhed and groaned; while wind roared through the laurel walk and swept over us.
"We must go in," said Mr. Rochester. "The weather is turning. I could have sat with you until morning, Jane."

"And so," I thought, "could I with you." I might have said it aloud, but a lurid, vivid spark leapt from a cloud I was watching, and there was a crack, a crash, and a close rattling peal of thunder; and I thought only of burying my dazzled eyes against Mr. Rochester's shoulder.

The rain poured down. He hurried me up the walk, through the grounds, and into the house; but we were thoroughly soaked before we could cross the threshold. He was taking off my shawl in the hall and shaking the water from my loosened hair when Mrs. Fairfax emerged from her room. I did not notice her at first, nor did Mr. Rochester. The lamp was lit. The clock was striking twelve.
"Hurry and get out of your wet things," he said; "and before you go, goodnight—goodnight, my darling!"

He kissed me again and again. When I looked up, stepping out of his arms, there stood the widow, pale, grave, and astonished. I only smiled at her and ran upstairs. "Explanations can wait for another time," I thought. Still, when I reached my room, I felt a pang at the thought that she might even temporarily misunderstand what she had seen. But joy soon swept away every other feeling; and loud as the wind blew, near and deep as the thunder crashed, fierce and frequent as the lightning flashed, and torrential as the rain fell during a storm that lasted two hours, I felt no fear and little awe. Mr. Rochester came three times to my door during the storm to ask if I was safe and calm; and that was comfort, that was strength for anything.

Before I left my bed the next morning, little Adèle came running in to tell me that the great horse-chestnut tree at the bottom of the orchard had been struck by lightning in the night, and half of it split away.

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: As I got up and dressed, I thought over what had happened and wondered if it had been a dream. I couldn't be sure it was real until I saw Mr. Rochester again and heard him repeat his words of love and promise.

While arranging my hair, I looked at my face in the mirror and felt it was no longer plain. There was hope in it, and colour in my cheeks. My eyes seemed as though they had glimpsed the source of all happiness and borrowed light from its glow. I had often been reluctant to look at my master, fearing my appearance would displease him. But now I felt sure I could lift my face to his without cooling his affection. I took a plain but clean, light summer dress from my drawer and put it on. No outfit had ever suited me so well, because I had never worn one in such a state of joy.

I was not surprised, when I ran down into the hall, to find that a brilliant June morning had followed the night's storm, and to feel, through the open glass door, the breath of a fresh, fragrant breeze. Nature had to be cheerful when I was so happy. A beggar woman and her little boy — both pale, ragged figures — were coming up the walk. I ran down and gave them all the money I happened to have in my purse, three or four shillings. Whether it brought them good or ill, they had to share in my celebration. The rooks cawed, and brighter birds sang, but nothing was so merry or so musical as my own rejoicing heart.

Mrs. Fairfax surprised me by looking out of the window with a sad face and saying gravely, "Miss Eyre, will you come to breakfast?" During the meal she was quiet and cool, but I could not set her right just then. I had to wait for my master to give explanations, and so did she. I ate what I could, then hurried upstairs. I met Adèle leaving the schoolroom.
"Where are you going? It's time for lessons."
"Mr. Rochester has sent me away to the nursery."
"Where is he?"
"In there," she said, pointing to the room she had just left. I went in, and there he stood.

"Come and bid me good morning," he said. I gladly went to him, and it was not merely a cold word now, or even a handshake that I received, but an embrace and a kiss. It seemed natural — it seemed right to be so well loved, so cherished by him.

"Jane, you look blooming, and smiling, and pretty," he said. "Truly pretty this morning. Is this my pale little elf? Is this my mustard-seed? This little sunny-faced girl with the dimpled cheek and rosy lips, the satin-smooth hazel hair and the radiant hazel eyes?" (I had green eyes, reader, but you must excuse the mistake. For him they were newly transformed, I suppose.)
"It is Jane Eyre, sir."
"Soon to be Jane Rochester," he added. "In four weeks, Janet. Not a day more. Do you hear that?"

I did, and I could not quite take it in. It made me dizzy. The feeling his announcement sent through me was something stronger than joy — something that struck and stunned. It was, I think, almost fear.
"You blushed, and now you are white, Jane. What is that for?"
"Because you gave me a new name — Jane Rochester — and it seems so strange."
"Yes, Mrs. Rochester," he said. "Young Mrs. Rochester — Fairfax Rochester's girl-bride."

"It can never be, sir. It doesn't sound real. Human beings never enjoy complete happiness in this world. I was not born for a different fate than the rest of my kind. To imagine such a destiny coming to me is a fairy tale — a daydream."

"Which I can and will make real. I shall begin today. This morning I wrote to my banker in London to send me certain jewels he has in his keeping — heirlooms for the ladies of Thornfield. In a day or two I hope to pour them into your lap, for every privilege, every attention shall be yours that I would give a nobleman's daughter if I were about to marry her."
"Oh, sir — never rain jewels! I don't like to hear them spoken of. Jewels for Jane Eyre sounds unnatural and strange. I would rather not have them."

"I will myself put the diamond chain around your neck and the circlet on your forehead — which will suit you, for nature, at least, has stamped her mark of nobility on this brow, Jane. And I will clasp the bracelets on these fine wrists and load these fairy-like fingers with rings."
"No, no, sir! Think of other subjects and speak of other things and in another tone. Don't address me as if I were a beauty. I am your plain, Quakerish governess."
"You are a beauty in my eyes, and a beauty just after the desire of my heart — delicate and ethereal."
"Puny and insignificant, you mean. You are dreaming, sir, or you are mocking me. For God's sake, don't be ironical!"

"I will make the world acknowledge you a beauty, too," he went on, while I truly grew uneasy at the tone he had adopted, because I felt he was either deceiving himself or trying to deceive me. "I will dress my Jane in satin and lace, and she shall have roses in her hair. And I will cover the head I love best with a priceless veil."

"And then you won't know me, sir, and I shall not be your Jane Eyre any longer, but a monkey in a clown's jacket — a jay in borrowed feathers. I would as soon see you, Mr. Rochester, decked out in stage costume as myself dressed in a court lady's gown. And I don't call you handsome, sir, though I love you most dearly — far too dearly to flatter you. Don't flatter me."

He pursued his theme, however, without noticing my objection. "This very day I shall take you in the carriage to Millcote, and you must choose some dresses for yourself. I told you we shall be married in four weeks. The wedding will take place quietly, in the church just down there. Then I shall whisk you away at once to London. After a brief stay, I shall carry my treasure to places nearer the sun: to French vineyards and Italian plains. She shall see whatever is famous in old legend and modern history. She shall taste the life of great cities, and she shall learn to value herself by fair comparison with others."
"Shall I travel? And with you, sir?"

"You shall stay in Paris, Rome, and Naples — in Florence, Venice, and Vienna. All the ground I have wandered over shall be walked again by you. Wherever I stamped my foot, your light step shall follow. Ten years ago I flew through Europe half mad, with disgust, hate, and rage as my companions. Now I shall revisit it healed and renewed, with an angel at my side as my comfort."

I laughed at him. "I am not an angel," I declared, "and I will not be one until I die. I will be myself. Mr. Rochester, you must neither expect nor demand anything heavenly of me — for you will not get it, any more than I shall get it from you, which I do not at all expect."
"What do you expect of me?"

"For a little while you will perhaps be as you are now — a very little while. Then you will turn cool. Then you will be unpredictable. Then you will be harsh, and I shall have a hard time pleasing you. But when you get well used to me, you will perhaps like me again — like me, I say, not love me. I suppose your love will fade within six months or less. I have observed in books written by men that period assigned as the farthest a husband's passion extends. Yet, after all, as a friend and companion, I hope never to become entirely distasteful to my dear master."
"Distasteful! And like you again! I think I shall like you again, and yet again, and I will make you confess that I do not only like but love you — with truth, passion, and constancy."
"Yet are you not unpredictable, sir?"

"To women who please me only by their faces, I am the very devil when I discover they have neither souls nor hearts — when they reveal a landscape of shallowness, triviality, and perhaps stupidity, coarseness, and bad temper. But to the clear eye and eloquent tongue, to the soul made of fire and the character that bends but does not break — at once flexible and strong, yielding and firm — I am ever tender and true."
"Had you ever experience of such a character, sir? Did you ever love such a person?"
"I love one now."
"But before me — if I, indeed, in any way measure up to your demanding standard?"

"I never met your equal. Jane, you please me and you master me — you seem to submit, and I like the sense of pliancy you give. But while I am winding the soft, silken thread around my finger, it sends a thrill up my arm to my heart. I am influenced — conquered. And the influence is sweeter than I can express, and the conquest I undergo has a power beyond any triumph I can win. Why do you smile, Jane? What does that mysterious, uncanny expression mean?"
"I was thinking, sir (you will excuse the idea — it was involuntary) — I was thinking of Hercules and Samson with their temptresses —"
"You were, you little imp —"

"Hush, sir! You don't talk very wisely just now, any more than those gentlemen acted very wisely. However, had they been married, they would no doubt have made up for their softness as suitors by their severity as husbands — and so will you, I fear. I wonder how you will answer me a year from now, should I ask a favour that doesn't suit your convenience or pleasure to grant."
"Ask me something now, Janet — the smallest thing. I long to be asked, and to say yes."
"Indeed I will, sir. I have my petition all ready."
"Speak! But if you look up and smile with that expression, I shall promise everything before I know what it is, and that will make a fool of me."
"Not at all, sir. I ask only this: don't send for the jewels, and don't crown me with roses. You might as well put a border of gold lace around that plain pocket handkerchief you have there."

"I might as well 'gild refined gold.' I know it. Your request is granted then — for now. I will cancel the order I sent to my banker. But you have not yet asked for anything. You have asked for a gift to be withdrawn. Try again."
"Well then, sir, have the goodness to satisfy my curiosity, which is very much aroused on one point."
He looked disturbed. "What? What?" he said hastily. "Curiosity is a dangerous request. It's a good thing I have not taken a vow to grant every wish —"
"But there can be no danger in granting this one, sir."
"Say it, Jane. But I wish that instead of a mere inquiry into, perhaps, a secret, it was a wish for half my estate."

"Now, King Ahasuerus! What do I want with half your estate? Do you think I am a moneylender seeking a good investment in land? I would much rather have all your trust. You will not shut me out of your confidence if you admit me to your heart?"
"You are welcome to all my confidence that is worth having, Jane. But for God's sake, don't desire a useless burden! Don't long for poison — don't turn out to be Eve on my hands!"

"Why not, sir? You have just been telling me how much you liked to be conquered, and how pleasant persuasion is to you. Don't you think I had better take advantage of the confession and begin to coax and plead — even cry and sulk if necessary — for the sake of testing my power?"
"I dare you to try any such thing. Push too far, and the game is up."

"Is it, sir? You give in very quickly. How stern you look now! Your eyebrows have grown as thick as my finger, and your forehead resembles what I once saw described in some very astonishing poetry as 'a blue-piled thunderloft.' Will that be your married look, sir, I suppose?"
"If that will be your married look, then I, as a Christian, will soon give up the idea of living with a mere sprite or salamander. But what did you have to ask, creature — out with it?"

"There, you are less than civil now, and I like rudeness a great deal better than flattery. I had rather be a creature than an angel. This is what I have to ask: why did you take such pains to make me believe you wished to marry Miss Ingram?"

"Is that all? Thank God it is no worse!" And now he relaxed his dark brows, looked down at me with a smile, and stroked my hair, as if well pleased at seeing a danger pass. "I think I may confess," he continued, "even though I should make you a little indignant, Jane — and I have seen what a fire-spirit you can be when you are indignant. You glowed in the cool moonlight last night, when you rebelled against fate and claimed your rank as my equal. Janet, by the way, it was you who made the proposal to me."
"Of course I did. But to the point, if you please, sir — Miss Ingram?"
"Well, I pretended to court Miss Ingram because I wished to make you as madly in love with me as I was with you, and I knew jealousy would be the best weapon I could use for that purpose."

"Excellent! Now you are small — not one bit bigger than the end of my little finger. It was a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace to act that way. Did you think nothing of Miss Ingram's feelings, sir?"
"Her feelings are concentrated in one — pride. And that needs humbling. Were you jealous, Jane?"

"Never mind, Mr. Rochester. It is in no way interesting to you to know that. Answer me truthfully once more. Do you think Miss Ingram will not suffer from your dishonest flirtation? Won't she feel abandoned and deserted?"
"Impossible! — when I told you how she, on the contrary, deserted me. The idea of my being penniless cooled, or rather extinguished, her passion in a moment."
"You have a curious, scheming mind, Mr. Rochester. I am afraid your principles on some points are rather unorthodox."
"My principles were never properly trained, Jane. They may have grown a little crooked for want of attention."
"Once again, seriously: may I enjoy the great happiness that has been given to me without fearing that someone else is suffering the bitter pain I myself felt a while ago?"

"That you may, my good little girl. There is not another being in the world who has the same pure love for me as yourself — for I take that comforting belief to heart, Jane, a faith in your affection."
I pressed my lips to the hand that lay on my shoulder. I loved him very much — more than I could trust myself to say — more than words had power to express.
"Ask something more," he said presently. "It is my delight to be asked, and to give in."

I was again ready with my request. "Tell Mrs. Fairfax what you intend, sir. She saw me with you last night in the hall, and she was shocked. Give her some explanation before I see her again. It pains me to be misjudged by such a good woman."

"Go to your room and put on your bonnet," he replied. "I mean you to come with me to Millcote this morning. While you get ready for the drive, I will enlighten the old lady. Did she think, Janet, that you had given up everything for love and considered it well lost?"
"I believe she thought I had forgotten my place, and yours, sir."
"Place! Place! — your place is in my heart, and on the necks of those who would insult you, now or hereafter. Go."

I was soon dressed. When I heard Mr. Rochester leave Mrs. Fairfax's parlour, I hurried down to it. The old lady had been reading her morning portion of Scripture — the lesson for the day. Her Bible lay open before her, and her spectacles were upon it. Her reading, interrupted by Mr. Rochester's announcement, seemed now forgotten. Her eyes, fixed on the blank wall opposite, expressed the surprise of a quiet mind stirred by unexpected news. Seeing me, she roused herself, made a sort of effort to smile, and framed a few words of congratulation. But the smile faded, and the sentence was left unfinished. She put on her spectacles, shut the Bible, and pushed her chair back from the table.

"I feel so astonished," she began, "that I hardly know what to say to you, Miss Eyre. I have surely not been dreaming, have I? Sometimes I half fall asleep when I am sitting alone and imagine things that have never happened. It has seemed to me more than once, when I have been dozing, that my dear husband, who died fifteen years ago, has come in and sat down beside me — and that I have even heard him call me by my name, Alice, as he used to do. Now, can you tell me whether it is actually true that Mr. Rochester has asked you to marry him? Don't laugh at me. But I really thought he came in here five minutes ago and said that in a month you would be his wife."
"He has said the same thing to me," I replied.
"He has! Do you believe him? Have you accepted him?"
"Yes."
She looked at me, bewildered.
"I could never have thought it. He is a proud man — all the Rochesters were proud — and his father, at least, liked money. He, too, has always been called careful. He means to marry you?"
"He tells me so."
She looked me over from head to foot. In her eyes I read that she had found no charm powerful enough to solve the puzzle.

"It's beyond me!" she continued. "But no doubt it is true since you say so. How it will turn out, I cannot tell. I really don't know. Equality of position and fortune is often advisable in such cases, and there are twenty years of difference in your ages. He might almost be your father."

"No, indeed, Mrs. Fairfax!" I exclaimed, stung. "He is nothing like my father! No one who saw us together would suppose it for an instant. Mr. Rochester looks as young, and is as young, as some men at twenty-five."
"Is it really for love that he is going to marry you?" she asked.
I was so hurt by her coldness and doubt that tears rose to my eyes.

"I am sorry to upset you," the widow went on. "But you are so young, and so little acquainted with men, that I wished to put you on your guard. It is an old saying that 'all that glitters is not gold,' and in this case I do fear there will be something found to be different from what either you or I expect."
"Why? Am I a monster?" I said. "Is it impossible that Mr. Rochester should have a sincere affection for me?"

"No, you are perfectly fine, and much improved of late. And Mr. Rochester, I daresay, is fond of you. I have always noticed that you were a sort of favourite of his. There are times when, for your sake, I have been a little uneasy at his obvious preference and have wished to warn you. But I did not like to suggest even the possibility of anything wrong. I knew such an idea would shock, perhaps offend you, and you were so sensible, so thoroughly modest and level-headed, that I hoped you could be trusted to look after yourself. Last night I cannot tell you what I suffered when I searched all over the house and could find neither you nor the master anywhere. And then, at midnight, I saw you come in with him."
"Well, never mind that now," I interrupted impatiently. "It is enough that everything was proper."

"I hope all will be right in the end," she said. "But believe me, you cannot be too careful. Try to keep Mr. Rochester at a distance. Be wary of yourself as well as of him. Gentlemen in his position are not accustomed to marrying their governesses."
I was growing truly irritated. Luckily, Adèle ran in.
"Let me go — let me go to Millcote too!" she cried. "Mr. Rochester won't let me, though there is so much room in the new carriage. Beg him to let me go, mademoiselle."

"That I will, Adèle." And I hurried away with her, glad to leave my gloomy adviser. The carriage was ready. They were bringing it around to the front, and my master was pacing the pavement, Pilot trotting back and forth behind him.
"Adèle may come with us, may she not, sir?"
"I told her no. I'll have no children along! I'll have only you."
"Do let her go, Mr. Rochester, if you please. It would be better."
"No, it wouldn't. She will be a nuisance."

He was quite commanding, both in look and voice. The chill of Mrs. Fairfax's warnings and the dampness of her doubts were upon me. Something flimsy and uncertain had crept into my hopes. I half lost my sense of power over him. I was about to obey him mechanically, without further protest. But as he helped me into the carriage, he looked at my face.
"What is the matter?" he asked. "All the sunshine is gone. Do you really wish the child to go? Will it annoy you if she is left behind?"
"I would far rather she went, sir."
"Then off for your bonnet, and back like a flash of lightning!" he cried to Adèle.
She obeyed him as fast as she could.
"After all, a single morning's interruption will not matter much," he said, "when I mean shortly to claim you — your thoughts, conversation, and company — for life."

Adèle, when lifted in, began kissing me to express her gratitude for my stepping in on her behalf. She was instantly deposited in a corner on the other side of him. She then peeked around to where I sat. So stern a neighbour was too restricting. To him, in his present grumpy mood, she dared whisper no remarks, nor ask him any questions.
"Let her come to me," I asked. "She will, perhaps, trouble you, sir. There is plenty of room on this side."
He handed her over as if she had been a lapdog. "I'll send her to school yet," he said, but now he was smiling.
Adèle heard him and asked if she was to go to school "without mademoiselle."

"Yes," he replied, "absolutely without mademoiselle, for I am to take mademoiselle to the moon, and there I shall find a cave in one of the white valleys among the volcano-tops, and mademoiselle shall live with me there, and only me."
"She will have nothing to eat. You will starve her," observed Adèle.
"I shall gather manna for her morning and night. The plains and hillsides on the moon are white with manna, Adèle."
"She will want to warm herself. What will she do for a fire?"
"Fire rises out of the lunar mountains. When she is cold, I'll carry her up to a peak and lay her down on the edge of a crater."
"Oh, she would be miserable there — not at all comfortable! And her clothes — they will wear out. How can she get new ones?"

Mr. Rochester pretended to be puzzled. "Hmm!" he said. "What would you do, Adèle? Rack your brains for a solution. How would a white or a pink cloud work for a gown, do you think? And one could cut a pretty enough scarf out of a rainbow."

"She is far better as she is," concluded Adèle, after thinking some time. "Besides, she would get tired of living with only you on the moon. If I were mademoiselle, I would never agree to go with you."
"She has agreed. She has pledged her word."
"But you can't get her there. There is no road to the moon. It is all air, and neither you nor she can fly."

"Adèle, look at that field." We were now outside Thornfield gates, bowling lightly along the smooth road to Millcote, where the dust was well settled by the thunderstorm, and the low hedges and tall trees on each side gleamed green and rain-freshened.

"In that field, Adèle, I was walking late one evening about two weeks ago — the evening of the day you helped me make hay in the orchard meadow. I was tired from raking, so I sat down to rest on a stile.
