I took out a little book and a pencil and began to write about a misfortune that befell me long ago, and a wish I had for happy days to come. I was writing away very fast, though daylight was fading from the page, when something came up the path and stopped two yards from me. I looked at it. It was a little thing with a veil of gossamer on its head. I beckoned it to come near. It stood soon at my knee. I never spoke to it, and it never spoke to me, in words. But I read its eyes and it read mine, and our silent conversation went something like this —

"It was a fairy, come from the land of elves, it said. Its errand was to make me happy. I must go with it out of the ordinary world to a lonely place — such as the moon, for instance — and it nodded its head toward her crescent, rising over Hay Hill. It told me of the alabaster cave and silver valley where we might live. I said I should like to go, but reminded it, as you reminded me, that I had no wings to fly.

"'Oh,' replied the fairy, 'that doesn't matter! Here is a charm that will remove all difficulties.' And she held out a pretty gold ring. 'Put it,' she said, 'on the fourth finger of my left hand, and I am yours and you are mine, and we shall leave earth and make our own heaven up there.' She nodded again at the moon. The ring, Adèle, is in my pocket, disguised as a gold coin. But I mean soon to change it back to a ring."
"But what has mademoiselle to do with it? I don't care about the fairy. You said it was mademoiselle you would take to the moon."

"Mademoiselle is a fairy," he said, whispering mysteriously. At which point I told Adèle not to mind his teasing. She, for her part, displayed a wealth of genuine French scepticism, calling Mr. Rochester "a true liar" and assuring him that she paid no attention whatever to his "fairy tales," and that "in any case, there were no fairies, and even if there were," she was sure they would never appear to him, nor ever give him rings, or offer to live with him on the moon.

The hour spent at Millcote was somewhat trying for me. Mr. Rochester made me go to a certain silk warehouse, where I was ordered to choose half a dozen dresses. I hated the business and begged to put it off — but no, it had to be done now. By means of urgent whispers, I reduced the half dozen to two. These, however, he vowed he would select himself. With anxiety I watched his eye roam over the colourful displays. He settled on a rich silk of the most brilliant amethyst and a superb pink satin. I told him in a fresh series of whispers that he might as well buy me a gold gown and a silver bonnet at once — I would certainly never dare to wear his choices. With enormous difficulty, for he was stubborn as a stone, I persuaded him to exchange them for a sober black satin and a pearl-grey silk. "It will do for the present," he said, "but he would yet see me glittering like a flower garden."

I was glad to get him out of the silk warehouse, and then out of a jeweller's shop. The more he bought me, the more my cheeks burned with annoyance and humiliation. As we got back into the carriage and I sat back, flushed and worn out, I remembered what, in the rush of events, dark and bright, I had completely forgotten — the letter from my uncle, John Eyre, to Mrs. Reed, about his intention to adopt me and make me his heir. "It would, indeed, be a relief," I thought, "if I had even the smallest independence. I can never bear being dressed like a doll by Mr. Rochester, or sitting like a second Danaë with the golden shower falling daily around me. I will write to Madeira the moment I get home and tell my uncle John I am going to be married, and to whom. If I had even the prospect of one day bringing Mr. Rochester an addition to his fortune, I could better endure being kept by him now." Somewhat comforted by this idea (which I carried out that very day), I ventured once more to meet my master's and lover's eye, which persistently sought mine, though I had been avoiding both his face and his gaze. He smiled, and I thought his smile was the kind a sultan might bestow, in a happy, fond moment, on a slave his gold and gems had enriched. I crushed his hand — which was forever chasing mine — vigorously, and thrust it back to him red from the passionate pressure.

"You need not look at me that way," I said. "If you do, I'll wear nothing but my old Lowood dresses to the end of the story. I'll be married in this lilac gingham. You may make a dressing gown for yourself out of the pearl-grey silk and an endless series of waistcoats out of the black satin."

He chuckled and rubbed his hands. "Oh, it is wonderful to see and hear her!" he exclaimed. "Is she original? Is she sharp? I would not exchange this one little English girl for the Grand Turk's whole harem, dark eyes, beautiful figures, and all!"

The Eastern reference stung me again. "I'll not stand in for a harem," I said, "so don't consider me a substitute for one. If you have a taste for anything in that line, away with you, sir, to the bazaars of Istanbul without delay, and spend some of that spare cash you seem at a loss to use up satisfactorily here."
"And what will you do, Janet, while I am bargaining for so many tons of flesh and such a variety of dark eyes?"

"I'll be preparing myself to go out as a missionary to preach liberty to the enslaved — your harem prisoners among the rest. I'll get admitted there, and I'll start a mutiny. And you, mighty overlord that you are, sir, shall in no time find yourself chained in our hands. Nor will I, for one, agree to cut your bonds until you have signed a charter — the most generous that any tyrant ever granted."
"I would consent to be at your mercy, Jane."

"I would have no mercy, Mr. Rochester, if you begged for it with an eye like that. While you looked so, I should be certain that whatever charter you might grant under force, your first act when released would be to violate its conditions."

"Why, Jane, what would you have? I fear you will compel me to go through a private marriage ceremony besides the one performed at the altar. You will insist, I see, on special terms. What will they be?"

"I only want peace of mind, sir — not crushed by piled-up obligations. Do you remember what you said of Céline Varens? Of the diamonds, the cashmeres you gave her? I will not be your English Céline Varens. I shall continue to serve as Adèle's governess. By that I shall earn my room and board and thirty pounds a year besides. I'll pay for my own clothes out of that money, and you shall give me nothing but —"
"Well, but what?"
"Your love. And if I give you mine in return, that debt will be settled."

"Well, for sheer natural boldness and pure inborn pride, you haven't your equal," he said. We were now approaching Thornfield. "Will it please you to dine with me today?" he asked, as we came back through the gates.
"No, thank you, sir."
"And why 'no, thank you,' if one may ask?"
"I have never dined with you, sir, and I see no reason why I should now — until —"
"Until what? You delight in half-finished sentences."
"Until I can't help it."
"Do you suppose I eat like an ogre or a ghoul, that you dread being the companion of my meal?"
"I have formed no opinion on the subject, sir. But I want to go on as usual for another month."
"You will give up your governess slavery at once."

"Indeed, begging your pardon, sir, I shall not. I shall just go on with it as usual. I shall keep out of your way all day, as I have been accustomed to do. You may send for me in the evening, when you feel like seeing me, and I'll come then — but at no other time."

"I need a smoke, Jane, or a pinch of snuff, to comfort me through all this — to keep my composure, as Adèle would say. Unfortunately I have neither my cigar case nor my snuff box. But listen — come closer. It is your turn now, little tyrant, but mine will come soon. And when once I have fairly seized you, to have and to hold, I'll just — figuratively speaking — attach you to a chain like this" (touching his watch chain). "Yes, bonny wee thing, I'll wear you close to my heart, lest my jewel I should lose."
He said this as he helped me down from the carriage. While he afterwards lifted out Adèle, I entered the house and made a swift retreat upstairs.

He duly summoned me to his presence that evening. I had prepared an occupation for him, for I was determined not to spend the whole time in private conversation. I remembered his fine voice. I knew he liked to sing — good singers generally do. I was no vocalist myself and, in his exacting judgment, no musician either, but I loved listening when the performance was good. No sooner had twilight begun to lower her blue and starry banner over the window than I rose, opened the piano, and begged him, for the love of heaven, to give me a song. He said I was a fickle witch and that he would rather sing another time, but I insisted that no time was like the present.
"Did I like his voice?" he asked.
"Very much." I was not fond of indulging that susceptible vanity of his, but for once, and for practical reasons, I would soothe and encourage it.
"Then, Jane, you must play the accompaniment."
"Very well, sir. I will try."

I did try, but was presently swept off the stool and declared "a little bungler." Being pushed unceremoniously to one side — which was precisely what I wanted — he took my place and proceeded to accompany himself, for he could play as well as sing. I retreated to the window recess. And while I sat there and looked out on the still trees and dim lawn, a sweet song was sung in mellow tones:
"The truest love that ever heart Felt at its kindled core, Did through each vein, in quickened start, The tide of being pour.
Her coming was my hope each day, Her parting was my pain; The chance that did her steps delay Was ice in every vein.
I dreamed it would be nameless bliss, As I loved, loved to be; And to this object did I press As blind as eagerly.
But wide as pathless was the space That lay our lives between, And dangerous as the foamy race Of ocean-surges green.
And haunted as a robber-path Through wilderness or wood; For Might and Right, and Woe and Wrath, Between our spirits stood.
I dangers dared; I hindrance scorned; I omens did defy: Whatever menaced, harassed, warned, I passed impetuous by.
On sped my rainbow, fast as light; I flew as in a dream; For glorious rose upon my sight That child of Shower and Gleam.
Still bright on clouds of suffering dim Shines that soft, solemn joy; Nor care I now, how dense and grim Disasters gather nigh.
I care not in this moment sweet, Though all I have rushed o'er Should come on pinion, strong and fleet, Proclaiming vengeance sore:
Though haughty Hate should strike me down, Right, bar approach to me, And grinding Might, with furious frown, Swear endless enmity.
My love has placed her little hand With noble faith in mine, And vowed that wedlock's sacred band Our nature shall entwine.
My love has sworn, with sealing kiss, With me to live — to die; I have at last my nameless bliss. As I love — loved am I!"

He rose and came towards me, and I saw his face all ablaze, his full falcon-eye flashing, tenderness and passion in every feature. I flinched for a moment — then I rallied. Soft scenes and daring displays of feeling I would not have, and I stood in danger of both. A weapon of defence had to be prepared — I sharpened my tongue. As he reached me, I asked sharply whom he was going to marry now.
"That was a strange question to be put by his darling Jane."

"Indeed! I considered it a very natural and necessary one. He had talked of his future wife dying with him. What did he mean by such a pagan idea? I had no intention of dying with him — he could depend on that."
"Oh, all he longed, all he prayed for, was that I might live with him! Death was not for such as I."
"Indeed it was. I had as good a right to die when my time came as he did. But I should wait for that time and not be carried off in some sacrificial ceremony."
"Would I forgive him for the selfish idea and prove my pardon by a reconciling kiss?"
"No. I would rather be excused."
Here I heard myself called a "hard little thing," and it was added that "any other woman would have been melted to the core at hearing such verses sung in her praise."

I assured him I was naturally hard — very flinty — and that he would often find me so. Moreover, I was determined to show him various rough edges of my character before the coming four weeks were up. He should know fully what sort of bargain he had made while there was still time to back out.
"Would I be quiet and talk rationally?"
"I would be quiet if he liked. And as to talking rationally, I flattered myself I was doing that now."

He fretted and fumed and grumbled. "Very good," I thought. "You may huff and fidget as you please, but this is the best approach to take with you, I am certain. I like you more than I can say, but I'll not sink into a swamp of sentiment. And with this needle of wit I'll keep you from the edge of the precipice too — and, moreover, maintain by its sharp point that distance between you and myself most helpful to our real mutual benefit."

Bit by bit, I worked him up to considerable irritation. Then, after he had retreated in a huff to the far end of the room, I got up and said, "I wish you good night, sir," in my natural and customary respectful manner. I slipped out by the side door and escaped.

The system I had started, I pursued throughout the whole trial period, and with great success. He was kept, to be sure, rather cross and grumpy. But on the whole I could see he was excellently entertained, and that a lamb-like submission and dove-like tenderness, while feeding his tyranny more, would have pleased his judgment, satisfied his common sense, and even suited his taste less.

In other people's presence I was, as before, respectful and quiet — any other behaviour being uncalled for. It was only in the evening sessions that I challenged and tormented him. He continued to send for me punctually the moment the clock struck seven. But when I appeared before him now, he had no such sweet terms as "love" and "darling" on his lips. The kindest words I got were "provoking puppet," "wicked elf," "sprite," and "changeling." In place of caresses I now got scowls. In place of a squeeze of the hand, a pinch on the arm. In place of a kiss on the cheek, a sharp tweak of the ear. It was all as it should be. At present I decidedly preferred these fierce favours to anything more tender. Mrs. Fairfax, I saw, approved of me — her anxiety on my account vanished — so I was certain I was doing the right thing. Meanwhile, Mr. Rochester declared I was wearing him to skin and bone and threatened terrible revenge for my present behaviour at some fast-approaching date. I laughed up my sleeve at his threats. "I can keep you in reasonable check now," I reflected, "and I don't doubt I'll be able to do it in the future. If one tactic loses its power, another must be devised."

Yet after all, my task was not an easy one. Often I would rather have pleased than teased him. My future husband was becoming my whole world — and more than the world: almost my hope of heaven. He stood between me and every thought of religion, as an eclipse comes between man and the broad sun. I could not, in those days, see God for His creature, of whom I had made an idol.

chapters.title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: The month of courtship had run its course. Its very last hours were being counted down. There was no putting off the day that was coming — the wedding day — and all preparations for its arrival were complete. I, at least, had nothing more to do. There were my trunks, packed, locked, corded, lined up in a row along the wall of my little room. Tomorrow, at this time, they would be far along the road to London, and so would I (God willing) — or rather, not I, but one Jane Rochester, a person I did not yet know. The address cards alone remained to be attached. They lay, four little squares, in the drawer. Mr. Rochester had himself written the direction, "Mrs. Rochester, —— Hotel, London," on each. I could not bring myself to attach them, or to have them attached. Mrs. Rochester! She did not exist. She would not be born until tomorrow, sometime after eight o'clock in the morning. I would wait to be assured she had come into the world alive before I assigned to her all that property. It was enough that in the closet opposite my dressing table, garments said to be hers had already displaced my black Lowood dress and straw bonnet. For that suit of wedding clothes did not belong to me — the pearl-coloured gown, the filmy veil hanging from the claimed trunk. I shut the closet to conceal the strange, ghost-like clothing it contained, which, at this evening hour — nine o'clock — certainly gave off a most eerie shimmer through the shadows of my room. "I will leave you by yourself, white dream," I said. "I am feverish. I hear the wind blowing. I will go outdoors and feel it."

It was not only the rush of preparation that made me feverish, nor only the anticipation of the great change — the new life to begin tomorrow. Both played their part, no doubt, in producing the restless, excited mood that drove me out at this late hour into the darkening grounds. But a third cause weighed on my mind more than either of them.

I had a strange and anxious thought at heart. Something had happened that I could not understand. No one knew of or had seen the event but myself. It had taken place the night before. Mr. Rochester had been away from home that night, and he had not yet returned. Business had called him to a small estate of two or three farms he owned thirty miles away — business he needed to settle in person before his planned departure from England. I waited now for his return, eager to unburden my mind and to seek from him the answer to the riddle that troubled me. Wait until he comes, reader. When I disclose my secret to him, you shall share the confidence.

I went to the orchard, driven to its shelter by the wind, which had blown strong and steady from the south all day without bringing a drop of rain. Instead of dying down as night approached, it seemed to grow stronger and deeper in its roar. The trees bent steadily in one direction, never twisting around and scarcely tossing back their boughs even once an hour — so constant was the force pushing their branching heads northward. The clouds drifted from pole to pole, fast following, mass upon mass. Not a glimpse of blue sky had been visible that July day.

It was not without a certain wild pleasure that I ran before the wind, delivering my troubled mind to the boundless storm thundering through space. Coming down the laurel walk, I faced the wreck of the chestnut tree. It stood black and torn apart, its trunk split down the centre, gaping wide. The two halves were not broken from each other, for the firm base and strong roots kept them joined below. But the shared life was destroyed — the sap could flow no more. Their great boughs on each side were dead, and next winter's storms would surely bring one or both crashing to earth. Yet for now, they could still be called one tree — a ruin, but a complete ruin.

"You did right to hold fast to each other," I said, as if the monstrous splinters were living things and could hear me. "I think, damaged as you look, charred and scorched, there must be a little sense of life in you yet, rising from that bond at the faithful, honest roots. You will never have green leaves again — never more see birds making nests and singing in your boughs. The time of pleasure and love is over with you. But you are not alone. Each of you has a companion to share in its decay." As I looked up at them, the moon appeared for a moment in the part of sky that filled their gap. Her disc was blood-red and half covered by cloud. She seemed to throw me one bewildered, dreary glance, then buried herself again instantly in the deep mass of cloud. The wind fell for a second around Thornfield, but far away over wood and water poured a wild, mournful wail. It was sad to hear, and I hurried on.

Here and there I wandered through the orchard, gathering up the apples that thickly carpeted the grass around the tree roots. Then I occupied myself separating the ripe ones from the unripe. I carried them into the house and put them away in the storeroom. Then I went to the library to check whether the fire was lit, for though it was summer, I knew on such a gloomy evening Mr. Rochester would like to see a cheerful hearth when he came in. Yes, the fire had been kindled some time ago and burned well. I placed his armchair by the chimney corner. I wheeled the table near it. I drew the curtain and had the candles brought in ready for lighting. More restless than ever, when I had finished these arrangements I could not sit still, nor even stay in the house. A little clock in the room and the old clock in the hall struck ten at the same moment.

"How late it's getting!" I said. "I will run down to the gates. It's moonlight at intervals, and I can see a good way along the road. He may be coming now, and meeting him will save some minutes of suspense."

The wind roared high in the great trees that arched over the gates. But the road, as far as I could see to the right and left, was all still and solitary — except for the shadows of clouds crossing it at intervals as the moon looked out. It was only a long, pale line, unbroken by a single moving figure.

A childish tear dimmed my eye as I looked — a tear of disappointment and impatience. Ashamed of it, I wiped it away. I lingered. The moon withdrew entirely into her chamber and drew close her curtain of dense cloud. The night grew dark. Rain came driving fast on the gale.

"I wish he would come! I wish he would come!" I exclaimed, seized with gloomy foreboding. I had expected his arrival before tea. Now it was dark. What could keep him? Had an accident happened? The events of the previous night came back to me. I interpreted them as a warning of disaster. I feared my hopes were too bright to come true, and I had enjoyed so much happiness lately that I imagined my fortune had passed its peak and must now decline.
"Well, I cannot return to the house," I thought. "I cannot sit by the fireside while he is abroad in this foul weather. Better tire my limbs than strain my heart. I will go forward and meet him."

I set out. I walked fast, but not far. Before I had covered a quarter of a mile, I heard the beat of hooves. A horseman came on at full gallop, a dog running at his side. Away with dark thoughts! It was he — there he was, mounted on Mesrour, followed by Pilot. He saw me, for the moon had opened a blue field in the sky and rode in it, watery and bright. He took his hat off and waved it around his head. I now ran to meet him.
"There!" he exclaimed, as he stretched out his hand and leaned from the saddle. "You can't do without me — that is obvious. Step on my boot-toe. Give me both hands. Mount!"

I obeyed. Joy made me nimble. I sprang up before him. A hearty round of kisses I got for a welcome, and some boastful triumph, which I swallowed as well as I could. He checked himself in his elation to ask, "But is there anything the matter, Janet, that you come to meet me at such an hour? Is there anything wrong?"
"No, but I thought you would never come. I could not bear to wait in the house for you, especially with this rain and wind."

"Rain and wind, indeed! Yes, you are dripping like a mermaid. Pull my cloak around you. But I think you are feverish, Jane — both your cheek and hand are burning hot. I ask again, is there anything the matter?"
"Nothing now. I am neither afraid nor unhappy."
"Then you have been both?"
"Rather. But I'll tell you all about it by and by, sir. And I daresay you will only laugh at me for my trouble."

"I'll laugh at you heartily when tomorrow is past. Until then I dare not — my prize is not certain. This is you, who have been as slippery as an eel this last month, and as thorny as a briar rose? I could not lay a finger anywhere without being pricked. And now I seem to have gathered up a stray lamb in my arms. You wandered out of the fold to seek your shepherd, did you, Jane?"
"I wanted you. But don't boast. Here we are at Thornfield. Now let me get down."

He set me down on the pavement. As the groom took his horse and he followed me into the hall, he told me to hurry and put on something dry, then return to him in the library. He stopped me as I headed for the staircase, to extract a promise that I would not be long. Nor was I long — in five minutes I rejoined him. I found him at supper.
"Take a seat and keep me company, Jane. Please God, it is the last meal but one you will eat at Thornfield Hall for a long time."
I sat down near him but told him I could not eat.
"Is it because you have a journey ahead of you, Jane? Is it the thought of going to London that takes away your appetite?"
"I cannot see my future clearly tonight, sir. And I hardly know what thoughts I have in my head. Everything in life seems unreal."
"Except me. I am solid enough — touch me."
"You, sir, are the most phantom-like of all. You are a mere dream."
He held out his hand, laughing. "Is that a dream?" he said, placing it close to my eyes. He had a rounded, muscular, vigorous hand, as well as a long, strong arm.
"Yes, though I touch it, it is a dream," I said, as I pushed it away from my face. "Sir, have you finished supper?"
"Yes, Jane."
I rang the bell and had the tray taken away. When we were alone again, I stirred the fire and then took a low seat at my master's knee.
"It is near midnight," I said.
"Yes. But remember, Jane, you promised to stay up with me the night before my wedding."
"I did. And I will keep my promise, for an hour or two at least. I have no wish to go to bed."
"Are all your arrangements complete?"
"All, sir."
"And on my part likewise," he returned. "I have settled everything, and we shall leave Thornfield tomorrow, within half an hour after our return from church."
"Very well, sir."
"With what an extraordinary smile you said that — 'very well,' Jane! What a bright spot of colour you have on each cheek! And how strangely your eyes glitter! Are you well?"
"I believe I am."
"Believe! What is the matter? Tell me what you feel."
"I could not, sir. No words could tell you what I feel. I wish this present hour would never end. Who knows what fate the next may bring?"
"This is morbid thinking, Jane. You have been over-excited or over-tired."
"Do you, sir, feel calm and happy?"
"Calm? — no. But happy — to the heart's core."
I looked up at him to read the signs of joy in his face. It was ardent and flushed.
"Give me your confidence, Jane," he said. "Relieve your mind of any weight that oppresses it by sharing it with me. What do you fear? That I shall not prove a good husband?"
"That is the idea farthest from my thoughts."
"Are you anxious about the new world you are about to enter? The new life you are stepping into?"
"No."
"You puzzle me, Jane. Your look and tone of sorrowful boldness confuse and pain me. I want an explanation."
"Then, sir, listen. You were away from home last night?"

"I was. I know that. And you hinted a while ago at something that had happened in my absence — nothing of consequence, probably. But, in short, it has disturbed you. Let me hear it. Has Mrs. Fairfax said something, perhaps? Or have you overheard the servants talking? Has your sensitive pride been wounded?"
"No, sir." The clock struck twelve. I waited until the timepiece had finished its silver chime and the big clock its deep, vibrating stroke. Then I continued.

"All day yesterday I was very busy and very happy in my constant activity. I am not, as you seem to think, troubled by any fears about the new life ahead of me. I think it a glorious thing to have the hope of living with you, because I love you. No, sir, don't caress me now — let me talk undisturbed. Yesterday I trusted in Providence, and believed that events were working together for your good and mine. It was a fine day, if you recall — the calm air and sky forbade worries about your safety or comfort on your journey. I walked a little while on the pavement after tea, thinking of you, and I pictured you so near me in my imagination that I scarcely missed your actual presence. I thought of the life that lay before me — your life, sir — an existence wider and more stirring than my own: as much more so as the depths of the ocean to which a brook runs are wider than the shallows of its own narrow channel. I wondered why moralists call this world a dreary wilderness. For me it blossomed like a rose. Just at sunset, the air turned cold and the sky cloudy. I went in. Sophie called me upstairs to look at my wedding dress, which they had just brought, and under it in the box I found your present — the veil which, in your princely extravagance, you had sent for from London, resolved, I suppose, since I would not have jewels, to trick me into accepting something equally costly. I smiled as I unfolded it, and planned how I would tease you about your aristocratic tastes and your efforts to disguise your common-born bride in the trappings of a noblewoman. I thought how I would carry down to you the square of plain lace I had prepared myself as a covering for my lowly head, and ask if that was not good enough for a woman who could bring her husband neither fortune, beauty, nor connections. I saw plainly how you would look, and heard your impatient protests and your proud dismissal of any need on your part to add to your wealth or raise your standing by marrying either a purse or a title."
"How well you read me, you witch!" Mr. Rochester broke in. "But what did you find in the veil besides its embroidery? Did you find poison, or a dagger, that you look so troubled now?"

"No, no, sir. Besides the delicacy and richness of the fabric, I found nothing but Fairfax Rochester's pride. And that did not frighten me, because I am used to seeing that particular demon. But, sir, as it grew dark, the wind rose. It blew yesterday evening, not as it blows now — wild and high — but with a low, moaning sound, far more unsettling. I wished you were home. I came into this room, and the sight of the empty chair and fireless hearth chilled me. For some time after I went to bed, I could not sleep. A sense of anxious excitement plagued me. The rising gale seemed to muffle some mournful under-sound. Whether it came from inside the house or outside I could not at first tell, but it returned, faint yet doleful, at every pause in the wind. At last I made out it must be some dog howling in the distance. I was glad when it stopped. When I fell asleep, I continued in dreams the idea of a dark and gusty night. I continued also the wish to be with you, and I felt a strange, sorrowful awareness of some barrier separating us. During all my first sleep, I was following the twists of an unknown road. Total darkness surrounded me. Rain pelted me. I was burdened with a little child — a very small creature, too young and weak to walk, which shivered in my cold arms and wailed miserably in my ear. I thought, sir, that you were on the road far ahead of me, and I strained every nerve to overtake you, and made effort upon effort to call your name and beg you to stop — but my movements were shackled, and my voice kept dying away, wordless. While you, I felt, drew farther and farther away with every moment."

"And these dreams weigh on your spirits now, Jane, when I am close to you? Nervous little creature! Forget your phantom sorrows and think only of real happiness! You say you love me, Janet — yes, I will not forget that, and you cannot deny it. Those words did not die unspoken on your lips. I heard them, clear and soft — perhaps too solemn, but sweet as music: 'I think it is a glorious thing to have the hope of living with you, Edward, because I love you.' Do you love me, Jane? Repeat it."
"I do, sir — I do, with my whole heart."

"Well," he said, after some minutes' silence, "it is strange, but that sentence has pierced my heart painfully. Why? I think because you said it with such earnest, almost religious intensity, and because your upward gaze at me now is the very essence of faith, truth, and devotion. It is too much as if some spirit were near me. Look wicked, Jane — as you know well how to look. Show me one of your wild, shy, teasing smiles. Tell me you hate me — tease me, provoke me. Do anything but move me. I would rather be angered than saddened."
"I will tease you and provoke you to your heart's content when I have finished my tale. But hear me to the end."
"I thought, Jane, you had told me all. I thought I had found the source of your sadness in a dream."
I shook my head. "What! Is there more? But I will not believe it to be anything important. I warn you of my disbelief beforehand. Go on."
The uneasiness of his manner, his somewhat apprehensive impatience, surprised me, but I continued.

"I dreamt another dream, sir — that Thornfield Hall was a dreary ruin, the haunt of bats and owls. I thought that of all the grand front nothing remained but a shell-like wall, very high and very fragile-looking. I wandered, on a moonlit night, through the grass-grown enclosure within. Here I stumbled over a marble hearth, and there over a fallen fragment of stonework. Wrapped in a shawl, I still carried the unknown little child. I could not set it down anywhere, however tired my arms — however much its weight slowed my progress, I had to keep hold of it. I heard the gallop of a horse at a distance on the road. I was sure it was you, and you were leaving for many years and for a distant country. I climbed the thin wall with frantic, reckless haste, desperate to catch one glimpse of you from the top. The stones rolled out from under my feet. The ivy branches I grasped gave way. The child clung around my neck in terror and almost strangled me. At last I gained the summit. I saw you like a speck on a white track, shrinking smaller every moment. The wind blew so strong I could not stand. I sat down on the narrow ledge. I hushed the frightened infant in my lap. You turned a bend in the road. I leaned forward to take a last look. The wall crumbled. I was shaken. The child rolled from my knee. I lost my balance, fell, and woke."
"Now, Jane, that is all."

"All the preface, sir. The tale is yet to come. On waking, a gleam dazzled my eyes. I thought — oh, it is daylight! But I was mistaken. It was only candlelight. Sophie, I supposed, had come in. There was a light on the dressing table, and the door of the closet, where I had hung my wedding dress and veil before going to bed, stood open. I heard a rustling there. I asked, 'Sophie, what are you doing?' No one answered. But a form emerged from the closet. It took the light, held it high, and examined the garments hanging from the trunk. 'Sophie! Sophie!' I called again — and still it was silent. I had sat up in bed. I leaned forward. First surprise, then bewilderment came over me — and then my blood ran cold. Mr. Rochester, this was not Sophie. It was not Leah. It was not Mrs. Fairfax. It was not — no, I was sure of it, and am still — it was not even that strange woman, Grace Poole."
"It must have been one of them," my master interrupted.
"No, sir, I solemnly assure you otherwise. The figure standing before me had never crossed my sight within the walls of Thornfield Hall before. The height, the shape were new to me."
"Describe it, Jane."

"It seemed, sir, a woman, tall and large, with thick, dark hair hanging long down her back. I don't know what she wore — it was white and straight — but whether it was a gown, a sheet, or a shroud, I cannot tell."
"Did you see her face?"

"Not at first. But presently she took my veil from its place. She held it up, gazed at it long, and then she threw it over her own head and turned to the mirror. At that moment I saw the reflection of her face and features quite distinctly in the dark oblong glass."
"And how were they?"

"Fearful and ghastly to me — oh, sir, I never saw a face like it! It was a discoloured face — a savage face. I wish I could forget the roll of the red eyes and the dreadful blackened swelling of the features!"
"Ghosts are usually pale, Jane."
"This, sir, was purple. The lips were swollen and dark. The brow was furrowed. The black eyebrows were raised wide over the bloodshot eyes. Shall I tell you what it reminded me of?"
"You may."
"Of the foul German spectre — the Vampire."
"Ah! What did it do?"
"Sir, it removed my veil from its gaunt head, tore it in two, and flinging both pieces on the floor, trampled on them."
It removed my veil from its gaunt head, tore it in two, and flinging both pieces on the floor, trampled on them.
"Afterwards?"

"It drew aside the window curtain and looked out. Perhaps it saw dawn approaching, for, taking the candle, it retreated to the door. Just at my bedside, the figure stopped. The fiery eyes glared at me — she thrust the candle close to my face and snuffed it out before my eyes. I was aware her ghastly face hovered over mine, and I lost consciousness. For the second time in my life — only the second time — I fainted from sheer terror."
"Who was with you when you came to?"

"No one, sir, but the broad daylight. I rose, bathed my head and face in water, drank a long draught. I felt that though I was weak I was not ill, and I decided that to no one but you would I confide this vision. Now, sir, tell me who and what that woman was."
"The creation of an overstimulated brain — that is certain. I must be careful with you, my treasure. Nerves like yours were not made for rough handling."
"Sir, believe me, my nerves were not at fault. The thing was real. The event actually happened."
"And your earlier dreams — were they real too? Is Thornfield Hall a ruin? Am I torn from you by impossible obstacles? Am I leaving you without a tear — without a kiss — without a word?"
"Not yet."
"Am I about to? Why, the day has already begun which is to bind us forever. And when we are once united, there shall be no return of these mental terrors. I guarantee that."
"Mental terrors, sir! I wish I could believe them to be only that. I wish it more now than ever, since even you cannot explain the mystery of that awful visitor."
"And since I cannot, Jane, it must have been unreal."

"But, sir, when I said as much to myself on rising this morning, and when I looked around the room to gather courage and comfort from the cheerful sight of each familiar object in full daylight, there — on the carpet — I saw what gave the flat lie to my theory: the veil, torn from top to bottom in two halves!"

I felt Mr. Rochester flinch and shudder. He hastily flung his arms around me. "Thank God!" he exclaimed. "That if anything evil did come near you last night, it was only the veil that was harmed. Oh, to think what might have happened!"
He drew his breath short and strained me so close to him I could scarcely breathe. After some minutes' silence, he continued, more cheerfully —

"Now, Janet, I'll explain it all to you. It was half dream, half reality. A woman did, I have no doubt, enter your room. And that woman was — must have been — Grace Poole. You call her a strange creature yourself, and from all you know you have reason to. What did she do to me? What to Mason? In a state between sleeping and waking, you noticed her entrance and her actions. But feverish, almost delirious as you were, you gave her a monstrous appearance different from her own. The long, wild hair, the swollen dark face, the exaggerated height — those were products of nightmare. The spiteful tearing of the veil was real — and that is just like her. I see you would ask why I keep such a woman in my house. When we have been married a year and a day, I will tell you — but not now. Are you satisfied, Jane? Do you accept my explanation?"

I thought about it, and in truth it seemed the only possible one. Satisfied I was not, but to please him I tried to appear so — and relieved I certainly did feel. So I answered him with a contented smile. And now, as it was long past one, I prepared to leave him.
"Does Sophie not sleep with Adèle in the nursery?" he asked, as I lit my candle.
"Yes, sir."

"And there is room enough in Adèle's little bed for you. You must share it with her tonight, Jane. It is no wonder the incident you have described should make you nervous, and I would rather you did not sleep alone. Promise me to go to the nursery."
"I shall be very glad to, sir."

"And fasten the door securely on the inside. Wake Sophie when you go upstairs, on the pretext of asking her to rouse you in good time tomorrow, for you must be dressed and have finished breakfast before eight. And now, no more dark thoughts. Chase dull care away, Janet. Don't you hear how softly the wind has dropped? And there is no more rain beating against the window-panes. Look here" — he lifted the curtain — "it is a lovely night!"
It was. Half the sky was pure and clear. The clouds, now retreating before the wind, which had shifted to the west, were filing off eastward in long, silver columns. The moon shone peacefully.
"Well," said Mr. Rochester, gazing searchingly into my eyes, "how is my Janet now?"
"The night is serene, sir, and so am I."
"And you will not dream of separation and sorrow tonight, but of happy love and blissful union."

This prediction was only half fulfilled. I did not indeed dream of sorrow, but neither did I dream of joy — for I never slept at all. With little Adèle in my arms, I watched the slumber of childhood — so peaceful, so calm, so innocent — and waited for the coming day. All my life was awake and stirring in my body. As soon as the sun rose, I rose too. I remember Adèle clung to me as I left her. I remember I kissed her as I loosened her little hands from my neck. And I cried over her with strange emotion, and left her because I feared my sobs would wake her still sound sleep. She seemed the emblem of my past life, and he whom I was now to dress myself to meet, the dread but adored figure of my unknown future day.

chapters.title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Sophie came at seven to dress me. She was very slow indeed in finishing the task — so slow that Mr. Rochester, grown impatient at my delay, I suppose, sent up to ask why I did not come. She was just fastening my veil (the plain square of lace, after all) to my hair with a brooch. I hurried from her hands as soon as I could.
"Stop!" she cried in French. "Look at yourself in the mirror. You have not taken one peep."

So I turned at the door. I saw a robed and veiled figure, so unlike my usual self that it seemed almost the image of a stranger. "Jane!" called a voice, and I hurried down. I was met at the foot of the stairs by Mr. Rochester.
"Dawdler!" he said. "My brain is on fire with impatience, and you take so long!"

He took me into the dining room, surveyed me keenly from head to foot, pronounced me "fair as a lily, and not only the pride of his life but the desire of his eyes," and then, telling me he would give me only ten minutes to eat some breakfast, he rang the bell. One of his recently hired servants, a footman, answered it.
"Is John getting the carriage ready?"
"Yes, sir."
"Is the luggage brought down?"
"They are bringing it down, sir."
"Go to the church. See if Mr. Wood the clergyman and the clerk are there. Come back and tell me."
The church, as the reader knows, was just beyond the gates. The footman soon returned.
"Mr. Wood is in the vestry, sir, putting on his surplice."
"And the carriage?"
"The horses are being harnessed."
"We shall not need it to go to church, but it must be ready the moment we return — all the boxes and luggage arranged and strapped on, and the coachman in his seat."
"Yes, sir."
"Jane, are you ready?"

I rose. There were no groomsmen, no bridesmaids, no relatives to wait for or arrange — none but Mr. Rochester and I. Mrs. Fairfax stood in the hall as we passed. I would have liked to speak to her, but my hand was held in a grip of iron. I was hurried along by a stride I could hardly match. And to look at Mr. Rochester's face was to understand that not a second of delay would be tolerated for any reason. I wonder what other bridegroom ever looked as he did — so bent on his purpose, so grimly determined — or who, under such set brows, ever revealed such blazing, flashing eyes.

I do not know whether the day was fair or foul. As we went down the drive, I gazed neither at sky nor earth. My heart was with my eyes, and both seemed to have migrated into Mr. Rochester's frame. I wanted to see the invisible thing on which, as we walked, he appeared to fix a gaze fierce and grim. I wanted to feel the thoughts whose force he seemed to be bracing against and resisting.
At the churchyard gate he stopped. He discovered I was completely out of breath. "Am I cruel in my love?" he said. "Wait a moment. Lean on me, Jane."

And now I can recall the picture of the grey old house of God rising calm before me, of a rook wheeling around the steeple, of a rosy morning sky beyond. I remember something, too, of the green grave-mounds. And I have not forgotten two figures of strangers wandering among the low hillocks and reading the inscriptions on the few mossy headstones. I noticed them because, as they saw us, they passed around to the back of the church. I had no doubt they were going to enter by the side-aisle door and witness the ceremony. Mr. Rochester did not notice them. He was earnestly looking at my face, from which the blood had, I imagine, momentarily drained. For I felt my forehead damp and my cheeks and lips cold. When I recovered, which I soon did, he walked gently with me up the path to the porch.

We entered the quiet and humble church. The priest waited in his white surplice at the modest altar, the clerk beside him. All was still. Two shadows only moved in a far corner. My guess had been correct. The strangers had slipped in before us, and they now stood by the Rochester family vault, their backs towards us, examining through the railings the old, time-stained marble tomb where a kneeling angel guarded the remains of Damer de Rochester, slain at Marston Moor during the civil wars, and of Elizabeth, his wife.

Our place was taken at the communion rail. Hearing a careful step behind me, I glanced over my shoulder. One of the strangers — a gentleman, clearly — was advancing up the central aisle. The service began. The explanation of the purpose of marriage was read through, and then the clergyman came a step further forward and, bending slightly towards Mr. Rochester, went on.

"I require and charge you both (as you will answer on the dreadful day of judgment, when the secrets of all hearts shall be disclosed), that if either of you know any impediment why you may not lawfully be joined together in matrimony, you do now confess it; for be well assured that so many as are coupled together otherwise than God's Word allows, are not joined together by God, neither is their marriage lawful."

He paused, as the custom is. When is the pause after that sentence ever broken by a reply? Not, perhaps, once in a hundred years. And the clergyman, who had not lifted his eyes from his book and had held his breath only for a moment, was proceeding. His hand was already stretched towards Mr. Rochester, his lips parting to ask, "Will you have this woman for your wedded wife?" — when a distinct and nearby voice said —
"The marriage cannot go on. I declare the existence of an impediment."

The clergyman looked up at the speaker and stood silent. The clerk did the same. Mr. Rochester moved slightly, as if an earthquake had rolled under his feet. Finding a firmer footing, and not turning his head or eyes, he said, "Proceed."
A deep silence fell when he had uttered that word, with quiet but low force. Presently Mr. Wood said —
"I cannot proceed without some investigation into what has been asserted, and evidence of its truth or falsehood."
"The ceremony is completely broken off," added the voice behind us. "I am in a position to prove my claim. An insurmountable impediment to this marriage exists."

Mr. Rochester heard, but did not react. He stood stubborn and rigid, making no movement but to seize my hand. What a hot and powerful grip he had! And how like quarried marble was his pale, firm, massive face at this moment! How his eye shone, still watchful, and yet wild beneath!
Mr. Wood seemed at a loss. "What is the nature of the impediment?" he asked. "Perhaps it may be overcome — explained away?"
"Hardly," was the answer. "I have called it insurmountable, and I speak with full knowledge."
The speaker came forward and leaned on the rails. He continued, uttering each word distinctly, calmly, steadily, but not loudly —
"It simply consists in the existence of a previous marriage. Mr. Rochester has a wife now living."

My nerves vibrated to those quietly spoken words as they had never vibrated to thunder — my blood felt their subtle violence as it had never felt frost or fire. But I was composed, and in no danger of fainting. I looked at Mr. Rochester. I made him look at me. His whole face was colourless rock. His eye was both spark and flint. He denied nothing. He seemed as if he would defy all things. Without speaking, without smiling, without seeming to recognise in me a human being, he only wrapped his arm around my waist and locked me to his side.
"Who are you?" he asked of the intruder.
"My name is Briggs, a solicitor of —— Street, London."
"And you would force a wife upon me?"
"I would remind you of your wife's existence, sir, which the law recognises, if you do not."
"Oblige me with an account of her — her name, her family, her place of residence."
"Certainly." Mr. Briggs calmly took a paper from his pocket and read out in a sort of official, nasal voice:

"'I affirm and can prove that on the 20th of October, A.D. —— (a date of fifteen years back), Edward Fairfax Rochester, of Thornfield Hall, in the county of ——, and of Ferndean Manor, in ——shire, England, was married to my sister, Bertha Antoinetta Mason, daughter of Jonas Mason, merchant, and of Antoinetta his wife, a Creole, at —— church, Spanish Town, Jamaica. The record of the marriage will be found in the register of that church — a copy of it is now in my possession. Signed, Richard Mason.'"
"That — if a genuine document — may prove I have been married, but it does not prove that the woman named as my wife is still living."
"She was living three months ago," returned the lawyer.
"How do you know?"
"I have a witness to the fact, whose testimony even you, sir, will scarcely dispute."
"Produce him — or go to hell."
"I will produce him first — he is on the spot. Mr. Mason, have the goodness to step forward."

Mr. Rochester, on hearing the name, clenched his teeth. He experienced, too, a sort of violent, convulsive tremor. Near to him as I was, I felt the spasm of fury or despair run through his body. The second stranger, who had until then lingered in the background, now drew near. A pale face looked over the solicitor's shoulder — yes, it was Mason himself. Mr. Rochester turned and glared at him. His eye, as I have often said, was a dark eye. It had now a tawny, even bloody light in its depth. His face flushed — his olive cheek and pale forehead received a glow as from a spreading, rising fire. He stirred, lifted his strong arm — he could have struck Mason, dashed him to the church floor, knocked the breath from his body with one ruthless blow — but Mason shrank away and cried faintly, "Good God!" Contempt fell cold on Mr. Rochester — his passion died as if a blight had withered it. He only asked — "What have you to say?"
An inaudible reply escaped Mason's white lips.
"The devil take you if you cannot answer clearly. I ask again — what have you to say?"

"Sir — sir," the clergyman interrupted, "do not forget you are in a sacred place." Then, turning to Mason, he inquired gently, "Are you aware, sir, whether or not this gentleman's wife is still living?"
"Courage," urged the lawyer. "Speak out."
"She is now living at Thornfield Hall," said Mason, in a clearer voice. "I saw her there last April. I am her brother."
"At Thornfield Hall!" exclaimed the clergyman. "Impossible! I am an old resident in this neighbourhood, sir, and I never heard of a Mrs. Rochester at Thornfield Hall."
I saw a grim smile twist Mr. Rochester's lips, and he muttered —
"No, by God! I took care that no one should hear of it — or of her under that name." He paused — for ten minutes he held counsel with himself. He formed his resolve and announced it —

"Enough! It shall all come out at once, like the bullet from the barrel. Wood, close your book and take off your surplice. John Green" — to the clerk — "leave the church. There will be no wedding today." The man obeyed.

Mr. Rochester continued, boldly and recklessly: "Bigamy is an ugly word! I meant, however, to be a bigamist. But fate has outmanoeuvred me, or Providence has checked me — perhaps the latter. I am little better than a devil at this moment, and, as my pastor there would tell me, deserve no doubt the harshest judgments of God, even to the unquenchable fire and the undying worm. Gentlemen, my plan is shattered. What this lawyer and his client say is true. I have been married, and the woman I married lives! You say you never heard of a Mrs. Rochester at the house up there, Wood? But I daresay you have many a time listened to gossip about the mysterious madwoman kept there under watch and guard. Some have whispered to you that she is my illegitimate half-sister. Some, my discarded mistress. I now inform you that she is my wife, whom I married fifteen years ago — Bertha Mason by name, sister of this brave fellow here, who is now, with his trembling limbs and white cheeks, showing you what stout hearts men may have. Cheer up, Dick! Don't be afraid of me! I'd almost as soon strike a woman as you. Bertha Mason is insane. She came from a mad family — idiots and lunatics through three generations! Her mother, the Creole, was both a madwoman and a drunkard! — as I found out after I had married the daughter, for they kept the family secrets hidden before the wedding. Bertha, like a dutiful child, took after her mother in both respects. I had a charming partner — pure, wise, modest. You can imagine I was a happy man. I went through glorious times! Oh, my experience has been heavenly, if you only knew! But I owe you no further explanation. Briggs, Wood, Mason, I invite you all to come up to the house and visit Mrs. Poole's patient, and my wife! You shall see what sort of being I was tricked into marrying, and judge whether or not I had a right to break the contract and seek companionship with something at least human. This girl," he continued, looking at me, "knew no more than you, Wood, of the disgusting secret. She thought all was fair and legal, and never dreamed she was going to be trapped into a sham union with a cheated wretch, already bound to a bad, mad, and degraded partner! Come, all of you — follow!"
Still holding me fast, he left the church. The three gentlemen came after. At the front door of the hall we found the carriage.
"Take it back to the coach-house, John," said Mr. Rochester coolly. "It will not be needed today."
At our entrance, Mrs. Fairfax, Adèle, Sophie, and Leah came forward to meet and greet us.
"About turn — every one of you!" cried the master. "Away with your congratulations! Who wants them? Not I! They are fifteen years too late!"

He strode on and climbed the stairs, still holding my hand, still beckoning the gentlemen to follow, which they did. We mounted the first staircase, passed along the gallery, continued to the third storey. The low, black door, opened by Mr. Rochester's master key, admitted us to the tapestried room with its great bed and its cabinet of paintings.
"You know this place, Mason," said our guide. "She bit and stabbed you here."

He lifted the hangings from the wall, uncovering a second door. This, too, he opened. In a room without a window, a fire burned, guarded by a high and strong fender, and a lamp hung from the ceiling by a chain. Grace Poole bent over the fire, apparently cooking something in a saucepan. In the deep shadow at the far end of the room, a figure moved back and forth. What it was, whether beast or human being, one could not at first sight tell. It seemed to grovel on all fours. It snatched and growled like some strange wild animal. But it was covered with clothing, and a mass of dark, grizzled hair, wild as a mane, hid its head and face.
"Good morning, Mrs. Poole!" said Mr. Rochester. "How are you? And how is your charge today?"
"We're tolerable, sir, I thank you," replied Grace, carefully setting the boiling pot on the hob. "Rather snappish, but not violent."
A fierce cry seemed to contradict her favourable report. The clothed creature rose up and stood tall on its hind feet.
"Ah! Sir, she sees you!" exclaimed Grace. "You had better not stay."
"Only a few moments, Grace. You must allow me a few moments."
"Take care then, sir! For God's sake, take care!"
The madwoman bellowed. She parted her tangled hair from her face and stared wildly at her visitors. I recognised that purple face — those bloated features. Mrs. Poole stepped forward.
"Keep out of the way," said Mr. Rochester, pushing her aside. "She has no knife now, I suppose, and I'm on my guard."
"One never knows what she has, sir. She is so cunning. It is beyond human wisdom to guess her tricks."
"We had better leave her," whispered Mason.
"Go to the devil!" was his brother-in-law's answer.

"Watch out!" cried Grace. The three gentlemen retreated at the same moment. Mr. Rochester flung me behind him. The madwoman sprang and seized his throat savagely, sinking her teeth into his cheek. They struggled. She was a big woman, nearly as tall as her husband, and heavy besides. She showed tremendous force in the fight — more than once she almost throttled him, athletic as he was. He could have brought her down with a single well-placed blow, but he would not strike. He would only wrestle. At last he mastered her arms. Grace Poole gave him a cord, and he tied them behind her. With more rope, which was near at hand, he bound her to a chair. The task was performed amid the fiercest screams and the most violent struggles. Mr. Rochester then turned to the onlookers. He looked at them with a smile both bitter and desolate.

"That is my wife," he said. "Such is the only embrace my marriage will ever know — such are the tender moments that will fill my leisure hours! And this is what I wished to have" — laying his hand on my shoulder — "this young girl, who stands so grave and quiet at the mouth of hell, looking calmly at the antics of a demon. I wanted her just as a change after that savage ordeal. Wood and Briggs, look at the difference! Compare these clear eyes with the red ones over there — this face with that mask — this figure with that bulk. Then judge me, priest of the gospel and man of the law, and remember that with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged! Off with you now. I must lock up my prize."
We all withdrew. Mr. Rochester stayed a moment behind us to give some further order to Grace Poole. The solicitor addressed me as he descended the stairs.
"You, madam," he said, "are cleared of all blame. Your uncle will be glad to hear it — if, indeed, he should still be living — when Mr. Mason returns to Madeira."
"My uncle! What of him? Do you know him?"

"Mr. Mason does. Mr. Eyre has been the Funchal correspondent of his firm for some years. When your uncle received your letter mentioning the planned union between yourself and Mr. Rochester, Mr. Mason, who was staying in Madeira to restore his health on his way back to Jamaica, happened to be with him. Mr. Eyre mentioned the news, for he knew that my client here was acquainted with a gentleman named Rochester. Mr. Mason, as astonished and distressed as you may imagine, revealed the true state of affairs. Your uncle, I am sorry to say, is now on his sickbed — from which, considering the nature of his disease and the stage it has reached, it is unlikely he will ever rise. He could not then hurry to England himself to rescue you from the trap you had fallen into, but he begged Mr. Mason to lose no time in taking steps to prevent the fraudulent marriage. He referred him to me for help. I acted with all speed, and am thankful I was not too late — as you, no doubt, must be also. Were I not morally certain that your uncle will be dead before you reach Madeira, I would advise you to accompany Mr. Mason back. But as it is, I think you had better remain in England until you can hear further, either from or of Mr. Eyre. Have we anything else to stay for?" he asked of Mr. Mason.

"No, no — let us be gone," was the anxious reply. Without waiting to take leave of Mr. Rochester, they made their exit at the hall door. The clergyman stayed to exchange a few words, either of caution or reproach, with his proud parishioner. This duty done, he too departed.

I heard him go as I stood at the half-open door of my own room, to which I had now retreated. The house emptied, I shut myself in, fastened the bolt so that no one might intrude, and proceeded — not to weep, not to mourn (I was yet too numb for that) — but mechanically to take off the wedding dress and replace it with the plain gown I had worn yesterday, as I thought, for the last time. I then sat down. I felt weak and tired. I leaned my arms on the table and my head dropped onto them. And now I thought. Until now I had only heard, seen, moved — followed up and down where I was led or dragged — watched event rush on event, revelation open beyond revelation. But now, I thought.

The morning had been quiet enough — all except the brief scene with the madwoman. The events in the church had not been noisy. There was no explosion of passion, no loud argument, no dispute, no defiance or challenge, no tears, no sobs. A few words had been spoken. A calmly pronounced objection to the marriage had been made. Some stern, brief questions had been put by Mr. Rochester. Answers and explanations had been given. Evidence had been presented. An open admission of the truth had been uttered by my master. Then the living proof had been seen. The intruders were gone, and all was over.

I was in my own room as usual — just myself, without obvious change. Nothing had struck me, or scarred me, or maimed me. And yet, where was the Jane Eyre of yesterday? Where was her life? Where were her prospects?

Jane Eyre, who had been a passionate, expectant woman — almost a bride — was a cold, solitary girl again. Her life was pale. Her prospects were desolate. A Christmas frost had come at midsummer. A white December storm had whirled over June. Ice glazed the ripe apples. Drifts crushed the blooming roses. On hayfield and cornfield lay a frozen shroud. Lanes which last night blushed full of flowers were today pathless with untrodden snow. And the woods, which twelve hours ago waved leafy and fragrant as tropical groves, now spread waste, wild, and white as pine forests in wintry Norway. My hopes were all dead — struck with a sudden doom, such as, in one night, fell on all the firstborn in the land of Egypt. I looked at my cherished wishes, yesterday so blooming and bright. They lay stark, cold, livid corpses that could never revive. I looked at my love — that feeling which was my master's, which he had created. It shivered in my heart like a suffering child in a cold cradle. Sickness and anguish had seized it. It could not seek Mr. Rochester's arms — it could not draw warmth from his breast. Oh, never more could it turn to him, for faith was shattered — trust was destroyed! Mr. Rochester was not to me what he had been, for he was not what I had thought him. I would not call him wicked. I would not say he had betrayed me. But the quality of untarnished truth was gone from my idea of him, and from his presence I must go. That I saw clearly. When — how — where, I could not yet determine. But he himself, I had no doubt, would hurry me from Thornfield. Real affection, it seemed, he could not have for me. It had been only fitful passion — that was thwarted, and he would want me no more. I should fear even to cross his path now. My very sight must be hateful to him. Oh, how blind my eyes had been! How weak my conduct!

My eyes were covered and closed. Swirling darkness seemed to swim around me, and thought came in as black and confused a flood. Abandoned by myself, emptied and powerless, I seemed to have lain down in the dried-up bed of a great river. I heard a flood unleashed in remote mountains and felt the torrent coming. To rise I had no will. To flee I had no strength. I lay faint, longing to be dead. One idea only still throbbed with life inside me — a memory of God. It stirred a wordless prayer. These words wandered up and down in my lightless mind, as something that should be whispered, but no energy was found to speak them —
"Be not far from me, for trouble is near: there is none to help."

It was near. And as I had lifted no prayer to heaven to avert it — as I had neither clasped my hands, nor bent my knees, nor moved my lips — it came, in full, heavy force. The torrent poured over me. The whole consciousness of my life destroyed, my love lost, my hope extinguished, my faith struck dead, swayed full and mighty above me in one crushing mass. That bitter hour cannot be described. In truth, "the waters came into my soul; I sank in deep mire: I felt no standing; I came into deep waters; the floods overflowed me."

chapters.title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: Sometime in the afternoon I raised my head, and looking around and seeing the western sun casting the sign of its decline on the wall, I asked myself, "What am I to do?"

But the answer my mind gave—"Leave Thornfield at once"—was so immediate, so terrifying, that I covered my ears. I told myself I could not bear such words right now. "That I am not Edward Rochester's bride is the least part of my grief," I argued. "That I have been woken from the most glorious dreams and found them all empty and meaningless—that is a horror I could bear and overcome. But that I must leave him—decisively, instantly, entirely—is intolerable. I cannot do it."

But then a voice inside me declared that I could do it, and predicted that I would. I wrestled with my own resolution. I wanted to be weak, so I could avoid the dreadful passage of further suffering I saw stretching out before me. And Conscience, turned tyrant, held Passion by the throat, told her mockingly that she had only dipped her dainty foot into the mire, and swore that with his iron arm he would plunge her down to depths of agony beyond measure.
"Let me be torn away, then!" I cried. "Let someone else help me!"

"No. You shall tear yourself away. No one shall help you. You shall pluck out your own right eye. You shall cut off your own right hand. Your heart shall be the victim, and you the priest who pierces it."

I rose up suddenly, terrified by the solitude that so ruthless a judge haunted—by the silence that so awful a voice filled. My head swam as I stood upright. I realized I was growing faint from agitation and hunger; I had eaten and drunk nothing all day, having skipped breakfast. And with a strange pang, I now reflected that, long as I had been shut in here, no one had sent a message to ask how I was or to invite me downstairs. Not even little Adèle had knocked at the door. Not even Mrs. Fairfax had come looking for me. "Friends always forget those whom fortune abandons," I murmured, as I unbolted the door and stepped out. I stumbled over an obstacle—my head was still dizzy, my vision dim, and my limbs feeble. I could not recover myself. I fell, but not to the ground: an outstretched arm caught me. I looked up—I was being held by Mr. Rochester, who sat in a chair across my bedroom threshold.

"You come out at last," he said. "I have been waiting for you a long time, and listening. Yet I heard not a single movement, not a single sob. Five more minutes of that deathlike silence, and I would have forced the lock like a burglar. So you avoid me? You shut yourself away and grieve alone! I would rather you had come and berated me furiously. You are passionate—I expected a scene of some kind. I was prepared for a downpour of tears; I only wanted them shed on my chest. Instead a senseless floor has received them, or your soaked handkerchief. But no—I am wrong: you have not wept at all! I see a white cheek and a faded eye, but no trace of tears. I suppose, then, your heart has been weeping blood?"

"Well, Jane! Not a word of reproach? Nothing bitter—nothing piercing? Nothing to wound a feeling or sting a passion? You sit quietly where I have placed you and look at me with a weary, passive expression."

"Jane, I never meant to wound you like this. If a man who had only one little lamb—dear to him as a daughter, that ate from his plate and drank from his cup and lay in his arms—had by some mistake slaughtered it at the butcher's, he would not have regretted his bloody blunder more than I now regret mine. Will you ever forgive me?"

Reader, I forgave him at that moment and on that spot. There was such deep remorse in his eye, such genuine pity in his tone, such manly energy in his manner. And besides, there was such unchanged love in his whole look and bearing—I forgave him everything. Yet not in words, not outwardly; only at the core of my heart.
"You know I am a scoundrel, Jane?" he asked after a while, wistfully—wondering, I suppose, at my continued silence and tameness, which came from weakness rather than choice.
"Yes, sir."
"Then tell me so bluntly and sharply—don't spare me."

"I cannot. I am tired and sick. I want some water." He let out a sort of shuddering sigh, and taking me in his arms, carried me downstairs. At first I did not know what room he had brought me to; everything was blurred to my glazed sight. Soon I felt the reviving warmth of a fire; for, summer as it was, I had grown ice-cold in my room. He put wine to my lips; I tasted it and revived. Then I ate something he offered me, and was soon myself again. I was in the library—sitting in his chair—he was very close. "If I could leave this life now, without too sharp a pang, it would be well for me," I thought. "Then I would not have to crack my heartstrings in tearing them away from Mr. Rochester. I must leave him, it seems. I do not want to leave him—I cannot leave him."
"How are you now, Jane?"
"Much better, sir. I shall be well soon."
"Taste the wine again, Jane."

I obeyed. Then he put the glass on the table, stood before me, and looked at me closely. Suddenly he turned away with an inarticulate exclamation, full of passionate emotion of some kind. He walked rapidly through the room and came back. He leaned toward me as if to kiss me; but I remembered that such gestures were now forbidden. I turned my face away and pushed his aside.
"What!—How is this?" he exclaimed quickly. "Oh, I know! You won't kiss the husband of Bertha Mason? You consider my arms full and my embraces spoken for?"
"At any rate, there is neither room nor claim for me, sir."
"Why, Jane? I will spare you the trouble of much talking. I will answer for you—Because I already have a wife, you would reply. Am I right?"
"Yes."

"If you think so, you must have a strange opinion of me. You must see me as a scheming scoundrel—a base and low rake who has been pretending to love you selflessly in order to lure you into a trap deliberately set, to strip you of your honor and rob you of your self-respect. What do you say to that? I see you can say nothing. In the first place, you are still faint and have all you can do just to breathe. In the second place, you cannot yet bring yourself to accuse and condemn me. And besides, the floodgates of tears are opening, and they would pour out if you spoke much. You have no desire to argue or reproach or make a scene: you are thinking how to act—talking, you believe, is pointless. I know you—I am on my guard."
"Sir, I do not wish to act against you," I said; and my unsteady voice warned me to cut my words short.

"Not in your sense of the word, but in mine you are plotting to destroy me. You have as good as said that I am a married man—as a married man you will avoid me, keep out of my way. Just now you refused to kiss me. You intend to make yourself a complete stranger to me: to live under this roof only as Adèle's governess. If ever I say a friendly word to you, if ever a friendly feeling draws you to me again, you will say, 'That man nearly made me his mistress: I must be ice and rock to him.' And ice and rock you will become."

I cleared and steadied my voice to reply: "Everything has changed around me, sir. I must change too—there is no doubt of that. And to avoid swings of feeling and constant battles with memories and associations, there is only one way—Adèle must have a new governess, sir."

"Oh, Adèle will go to school—I have already settled that. Nor do I mean to torment you with the hideous associations and memories of Thornfield Hall—this accursed place—this tent of Achan—this vault of insolence, offering the ghastliness of living death to the light of the open sky—this narrow stone hell, with its one real demon, worse than a legion of the kind we imagine. Jane, you shall not stay here, and neither will I. I was wrong ever to bring you to Thornfield Hall, knowing as I did how it was haunted. I ordered them to hide from you, before I ever met you, all knowledge of the curse on this place—simply because I feared Adèle would never keep a governess if the woman knew what fellow resident she shared the house with. And my plans would not let me move the madwoman elsewhere—though I own an old house, Ferndean Manor, even more remote and hidden than this, where I could have housed her safely enough, had not a scruple about the unhealthy location, deep in the woods, made my conscience recoil from the arrangement. Probably those damp walls would soon have relieved me of her. But to each villain his own vice; and mine is not a tendency toward indirect murder, even of what I most hate."

"However, concealing the madwoman's presence from you was something like covering a child with a cloak and laying it near a poison tree: that demon's proximity is toxic, and always was. But I will shut up Thornfield Hall. I will nail up the front door and board the lower windows. I will pay Mrs. Poole two hundred a year to live here with my wife, as you call that fearful creature. Grace will do much for money, and she shall have her son—the keeper at Grimsby Retreat—to bear her company and help her during the fits, when my wife is driven by her demons to burn people in their beds at night, to stab them, to tear the flesh from their bones, and so on—"
"Sir," I interrupted him, "you are merciless toward that unfortunate woman. You speak of her with hatred—with vindictive hostility. It is cruel—she cannot help being mad."

"Jane, my little darling (I will call you that, because you are), you don't know what you are talking about. You misjudge me again: it is not because she is mad that I hate her. If you were mad, do you think I would hate you?"
"I do indeed, sir."

"Then you are mistaken, and you know nothing about me, and nothing about the kind of love I am capable of. Every atom of your body is as dear to me as my own. In pain and sickness it would still be dear. Your mind is my treasure, and if it were shattered, it would be my treasure still. If you raved, my arms should hold you—not a straitjacket. Your grip, even in fury, would have a charm for me. If you flew at me as wildly as that woman did this morning, I would receive you in an embrace at least as tender as it was firm. I would not shrink from you with disgust as I did from her. In your quiet moments you would have no watcher and no nurse but me. I could bend over you with untiring tenderness, though you gave me no smile in return, and never tire of gazing into your eyes, though they no longer held a ray of recognition for me.—But why do I follow that line of thought? I was talking about taking you away from Thornfield. Everything, you know, is ready for an immediate departure. Tomorrow you shall go. I only ask you to endure one more night under this roof, Jane; and then, farewell to its miseries and terrors forever! I have a place to go to that will be a safe refuge from hateful memories, from unwelcome intrusion—even from lies and slander."
"And take Adèle with you, sir," I interrupted. "She will be a companion for you."

"What do you mean, Jane? I told you I would send Adèle to school. And what would I want with a child for a companion—and not my own child, but a French dancer's bastard? Why do you press me about her! I say, why do you suggest Adèle as my companion?"
"You spoke of a retreat, sir; and retreat and solitude are dull. Too dull for you."
"Solitude! Solitude!" he repeated with irritation. "I see I must explain myself. I don't know what sphinx-like expression is forming on your face. You are to share my solitude. Do you understand?"

I shook my head. It took a degree of courage, agitated as he was becoming, even to risk that mute sign of refusal. He had been pacing rapidly around the room, and he stopped, as if suddenly rooted to one spot. He looked at me long and hard. I turned my eyes away from him, fixed them on the fire, and tried to assume and maintain a quiet, composed expression.

"Now for the snag in Jane's character," he said at last, speaking more calmly than his look had led me to expect. "The reel of silk has run smoothly enough so far; but I always knew there would come a knot and a tangle: here it is. Now for frustration, and fury, and endless trouble! By God! I long to use a fraction of Samson's strength and snap the entanglement like string!"
He resumed his pacing, but soon stopped again, this time right in front of me.

"Jane! Will you listen to reason?" (He stooped and brought his lips to my ear.) "Because if you won't, I'll try force." His voice was hoarse; his look that of a man about to snap an unbearable restraint and plunge headlong into wild abandon. I saw that in another moment, with one more surge of frenzy, I would be able to do nothing with him. The present—the passing second—was all I had in which to control and restrain him. A movement of rejection, flight, or fear would have sealed my fate—and his. But I was not afraid. Not in the least. I felt an inner power, a sense of influence, that supported me. The crisis was dangerous, but not without its thrill: like, perhaps, what a man feels when he slips over the rapids in his canoe. I took hold of his clenched fist, loosened the knotted fingers, and said to him soothingly—
"Sit down. I will talk to you as long as you like, and hear everything you have to say, whether reasonable or unreasonable."

He sat down, but he did not get to speak right away. I had been fighting back tears for some time, taking great pains to suppress them because I knew he would not want to see me cry. Now, however, I decided it was better to let them flow as freely and as long as they wished. If the flood annoyed him, so much the better. So I gave in and wept hard.
Soon I heard him earnestly begging me to compose myself. I said I could not while he was in such a state.
"But I am not angry, Jane. I only love you too much. And you had set your little pale face with such a resolute, frozen look—I could not bear it. Hush now, and dry your eyes."
His softened voice told me he was subdued; so I, in turn, became calm. Now he tried to rest his head on my shoulder, but I would not allow it. Then he tried to draw me to him: no.
