He declared it unnecessary to send for a doctor: nature, he was sure, would manage best on her own. He said every nerve had been overstrained somehow, and the whole system needed to sleep heavily for a while. There was no disease. He expected my recovery would be quick enough once it began. These opinions he delivered in a few words, in a quiet, low voice; and added, after a pause, in the tone of a man not given to elaborate comment, "Rather an unusual face; certainly not suggestive of low birth or degradation."
"Quite the opposite," responded Diana. "To tell the truth, St. John, my heart goes out to the poor little soul. I hope we may be able to help her permanently."

"That is unlikely," was the reply. "You will find she is some young lady who has had a falling-out with her family and has probably left them rashly. We may perhaps succeed in reuniting her with them, if she is not stubborn: but I see lines of resolve in her face that make me doubt how easy she will be to manage." He stood studying me for some minutes; then added, "She looks sensible, but not at all pretty."
"She is so ill, St. John."
"Ill or well, she would always be plain. The grace and harmony of beauty are completely absent from those features."

On the third day I was better; on the fourth, I could speak, move, and sit up in bed. Hannah had brought me some porridge and dry toast at what I supposed was dinnertime. I had eaten with appetite: the food was good—free of the feverish taste that had poisoned everything I had swallowed before. When she left me, I felt comparatively strong and revived: before long, restlessness and a desire for activity stirred in me. I wanted to get up; but what could I put on? Only my damp and mud-caked clothes, in which I had slept on the ground and fallen in the marsh. I felt ashamed to appear before my rescuers so dressed. I was spared the embarrassment.

On a chair by the bed were all my own things, clean and dry. My black silk dress hung on the wall. The traces of the bog had been removed; the creases left by the wet had been smoothed out: it was perfectly respectable. Even my shoes and stockings had been cleaned and made presentable. There were means of washing in the room, and a comb and brush to smooth my hair. After a slow process, resting every five minutes, I managed to dress myself. My clothes hung loose on me; for I was much wasted, but I covered the gaps with a shawl, and once more—clean and decent-looking, no speck of dirt, no trace of the disorder I so hated and which seemed so to degrade me—I crept down a stone staircase with the help of the banister, into a narrow, low passage, and found my way to the kitchen.

It was full of the fragrance of fresh bread and the warmth of a generous fire. Hannah was baking. Prejudices, it is well known, are hardest to uproot from a mind that has never been opened by education: they grow there as firmly as weeds among stones. Hannah had been cold and stiff at first: lately she had begun to soften a little; and when she saw me come in tidy and properly dressed, she actually smiled.
"What, you're up!" she said. "You're better, then. You can sit yourself down in my chair by the fireplace, if you like."
She pointed to the rocking chair: I took it. She bustled about, examining me now and then from the corner of her eye. Turning to me as she took some loaves from the oven, she asked bluntly—
"Had you ever gone begging before you came here?"
I was offended for a moment; but remembering that anger was pointless, and that I had indeed appeared as a beggar to her, I answered quietly but with a certain deliberate firmness—
"You are wrong to think me a beggar. I am no beggar; no more than you are, or your young ladies."
After a pause she said, "I don't understand that: you've got no house, and no money, I suppose?"
"The lack of a house or money does not make a beggar in the way you mean."
"Are you educated?" she asked after a moment.
"Yes, very."
"But you've never been to a boarding school?"
"I was at a boarding school for eight years."
She opened her eyes wide. "Then why on earth can't you support yourself?"
"I have supported myself; and I trust I shall do so again. What are you going to do with these gooseberries?" I asked, as she brought out a basket of the fruit.
"Make them into pies."
"Give them to me and I'll sort them."
"No; I don't want you to do anything."
"But I must do something. Let me have them."
She agreed; she even brought me a clean towel to spread over my dress, "in case," as she said, "I should get it dirty."
"You haven't been used to servant's work, I can see by your hands," she remarked. "I suppose you've been a dressmaker?"
"No, you are wrong. And now, never mind what I have been: don't worry about me any further; but tell me the name of the house where we are."
"Some call it Marsh End, and some call it Moor House."
"And the gentleman who lives here is called Mr. St. John?"
"No; he doesn't live here: he is only staying for a while. When he is at home, he is in his own parish at Morton."
"That village a few miles away?"
"Yes."
"And what is he?"
"He is a clergyman."
I remembered the answer of the old housekeeper at the parsonage when I had asked to see the clergyman. "This, then, was his father's house?"
"Yes; old Mr. Rivers lived here, and his father, and grandfather, and great-grandfather before him."
"The gentleman's name, then, is Mr. St. John Rivers?"
"Yes; St. John is his first name."
"And his sisters are called Diana and Mary Rivers?"
"Yes."
"Their father is dead?"
"Dead three weeks ago, of a stroke."
"They have no mother?"
"The mistress has been dead for many a year."
"Have you lived with the family long?"
"I've lived here thirty years. I nursed all three of them."
"That proves you must have been an honest and faithful servant. I will say that much for you, though you had the rudeness to call me a beggar."
She stared at me again in surprise. "I believe," she said, "I was quite wrong about you: but there are so many cheats about, you must forgive me."
"And yet," I continued, rather severely, "you were ready to shut me out on a night when you should not have turned away a dog."
"Well, it was hard: but what can a body do? I was thinking more of the children than of myself: poor things! They've got nobody to look after them but me. I have to be careful."
I maintained a solemn silence for some minutes.
"You mustn't think too badly of me," she said again.

"But I do think badly of you," I said; "and I'll tell you why—not so much because you refused me shelter, or suspected me of being a fraud, but because you just now treated it as a kind of disgrace that I had no money and no house. Some of the best people who ever lived have been as poor as I am; and if you are a Christian, you ought not to regard poverty as a crime."
"No more I should," she said. "Mr. St. John tells me so too; and I see I was wrong—but I have a very different opinion of you now from what I had. You look like a truly decent little creature."
"That will do—I forgive you now. Shake hands."
She put her floury, work-hardened hand into mine; another and warmer smile lit up her rough face, and from that moment we were friends.

Hannah was clearly fond of talking. While I sorted the fruit and she made the pastry for the pies, she gave me various details about her late master and mistress, and "the children," as she called the young people.

Old Mr. Rivers, she said, was a simple man, but a gentleman and from as ancient a family as you could find. Marsh End had belonged to the Rivers family for as long as it had been a house: and it was, she declared, over two hundred years old—though it looked just a small, humble place, nothing compared to Mr. Oliver's grand hall down in Morton Vale. But she could remember Bill Oliver's father as a common needlemaker; and the Rivers had been gentry since the days of the Henrys, as anyone could see by looking in the church registers at Morton. Still, she admitted, the old master was like other folk—nothing much out of the ordinary: passionate about shooting, farming, and such things. The mistress was different. She was a great reader and studied a great deal; and the children had taken after her. There was no one like them in these parts, nor had there ever been; they had loved learning, all three, almost from the time they could talk; and they had always been "their own sort." Mr. St. John, when he grew up, would go to university and become a clergyman; and the girls, as soon as they left school, would look for positions as governesses: for they had told her that their father had some years ago lost a great deal of money through a man he trusted going bankrupt; and as he was no longer rich enough to give them inheritances, they would have to provide for themselves. They had lived very little at home for a long while, and were only here now to stay a few weeks on account of their father's death; but they did so love Marsh End and Morton and all these moors and hills. They had been in London and many other great cities; but they always said there was no place like home; and they were so good with each other—never quarreled or argued. She did not know where you could find such a close family.
Having finished sorting the gooseberries, I asked where the two ladies and their brother were now.
"Gone over to Morton for a walk; but they would be back in half an hour for tea."

They returned within the time Hannah had predicted: they came in through the kitchen door. Mr. St. John, seeing me, merely nodded and walked through; the two ladies stopped: Mary, in a few words, kindly and calmly expressed her pleasure at seeing me well enough to come downstairs; Diana took my hand. She shook her head at me.
"You should have waited for my permission to come down," she said. "You still look very pale—and so thin! Poor child—poor girl!"

Diana had a voice that sounded, to my ear, like the cooing of a dove. She had eyes whose gaze I delighted in meeting. Her whole face seemed to me full of charm. Mary's expression was equally intelligent—her features equally pretty; but her look was more reserved, and her manners, though gentle, more distant. Diana looked and spoke with a certain authority: she had a strong will, clearly. It was in my nature to take pleasure in yielding to authority like hers, and to bend, where my conscience and self-respect permitted, to a decisive will.

"And what business do you have here?" she continued. "This is not your place. Mary and I sit in the kitchen sometimes, because at home we like to be free, even to the point of doing whatever we please—but you are a guest and must go into the parlor."
"I am perfectly fine here."
"Not at all, with Hannah bustling about and dusting you with flour."
"Besides, the fire is too hot for you," put in Mary.
"Of course," added her sister. "Come, you must do as you're told." And still holding my hand, she made me stand and led me into the inner room.

"Sit there," she said, placing me on the sofa, "while we take off our things and get the tea ready; it is another privilege we enjoy in our little moorland home—preparing our own meals when we feel like it, or when Hannah is baking, brewing, washing, or ironing."
She closed the door, leaving me alone with Mr. St. John, who sat opposite with a book or newspaper in hand. I examined, first, the parlor, and then its occupant.

The parlor was a rather small room, very simply furnished, yet comfortable because it was clean and neat. The old-fashioned chairs were highly polished, and the walnut table gleamed like a mirror. A few strange, antique portraits of men and women from earlier times decorated the stained walls; a glass-fronted cabinet held some books and an ancient set of china. There was no unnecessary ornament in the room—not a single modern piece of furniture, except a pair of work boxes and a lady's writing desk in rosewood, which stood on a side table: everything—including the carpet and curtains—looked at once well-worn and well-preserved.

Mr. St. John—sitting as still as one of the dusty portraits on the walls, eyes fixed on the page he was reading, lips silently sealed—was easy enough to study. Had he been a statue instead of a man, he could not have been easier. He was young—perhaps twenty-eight to thirty—tall, slender; his face held the eye: it was like a Greek face, very pure in its lines. A perfectly straight, classical nose; a distinctly Athenian mouth and chin. It is rare indeed for an English face to come so close to the ancient models as his did. He might well be a little taken aback by the irregularity of my features, his own being so perfectly balanced. His eyes were large and blue, with brown lashes; his high forehead, colorless as ivory, was partially streaked with careless locks of fair hair.

This is a gentle portrait, is it not, reader? Yet the man it describes hardly gave the impression of a gentle, yielding, sensitive, or even a calm nature. Quiet as he sat now, there was something about his nostrils, his mouth, his brow that, to my perception, signaled qualities within that were either restless, or hard, or eager. He did not speak a word to me, nor even direct a glance my way, until his sisters returned. Diana, as she went in and out preparing tea, brought me a little cake baked on top of the oven.
"Eat that now," she said. "You must be hungry. Hannah says you have had nothing but some porridge since breakfast."

I did not refuse, for my appetite was awake and keen. Mr. Rivers now closed his book, came to the table, and as he sat down, fixed his blue, portrait-like eyes squarely on me. There was a frank directness, a searching, deliberate steadiness in his gaze now, which told me that intention, not shyness, had kept it turned away from the stranger until now.
"You are very hungry," he said.
"I am, sir." It is my way—it always was my way, by instinct—to meet brevity with brevity, directness with plainness.
"It is fortunate that a mild fever forced you to fast for the last three days: there would have been danger in giving in to your appetite at first. Now you may eat, though still in moderation."
"I trust I shall not eat at your expense for long, sir," was my very clumsily phrased, unpolished answer.
"No," he said coolly. "When you have told us where your family and friends live, we can write to them, and you can be restored to your home."
"That, I must tell you plainly, is not in my power to do; being entirely without home and friends."

The three looked at me, but not with suspicion; I sensed no distrust in their glances: there was more of curiosity. I speak particularly of the young ladies. St. John's eyes, though clear enough in the literal sense, were hard to read in the figurative one. He seemed to use them more as instruments for probing other people's thoughts than as windows for revealing his own: a combination of sharpness and reserve more likely to unsettle than to encourage.
"Do you mean to say," he asked, "that you are completely cut off from every connection?"
"I do. Not a single tie links me to any living being: not a claim do I have to shelter under any roof in England."
"A most unusual position for someone your age!"
Here I noticed his glance directed to my hands, which were folded on the table before me. I wondered what he was looking for: his words soon explained.
"You have never been married? You are unmarried?"
Diana laughed. "Why, she can't be more than seventeen or eighteen, St. John," she said.
"I am nearly nineteen: but I am not married. No."

I felt a burning flush rise to my face; for bitter and painful memories were stirred by any reference to marriage. They all saw my embarrassment and emotion. Diana and Mary helped me by looking elsewhere; but the colder, sterner brother continued to stare until the discomfort he had caused forced out tears as well as color.
"Where did you last live?" he now asked.
"You are too inquisitive, St. John," murmured Mary in a low voice; but he leaned across the table and demanded an answer with a second firm, piercing look.
"The name of the place where, and the person with whom, I lived is my secret," I replied concisely.
"Which, if you wish, you have every right to keep, both from St. John and every other questioner," remarked Diana.
"Yet if I know nothing about you or your history, I cannot help you," he said. "And you do need help, do you not?"
"I do need it, and I seek it to this extent, sir: that some truly kind person will point me toward work that I can do, and for which the pay will keep me in the barest necessities of life."

"I do not know whether I am a truly kind person; but I am willing to help you to the best of my ability in so honest a purpose. First, then, tell me what you have been used to doing, and what you can do."

I had now finished my tea. I was enormously refreshed by the drink; as much revived as a giant by wine. It gave new strength to my weakened nerves and enabled me to address this penetrating young judge steadily.

"Mr. Rivers," I said, turning to him and looking at him as directly as he looked at me, "you and your sisters have done me a great service—the greatest one person can do for another: you have rescued me, through your generous hospitality, from death. This gift gives you an unlimited claim on my gratitude, and a claim, to some extent, on my honesty. I will tell you as much of the history of the wanderer you have sheltered as I can tell without compromising my own peace of mind—my own safety, moral and physical, and that of others."

"I am an orphan, the daughter of a clergyman. My parents died before I could know them. I was raised as a dependent; educated in a charitable institution. I will even tell you the name of the school where I spent six years as a pupil and two as a teacher—Lowood Orphan Asylum, in ——shire: you will have heard of it, Mr. Rivers? The Reverend Robert Brocklehurst is the treasurer."
"I have heard of Mr. Brocklehurst, and I have seen the school."

"I left Lowood nearly a year ago to become a private governess. I found a good position and was happy. This place I was forced to leave four days before I came here. The reason for my departure I cannot and should not explain: it would be useless, dangerous, and would sound unbelievable. No blame rests on me: I am as free from guilt as any of you three. Miserable I am, and must be for a time; for the disaster that drove me from a house I had found to be a paradise was of a strange and terrible nature. In planning my departure I focused on only two things—speed and secrecy: to ensure these, I had to leave behind everything I owned except a small parcel; which, in my haste and distress, I forgot to take from the coach that brought me to Whitcross. To this neighborhood, then, I came completely destitute. I slept two nights in the open air and wandered two days without crossing a doorstep: only twice in that time did I taste food. It was when hunger, exhaustion, and despair had brought me almost to my last breath that you, Mr. Rivers, stopped me from dying of starvation at your door and took me under your roof. I know everything your sisters have done for me since—for I was not truly unconscious during my seeming stupor—and I owe to their instinctive, genuine, warm compassion as great a debt as to your Christian charity."
"Don't make her talk any more now, St. John," said Diana, as I paused. "She is clearly not yet strong enough for excitement. Come to the sofa and sit down, Miss Elliott."
I gave an involuntary start at hearing the false name: I had forgotten my alias. Mr. Rivers, from whom nothing seemed to escape, noticed it immediately.
"You said your name was Jane Elliott?" he observed.
"I did; and it is the name I think it wise to go by for now, but it is not my real name, and when I hear it, it sounds strange to me."
"Your real name you will not give?"
"No: I fear discovery above all things; and anything that might lead to it, I avoid."
"You are quite right, I'm sure," said Diana. "Now do, brother, let her have some peace."
But when St. John had reflected for a few moments, he resumed as steadily and as shrewdly as before.

"You would not like to be dependent on our hospitality for long—you would wish, I see, to move beyond my sisters' kindness and, above all, beyond my charity (I am quite aware of the distinction you draw, and I do not resent it—it is fair): you want to be independent of us?"

"I do: I have already said so. Show me how to work, or how to find work: that is all I ask now; then let me go, even if it is to the meanest cottage; but until then, allow me to stay here: I dread another encounter with the horrors of homelessness."
"Indeed you shall stay here," said Diana, placing her white hand on my head. "You shall," repeated Mary, in the tone of quiet sincerity that seemed natural to her.

"My sisters, you see, take pleasure in keeping you," said Mr. St. John, "as they would take pleasure in keeping and nursing a half-frozen bird that some winter wind might have blown through their window. I feel more inclined to set you on the path to keeping yourself, and shall try to do so; but understand, my world is small. I am merely the minister of a poor country parish: my help must be of the humblest kind. And if you are inclined to look down on modest beginnings, seek more effective aid than I can offer."

"She has already said that she is willing to do anything honest she can do," answered Diana on my behalf; "and you know, St. John, she has no choice of helpers: she is forced to put up with crusty people like you."
"I will be a dressmaker; I will be a seamstress; I will be a servant, a nursemaid, if I can do no better," I answered.
"Good," said Mr. St. John, quite coolly. "If that is your spirit, I promise to help you, in my own time and way."
He resumed the book he had been reading before tea. I soon withdrew, for I had talked as much and sat up as long as my current strength would allow.

chapters.title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: The more I came to know the residents of Moor House, the better I liked them. In a few days I had recovered enough to sit up all day and sometimes go for walks. I could join Diana and Mary in all their activities; talk with them as much as they wished, and help them whenever and wherever they let me. There was a reviving pleasure in this companionship, of a kind I was tasting for the first time—the pleasure that comes from a perfect match of tastes, feelings, and principles.

I liked to read what they liked to read: what delighted them, delighted me; what they valued, I respected. They loved their secluded home. I, too, in the gray, small, ancient building, with its low roof, its latticed windows, its crumbling walls, its avenue of old firs—all bent sideways by mountain winds; its garden, dark with yew and holly, where no flowers but the hardiest would bloom—found a charm both powerful and lasting. They were attached to the purple moors behind and around their home—to the hollow valley into which the pebbly bridle path from their gate descended, winding first between fern-covered banks and then among a few of the wildest little pastures that ever bordered a wilderness of heath or fed a flock of gray moorland sheep with their small moss-faced lambs. They clung to this place, I say, with a perfect passion of devotion. I could understand the feeling and share both its depth and its truth. I saw the fascination of the landscape. I felt the sacred quality of its loneliness: my eyes feasted on the curves of hill and valley—on the wild coloring given to ridge and hollow by moss, by heather bells, by flower-sprinkled turf, by bright bracken, and weathered granite crags. These details meant as much to me as to them—just as many pure and sweet sources of pleasure. The strong blast and the gentle breeze; the rough day and the calm; the hours of sunrise and sunset; moonlit nights and cloudy ones—all stirred in me, in these surroundings, the same attraction they felt. The same spell that enchanted them wound itself around my heart.

Indoors we got along just as well. They were both more accomplished and better read than I was; but eagerly I followed the path of knowledge they had already traveled. I devoured the books they lent me: then it was deeply satisfying to discuss with them in the evening what I had read during the day. Thought matched thought; opinion met opinion: we agreed, in short, perfectly.

If our trio had a leader, it was Diana. Physically, she far surpassed me: she was beautiful; she was robust. In her spirit there was an abundance of life and a confident vitality that amazed me even as it baffled my understanding. I could hold my own in conversation when the evening began, but once my first burst of energy was spent, I was glad to sit on a stool at Diana's feet, rest my head on her knee, and listen while she and Mary thoroughly explored a topic I had only touched on. Diana offered to teach me German. I liked learning from her: I saw that the role of teacher pleased and suited her; the role of student pleased and suited me equally. Our natures fitted together: a deep mutual affection was the result. They discovered I could draw: their pencils and paint boxes were immediately at my disposal. My skill, greater in this area than theirs, surprised and charmed them. Mary would sit and watch me for hours; then she would take lessons, and she made a willing, intelligent, dedicated student. Occupied this way, and entertaining one another, days passed like hours and weeks like days.

As for Mr. St. John, the friendship that had sprung up so naturally and quickly between me and his sisters did not extend to him. One reason for the distance still between us was that he was comparatively seldom at home: a large part of his time seemed devoted to visiting the sick and poor among the scattered population of his parish.

No weather seemed to deter him from these pastoral rounds: rain or shine, he would, when his morning hours of study were over, take his hat, and, followed by his father's old pointer, Carlo, go out on his mission of love or duty—I was not sure which he considered it. Sometimes, when the day was especially bad, his sisters would protest. He would then say, with a particular smile, more solemn than cheerful—
"And if I let a gust of wind or a sprinkle of rain turn me aside from these easy tasks, what preparation would such laziness be for the future I have planned for myself?"
Diana and Mary's usual response to this was a sigh and some minutes of apparently sorrowful reflection.

But beyond his frequent absences, there was another barrier to friendship with him: he seemed reserved, abstracted, and even brooding by nature. Devoted in his pastoral duties, blameless in his life and habits, he nonetheless did not appear to enjoy the mental peace, the inner contentment, that should be the reward of every sincere Christian and practical philanthropist. Often in the evening, sitting by the window with his desk and papers before him, he would stop reading or writing, rest his chin on his hand, and give himself up to some train of thought; but that it was troubled and intense could be seen in the frequent flash and restless widening of his eyes.

I think, moreover, that Nature was not the treasure to him that it was to his sisters. He expressed once, and only once in my hearing, a strong appreciation for the rugged charm of the hills and an inborn love for the dark roof and ancient walls he called home; but there was more of gloom than pleasure in the tone and words with which the feeling was expressed; and never did he seem to roam the moors for the sake of their soothing silence—never did he seek out or linger over the thousand peaceful pleasures they could offer.

Uncommunicative as he was, some time passed before I had a chance to gauge his mind. I first got a sense of its depth when I heard him preach in his own church at Morton. I wish I could describe that sermon: but it is beyond my ability. I cannot even faithfully convey the effect it had on me.

It began calmly—and indeed, in terms of delivery and tone of voice, it remained calm to the end: but a deeply felt, tightly controlled passion soon breathed through the precise words and drove the powerful language. This grew to force—compressed, concentrated, restrained. The heart was stirred, the mind astonished by the preacher's power: neither was comforted. Throughout there ran a strange bitterness; an absence of gentle consolation; stern references to Calvinist doctrines—election, predestination, damnation—were frequent; and each mention of these ideas sounded like a sentence of doom pronounced. When he finished, instead of feeling better, calmer, more enlightened by his words, I experienced an inexpressible sadness; for it seemed to me—whether equally so to others I cannot say—that the eloquence I had been hearing had sprung from a depth where stirred dark sediments of disappointment, where troubled currents of unsatisfied yearning and restless ambition flowed. I was certain St. John Rivers—clean-living, conscientious, zealous as he was—had not yet found that peace of God which passes all understanding: he had no more found it, I thought, than I had with my hidden, gnawing grief for my shattered idol and lost paradise—grief I have lately avoided mentioning, but which possessed me and tyrannized over me without mercy.

Meanwhile a month had passed. Diana and Mary were soon to leave Moor House and return to the very different life and world that awaited them as governesses in a large, fashionable, south-of-England city, where each held a position in a household whose wealthy and haughty members regarded them only as humble employees, neither knowing nor valuing their inner qualities, and appreciating only their acquired skills as they might value the talent of their cook or the taste of their lady's maid. Mr. St. John had said nothing to me yet about the employment he had promised to find me; yet it was becoming urgent that I have some occupation. One morning, finding myself alone with him for a few minutes in the parlor, I ventured to approach the window alcove—which his table, chair, and desk had made into a kind of study—and I was about to speak, though unsure what words to use—for it is always hard to break the ice of reserve that coats a nature like his—when he saved me the trouble by speaking first.
Looking up as I drew near—"You have a question to ask me?" he said.
"Yes; I want to know whether you have heard of any work I can take on."

"I found or devised something for you three weeks ago; but as you seemed both useful and happy here—as my sisters had clearly become attached to you, and your company gave them unusual pleasure—I thought it unwise to interrupt your mutual comfort until their approaching departure from Marsh End should make yours necessary."
"And they will leave in three days?" I said.
"Yes; and when they go, I shall return to the parsonage at Morton: Hannah will come with me; and this old house will be closed up."

I waited a few moments, expecting him to continue on the subject he had raised: but he seemed to have drifted into another line of thought. His expression showed his mind was elsewhere—far from me and my concerns. I had to bring him back to a topic of close and urgent interest to me.
"What is the work you had in mind, Mr. Rivers? I hope this delay has not made it harder to secure."
"Oh, no; since it is work that depends only on me to offer and you to accept."

He paused again: there seemed to be a reluctance to go on. I grew impatient: a restless movement or two, and an eager, insistent look fixed on his face, conveyed my feeling as effectively as words could have, and with less effort.

"You need not be in any hurry to hear," he said. "Let me be frank: I have nothing attractive or lucrative to suggest. Before I explain, please recall my clear warning that if I helped you, it would be as the blind helping the lame. I am poor; for I find that, when I have paid my father's debts, all the inheritance remaining to me will be this crumbling house, the row of damaged firs behind, and the patch of boggy ground with the yew trees and holly bushes in front. I am obscure: Rivers is an old name; but of the three sole descendants of the line, two earn a dependent's wages among strangers, and the third considers himself an exile from his native land—not only for life but in death. Yes, and deems, and is bound to deem, himself honored by this fate, and aspires only for the day when the cross of separation from earthly ties shall be laid on his shoulders, and when the Head of that Church Militant of whose humblest members he is one shall give the word: 'Rise, follow Me!'"
St. John spoke these words as he delivered his sermons, with a quiet, deep voice; with an unflushed cheek and a burning glow in his eyes. He continued—

"And since I myself am poor and obscure, I can offer you only the service of poverty and obscurity. You may even think it degrading—for I can see your habits have been what the world calls refined: your tastes lean toward the ideal, and your society has at least been among the educated; but I believe that no service degrades which can better the human race. I hold that the more barren and unpromising the soil where the Christian worker is assigned his task of cultivation—the scantier the reward his labor brings—the higher the honor. His, in such circumstances, is the destiny of the pioneer; and the first pioneers of the Gospel were the Apostles—their captain was Jesus, the Redeemer, Himself."
"Well?" I said, as he paused again. "Go on."

He looked at me before continuing: indeed, he seemed to be carefully reading my face, as if its features and lines were words on a page. The conclusions he drew from this examination he partly expressed in his next remarks.

"I believe you will accept the position I am offering you," he said, "and hold it for a while—though not permanently: any more than I could permanently keep the narrow and narrowing—the quiet, hidden office of English country clergyman; for in your nature there is a restlessness as hostile to peace as the one in mine, though of a different kind."
"Please explain," I urged, when he stopped yet again.

"I will; and you shall hear how modest the proposal is—how small—how limiting. I shall not stay long at Morton, now that my father is dead and I am my own master. I shall leave the place probably within a year; but while I do stay, I will throw myself fully into improving it. Morton, when I came to it two years ago, had no school: the children of the poor were shut out from every hope of advancement. I started one for boys: I now intend to open a second school for girls. I have rented a building for the purpose, with a two-room cottage attached for the teacher's house. Her salary will be thirty pounds a year: her house is already furnished, very simply but adequately, through the kindness of a lady, Miss Oliver—the only daughter of the sole wealthy man in my parish, Mr. Oliver, the owner of a needle factory and iron foundry in the valley. The same lady pays for the education and clothing of an orphan from the workhouse, on the condition that the girl will help the teacher with such domestic tasks as her teaching duties leave her no time to handle herself. Will you be this teacher?"

He put the question somewhat hurriedly; he seemed half to expect an indignant, or at least a scornful, rejection of the offer: not knowing all my thoughts and feelings, though guessing some, he could not tell how the prospect would look to me. In truth it was humble—but it was sheltered, and I wanted a safe haven. It was dull—but compared to the life of a governess in a wealthy household, it was independent; and the fear of servitude among strangers cut deep into my soul. It was not ignoble—not unworthy—not intellectually degrading. I made my decision.
"I thank you for the offer, Mr. Rivers, and I accept it with all my heart."

"But you understand me?" he said. "It is a village school: your students will be only poor girls—farm workers' children, at best farmers' daughters. Knitting, sewing, reading, writing, arithmetic—that will be all you teach. What will you do with your accomplishments? What about the larger part of your mind—your feelings—your tastes?"
"Save them until they are needed. They will keep."
"You know what you are taking on, then?"
"I do."
He smiled now: and not a bitter or sad smile, but one of genuine, deep satisfaction.
"And when will you begin?"
"I will go to my house tomorrow, and open the school next week, if you like."
"Very well: so be it."
He rose and walked across the room. Stopping, he looked at me again. He shook his head.
"What do you disapprove of, Mr. Rivers?" I asked.
"You will not stay at Morton long: no, no!"
"Why? What makes you say so?"
"I read it in your eye; it is not the kind that promises a steady, even course through life."
"I am not ambitious."
He startled at the word "ambitious." He repeated, "No. What made you think of ambition? Who is ambitious? I know I am: but how did you find that out?"
"I was speaking of myself."
"Well, if you are not ambitious, you are—" He paused.
"What?"

"I was going to say passionate: but perhaps you would misunderstand the word and be offended. I mean that human bonds and sympathies have a very powerful hold on you. I am sure you cannot long be content to spend your free time in solitude and devote your working hours to monotonous labor completely devoid of stimulation: any more than I can be content," he added with emphasis, "to live here buried in marshland, hemmed in by mountains—my nature, God-given, thwarted; my abilities, heaven-bestowed, paralyzed—rendered useless. You hear how I contradict myself. I, who preached contentment with a humble lot and defended the calling even of woodcutters and water-carriers in God's service—I, His ordained minister, nearly rave in my restlessness. Well, ambitions and principles must somehow be reconciled."
He left the room. In this brief hour I had learned more about him than in the whole previous month: yet he still puzzled me.

Diana and Mary Rivers grew sadder and quieter as the day of leaving their brother and their home drew near. They both tried to appear as usual; but the sorrow they struggled against was one that could not be fully conquered or hidden. Diana confided that this would be a different parting from any they had ever known. It would probably, as far as St. John was concerned, be a parting for years: it might be a parting for life.

"He will sacrifice everything to his long-held plans," she said. "Natural affection and even stronger feelings. St. John looks quiet, Jane; but he hides a fever inside him. You would think him gentle, yet in some things he is as unyielding as death; and the worst of it is, my conscience can hardly let me try to talk him out of his stern decision: certainly, I cannot for a moment blame him for it. It is right, noble, Christian: yet it breaks my heart!" And the tears sprang to her beautiful eyes. Mary bent her head low over her work.
"We are already without a father: we shall soon be without home and brother," she murmured.

At that moment a small event occurred that seemed decreed by fate specifically to confirm the truth of the saying that "misfortunes never come alone," and to add to their troubles the maddening one of a last-minute disappointment. St. John passed the window reading a letter. He came in.
"Our uncle John is dead," he said.
Both sisters seemed struck: not shocked or grief-stricken; the news appeared in their eyes more significant than sad.
"Dead?" repeated Diana.
"Yes."
She fixed a searching gaze on her brother's face. "And what then?" she asked, in a low voice.
"What then, Die?" he replied, maintaining a marble stillness of expression. "What then? Why—nothing. Read."

He tossed the letter into her lap. She glanced over it and passed it to Mary. Mary read it in silence and returned it to her brother. All three looked at each other, and all three smiled—a bleak, pensive smile.
"So be it! We can still survive," said Diana at last.
"At any rate, it leaves us no worse off than before," remarked Mary.
"It only presses rather forcefully on the mind the picture of what might have been," said Mr. Rivers, "and contrasts it a bit too sharply with what is."
He folded the letter, locked it in his desk, and went out again.
For some minutes no one spoke. Then Diana turned to me.

"Jane, you will wonder at us and our mysteries," she said, "and think us hard-hearted for not being more upset at the death of so close a relative as an uncle; but we have never met him or known him. He was my mother's brother. My father and he quarreled long ago. It was on his advice that my father risked most of his money in the speculation that ruined him. Bitter accusations flew between them: they parted in anger and were never reconciled. My uncle went on to more successful ventures: it appears he accumulated a fortune of twenty thousand pounds. He never married and had no close family but ourselves and one other person, no more closely related than we are. My father always clung to the hope that he would make amends for his error by leaving his money to us; that letter informs us that he has left every penny to the other relative, except for thirty guineas to be split between St. John, Diana, and Mary Rivers, for the purchase of three mourning rings. He had every right, of course, to do as he pleased: and yet it dampens the spirits to receive such news. Mary and I would have counted ourselves rich with a thousand pounds each; and to St. John such a sum would have been valuable for the good it would have enabled him to do."

With this explanation given, the subject was dropped, and neither Mr. Rivers nor his sisters mentioned it again. The next day I left Marsh End for Morton. The day after, Diana and Mary departed for distant B——. Within a week, Mr. Rivers and Hannah moved to the parsonage: and so the old house was left empty.

chapters.title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: My home, then, when at last I find one, is a cottage; a little room with whitewashed walls and a sanded floor, containing four painted chairs and a table, a clock, a cupboard, and two or three plates, dishes, and a set of earthenware tea things. Above, a bedroom the same size as the kitchen, with a plain bedstead and a chest of drawers; small, yet too large to be filled with my meager wardrobe: though the kindness of my gentle and generous friends has added to it a modest supply of essentials.

It is evening. I have sent away, with an orange as payment, the little orphan who serves as my maid. I am sitting alone by the fire. This morning the village school opened. I had twenty students. But only three of them can read: none can write or do arithmetic. Several knit, and a few sew a little. They speak with the broadest local accent. For now, they and I have trouble understanding each other's speech. Some of them are rude, rough, and unmanageable, as well as ignorant; but others are willing, eager to learn, and show a character that pleases me. I must not forget that these coarsely dressed little country children are made of flesh and blood as good as the offspring of the noblest families; and that the seeds of native excellence, refinement, intelligence, and kindness are as likely to exist in their hearts as in those of the best-born. My duty will be to nurture these seeds: surely I shall find some happiness in that task. I do not expect much enjoyment in the life opening before me: yet it will, no doubt, if I manage my mind and use my abilities as I should, give me enough to sustain me from day to day.

Was I very cheerful, settled, content during the hours I spent in that bare, humble schoolroom this morning and afternoon? To be honest with myself, the answer is no: I felt desolate to an extreme degree. I felt—yes, fool that I am—I felt degraded. I feared I had taken a step that lowered rather than raised me in the scale of social existence. I was feebly dismayed at the ignorance, the poverty, the coarseness of everything I heard and saw around me. But let me not hate and despise myself too much for these feelings; I know them to be wrong—and knowing that is a great step forward; I shall fight to overcome them. Tomorrow, I trust, I shall partly succeed; and in a few weeks, perhaps, they will be fully conquered. In a few months, it is possible, the happiness of seeing progress and improvement in my students may replace disgust with satisfaction.

Meanwhile, let me ask myself one question—Which is better? To have given in to temptation; listened to passion; made no painful effort—no struggle; but to have sunk down into the silken trap; fallen asleep on the flowers covering it; woken in a southern land, among the luxuries of a villa: to have been living now in France, Mr. Rochester's mistress; delirious with his love half the time—for he would—oh yes, he would have loved me well for a while. He did love me—no one will ever love me like that again. I shall never again know the sweet tribute paid to beauty, youth, and grace—for never to anyone else shall I seem to possess those charms. He was fond and proud of me—and no other man ever will be.—But where am I wandering, and what am I saying, and above all feeling? The question is: is it better to be a slave in a fool's paradise at Marseilles—drunk on false happiness one hour, choking on the bitterest tears of remorse and shame the next—or to be a village schoolmistress, free and honest, in a breezy mountain valley in the healthy heart of England?

Yes; I feel now that I was right when I held to principle and law, and scorned and crushed the mad urgings of a frenzied moment. God directed me to the right choice: I thank His providence for the guidance!

Having brought my evening reflections to this point, I rose, went to my door, and looked at the sunset of the harvest day, and at the quiet fields before my cottage, which, along with the school, was half a mile from the village. The birds were singing their last notes—
"The air was mild, the dew was balm."

While I looked, I thought myself happy, and was surprised to find myself before long weeping—and why? For the fate that had torn me from my master: for him I was never to see again; for the desperate grief and destructive fury—consequences of my departure—that might now, perhaps, be dragging him from the right path, too far to hope for his eventual return. At this thought, I turned my face from the lovely evening sky and the lonely vale of Morton—I say lonely, for in the stretch of it visible to me there was no building except the church and the parsonage, half-hidden in trees, and, at the very far end, the roof of Vale Hall, where the rich Mr. Oliver and his daughter lived. I covered my eyes and leaned my head against the stone doorframe; but soon a slight sound near the little gate that separated my tiny garden from the meadow beyond made me look up. A dog—old Carlo, Mr. Rivers' pointer, as I saw at once—was pushing the gate with his nose, and St. John himself leaned on it with folded arms; his brow furrowed, his gaze stern almost to displeasure, fixed on me. I asked him to come in.
"No, I cannot stay; I have only brought you a small parcel my sisters left for you. I think it contains a paint box, pencils, and paper."
I came forward to take it: a welcome gift it was. He studied my face, I thought, with severity as I approached: the traces of tears were no doubt clearly visible.
"Have you found your first day's work harder than you expected?" he asked.
"Oh, no! On the contrary, I think in time I shall get along very well with my students."
"But perhaps your accommodations—your cottage—your furniture—have disappointed you? They are, admittedly, meager enough; but—" I interrupted—

"My cottage is clean and weatherproof; my furniture adequate and comfortable. Everything I see has made me grateful, not despondent. I am not such a fool or hedonist as to mourn the absence of a carpet, a sofa, and silver plate; besides, five weeks ago I had nothing—I was an outcast, a beggar, a vagrant; now I have friends, a home, a profession. I marvel at the goodness of God; the generosity of my friends; the bounty of my lot. I am not complaining."
"But you feel loneliness weighing on you? The little house behind you is dark and empty."
"I have hardly had time yet to enjoy a sense of peace, much less to grow impatient with loneliness."

"Very well; I hope you truly feel the contentment you describe. At any rate, your good sense will tell you that it is too early to give in to the wavering fears of Lot's wife. What you left behind before I found you, I do not of course know; but I advise you to resist firmly every temptation that would make you look back: pursue your present course steadily, for at least some months."
"That is exactly what I intend," I answered. St. John continued—

"It is hard work to control the pull of desire and redirect the bent of nature; but that it can be done, I know from experience. God has given us, to a degree, the power to shape our own fate; and when our energies seem to demand nourishment they cannot get—when our will strains after a path we may not follow—we need neither starve from lack, nor stand still in despair: we have only to seek different nourishment for the mind, as strong as the forbidden food it craved—and perhaps purer; and to carve out for the restless foot a road as direct and broad as the one Fortune has blocked, if rougher."

"A year ago I was myself deeply miserable, because I thought I had made a mistake in entering the ministry: its routine duties bored me to death. I burned for the more active life of the wider world—for the more exciting work of a literary career—for the destiny of an artist, author, orator; anything rather than that of a clergyman. Yes, the heart of a politician, of a soldier, of a seeker of glory, a lover of fame, a pursuer of power, beat under my curate's vestment. I thought about it; my life was so wretched it must be changed, or I must die. After a season of darkness and struggle, light broke and relief came: my cramped existence suddenly opened out into a boundless plain—my abilities heard a call from heaven to rise, gather their full strength, spread their wings, and soar beyond sight. God had a mission for me; to carry it far, to deliver it well, skill and strength, courage and eloquence—the best qualities of soldier, statesman, and orator—were all needed: for all of these come together in the good missionary."

"A missionary I resolved to be. From that moment my state of mind changed; the chains dissolved and fell from every faculty, leaving only their painful marks—which only time can heal. My father, it is true, reinforced the decision, but since his death I have no legitimate obstacle left to contend with; some affairs to settle, a successor for Morton to arrange, an attachment or two of the heart to break through or cut away—a last conflict with human weakness, which I know I shall win because I have vowed that I will win—and I leave Europe for the East."

He said this in his particular, subdued yet emphatic voice; looking, when he had finished speaking, not at me but at the setting sun, which I looked at too. Both of us had our backs toward the path leading up the field to the gate. We had heard no step on that grass-covered track; the water running in the valley was the only soothing sound of the hour and the scene; so we both startled when a bright voice, sweet as a silver bell, exclaimed—

"Good evening, Mr. Rivers. And good evening, old Carlo. Your dog is quicker to recognize his friends than you are, sir; he pricked his ears and wagged his tail when I was at the bottom of the field, and you still have your back to me."

It was true. Though Mr. Rivers had started at the first of those musical tones as if lightning had split a cloud over his head, he still stood, at the end of her sentence, in the same position she had caught him in—his arm resting on the gate, his face turned toward the west. He turned at last, with measured deliberation. A vision, it seemed to me, had appeared at his side. There stood, within three feet of him, a figure dressed in pure white—a youthful, graceful form: full yet fine in outline; and when, after stooping to pet Carlo, she raised her head and threw back a long veil, there bloomed under his gaze a face of perfect beauty. Perfect beauty is a bold claim; but I do not take it back or soften it: features as sweet as any ever shaped by England's temperate climate; colors of rose and lily as pure as any her misty skies and damp breezes ever produced—these justified the term in this case. No charm was missing, no flaw was visible; the young woman had regular, delicate features; eyes shaped and colored like those in beautiful paintings—large, dark, and full; the long, shadowy lash that frames a fine eye with such soft allure; the finely drawn brow that gives such clarity; the white, smooth forehead that adds such calm to the livelier beauties of color and light; the cheek, oval, fresh, and smooth; the lips, fresh too, rosy, healthy, sweetly shaped; the even, gleaming teeth without a flaw; the small dimpled chin; the crowning glory of rich, abundant hair—every advantage, in short, which, combined, embodies the ideal of beauty, was fully hers. I gazed at this lovely creature in wonder: I admired her with my whole heart. Nature had surely formed her in a generous mood; and, forgetting her usual stingy allotment of gifts, had showered this favorite child with a grandmother's bounty.

What did St. John Rivers think of this earthly angel? I naturally asked myself that question as I saw him turn to her and look at her; and naturally I sought the answer in his expression. He had already withdrawn his eyes from the vision and was staring at a humble tuft of daisies growing by the gate.
"A lovely evening, but late for you to be out alone," he said, as he crushed the white heads of the closed flowers with his foot.

"Oh, I only came back from S——" (she named a large town some twenty miles away) "this afternoon. Papa told me you had opened your school and that the new teacher had arrived; so I put on my bonnet after tea and walked up the valley to see her: is this she?" pointing to me.
"It is," said St. John.
"Do you think you will like Morton?" she asked me, with a direct and innocent simplicity of tone and manner—pleasing, if childlike.
"I hope so. I have many reasons to."
"Did you find your students as attentive as you expected?"
"Quite."
"Do you like your house?"
"Very much."
"Have I furnished it nicely?"
"Very nicely indeed."
"And made a good choice of assistant for you in Alice Wood?"

"You certainly have. She is quick to learn and handy." (This, then, I thought, is Miss Oliver, the heiress; favored, it seems, in the gifts of fortune as well as nature! What lucky alignment of the stars presided over her birth, I wonder?)

"I shall come up and help you teach sometimes," she added. "It will be a nice change for me to visit you now and then; and I do like a change. Mr. Rivers, I have been so merry during my stay at S——. Last night, or rather this morning, I was dancing until two o'clock. The ——th regiment is stationed there since the riots; and the officers are the most delightful men in the world: they put all our young knife-grinders and scissor merchants to shame."

It seemed to me that Mr. St. John's lower lip jutted and his upper lip curled for a moment. His mouth certainly looked very compressed, and the lower half of his face unusually stern and square, as the laughing girl gave him this information. He raised his eyes, too, from the daisies and turned them on her. It was an unsmiling, searching, pointed look. She met it with another laugh, and laughter suited her well—her youth, her roses, her dimples, her bright eyes.
As he stood, silent and grave, she went back to petting Carlo. "Poor Carlo loves me," she said. "He is not stern and distant to his friends; and if he could talk, he would not be silent."

As she stroked the dog's head, bending with natural grace before his young and severe master, I saw a flush rise to that master's face. I saw his solemn eye soften with sudden fire and flicker with irresistible emotion. Lit up like this, he looked nearly as beautiful as a man can be, as she was as a woman. His chest rose once, as if his large heart, weary of its iron restraint, had swelled in spite of his will and made a powerful leap for freedom. But he checked it, I think, as a determined rider would check a rearing horse. He responded with neither word nor movement to the gentle advances she made.

"Papa says you never come to see us anymore," continued Miss Oliver, looking up. "You are quite a stranger at Vale Hall. He is alone this evening and not very well: will you come back with me and visit him?"
"It is not an appropriate hour to call on Mr. Oliver," answered St. John.

"Not appropriate! But I insist it is. It is exactly the time when Papa most wants company: when the factory is closed and he has nothing to occupy him. Now, Mr. Rivers, do come. Why are you so terribly shy and so terribly gloomy?" She filled the gap his silence left with an answer of her own.

"I forgot!" she exclaimed, shaking her beautiful curled head as if shocked at herself. "I am so giddy and thoughtless! Do excuse me. It slipped my mind that you have good reasons to be in low spirits. Diana and Mary have left you, and Moor House is shut up, and you are so lonely. I am sure I pity you. Do come and see Papa."
"Not tonight, Miss Rosamond, not tonight."
Mr. St. John spoke almost like a machine: only he himself knew what it cost him to refuse.
"Well, if you are so stubborn, I will leave you; for I dare not stay any longer: the dew is starting to fall. Good evening!"
She held out her hand. He barely touched it. "Good evening!" he repeated, in a voice as low and hollow as an echo. She turned away, but came back after a moment.
"Are you well?" she asked. Well might she ask: his face was as white as her gown.

"Perfectly well," he said; and, with a bow, he left the gate. She went one way; he went another. She turned twice to look after him as she tripped lightly down the field; he, as he strode firmly across it, never once looked back.
This spectacle of another person's suffering and self-denial drew my thoughts away from exclusive focus on my own. Diana Rivers had called her brother "unyielding as death." She had not exaggerated.

chapters.title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: I continued the work of the village school as actively and faithfully as I could. It was truly hard at first. Some time passed before, despite all my efforts, I could understand my students and their natures. Completely untaught, their minds still dormant, they seemed hopelessly dull to me; and at first glance, all equally so. But I soon found I was wrong. There was as much variety among them as among the educated; and when I came to know them and they me, this variety quickly showed itself. Their amazement at me, my speech, my rules, and my ways, once it faded, revealed that some of these heavy-looking, slack-jawed country girls were sharp-witted enough. Many proved obliging and pleasant too; and I discovered among them more than a few examples of natural courtesy and innate self-respect, as well as excellent ability, that won both my affection and my admiration. These girls soon took pride in doing their work well, keeping themselves tidy, learning their lessons regularly, and acquiring quiet, orderly manners. The speed of their progress, in some cases, was even surprising; and I took an honest, happy pride in it. Besides, I began personally to like some of the best girls; and they liked me. Among my students were several farmers' daughters: young women, nearly grown. These could already read, write, and sew; and to them I taught the basics of grammar, geography, history, and finer needlework. I found admirable characters among them—characters eager for knowledge and disposed toward improvement—with whom I spent many a pleasant evening in their own homes. Their parents (the farmer and his wife) showered me with kindnesses. There was pleasure in accepting their simple warmth, and in repaying it with a thoughtfulness—a careful regard for their feelings—that they were not, perhaps, always accustomed to, and which both charmed and benefited them; because, while it raised them in their own estimation, it made them eager to deserve the respectful treatment they received.

I felt I was becoming a favorite in the neighborhood. Whenever I went out, I heard cordial greetings on all sides and was welcomed with friendly smiles. To live amid general goodwill, even if it is only the goodwill of working people, is like sitting in calm, sweet sunshine; serene inner feelings bud and bloom in that warmth. At this point in my life, my heart far more often swelled with gratitude than sank with despair: and yet, reader, to tell you everything, in the midst of this calm, useful existence—after a day spent in honorable work among my students, an evening passed drawing or reading contentedly alone—I would plunge into strange dreams at night: dreams vivid, turbulent, full of the ideal, the exciting, the stormy—dreams where, amid extraordinary scenes charged with adventure, thrilling danger, and romantic chance, I met Mr. Rochester again and again, always at some intense crisis; and then the feeling of being in his arms, hearing his voice, meeting his eyes, touching his hand and cheek, loving him, being loved by him—the hope of spending a lifetime at his side—would be renewed with all its first force and fire. Then I would wake. Then I would remember where I was and how I was situated. Then I would sit up in my curtainless bed, trembling and shaking; and the still, dark night would witness the convulsion of despair and hear the burst of passion. By nine o'clock the next morning I was punctually opening the school; calm, steady, ready for the day's duties.

Rosamond Oliver kept her word about visiting me. She usually called at the school during her morning ride. She would canter up to the door on her pony, followed by a mounted servant in livery. Nothing more exquisite than her appearance could be imagined, in her purple riding habit with her velvet cap set gracefully above the long curls that brushed her cheek and floated to her shoulders: and this is how she would enter the rustic building and glide through the dazzled ranks of village children. She generally came at the hour when Mr. Rivers was giving his daily lesson in religious instruction. Her gaze, I fear, pierced the young clergyman's heart to the quick. A kind of instinct seemed to warn him of her entrance, even when he was not looking; and when his back was to the door, if she appeared, his cheek would glow, and his marble-like features, though they refused to relax, changed in some indescribable way and, in their very stillness, became expressive of a repressed passion stronger than any flexing muscle or darting glance could show.

She knew her power over him, of course: indeed, he could not conceal it from her, try as he might. Despite his Christian self-control, when she approached and addressed him, smiling brightly, encouragingly, even tenderly into his face, his hand would tremble and his eyes would burn. He seemed to say, with his sad and resolute expression, if not with his lips, "I love you, and I know you prefer me. It is not fear of rejection that keeps me silent. If I offered my heart, I believe you would accept it. But that heart is already laid on a sacred altar: the fire is arranged around it. Soon it will be nothing but a consumed offering."

And then she would pout like a disappointed child; a wistful cloud would soften her radiant liveliness; she would snatch her hand from his and turn away in brief irritation from his look, at once so heroic and so martyrlike. St. John, no doubt, would have given the world to follow her, call her back, hold on to her when she left him like this; but he would not give one chance at heaven, nor surrender, for the paradise of her love, one hope of the true, eternal Paradise. Besides, he could not confine everything in his nature—the wanderer, the dreamer, the poet, the priest—within the limits of a single passion. He could not—he would not—trade his wild field of missionary work for the drawing rooms and the peace of Vale Hall. I learned this much from him directly, in an advance I once, despite his reserve, dared to make upon his confidence.

Miss Oliver had already honored me with frequent visits to my cottage. I had come to know her whole character, which had no mystery or pretense: she was flirtatious but not heartless; demanding, but not worthlessly selfish. She had been spoiled since birth, but was not ruined by it. She was impulsive but good-natured; vain (she could not help it, when every glance in the mirror showed her such a flood of loveliness) but not affected; generous; free of the arrogance of wealth; straightforward; reasonably intelligent; cheerful, lively, and carefree: she was very charming, in short, even to a cool female observer like me; but she was not deeply interesting or truly impressive. Her mind was of a very different sort from that of St. John's sisters, for instance. Still, I liked her almost as much as I liked my former pupil Adèle; except that for a child we have watched over and taught, a closer affection develops than we can give an equally appealing adult acquaintance.

She had taken a friendly liking to me. She said I was like Mr. Rivers, only, she allowed, "not one-tenth as handsome, though I was a nice, neat little soul enough, but he was an angel." I was, however, good, clever, composed, and steady, like him. I was a freak of nature, she declared, to be a village schoolmistress: she was sure my past, if it were known, would make a wonderful novel.

One evening, while, with her usual childlike energy and thoughtless but inoffensive curiosity, she was rummaging through the cupboard and table drawer of my little kitchen, she discovered first two French books, a volume of Schiller, a German grammar and dictionary, and then my drawing materials and some sketches, including a pencil portrait of a pretty little cherub-faced girl, one of my students, and various views from nature, taken in the Vale of Morton and on the surrounding moors. She was first struck dumb with surprise, and then electrified with delight.

"Had I done these pictures? Did I know French and German? What a wonder—what a miracle I was! I drew better than her teacher at the finest school in S——. Would I sketch a portrait of her, to show to Papa?"

"With pleasure," I replied; and I felt a thrill of artistic delight at the idea of copying from such a perfect and radiant model. She was wearing a dark blue silk dress; her arms and neck were bare; her only ornament was her chestnut hair, which waved over her shoulders with all the wild grace of natural curls. I took a sheet of fine cardboard and drew a careful outline. I promised myself the pleasure of adding color later; and, as it was getting late, I told her she must come and sit for me another day.

She gave her father such a report of me that Mr. Oliver himself accompanied her the next evening—a tall, heavy-featured, middle-aged, gray-haired man, beside whom his lovely daughter looked like a bright flower next to a weathered tower. He seemed a quiet, and perhaps a proud man; but he was very kind to me. The sketch of Rosamond's portrait pleased him greatly: he said I must make a finished painting of it. He also insisted on my coming the next day to spend the evening at Vale Hall.

I went. I found it a large, handsome house, showing clear signs of its owner's wealth. Rosamond was full of glee and pleasure the entire time I was there. Her father was friendly; and when he drew me into conversation after tea, he expressed strong approval of what I had accomplished at the Morton school, and said he only feared, from what he could see and hear, that I was too good for the place and would soon leave it for one more suitable.
"Indeed," cried Rosamond, "she is clever enough to be a governess in a high family, Papa."

I thought I would far rather be where I was than in any grand household in the land. Mr. Oliver spoke of Mr. Rivers—of the Rivers family—with great respect. He said it was a very old name in that area; that the family's ancestors had been wealthy; that all of Morton had once belonged to them; that even now he considered the head of the family could, if he wished, marry into the best circles. He thought it a pity that so fine and talented a young man had resolved to go out as a missionary; it was throwing away a valuable life. It appeared, then, that her father would put no obstacle in the way of Rosamond's union with St. John. Mr. Oliver clearly regarded the young clergyman's good birth, old name, and sacred profession as sufficient compensation for his lack of fortune.

It was the fifth of November, and a holiday. My little servant, after helping me clean my house, had gone, well satisfied with a penny for her trouble. Everything around me was spotless and bright—scrubbed floor, polished grate, and well-rubbed chairs. I had also tidied myself up, and now had the afternoon free to spend as I wished.

Translating a few pages of German took an hour; then I got out my palette and pencils and turned to the more soothing, because easier, task of finishing Rosamond Oliver's miniature portrait. The face was already done: only the background needed coloring and the drapery shading; a touch of red to add to the full lips—a soft curl here and there in the hair—a deeper tint to the shadow of the lashes beneath the blue-tinged eyelids. I was absorbed in these fine details when, after one quick tap, my door opened to admit St. John Rivers.

"I have come to see how you are spending your holiday," he said. "Not in gloomy thought, I hope? No, that is good: while you draw you will not feel lonely. You see, I still worry about you, though you have held up wonderfully so far. I have brought you a book for the evening," and he laid on the table a new publication—a poem: one of those genuine masterworks so often granted to the fortunate public of those days—the golden age of modern literature. Alas! the readers of our time are less blessed. But take heart! I will not stop to accuse or lament. I know poetry is not dead, nor genius lost; nor has greed gained power over either, to bind or destroy them: they will both assert their existence, their presence, their freedom and their strength again one day. Mighty angels, safe in heaven! They smile when base souls triumph and timid ones weep over their destruction. Poetry destroyed? Genius banished? No! Mediocrity—no: do not let envy suggest that thought. No; they not only survive but reign and redeem: and without their divine influence everywhere, you would live in hell—the hell of your own smallness.

While I was eagerly scanning the bright pages of Marmion (for Marmion it was), St. John bent down to examine my painting. His tall figure sprang upright again with a start: he said nothing. I looked up at him: he avoided my eye. I knew his thoughts well and could read his heart plainly; at that moment I felt calmer and cooler than he. I had temporarily the advantage, and I decided to do him some good, if I could.

"With all his firmness and self-control," I thought, "he pushes himself too hard: locks every feeling and pang inside—expresses, confesses, shares nothing. I am sure it would do him good to talk a little about this sweet Rosamond, whom he thinks he should not marry. I will make him talk."

I said first, "Take a seat, Mr. Rivers." But he answered, as he always did, that he could not stay. "Very well," I responded mentally, "stand if you like; but you shall not leave just yet, I am determined. Solitude is at least as harmful for you as it is for me. I will see if I can find the secret spring of your reserve, and an opening in that marble chest through which I can pour one drop of the balm of sympathy."
"Is this portrait a good likeness?" I asked bluntly.
"Likeness! Of whom? I did not look at it closely."
"You did, Mr. Rivers."

He nearly started at my sudden and bold directness: he looked at me in astonishment. "Oh, that is nothing yet," I thought. "I don't intend to be put off by a little stiffness on your part; I am prepared to go much further." I continued, "You studied it closely and carefully; but I have no objection to your looking again," and I got up and placed it in his hand.
"A well-executed picture," he said; "very soft, clear coloring; very graceful and accurate drawing."
"Yes, yes; I know all that. But what about the likeness? Who does it look like?"
Overcoming some hesitation, he answered, "Miss Oliver, I presume."

"Of course. And now, sir, to reward you for the accurate guess, I will promise to paint you a careful and faithful copy of this very picture, provided you admit that the gift would be welcome. I don't want to waste my time and effort on an offering you would consider worthless."

He continued to gaze at the picture: the longer he looked, the more firmly he held it, the more he seemed to want it. "It is like her!" he murmured; "the eye is perfectly done: the color, light, expression are all right. It smiles!"

"Would it comfort you, or would it pain you, to have a painting like it? Tell me. When you are in Madagascar, or at the Cape, or in India, would it be a consolation to have that keepsake in your possession? Or would the sight of it bring memories that would weaken and distress you?"
He now furtively raised his eyes: he glanced at me, uncertain, troubled: he looked at the picture again.
"That I should like to have it is certain: whether it would be wise is another question."

Since I had discovered that Rosamond genuinely preferred him and that her father was unlikely to oppose the match, I—less lofty in my views than St. John—had been strongly inclined to argue for their union. It seemed to me that, should he gain possession of Mr. Oliver's large fortune, he might do as much good with it as if he went abroad and left his brilliance to wither and his strength to waste under a tropical sun. With this conviction I now answered—
"As far as I can see, it would be wiser and more sensible if you simply took the original at once."

By this time he had sat down: he had laid the picture on the table before him and, with his forehead propped on both hands, was gazing at it adoringly. I could see he was now neither angry nor shocked at my boldness. I saw that to be addressed so frankly on a subject he had considered untouchable—to hear it handled so freely—was beginning to feel like a new pleasure to him, an unhoped-for relief. Reserved people often truly need frank discussion of their feelings and sorrows more than the naturally open do. The most stone-faced stoic is human after all; and to burst with courage and goodwill into the silent sea of their souls is often to give them the greatest of gifts.

"She likes you, I am sure," I said, standing behind his chair, "and her father respects you. Moreover, she is a sweet girl—rather thoughtless; but you would have enough thought for both of you. You ought to marry her."
"Does she like me?" he asked.
"Definitely; more than anyone else. She talks about you constantly: there is no subject she enjoys more or returns to more often."
"It is very pleasant to hear this," he said—"very pleasant: go on for another quarter of an hour." And he actually took out his watch and laid it on the table to time the interval.
"But what is the use of going on," I asked, "when you are probably preparing some crushing rebuttal, or forging a fresh chain to shackle your heart?"

"Don't imagine such harsh things. Picture me yielding and melting, as I am now: human love rising like a freshly opened spring in my mind and flooding with sweet water the whole field I have so carefully and laboriously prepared—so painstakingly sown with seeds of good intentions and self-denying plans. And now it is drenched with sweet nectar—the young shoots drowned—delicious poison corrupting them. Now I see myself stretched on a sofa in the drawing room at Vale Hall, at the feet of my bride Rosamond Oliver: she is talking to me with her sweet voice—gazing down at me with those eyes your skillful hand has copied so well—smiling at me with those coral lips. She is mine—I am hers—this present life and passing world are enough for me. Hush! Say nothing—my heart is full of delight—my senses are enchanted—let the time I marked pass in peace."

I humored him: the watch ticked on: he breathed fast and shallow: I stood silent. In this hush the quarter-hour flew by; he put the watch away, laid the picture down, stood up, and took his place by the fire.

"Now," he said, "that little space was given over to fever and fantasy. I rested my head on the breast of temptation and willingly placed my neck under her garland of flowers; I tasted her cup. The pillow was burning: there is a serpent in the garland: the wine has a bitter taste: her promises are hollow—her offers false. I see and know all this."
I stared at him in wonder.

"It is strange," he went on, "that while I love Rosamond Oliver so wildly—with all the intensity of a first passion, whose object is exquisitely beautiful, graceful, and captivating—I experience at the same time a calm, clear awareness that she would not make me a good wife; that she is not the partner suited to me; that I should discover this within a year of marrying; and that twelve months of rapture would give way to a lifetime of regret. This I know."
"Strange indeed!" I could not help exclaiming.

"While something in me," he continued, "is keenly alive to her charms, something else is just as deeply aware of her flaws: they are such that she could share in nothing I aspired to—cooperate in nothing I undertook. Rosamond a sufferer, a laborer, a woman apostle? Rosamond a missionary's wife? No!"
"But you don't have to be a missionary. You could give up that plan."

"Give it up! What! My calling? My great work? My foundation laid on earth for a mansion in heaven? My hopes of being counted among those who have merged all ambitions into the glorious one of bettering humanity—of carrying knowledge into the realms of ignorance—of replacing war with peace—bondage with freedom—superstition with faith—the fear of hell with the hope of heaven? Must I give that up? It is dearer than the blood in my veins. It is what I have to look forward to, and to live for."
After a long pause, I said—"And Miss Oliver? Do her disappointment and sorrow not concern you?"

"Miss Oliver is always surrounded by admirers and flatterers: in less than a month, my image will be erased from her heart. She will forget me; and will marry, probably, someone who will make her far happier than I ever could."
"You speak coolly enough; but you are suffering in this struggle. You are wasting away."

"No. If I have grown a little thin, it is from anxiety about my plans, still unsettled—my departure, continually postponed. Only this morning I received word that the successor whose arrival I have been waiting for so long cannot be ready to replace me for another three months; and those three months may stretch to six."
"You tremble and flush whenever Miss Oliver enters the schoolroom."

Again the surprised expression crossed his face. He had not imagined that a woman would dare speak so directly to a man. For my part, I felt comfortable in this kind of conversation.
