I could never be at ease with strong, thoughtful, and refined minds, whether male or female, until I had gotten past the outer walls of conventional reserve, crossed the threshold of confidence, and won a place by the very fireside of their hearts.

"You are original," he said, "and not timid. There is something brave in your spirit, as well as penetrating in your eye; but allow me to assure you that you partly misread my emotions. You think them deeper and more powerful than they are. You credit me with more feeling than I have a right to claim. When I flush and when I tremble before Miss Oliver, I do not pity myself. I despise the weakness. I know it is base: a mere fever of the flesh, not, I declare, a convulsion of the soul. That is as fixed as a rock, set firm in the depths of a restless sea. Know me for what I am—a cold, hard man."
I smiled skeptically.

"You have taken my confidence by storm," he continued, "and now it is at your disposal. In my original state—stripped of the blood-bleached robe with which Christianity covers human deformity—I am a cold, hard, ambitious man. Natural affection alone, of all feelings, has any lasting hold on me. Reason, not emotion, is my guide; my ambition is limitless: my desire to rise higher, to achieve more than others, is insatiable. I value endurance, persistence, industry, talent; because these are the means by which men accomplish great things and climb to lofty heights. I watch your progress with interest because I consider you an example of a diligent, orderly, energetic woman: not because I deeply sympathize with what you have suffered, or what you still endure."
"You would describe yourself as a mere pagan philosopher," I said.

"No. There is this difference between me and godless philosophers: I believe; and I believe the Gospel. You chose the wrong word. I am not a pagan but a Christian philosopher—a follower of the faith of Jesus. As His disciple I embrace His pure, merciful, generous teachings. I champion them: I am sworn to spread them. Won over to religion in my youth, she has cultivated my original qualities like this: from the tiny seed of natural affection, she has grown the towering tree of love for humanity. From the wild, stringy root of human integrity, she has raised a proper sense of divine justice. The ambition to win power and fame for my wretched self, she has transformed into the ambition to expand my Master's kingdom; to win victories for the banner of the cross. This is what religion has done for me; making the best use of the raw material; pruning and training nature. But she could not root out nature: nor will nature be rooted out until this mortal puts on immortality."
Having said this, he picked up his hat from the table beside my palette. Once more he looked at the portrait.
"She is lovely," he murmured. "She is well named the Rose of the World, indeed!"
"And may I not paint a copy for you?"
"What would be the point? No."

He drew across the picture the sheet of thin paper on which I usually rested my hand while painting, to keep the cardboard from being smudged. What he suddenly noticed on this blank paper, I could not tell; but something had caught his eye. He snatched it up; he looked at the edge; then shot me a look that was indescribably peculiar and completely incomprehensible: a glance that seemed to take in and register every detail of my figure, face, and dress; for it swept over everything, quick and keen as lightning. His lips parted as if to speak: but he checked whatever he had been about to say.
"What is the matter?" I asked.

"Nothing in the world," was the reply; and, replacing the paper, I saw him deftly tear a narrow strip from the margin. It vanished into his glove; and with one hasty nod and "good afternoon," he was gone.
"Well!" I exclaimed, using a local expression, "that beats everything!"

I in my turn examined the paper; but saw nothing on it except a few faint smudges of paint where I had tested colors with my brush. I puzzled over the mystery for a minute or two; but finding it unsolvable and certain it could not matter much, I put it out of my mind and soon forgot it.

chapters.title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: When Mr. St. John left, it was beginning to snow; the whirling storm continued all night. The next day a biting wind brought fresh, blinding falls; by twilight the valley was buried under drifts and nearly impassable. I had closed my shutters, laid a mat against the door to keep the snow from blowing in underneath, and stoked my fire. After sitting nearly an hour on the hearth listening to the muffled fury of the storm, I lit a candle, took down Marmion, and began—

"Day set on Norham's castled steep, And Tweed's fair river broad and deep, And Cheviot's mountains lone; The massive towers, the donjon keep, The flanking walls that round them sweep, In yellow lustre shone"—
I soon forgot the storm in the music of the verse.

I heard a noise: the wind, I thought, shaking the door. No; it was St. John Rivers, who, lifting the latch, stepped in out of the frozen hurricane—the howling darkness—and stood before me: the cloak that covered his tall figure all white as a glacier. I was nearly stunned with surprise, so little had I expected any visitor from the snowbound valley that night.
"Any bad news?" I demanded. "Has something happened?"

"No. How easily alarmed you are!" he answered, removing his cloak and hanging it against the door, toward which he calmly pushed back the mat his entrance had displaced. He stamped the snow from his boots.

"I shall ruin the cleanness of your floor," he said, "but you must excuse me just this once." Then he approached the fire. "I had a hard time getting here, I assure you," he observed, warming his hands over the flame. "One drift came up to my waist; fortunately the snow is still quite soft."
"But why have you come?" I could not help asking.

"A rather unwelcoming question for a visitor; but since you ask, I'll answer simply: to have a little conversation with you. I grew tired of my silent books and empty rooms. Besides, since yesterday I have felt the excitement of someone who has been told half a story and is impatient to hear the rest."

He sat down. I recalled his strange behavior of the day before, and I genuinely began to wonder if his mind was affected. If he was mad, however, his was a very cool and collected madness. I had never seen that handsome face of his look more like chiseled marble than it did right now, as he pushed his snow-wet hair back from his forehead and let the firelight fall freely on his pale brow and equally pale cheek, where I was sorry to see the hollow mark of worry or sorrow now so plainly etched. I waited, expecting him to say something I could at least understand; but his hand was at his chin, his finger on his lip: he was thinking. It struck me that his hand looked as wasted as his face. A perhaps unwarranted surge of pity swept over me: I was moved to say—
"I wish Diana or Mary would come and live with you: it is too bad that you should be entirely alone; and you are recklessly careless about your own health."
"Not at all," he said; "I take care of myself when necessary. I am fine now. What do you see wrong with me?"
This was said with a careless, distracted indifference that showed my concern was, in his view at least, entirely unnecessary. I fell silent.

He still slowly traced his finger across his upper lip, and still his gaze rested dreamily on the glowing grate; feeling I should say something, I asked him after a moment if he felt any cold draft from the door behind him.
"No, no!" he answered shortly and somewhat irritably.
"Well," I thought, "if you won't talk, you can sit in silence; I will leave you alone and go back to my book."

So I trimmed the candle and returned to Marmion. He soon stirred; my eye was instantly drawn to his movements; he only took out a leather notebook, produced a letter from it, read it in silence, folded it, put it back, and sank again into thought. It was useless to try to read with such an inscrutable figure before me; nor could I, in my impatience, agree to stay quiet; he could rebuff me if he liked, but talk I would.
"Have you heard from Diana and Mary lately?"
"Not since the letter I showed you a week ago."
"There has not been any change in your own plans? You will not be called away from England sooner than you expected?"
"I'm afraid not: such luck is too good for me." Blocked in that direction, I changed my approach. I thought to talk about the school and my students.
"Mary Garrett's mother is better, and Mary came back to the school this morning. And I shall have four new girls next week from Foundry Close—they would have come today but for the snow."
"Indeed!"
"Mr. Oliver is paying for two of them."
"Is he?"
"He intends to give the whole school a treat at Christmas."
"I know."
"Was it your idea?"
"No."
"Whose, then?"
"His daughter's, I think."
"That sounds like her: she is so good-natured."
"Yes."
Again came the blankness of a pause: the clock struck eight. It roused him; he uncrossed his legs, sat up straight, and turned to me.
"Put your book aside for a moment and come a little closer to the fire," he said.
Puzzled, and finding no end to my puzzlement, I did as he asked.

"Half an hour ago," he went on, "I mentioned my impatience to hear the rest of a story. On reflection, I think the matter will be better handled if I take the narrator's part and make you the listener. Before I begin, it is only fair to warn you that the story will sound rather familiar to your ears; but stale details often gain a certain freshness when they pass through new lips. For the rest, whether familiar or new, it is short."

"Twenty years ago, a poor curate—never mind his name for now—fell in love with a rich man's daughter; she fell in love with him and married him, against the advice of all her friends, who consequently disowned her immediately after the wedding. Before two years had passed, the rash pair were both dead, and laid quietly side by side under one slab. (I have seen their grave; it formed part of the pavement of a huge churchyard surrounding the grim, soot-black old cathedral of an overgrown factory town in ——shire.) They left a daughter, which Charity received in her arms at birth—cold as the snowdrift I nearly got stuck in tonight. Charity carried the friendless child to the house of its rich maternal relations; it was raised by an aunt-in-law called (I come to names now) Mrs. Reed of Gateshead. You flinch—did you hear a noise? It is probably just a rat scuttling along the rafters of the schoolroom next door: it was a barn before I had it repaired and converted, and barns usually have rats.—To continue. Mrs. Reed kept the orphan ten years: whether she was happy there or not, I cannot say, never having been told; but at the end of that time she transferred her to a place you know—none other than Lowood School, where you yourself lived so long. It seems her career there was very honorable: from a pupil she became a teacher, like you—really, it strikes me there are parallel points in her history and yours—she left it to become a governess: there, again, your fates were similar; she undertook the education of the ward of a certain Mr. Rochester."
"Mr. Rivers!" I interrupted.

"I can guess your feelings," he said, "but control them for now. I have nearly finished; hear me to the end. Of Mr. Rochester's character I know nothing, except the single fact that he proposed what he called honorable marriage to this young woman, and that at the very altar she discovered he already had a wife, though a madwoman. What his subsequent behavior and proposals were is pure guesswork; but when an event occurred that made it necessary to find the governess, it was discovered she was gone—no one could say when, where, or how. She had left Thornfield Hall in the night; every search for her trail had been fruitless: the countryside had been scoured far and wide; not a trace of information about her could be found. Yet she must be found—it has become a matter of serious urgency: advertisements have been placed in all the papers; I myself have received a letter from a Mr. Briggs, a solicitor, giving the details I have just shared. Is it not a remarkable story?"
"Just tell me this," said I, "and since you know so much, you surely can tell me—what of Mr. Rochester? How and where is he? What is he doing? Is he well?"

"I know nothing about Mr. Rochester: the letter never mentions him except to describe the fraudulent and illegal attempt I have referred to. You should be asking the governess's name—the nature of the event that requires her appearance."
"Did no one go to Thornfield Hall, then? Did no one see Mr. Rochester?"
"I suppose not."
"But they wrote to him?"
"Of course."
"And what did he say? Who has his letters?"
"Mr. Briggs indicates that the reply to his inquiry came not from Mr. Rochester but from a lady: it is signed 'Alice Fairfax.'"

I went cold with dread: my worst fears were probably true. He had in all likelihood left England and rushed in reckless desperation to some former haunt on the Continent. And what comfort for his terrible suffering—what outlet for his strong passions—had he sought there? I dared not answer the question. Oh, my poor master—once almost my husband—whom I had so often called "my dear Edward!"
"He must have been a bad man," observed Mr. Rivers.
"You don't know him—don't pass judgment on him," I said with heat.

"Very well," he answered quietly; "and indeed my mind is occupied with other matters than him. I have my story to finish. Since you won't ask the governess's name, I must tell you myself. Wait! I have it here—it is always more satisfactory to see important details in writing, committed to black and white."

And the notebook was once again deliberately produced, opened, searched through; from one of its compartments he drew a shabby slip of paper, hastily torn off. I recognized in its texture and its stains of blue, crimson, and vermilion the stolen margin of my portrait's protective sheet. He stood, held it close to my eyes: and I read, traced in ink, in my own handwriting, the words "JANE EYRE"—the work, no doubt, of some absent-minded moment.

"Briggs wrote to me about a Jane Eyre," he said; "the advertisements called for a Jane Eyre. I knew a Jane Elliott.—I confess I had my suspicions, but it was only yesterday afternoon that they were confirmed beyond doubt. You acknowledge the name and give up the alias?"
"Yes—yes; but where is Mr. Briggs? He may know more of Mr. Rochester than you do."

"Briggs is in London. I doubt he knows anything at all about Mr. Rochester; it is not Mr. Rochester he is interested in. Meanwhile, you are ignoring the important points to chase after trifles: you do not ask why Mr. Briggs was looking for you—what he wanted with you."
"Well, what did he want?"
"Simply to tell you that your uncle, Mr. Eyre of Madeira, is dead; that he has left you all his property, and that you are now rich—simply that—nothing more."
"I—rich?"
"Yes, you, rich—quite an heiress."
Silence followed.

"You will need to prove your identity, of course," resumed St. John after a moment, "a step that should present no difficulty; you can then take immediate possession. Your fortune is invested in English government bonds; Briggs has the will and the necessary documents."

Here was an unexpected card turned up! It is a fine thing, reader, to be lifted in a moment from poverty to wealth—a very fine thing; but not something you can grasp, or consequently enjoy, all at once. And there are other turns in life far more thrilling and joy-giving: this is solid, a matter of the real world, nothing ideal about it; all its associations are practical and sober, and its effects the same. You do not jump and spring and shout hurrah! on hearing you have a fortune; you start thinking about responsibilities and pondering business; on a foundation of steady satisfaction rise certain serious concerns, and you restrain yourself, and brood over your good luck with a solemn brow.

Besides, the words legacy, bequest walk hand in hand with the words death, funeral. My uncle, I had heard, was dead—my only relative; ever since learning of his existence, I had cherished the hope of one day meeting him: now I never would. And then this money came only to me: not to me and a rejoicing family, but to my solitary self. It was a great gift, no doubt; and independence would be glorious—yes, I felt that—that thought swelled my heart.
"You unbend your forehead at last," said Mr. Rivers. "I thought Medusa had looked at you and you were turning to stone. Perhaps now you will ask how much you are worth?"
"How much am I worth?"
"Oh, a trifle! Nothing worth mentioning, of course—twenty thousand pounds, I think they say—but what is that?"
"Twenty thousand pounds?"
Here was another shock—I had been calculating on four or five thousand. This news actually took my breath for a moment: Mr. St. John, whom I had never heard laugh before, laughed now.
"Well," he said, "if you had committed a murder and I had told you your crime was discovered, you could scarcely look more horrified."
"It is an enormous sum—are you sure there is no mistake?"
"No mistake at all."
"Perhaps you read the figures wrong—it may be two thousand!"
"It is written in words, not figures—twenty thousand."
I again felt rather like a person of average appetite sitting down to eat alone at a table set for a hundred. Mr. Rivers stood and put on his cloak.

"If it were not such a wild night," he said, "I would send Hannah down to keep you company: you look too desperately miserable to be left alone. But Hannah, poor woman, could not wade through the drifts as well as I: her legs are not quite as long. So I must leave you to your troubles. Good night."
He was lifting the latch: a sudden thought struck me.
"Wait a moment!" I cried.
"Yes?"
"It puzzles me to know why Mr. Briggs wrote to you about me; or how he knew you, or could imagine that you, living in such a remote place, could help find me."
"Oh! I am a clergyman," he said; "and the clergy are often asked about odd matters." Again the latch rattled.
"No; that doesn't satisfy me!" I exclaimed; and indeed there was something in his hasty, evasive reply that, instead of calming my curiosity, only sharpened it.
"It is a very strange business," I added; "I must know more about it."
"Another time."
"No; tonight!—tonight!" and as he turned toward the door, I planted myself between it and him. He looked rather uncomfortable.
"You certainly shall not leave until you have told me everything," I said.
"I would rather not, just now."
"You shall!—you must!"
"I would rather Diana or Mary told you."
Of course these objections only drove my eagerness to a peak: satisfied it must be, and without delay; and I told him so.
"But I warned you that I am a stubborn man," he said, "hard to persuade."
"And I am a stubborn woman—impossible to put off."
And I am a stubborn woman—impossible to put off.
"And besides," he went on, "I am cold: no passion touches me."

"Whereas I am hot, and fire melts ice. The blaze over there has thawed all the snow from your cloak; and by the same token, it has streamed across my floor and made it look like a trampled street. As you hope ever to be forgiven, Mr. Rivers, the high crime and offense of ruining a sanded kitchen, tell me what I want to know."

"Well, then," he said, "I give in; if not to your earnestness, then to your persistence: as stone is worn by constant dripping. Besides, you must find out someday—as well now as later. Your name is Jane Eyre?"
"Of course: that was all settled before."
"You are not, perhaps, aware that I share your surname?—that I was christened St. John Eyre Rivers?"
"No, indeed! I remember now seeing the letter E. included in your initials, written in books you have lent me at various times; but I never asked what name it stood for. But what then? Surely—"

I stopped: I could not trust myself to entertain, much less to speak, the thought that rushed upon me—that took shape—that, in a second, stood out as a strong, solid probability. Circumstances linked themselves, fitted together, fell into order: the chain that had been lying in a formless heap of links was drawn out straight—every ring was perfect, the connection complete. I knew, by instinct, how things stood, before St. John had said another word; but I cannot expect the reader to have the same intuitive grasp, so I must repeat his explanation.

"My mother's name was Eyre; she had two brothers; one a clergyman, who married Miss Jane Reed of Gateshead; the other, John Eyre, Esquire, merchant, late of Funchal, Madeira. Mr. Briggs, being Mr. Eyre's solicitor, wrote to us last August to inform us of our uncle's death and to say that he had left his property to his brother the clergyman's orphan daughter, bypassing us because of a quarrel, never forgiven, between him and my father. He wrote again a few weeks ago to say that the heiress had disappeared, and to ask if we knew anything about her. A name casually written on a slip of paper has allowed me to find her. You know the rest." Again he was going, but I set my back against the door.
"Do let me speak," I said; "give me one moment to catch my breath and think." I paused—he stood before me, hat in hand, looking composed enough. I went on—
"Your mother was my father's sister?"
"Yes."
"My aunt, then?"
He nodded.
"My uncle John was your uncle John? You, Diana, and Mary are his sister's children, as I am his brother's child?"
"Undeniably."
"You three, then, are my cousins; half the blood on each side flows from the same source?"
"We are cousins; yes."

I studied him. It seemed I had found a brother: one I could be proud of—one I could love; and two sisters, whose qualities were such that when I knew them only as strangers, they had inspired me with genuine affection and admiration. The two women on whom, kneeling on the wet ground and peering through the low, latticed window of Moor House kitchen, I had gazed with so bitter a mixture of fascination and despair—they were my close relatives; and the young, distinguished gentleman who had found me almost dying on his doorstep was my own blood relation. Glorious discovery for a lonely soul! This was wealth indeed!—wealth for the heart!—a mine of pure, warm affections. This was a blessing, bright, vivid, and exhilarating;—not like the heavy gift of gold: welcome enough in its way, but sobering under its weight. I clapped my hands in sudden joy—my pulse leapt, my blood thrilled.
"Oh, I am glad!—I am glad!" I exclaimed.

St. John smiled. "Did I not say you neglected the important things to chase after trifles?" he asked. "You were serious when I told you that you had a fortune; and now, for something that hardly matters, you are overjoyed."

"What can you mean? It may not matter to you; you have sisters and don't need a cousin; but I had nobody; and now three relatives—or two, if you refuse to be counted—have been born into my world, fully grown. I say again, I am glad!"

I paced quickly through the room. I stopped, half suffocating with thoughts that rose faster than I could absorb, understand, or sort them:—thoughts of what might, could, would, and should happen, and soon. I looked at the blank wall: it seemed a sky thick with rising stars—every one lighting me toward a purpose or a joy. Those who had saved my life, whom until this moment I had loved without the power to give anything back, I could now benefit. They were under a yoke—I could free them; they were scattered—I could reunite them. The independence, the abundance that was mine could be theirs too. Were we not four? Twenty thousand pounds divided equally would be five thousand each. Enough and to spare: justice would be done—mutual happiness secured. Now the wealth did not weigh on me: now it was not merely a bequest of coins—it was a gift of life, hope, and joy.

How I looked while these ideas were storming through my mind, I cannot say; but I soon noticed that Mr. Rivers had placed a chair behind me and was gently trying to get me to sit down. He also advised me to be calm; I scorned the suggestion that I was helpless and hysterical, shook off his hand, and began pacing again.

"Write to Diana and Mary tomorrow," I said, "and tell them to come home at once. Diana said they would both consider themselves rich with a thousand pounds, so with five thousand they will do very well."
"Tell me where I can get you a glass of water," said St. John; "you really must try to calm yourself."
"Nonsense! And what effect will this bequest have on you? Will it keep you in England, persuade you to marry Miss Oliver, and settle down like an ordinary person?"
"You are rambling: your mind is confused. I have been too sudden in breaking the news; it has excited you beyond your strength."
"Mr. Rivers! You are driving me mad with frustration: I am perfectly rational; it is you who misunderstand, or pretend to misunderstand."
"Perhaps if you explained yourself a little more clearly, I would grasp your meaning better."

"Explain! What is there to explain? You must see that twenty thousand pounds, the sum in question, divided equally between the nephew and three nieces of our uncle, gives five thousand to each? What I want is for you to write to your sisters and tell them about the fortune that has come to them."
"To you, you mean."

"I have stated my view of the case: I am incapable of taking any other. I am not brutally selfish, blindly unjust, or monstrously ungrateful. Besides, I am determined to have a home and a family. I like Moor House, and I will live at Moor House; I like Diana and Mary, and I will attach myself to Diana and Mary for life. It would please and benefit me to have five thousand pounds; it would torment and oppress me to have twenty thousand; which, moreover, could never be mine in fairness, though it might be in law. I give up to you, then, what is absolutely surplus to my needs. Let there be no arguments and no debate about it; let us agree among ourselves and settle the matter at once."
"This is acting on impulse; you must take days to consider such a thing before your word can be taken seriously."
"Oh! If all you doubt is my sincerity, I am at ease: you see the justice of the case?"

"I do see a certain justice; but it goes against all custom. Besides, the entire fortune is yours by right: my uncle earned it by his own efforts; he was free to leave it to whomever he wished. He left it to you. After all, justice does permit you to keep it: you may, with a clear conscience, consider it absolutely your own."

"With me," I said, "it is fully as much a matter of feeling as of conscience: I must follow my feelings; I so rarely have the chance. If you were to argue, object, and annoy me for a year, I could not give up the delicious pleasure I have glimpsed—that of partly repaying an enormous debt, and gaining lifelong friends."

"You think so now," replied St. John, "because you do not know what it means to possess, or consequently to enjoy, wealth: you cannot imagine the importance twenty thousand pounds would give you; the place in society it would allow you; the prospects it would open—you cannot—"

"And you," I interrupted, "cannot begin to imagine the hunger I have for family love. I never had a home, I never had brothers or sisters; I must and will have them now: you are not reluctant to acknowledge me and accept me, are you?"
"Jane, I will be your brother—my sisters will be your sisters—without requiring this sacrifice of your rightful inheritance."

"Brother? Yes; at a distance of a thousand miles! Sisters? Yes; slaving among strangers! I, wealthy—gorged with gold I never earned and do not deserve! You, penniless! Fine equality and brotherhood! Close union! Intimate bond!"
"But, Jane, your longing for family ties and domestic happiness may be fulfilled by other means than what you are proposing: you could marry."
"Nonsense, again! Marry! I do not want to marry, and never shall."
"That is saying too much: such rash claims prove you are speaking under great excitement."

"It is not saying too much: I know what I feel, and how completely opposed I am to the very idea of marriage. No one would take me for love; and I refuse to be seen as a mere financial opportunity. And I do not want a stranger—cold, alien, different from me; I want my own family: people with whom I feel a complete bond. Say again you will be my brother: when you spoke those words I was satisfied, happy; repeat them, if you can, and mean them."

"I think I can. I know I have always loved my own sisters; and I know what my affection for them rests on—respect for their worth and admiration for their talents. You too have principle and intelligence: your tastes and habits resemble Diana's and Mary's; your company is always agreeable to me; in your conversation I have already for some time found a wholesome comfort. I feel I can easily and naturally make room in my heart for you, as my third and youngest sister."
"Thank you: that is enough for tonight. Now you had better go; for if you stay longer, you will probably annoy me again with some mistrustful objection."
"And the school, Miss Eyre? It must be closed now, I suppose?"
"No. I will keep my post as teacher until you find a replacement."
He smiled approvingly: we shook hands, and he left.

I need not describe in detail the further battles I fought and arguments I used to get the inheritance settled as I wished. My task was very difficult; but as I was absolutely resolved—as my cousins eventually saw that my mind was truly and unshakably fixed on making a fair division of the property—as they must in their own hearts have felt the justice of the intention, and must, besides, have known instinctively that in my place they would have done exactly what I wished to do—they yielded at last so far as to agree to put the matter to arbitration. The judges chosen were Mr. Oliver and a skilled lawyer: both agreed with my view. I got my way. The legal documents were drawn up: St. John, Diana, Mary, and I each received a competence.

chapters.title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: It was near Christmas by the time everything was settled: the season of general holiday was approaching. I now closed Morton school, taking care that the parting should not be empty-handed on my side. Good fortune opens the hand as well as the heart wonderfully; and to give something when we have received much is but to give vent to the unusual surge of feeling. I had long felt with pleasure that many of my rustic scholars liked me, and when we parted, that awareness was confirmed: they showed their affection plainly and strongly. Deep was my gratification to find I truly had a place in their unsophisticated hearts: I promised them that never a week should pass in future without my visiting them and giving them an hour’s teaching in their school.

Mr. Rivers came up just as I had watched the classes — now numbering sixty girls — file out before me and had locked the door. I stood with the key in my hand, exchanging a few words of special farewell with some half-dozen of my best pupils: as decent, respectable, modest, and well-informed young women as could be found in the ranks of the British peasantry. And that is saying a great deal; for after all, the British peasantry are the best taught, best mannered, and most self-respecting of any in Europe: since those days I have seen paysannes and Bäuerinnen, and the best of them seemed to me ignorant, coarse, and besotted compared with my Morton girls.

“Do you consider you have earned your reward for a season of exertion?” asked Mr. Rivers, when they were gone. “Does not the awareness of having done some real good in your day and generation give you pleasure?”
“Undoubtedly.”
“And you have only toiled a few months! Would not a life devoted to the task of regenerating your race be well spent?”

“Yes,” I said; “but I could not go on like that forever. I want to enjoy my own faculties as well as to cultivate those of other people. I must enjoy them now; don’t call either my mind or body back to the school. I am out of it and ready for a full holiday.”
He looked grave. “What now? What sudden eagerness is this you are showing? What are you going to do?”
“To be active — as active as I can. And first I must beg you to set Hannah at liberty, and get someone else to wait on you.”
“Do you want her?”
“Yes — to go with me to Moor House. Diana and Mary will be home in a week, and I want to have everything in order for their arrival.”
“I understand. I thought you were about to fly off on some excursion. It is better this way: Hannah shall go with you.”
“Tell her to be ready by tomorrow then; and here is the schoolroom key. I will give you the key of my cottage in the morning.”

He took it. “You give it up very gleefully,” he said. “I don’t quite understand your light-heartedness, because I cannot tell what employment you propose to yourself as a substitute for the one you are relinquishing. What aim, what purpose, what ambition in life have you now?”

“My first aim will be to _clean down_ (do you grasp the full force of the expression?) — to _clean down_ Moor House from attic to cellar; my next to rub it up with beeswax, oil, and an endless number of cloths, till it glitters again; my third, to arrange every chair, table, bed, and carpet with mathematical precision; afterwards I shall come near to ruining you in coals and peat to keep up good fires in every room; and lastly, the two days before your sisters are expected will be devoted by Hannah and me to such a beating of eggs, sorting of currants, grating of spices, compounding of Christmas cakes, chopping up of materials for mince-pies, and solemnising of other culinary rites as words can convey but an inadequate notion of to the uninitiated like you. My purpose, in short, is to have all things in an absolutely perfect state of readiness for Diana and Mary before next Thursday; and my ambition is to give them a perfect welcome when they come.”
St. John smiled slightly — still he was dissatisfied.
“It is all very well for the present,” he said; “but seriously, I trust that when the first flush of excitement is over, you will look a little higher than domestic endearments and household joys.”
“The best things the world has!” I interrupted.
“No, Jane, no: this world is not the scene of fulfilment; do not try to make it so — nor of rest; do not turn slothful.”
“I mean, on the contrary, to be busy.”

“Jane, I excuse you for the present: I allow you two months’ grace for the full enjoyment of your new position, and for pleasing yourself with this late-found charm of relationship; but _then_, I hope you will begin to look beyond Moor House and Morton, and sisterly society, and the selfish calm and sensual comfort of civilised affluence. I hope your energies will then once more trouble you with their strength.”
I looked at him with surprise. “St. John,” I said, “I think you are almost wicked to talk this way. I am ready to be as content as a queen, and you try to stir me up to restlessness! To what end?”

“To the end of turning to good account the talents which God has entrusted to your keeping, and of which He will surely one day demand a strict account. Jane, I shall watch you closely and anxiously — I warn you of that. And try to restrain the disproportionate fervour with which you throw yourself into commonplace home pleasures. Don’t cling so tenaciously to ties of the flesh; save your constancy and ardour for an adequate cause; refrain from wasting them on trite, transient objects. Do you hear, Jane?”
“Yes — just as if you were speaking Greek. I feel I have adequate cause to be happy, and I _will_ be happy. Goodbye!”

Happy at Moor House I was, and hard I worked; and so did Hannah. She was charmed to see how jovial I could be amid the bustle of a house turned upside down — how I could brush, and dust, and clean, and cook. And really, after a day or two of confusion compounded upon confusion, it was delightful by degrees to summon order from the chaos we ourselves had made. I had previously taken a journey to S—— to purchase some new furniture, my cousins having given me _carte blanche_ to make what alterations I pleased, and a sum having been set aside for that purpose. The ordinary sitting-room and bedrooms I left much as they were: for I knew Diana and Mary would derive more pleasure from seeing again the old homely tables, chairs, and beds than from the spectacle of the smartest innovations. Still, some novelty was necessary to give to their return the piquancy with which I wished it to be invested. Dark handsome new carpets and curtains, an arrangement of some carefully selected antique ornaments in porcelain and bronze, new coverings and mirrors and dressing-cases for the toilet tables, served the purpose: they looked fresh without being glaring. A spare parlour and bedroom I refurnished entirely, with old mahogany and crimson upholstery: I laid canvas in the passage and carpets on the stairs. When all was finished, I thought Moor House as complete a model of bright, modest snugness within as it was, at this season, a specimen of wintry waste and desert dreariness without.

The eventful Thursday at length came. They were expected about dark, and before dusk fires were lit upstairs and below; the kitchen was in perfect trim; Hannah and I were dressed, and all was in readiness.

St. John arrived first. I had begged him to keep quite clear of the house till everything was arranged, and indeed the bare idea of the commotion — at once sordid and trivial — going on within its walls was enough to drive him to stay away. He found me in the kitchen, watching the progress of certain cakes for tea, then baking. Approaching the hearth, he asked, “If I was at last satisfied with housemaid’s work?” I answered by inviting him to accompany me on a general inspection of the result of my labours. With some difficulty, I got him to make the tour of the house. He just looked in at the doors I opened; and when he had wandered upstairs and downstairs, he said I must have gone through a great deal of fatigue and trouble to have effected such considerable changes in so short a time — but not a syllable did he utter to indicate pleasure in the improved appearance of his home.
This silence damped me. I thought perhaps the alterations had disturbed some old associations he valued. I asked whether this was the case — no doubt in a somewhat crestfallen tone.

“Not at all; he had, on the contrary, noticed that I had scrupulously respected every association: he feared, indeed, I must have bestowed more thought on the matter than it was worth. How many minutes, for instance, had I devoted to studying the arrangement of this very room? — By the way, could I tell him where such a book was?”
I showed him the volume on the shelf. He took it down, and withdrawing to his accustomed window recess, he began to read it.

Now, I did not like this, reader. St. John was a good man; but I began to feel he had spoken truth of himself when he said he was hard and cold. The humanities and amenities of life had no attraction for him — its peaceful enjoyments no charm. Literally, he lived only to aspire — after what was good and great, certainly; but still he would never rest, nor approve of others resting around him. As I looked at his lofty forehead, still and pale as a white stone — at his fine features fixed in study — I understood all at once that he would hardly make a good husband: that it would be a trying thing to be his wife. I understood, as by inspiration, the nature of his love for Miss Oliver; I agreed with him that it was only a love of the senses. I understood how he should despise himself for the feverish influence it exercised over him; how he should wish to stifle and destroy it; how he should mistrust its ever conducting permanently to his happiness or hers. I saw he was of the material from which nature hews her heroes — Christian and Pagan — her lawgivers, her statesmen, her conquerors: a steadfast bulwark for great interests to rest upon; but, at the fireside, too often a cold, cumbersome column, gloomy and out of place.

“This parlour is not his sphere,” I reflected. “The Himalayan ridge or Caffre bush, even the plague-cursed Guinea Coast swamp would suit him better. Well may he shun the calm of domestic life; it is not his element — there his faculties stagnate, they cannot develop or appear to advantage. It is in scenes of strife and danger — where courage is proved, and energy exercised, and fortitude tested — that he will speak and move, the leader and superior. A merry child would have the advantage of him on this hearth. He is right to choose a missionary’s career — I see it now.”

“They are coming! they are coming!” cried Hannah, throwing open the parlour door. At the same moment old Carlo barked joyfully. Out I ran. It was now dark, but a rumbling of wheels was audible. Hannah soon had a lantern lit. The carriage had stopped at the wicket; the driver opened the door: first one well-known figure, then another, stepped out. In a minute I had my face under their bonnets, in contact first with Mary’s soft cheek, then with Diana’s flowing curls. They laughed — kissed me — then Hannah; patted Carlo, who was half wild with delight; asked eagerly if all was well; and, being assured it was, hurried into the house.

They were stiff from their long and jolting drive from Whitcross, and chilled from the frosty night air; but their pleasant faces brightened in the cheerful firelight. While the driver and Hannah brought in the boxes, they asked for St. John. At that moment he came out from the parlour. They both threw their arms round his neck at once. He gave each one quiet kiss, said in a low tone a few words of welcome, stood a while to be talked to, and then, hinting that he supposed they would soon rejoin him in the parlour, withdrew there as to a place of refuge.

I had lit their candles to go upstairs, but Diana had first to give hospitable orders about the driver. This done, both followed me. They were delighted with the renovation and decoration of their rooms — with the new drapery, the fresh carpets, and the richly tinted china vases: they expressed their pleasure ungrudgingly. I had the pleasure of feeling that my arrangements met their wishes exactly, and that what I had done added a vivid charm to their joyous return home.

Sweet was that evening. My cousins, full of exhilaration, were so eloquent in narrative and comment that their fluency covered St. John’s silence. He was sincerely glad to see his sisters, but in their glow of warmth and flow of joy he could not share. The event of the day — that is, the return of Diana and Mary — pleased him; but the accompaniments of that event — the glad tumult, the garrulous glee of the reception — irked him: I saw he wished the calmer morrow had already come. At the very height of the night’s enjoyment, about an hour after tea, a rap was heard at the door. Hannah entered with word that “a poor lad was come, at this unlikely time, to fetch Mr. Rivers to see his mother, who was drawing away.”
“Where does she live, Hannah?”
“Right up at Whitcross Brow, almost four miles off, and moor and bog all the way.”
“Tell him I will go.”

“I’m sure, sir, you had better not. It’s the worst road to travel after dark that can be: there’s no track at all across the bog. And then it is such a bitter night — the keenest wind you ever felt. You had better send word, sir, that you will be there in the morning.”

But he was already in the passage, putting on his cloak; and without one objection, one murmur, he departed. It was then nine o’clock: he did not return till midnight. Starved and tired enough he was, but he looked happier than when he had set out. He had performed an act of duty, made an exertion, felt his own strength to do and deny, and was on better terms with himself.

I am afraid the whole of the following week tried his patience. It was Christmas week: we took up no settled employment, but spent it in a sort of merry domestic dissipation. The air of the moors, the freedom of home, the dawn of prosperity, acted on Diana and Mary’s spirits like some life-giving elixir: they were gay from morning till noon, and from noon till night. They could always talk; and their conversation, witty, pithy, and original, had such charms for me that I preferred listening to it and sharing in it to doing anything else. St. John did not rebuke our vivacity, but he escaped from it: he was seldom in the house; his parish was large, the population scattered, and he found daily business in visiting the sick and poor in its different districts.
One morning at breakfast, Diana, after looking a little pensive for some minutes, asked him “if his plans were still unchanged.”
“Unchanged and unchangeable,” was the reply. And he went on to inform us that his departure from England was now definitively fixed for the next year.

“And Rosamond Oliver?” suggested Mary, the words seeming to escape her lips involuntarily: for no sooner had she uttered them than she made a gesture as if wishing to take them back. St. John had a book in his hand — it was his unsocial custom to read at meals — he closed it and looked up.

“Rosamond Oliver,” he said, “is about to be married to Mr. Granby, one of the best-connected and most estimable residents in S——, grandson and heir to Sir Frederic Granby. I had the news from her father yesterday.”
His sisters looked at each other and at me; we all three looked at him: he was serene as glass.
“The match must have been got up hastily,” said Diana. “They cannot have known each other long.”

“But two months: they met in October at the county ball at S——. But where there are no obstacles to a union, as in the present case, where the connection is in every way desirable, delays are unnecessary: they will be married as soon as S—— Place, which Sir Frederic gives up to them, can be refitted for their reception.”

The first time I found St. John alone after this communication, I felt tempted to ask if the event distressed him; but he seemed so little to need sympathy that, far from venturing to offer him more, I felt some shame at the recollection of what I had already hazarded. Besides, I was out of practice in talking to him: his reserve was again frozen over, and my frankness was congealed beneath it. He had not kept his promise of treating me like his sisters; he continually made little chilling distinctions between us, which did not at all tend to develop cordiality. In short, now that I was acknowledged his kinswoman, and lived under the same roof with him, I felt the distance between us to be far greater than when he had known me only as the village schoolmistress. When I remembered how far I had once been admitted to his confidence, I could hardly understand his present coldness.
Such being the case, I felt not a little surprised when he raised his head suddenly from the desk over which he was stooping, and said —
“You see, Jane, the battle is fought and the victory won.”
Startled at being addressed like this, I did not immediately reply. After a moment’s hesitation I answered —
“But are you sure you are not in the position of those conquerors whose triumphs have cost them too dear? Would not another such victory ruin you?”

“I think not; and if I were, it does not much matter; I shall never be called upon to fight such another. The outcome of the conflict is decisive: my way is now clear; I thank God for it!” So saying, he returned to his papers and his silence.

As our mutual happiness (_i.e._, Diana’s, Mary’s, and mine) settled into a quieter character, and we resumed our usual habits and regular studies, St. John stayed more at home: he sat with us in the same room, sometimes for hours together. While Mary drew, Diana pursued a course of encyclopaedic reading she had (to my awe and amazement) undertaken, and I toiled away at German, he pondered a mystic lore of his own: that of some Eastern tongue, the acquisition of which he thought necessary to his plans.

Thus occupied, he appeared, sitting in his own recess, quiet and absorbed enough; but that blue eye of his had a habit of leaving the outlandish-looking grammar and wandering over — and sometimes fixing upon — us, his fellow-students, with a curious intensity of observation. If caught, it would be instantly withdrawn; yet every now and then it returned searchingly to our table. I wondered what it meant. I wondered, too, at the punctual satisfaction he never failed to show on an occasion that seemed to me of small moment — namely, my weekly visit to Morton school; and still more was I puzzled when, if the day was unfavourable — if there was snow, rain, or high wind — and his sisters urged me not to go, he would invariably make light of their concern and encourage me to accomplish the task regardless of the elements.

“Jane is not such a weakling as you would make her,” he would say. “She can bear a mountain blast, or a shower, or a few flakes of snow, as well as any of us. Her constitution is both sound and elastic — better calculated to endure variations of climate than many more robust.”

And when I returned, sometimes quite tired, and not a little weather-beaten, I never dared complain, because I saw that to murmur would be to vex him: on all occasions fortitude pleased him; the opposite was a special annoyance.

One afternoon, however, I got leave to stay at home, because I really had a cold. His sisters had gone to Morton in my stead. I sat reading Schiller; he, deciphering his crabbed Oriental scrolls. As I exchanged a translation for an exercise, I happened to glance his way: there I found myself under the influence of the ever-watchful blue eye. How long it had been searching me through and through, and over and over, I cannot tell: so keen it was, and yet so cold, that for the moment I felt superstitious — as if I were sitting in the room with something uncanny.
“Jane, what are you doing?”
“Learning German.”
“I want you to give up German and learn Hindostanee.”
“You are not serious?”
“So serious that I must have it so: and I will tell you why.”

He then went on to explain that Hindostanee was the language he was himself studying at present; that as he advanced, he was apt to forget the beginning; that it would help him greatly to have a pupil with whom he might go over the elements again and again, and so fix them thoroughly in his mind; that his choice had hovered for some time between me and his sisters; but that he had settled on me because he saw I could sit at a task the longest of the three. Would I do him this favour? I should not, perhaps, have to make the sacrifice long, as it now wanted barely three months to his departure.

St. John was not a man to be lightly refused: you felt that every impression made on him, either for pain or pleasure, was deeply engraved and permanent. I consented. When Diana and Mary returned, the former found her pupil transferred from her to her brother: she laughed, and both she and Mary agreed that St. John should never have persuaded them to such a step. He answered quietly —
“I know it.”

I found him a very patient, very forbearing, and yet an exacting master: he expected me to do a great deal; and when I fulfilled his expectations, he, in his own way, fully showed his approval. By degrees, he gained a certain influence over me that took away my liberty of mind: his praise and notice were more restraining than his indifference. I could no longer talk or laugh freely when he was by, because a tiresomely insistent instinct reminded me that vivacity (at least in me) was distasteful to him. I was so fully aware that only serious moods and occupations were acceptable, that in his presence every effort to sustain or follow any other became vain: I fell under a freezing spell. When he said “go,” I went; “come,” I came; “do this,” I did it. But I did not love my servitude: I wished, many a time, he had continued to neglect me.

One evening when, at bedtime, his sisters and I stood round him, bidding him good-night, he kissed each of them, as was his custom; and, as was equally his custom, he gave me his hand. Diana, who happened to be in a playful humour (_she_ was not painfully controlled by his will, for hers, in another way, was as strong), exclaimed —
“St. John! you used to call Jane your third sister, but you don’t treat her as such: you should kiss her too.”

She pushed me towards him. I thought Diana very provoking, and felt uncomfortably embarrassed; and while I was thus thinking and feeling, St. John bent his head; his Greek face was brought to a level with mine, his eyes questioned mine piercingly — he kissed me. There are no such things as marble kisses or ice kisses, or I should say my ecclesiastical cousin’s salute belonged to one of these classes; but there may be experimental kisses, and his was an experimental kiss. When given, he looked at me to see the result; it was not striking: I am sure I did not blush; perhaps I might have turned a little pale, for I felt as if this kiss were a seal affixed to my fetters. He never omitted the ceremony afterwards, and the gravity and calm with which I underwent it seemed to invest it for him with a certain charm.

As for me, I daily wished more to please him; but to do so, I felt daily more and more that I must disown half my nature, stifle half my faculties, wrest my tastes from their original bent, force myself to take up pursuits for which I had no natural vocation. He wanted to train me to an elevation I could never reach; it tormented me hourly to aspire to the standard he held up. The thing was as impossible as to reshape my irregular features to his correct and classic pattern, to give to my changeable green eyes the sea-blue tint and solemn lustre of his own.

Not his ascendancy alone, however, held me in thrall at present. Of late it had been easy enough for me to look sad: a cankering evil sat at my heart and drained my happiness at its source — the evil of suspense.

Perhaps you think I had forgotten Mr. Rochester, reader, amid these changes of place and fortune. Not for a moment. His idea was still with me, because it was not a vapour that sunshine could disperse, nor a figure traced in sand that storms could wash away; it was a name graven on a tablet, fated to last as long as the marble it was inscribed on. The craving to know what had become of him followed me everywhere; when I was at Morton, I re-entered my cottage every evening to think of that; and now at Moor House, I sought my bedroom each night to brood over it.

In the course of my necessary correspondence with Mr. Briggs about the will, I had asked if he knew anything of Mr. Rochester’s present residence and state of health; but, as St. John had guessed, he was quite ignorant of everything concerning him. I then wrote to Mrs. Fairfax, begging her for information on the subject. I had calculated with certainty on this step answering my purpose: I felt sure it would draw an early answer. I was astonished when a fortnight passed without a reply; but when two months wore away, and day after day the post arrived and brought nothing for me, I fell prey to the keenest anxiety.

I wrote again: there was a chance that my first letter had gone astray. Renewed hope followed renewed effort: it shone like the former for some weeks, then, like it, faded and flickered: not a line, not a word reached me. When half a year had been wasted in vain expectation, my hope died out, and then I felt dark indeed.

A fine spring shone round me, which I could not enjoy. Summer approached; Diana tried to cheer me: she said I looked ill, and wished to accompany me to the seaside. This St. John opposed; he said I did not need dissipation, I needed employment; my present life was too purposeless, I needed an aim; and, I suppose, by way of supplying deficiencies, he prolonged still further my lessons in Hindostanee, and grew more urgent in demanding their completion: and I, like a fool, never thought of resisting him — I could not resist him.

One day I had come to my studies in lower spirits than usual; the ebb was caused by a sharply felt disappointment. Hannah had told me in the morning there was a letter for me, and when I went down to take it, almost certain that the long-looked-for tidings were granted me at last, I found only an unimportant note from Mr. Briggs on business. The bitter check had wrung some tears from me; and now, as I sat poring over the crabbed characters and flourishing tropes of an Indian scribe, my eyes filled again.

St. John called me to his side to read; in attempting to do this my voice failed me: words were lost in sobs. He and I were the only occupants of the parlour: Diana was practising her music in the drawing-room, Mary was gardening — it was a very fine May day, clear, sunny, and breezy. My companion expressed no surprise at this emotion, nor did he question me as to its cause; he only said —

“We will wait a few minutes, Jane, till you are more composed.” And while I smothered the fit as quickly as I could, he sat calm and patient, leaning on his desk, and looking like a physician watching with the eye of science an expected and fully understood crisis in a patient’s illness. Having stifled my sobs, wiped my eyes, and muttered something about not being very well that morning, I resumed my task and succeeded in completing it. St. John put away my books and his, locked his desk, and said —
“Now, Jane, you shall take a walk; and with me.”
“I will call Diana and Mary.”
“No; I want only one companion this morning, and that must be you. Put on your things; go out by the kitchen door: take the road towards the head of Marsh Glen. I will join you in a moment.”

I know no middle ground: I never in my life have known any middle ground in my dealings with positive, hard characters opposed to my own, between absolute submission and determined revolt. I have always faithfully kept to the one, up to the very moment of bursting, sometimes with volcanic vehemence, into the other; and as neither present circumstances warranted mutiny, nor my present mood inclined me to it, I observed careful obedience to St. John’s directions; and in ten minutes I was treading the wild track of the glen, side by side with him.

The breeze was from the west: it came over the hills, sweet with scents of heath and rush; the sky was of stainless blue; the stream descending the ravine, swelled with past spring rains, poured along plentiful and clear, catching golden gleams from the sun and sapphire tints from the firmament. As we advanced and left the track, we trod a soft turf, mossy fine and emerald green, minutely enamelled with a tiny white flower, and spangled with a star-like yellow blossom: the hills, meanwhile, shut us quite in; for the glen, towards its head, wound into their very core.

“Let us rest here,” said St. John, as we reached the first stragglers of a battalion of rocks, guarding a sort of pass, beyond which the stream rushed down in a waterfall; and where, still a little farther, the mountain shook off turf and flower, and had only heath for raiment and crag for gem — where it exaggerated the wild to the savage, and exchanged the fresh for the frowning — where it guarded the forlorn hope of solitude, and a last refuge for silence.

I took a seat: St. John stood near me. He looked up the pass and down the hollow; his glance wandered away with the stream, and returned to traverse the unclouded heaven which coloured it: he removed his hat, let the breeze stir his hair and kiss his brow. He seemed in communion with the genius of the haunt: with his eye he bade farewell to something.
“And I shall see it again,” he said aloud, “in dreams when I sleep by the Ganges; and again in a more remote hour — when another slumber overcomes me — on the shore of a darker stream!”

Strange words of a strange love! An austere patriot’s passion for his fatherland! He sat down; for half an hour we never spoke; neither he to me nor I to him. When that interval had passed, he began again —
“Jane, I go in six weeks; I have taken my berth in an East Indiaman which sails on the 20th of June.”
“God will protect you; for you have undertaken His work,” I answered.

“Yes,” he said, “there is my glory and joy. I am the servant of an infallible Master. I am not going out under human guidance, subject to the defective laws and erring control of my feeble fellow-worms: my king, my lawgiver, my captain, is the All-perfect. It seems strange to me that all round me do not burn to enlist under the same banner — to join in the same enterprise.”
“All have not your powers, and it would be folly for the feeble to wish to march with the strong.”
“I do not speak to the feeble, or think of them: I address only such as are worthy of the work, and competent to accomplish it.”
“Those are few in number, and difficult to find.”

“You say truly; but when found, it is right to stir them up — to urge and exhort them to the effort — to show them what their gifts are, and why they were given — to speak Heaven’s message in their ear — to offer them, direct from God, a place in the ranks of His chosen.”
“If they are truly qualified for the task, will not their own hearts be the first to inform them of it?”
I felt as if an awful charm was forming round me and gathering over me: I trembled to hear some fatal word spoken which would at once declare and rivet the spell.
“And what does _your_ heart say?” demanded St. John.
“My heart is mute — my heart is mute,” I answered, struck and thrilled.
“Then I must speak for it,” continued the deep, relentless voice. “Jane, come with me to India: come as my helpmeet and fellow-labourer.”

The glen and sky spun round: the hills heaved! It was as if I had heard a summons from Heaven — as if a visionary messenger, like him of Macedonia, had called out, “Come over and help us!” But I was no apostle — I could not see the herald — I could not receive his call.
“Oh, St. John!” I cried, “have some mercy!”
I appealed to one who, in the discharge of what he believed his duty, knew neither mercy nor remorse. He continued —

“God and nature intended you for a missionary’s wife. It is not personal, but mental endowments they have given you: you are formed for labour, not for love. A missionary’s wife you must — shall be. You shall be mine: I claim you — not for my pleasure, but for my Sovereign’s service.”
“I am not fit for it: I have no vocation,” I said.

He had counted on these first objections: he was not irritated by them. Indeed, as he leaned back against the crag behind him, folded his arms on his chest, and fixed his countenance, I saw he was prepared for a long and trying opposition, and had taken in a stock of patience to last him to its close — resolved, however, that the close should be conquest for him.

“Humility, Jane,” he said, “is the groundwork of Christian virtues: you say rightly that you are not fit for the work. Who is fit for it? Or who, that was ever truly called, believed himself worthy of the summons? I, for instance, am but dust and ashes. With St. Paul, I acknowledge myself the chief of sinners; but I do not allow this sense of my personal vileness to daunt me. I know my Leader: that He is just as well as mighty; and while He has chosen a feeble instrument to perform a great task, He will, from the boundless stores of His providence, supply the inadequacy of the means to the end. Think like me, Jane — trust like me. It is the Rock of Ages I ask you to lean on: do not doubt but it will bear the weight of your human weakness.”
“I do not understand a missionary life: I have never studied missionary labours.”

“There I, humble as I am, can give you the aid you need: I can set you your task from hour to hour; stand by you always; help you from moment to moment. This I could do in the beginning: soon (for I know your powers) you would be as strong and apt as myself, and would not require my help.”

“But my powers — where are they for this undertaking? I do not feel them. Nothing speaks or stirs in me while you talk. I am aware of no light kindling — no life quickening — no voice counselling or cheering. Oh, I wish I could make you see how much my mind is at this moment like a rayless dungeon, with one shrinking fear fettered in its depths — the fear of being persuaded by you to attempt what I cannot accomplish!”

“I have an answer for you — hear it. I have watched you ever since we first met: I have made you my study for ten months. I have tested you in that time by various trials: and what have I seen and drawn out? In the village school I found that you could perform well, punctually, uprightly, labour uncongenial to your habits and inclinations; I saw you could perform it with capability and tact: you could win while you controlled. In the calm with which you learnt you had suddenly become rich, I read a mind clear of the vice of Demas: lucre had no undue power over you. In the resolute readiness with which you cut your wealth into four shares, keeping but one to yourself, and giving the three others to the claim of abstract justice, I recognised a soul that revelled in the flame and excitement of sacrifice. In the tractability with which, at my wish, you forsook a study in which you were interested, and adopted another because it interested me; in the untiring diligence with which you have since persevered in it — in the unflagging energy and unshaken temper with which you have met its difficulties — I acknowledge the complement of the qualities I seek. Jane, you are docile, diligent, disinterested, faithful, constant, and courageous; very gentle, and very heroic: cease to mistrust yourself — I can trust you unreservedly. As a conductress of Indian schools, and a helper amongst Indian women, your assistance will be invaluable to me.”

My iron shroud contracted round me; persuasion advanced with slow, sure step. Shut my eyes as I would, these last words of his succeeded in making the way, which had seemed blocked up, comparatively clear. My work, which had seemed so vague, so hopelessly diffuse, condensed itself as he proceeded, and took on a definite form under his shaping hand. He waited for an answer. I demanded a quarter of an hour to think before I again hazarded a reply.
“Very willingly,” he rejoined; and rising, he strode a little distance up the pass, threw himself down on a swell of heath, and there lay still.
He threw himself down on a swell of heath, and there lay still.

“I _can_ do what he wants me to do: I am forced to see and acknowledge that,” I meditated — “that is, if life be spared me. But I feel mine is not the existence to be long protracted under an Indian sun. What then? He does not care for that: when my time came to die, he would resign me, in all serenity and sanctity, to the God who gave me. The case is very plain before me. In leaving England, I should leave a loved but empty land — Mr. Rochester is not there; and if he were, what is, what can that ever be to me? My business is to live without him now: nothing so absurd, so weak as to drag on from day to day, as if I were waiting for some impossible change in circumstances which might reunite me to him. Of course (as St. John once said) I must seek another interest in life to replace the one lost: is not the occupation he now offers me truly the most glorious man can adopt or God assign? Is it not, by its noble cares and sublime results, the one best calculated to fill the void left by uprooted affections and demolished hopes? I believe I must say, Yes — and yet I shudder. Alas! If I join St. John, I abandon half myself: if I go to India, I go to premature death. And how will the interval between leaving England for India, and India for the grave, be filled? Oh, I know well! That, too, is very clear to my vision. By straining to satisfy St. John till my sinews ache, I _shall_ satisfy him — to the finest central point and farthest outward circle of his expectations. If I _do_ go with him — if I _do_ make the sacrifice he urges, I will make it absolutely: I will throw all on the altar — heart, vitals, the entire victim. He will never love me; but he shall approve me; I will show him energies he has not yet seen, resources he has never suspected. Yes, I can work as hard as he can, and with as little grudging.

“Consent, then, to his demand is possible: but for one item — one dreadful item. It is — that he asks me to be his wife, and has no more of a husband’s heart for me than that frowning giant of a rock, down which the stream is foaming in yonder gorge. He prizes me as a soldier would a good weapon; and that is all. Unmarried to him, this would never grieve me; but can I let him complete his calculations — coolly put into practice his plans — go through the wedding ceremony? Can I receive from him the bridal ring, endure all the forms of love (which I doubt not he would scrupulously observe) and know that the spirit was quite absent? Can I bear the awareness that every endearment he bestows is a sacrifice made on principle? No: such a martyrdom would be monstrous. I will never undergo it. As his sister, I might accompany him — not as his wife: I will tell him so.”
I looked towards the knoll: there he lay, still as a fallen column; his face turned to me: his eye beaming watchful and keen. He started to his feet and approached me.
“I am ready to go to India, if I may go free.”
“Your answer requires a commentary,” he said; “it is not clear.”
“You have until now been my adopted brother — I, your adopted sister: let us continue as such: you and I had better not marry.”

He shook his head. “Adopted fraternity will not do in this case. If you were my real sister it would be different: I should take you, and seek no wife. But as it is, either our union must be consecrated and sealed by marriage, or it cannot exist: practical obstacles oppose themselves to any other plan. Do you not see it, Jane? Consider a moment — your strong sense will guide you.”

I did consider; and still my sense, such as it was, directed me only to the fact that we did not love each other as man and wife should: and therefore it inferred we ought not to marry. I said so. “St. John,” I returned, “I regard you as a brother — you, me as a sister: so let us continue.”
“We cannot — we cannot,” he answered, with short, sharp determination: “it would not do. You have said you will go with me to India: remember — you have said that.”
“Conditionally.”

“Well — well. To the main point — the departure with me from England, the co-operation with me in my future labours — you do not object. You have already as good as put your hand to the plough: you are too consistent to withdraw it. You have but one end to keep in view — how the work you have undertaken can best be done. Simplify your complicated interests, feelings, thoughts, wishes, aims; merge all considerations in one purpose: that of fulfilling with effect — with power — the mission of your great Master. To do so, you must have a coadjutor: not a brother — that is a loose tie — but a husband. I, too, do not want a sister: a sister might any day be taken from me. I want a wife: the sole helpmeet I can influence effectively in life, and retain absolutely till death.”
I shuddered as he spoke: I felt his influence in my marrow — his hold on my limbs.
“Seek one elsewhere than in me, St. John: seek one fitted to you.”

“One fitted to my purpose, you mean — fitted to my vocation. Again I tell you it is not the insignificant private individual — the mere man, with the man’s selfish senses — I wish to mate: it is the missionary.”
“And I will give the missionary my energies — it is all he wants — but not myself: that would be only adding the husk and shell to the kernel. For them he has no use: I retain them.”

“You cannot — you ought not. Do you think God will be satisfied with half an offering? Will He accept a mutilated sacrifice? It is the cause of God I advocate: it is under His standard I enlist you. I cannot accept on His behalf a divided allegiance: it must be entire.”
“Oh! I will give my heart to God,” I said. “_You_ do not want it.”

I will not swear, reader, that there was not something of repressed sarcasm both in the tone in which I uttered this sentence, and in the feeling that accompanied it. I had silently feared St. John till now, because I had not understood him. He had held me in awe, because he had held me in doubt. How much of him was saint, how much mortal, I could not tell before: but revelations were being made in this conference: the analysis of his nature was proceeding before my eyes. I saw his fallibilities: I understood them. I understood that, sitting there where I did, on the bank of heath, and with that handsome form before me, I sat at the feet of a man, erring as I. The veil fell from his hardness and despotism. Having felt in him the presence of these qualities, I felt his imperfection and took courage. I was with an equal — one with whom I might argue — one whom, if I saw good, I might resist.

He was silent after I had uttered the last sentence, and I presently risked an upward glance at his face. His eye, bent on me, expressed at once stern surprise and keen inquiry. “Is she sarcastic, and sarcastic to _me!_” it seemed to say. “What does this signify?”

“Do not let us forget that this is a solemn matter,” he said at length; “one of which we may neither think nor talk lightly without sin. I trust, Jane, you are in earnest when you say you will give your heart to God: it is all I want. Once wrench your heart from man, and fix it on your Maker, the advancement of that Maker’s spiritual kingdom on earth will be your chief delight and endeavour; you will be ready to do at once whatever furthers that end. You will see what impetus would be given to your efforts and mine by our physical and mental union in marriage: the only union that gives a character of permanent conformity to the destinies and designs of human beings; and, passing over all minor caprices — all trivial difficulties and delicacies of feeling — all scruple about the degree, kind, strength, or tenderness of mere personal inclination — you will hasten to enter into that union at once.”

“Shall I?” I said briefly; and I looked at his features, beautiful in their harmony, but strangely formidable in their still severity; at his brow, commanding but not open; at his eyes, bright and deep and searching, but never soft; at his tall imposing figure; and fancied myself in idea _his wife_. Oh! it would never do! As his curate, his comrade, all would be right: I would cross oceans with him in that capacity; toil under Eastern suns, in Asian deserts with him in that office; admire and emulate his courage and devotion and vigour; accommodate quietly to his masterhood; smile undisturbed at his ineradicable ambition; distinguish the Christian from the man: profoundly esteem the one, and freely forgive the other. I should suffer often, no doubt, attached to him only in this capacity: my body would be under rather a stringent yoke, but my heart and mind would be free. I should still have my unblighted self to turn to: my natural unenslaved feelings with which to commune in moments of loneliness. There would be recesses in my mind which would be only mine, to which he never came, and sentiments growing there fresh and sheltered which his austerity could never blight, nor his measured warrior-march trample down: but as his wife — at his side always, and always restrained, and always checked — forced to keep the fire of my nature continually low, to compel it to burn inwardly and never utter a cry, though the imprisoned flame consumed vital after vital — _this_ would be unendurable.
“St. John!” I exclaimed, when I had got so far in my meditation.
“Well?” he answered icily.
“I repeat I freely consent to go with you as your fellow-missionary, but not as your wife; I cannot marry you and become part of you.”

“A part of me you must become,” he answered steadily; “otherwise the whole bargain is void. How can I, a man not yet thirty, take out with me to India a girl of nineteen, unless she be married to me? How can we be forever together — sometimes in solitudes, sometimes amidst savage tribes — and unwed?”
“Very well,” I said shortly; “under the circumstances, quite as well as if I were either your real sister, or a man and a clergyman like yourself.”

“It is known that you are not my sister; I cannot introduce you as such: to attempt it would be to fasten harmful suspicions on us both. And for the rest, though you have a man’s vigorous brain, you have a woman’s heart and — it would not do.”

“It would do,” I affirmed with some disdain, “perfectly well. I have a woman’s heart, but not where you are concerned; for you I have only a comrade’s constancy; a fellow-soldier’s frankness, fidelity, fraternity, if you like; a neophyte’s respect and submission to his hierophant: nothing more — don’t fear.”

“It is what I want,” he said, speaking to himself; “it is just what I want. And there are obstacles in the way: they must be hewn down. Jane, you would not repent marrying me — be certain of that; we _must_ be married. I repeat it: there is no other way; and undoubtedly enough of love would follow upon marriage to render the union right even in your eyes.”

“I scorn your idea of love,” I could not help saying, as I rose up and stood before him, leaning my back against the rock. “I scorn the counterfeit sentiment you offer: yes, St. John, and I scorn you when you offer it.”
He looked at me fixedly, compressing his well-cut lips while he did so. Whether he was angered or surprised, or what, it was not easy to tell: he could command his countenance thoroughly.
“I scarcely expected to hear that expression from you,” he said: “I think I have done and said nothing to deserve scorn.”
I was touched by his gentle tone, and overawed by his high, calm mien.

“Forgive me the words, St. John; but it is your own fault that I have been roused to speak so unguardedly. You have introduced a topic on which our natures are at variance — a topic we should never discuss: the very name of love is an apple of discord between us. If the reality were required, what should we do? How should we feel? My dear cousin, abandon your scheme of marriage — forget it.”

“No,” he said; “it is a long-cherished scheme, and the only one which can secure my great end: but I shall urge you no further at present. Tomorrow, I leave home for Cambridge: I have many friends there to whom I should wish to say farewell. I shall be absent a fortnight — take that space of time to consider my offer: and do not forget that if you reject it, it is not me you deny, but God. Through my means, He opens to you a noble career; as my wife only can you enter upon it. Refuse to be my wife, and you limit yourself forever to a track of selfish ease and barren obscurity. Tremble lest in that case you should be numbered with those who have denied the faith, and are worse than infidels!”
He had done. Turning from me, he once more
“Looked to river, looked to hill.”

But this time his feelings were all pent in his heart: I was not worthy to hear them uttered. As I walked by his side homeward, I read well in his iron silence all he felt towards me: the disappointment of an austere and despotic nature, which has met resistance where it expected submission — the disapproval of a cool, inflexible judgment, which has detected in another feelings and views in which it has no power to sympathise: in short, as a man, he would have wished to coerce me into obedience: it was only as a sincere Christian that he bore so patiently with my perversity, and allowed so long a space for reflection and repentance.
