That night, after he had kissed his sisters, he thought proper to forget even to shake hands with me, but left the room in silence. I — who, though I had no love, had much friendship for him — was hurt by the marked omission: so much hurt that tears started to my eyes.
“I see you and St. John have been quarrelling, Jane,” said Diana, “during your walk on the moor. But go after him; he is now lingering in the passage expecting you — he will make it up.”
I have not much pride under such circumstances: I would always rather be happy than dignified; and I ran after him — he stood at the foot of the stairs.
“Good-night, St. John,” I said.
“Good-night, Jane,” he replied calmly.
“Then shake hands,” I added.

What a cold, loose touch he impressed on my fingers! He was deeply displeased by what had occurred that day; cordiality would not warm him, nor tears move him. No happy reconciliation was to be had with him — no cheering smile or generous word: but still the Christian was patient and placid; and when I asked him if he forgave me, he answered that he was not in the habit of cherishing the remembrance of vexation; that he had nothing to forgive, not having been offended.
And with that answer he left me. I would much rather he had knocked me down.

chapters.title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: He didn't leave for Cambridge the next day as he'd said he would. He delayed his departure a full week. During that time he made me feel what severe punishment a good yet stern, conscientious yet unforgiving man can inflict on someone who has offended him. Without a single hostile act, without one reproachful word, he managed to impress on me constantly that I had been cast out of his favor.

Not that St. John harbored any spirit of unchristian revenge—not that he would have harmed a hair on my head if he could. By both nature and principle, he was above petty vengeance. He had forgiven me for saying I scorned him and his love. But he had not forgotten the words. As long as he and I both lived, he never would forget them. I saw by his look, whenever he turned to me, that they hung permanently in the air between us. Whenever I spoke, they sounded in my voice. They colored my every word and action.

He didn't stop talking to me. He even called me each morning to join him at his desk as usual. But I fear the imperfect human inside him took a pleasure the pure Christian did not share—pleasure in showing how skillfully he could, while acting and speaking exactly as always, drain every drop of warmth and interest from his words and manner. To me, he had become nothing more than a marble guardian angel. He was still protecting me, still watching over me, but the kindness had turned to ice.

All this was torture—refined, lingering torture. It kept up a slow fire of frustration and a trembling grief that wore me down completely. I felt how—if I were his wife—this good man, pure as a deep, sunless spring, could slowly kill me without drawing a single drop of blood, and without staining his crystal conscience with even the faintest mark of crime. I felt this especially when I tried to make peace. No compassion met mine. He felt no suffering in return. He hadn't given himself to me or tried to win me. He stood apart from me as if we were different species. He was quietly confident that he was right, and I was wrong. This conviction showed clearly in everything he said and did.

The night before he was to leave, I happened to see him walking in the garden at sunset. Remembering that this man, distant as he now was, had once saved my life—and that we were family—I was moved to make one last attempt at friendship. I went out and approached him at the little gate. I spoke directly.
"St. John, I'm unhappy because you're still angry with me. Let us be friends."
"I hope we are friends," came the unmoved reply. He continued watching the rising moon.
"No, St. John, we are not friends as we were. You know that."
"Aren't we? That's wrong. For my part, I wish you no ill and all good."
"I believe you, St. John. I'm sure you're incapable of wishing anyone ill. But as your relative, I want something more than the general goodwill you extend to strangers."
"Of course," he said. "Your wish is reasonable. And I'm far from considering you a stranger."

This, spoken in a cool, even tone, was both humiliating and baffling. If I'd listened to my pride, I would have walked away at once. But something worked in me more powerfully than pride. I deeply respected my cousin's talent and principles. His friendship meant a great deal to me. Losing it was hard to bear. I wouldn't give up the attempt to regain it so easily.
"Must we part this way, St. John? When you go to India, will you leave me like this—without a kinder word than any you've yet spoken?"
He turned from the moon and faced me.
"When I go to India, Jane, will I leave you? What! Are you not going to India?"
"You said I couldn't unless I married you."
"And you will not marry me? You hold to that decision?"

Reader, do you know, as I do, the terror that cold people can put into the ice of their questions? How much of an avalanche is in their anger? How much of a frozen sea breaking apart is in their displeasure?
"No. St. John, I will not marry you. I stand by my decision."
The avalanche had shaken and shifted slightly forward. But it hadn't crashed down yet.
"Once more, why this refusal?" he asked.
"Before," I answered, "because you didn't love me. Now, because you almost hate me. If I married you, you would kill me. You are killing me now."
His lips and cheeks turned white—deathly white.

"I should kill you—I am killing you? Those words should not be used. They are violent, unfeminine, and untrue. They reveal an unfortunate state of mind. They deserve severe correction. They would seem inexcusable, except that it is man's duty to forgive his fellow even seventy-seven times over."
I had done it now. In trying to erase the mark of my earlier offense from his mind, I had stamped a new one—far deeper. I had burned it in.
"Now you will truly hate me," I said. "It's useless to try to make peace. I've made an eternal enemy of you."
These words inflicted a fresh wound—worse because they touched on the truth. That bloodless lip trembled briefly. I knew the steel-hard anger I had sharpened. My heart ached.
"You completely misread my words," I said, seizing his hand. "I had no intention of hurting you—truly, I didn't."
He smiled bitterly and pulled his hand firmly away. "And now I suppose you're taking back your promise to go to India altogether?" he said after a long pause.
"Yes, I'll still go—as your assistant," I answered.

A very long silence followed. What struggle between nature and duty took place in him during that pause, I cannot say. Only strange gleams flickered in his eyes, and dark shadows crossed his face. At last he spoke.

"I've already explained why a single woman of your age cannot accompany a single man of mine abroad. I explained it in terms that, I would have thought, would prevent you from ever mentioning the plan again. That you've done so, I regret—for your sake."

I cut in. Any clear reproach actually gave me courage. "Stick to common sense, St. John—you're drifting into nonsense. You pretend to be shocked by what I've said. You're not really shocked. With your intelligence, you can't be so dense or so vain as to misunderstand me. I say again: I will be your assistant, if you like, but never your wife."
Again he turned deathly pale. But, as before, he controlled his emotions perfectly. He answered firmly but calmly—

"A female assistant who is not my wife would never work. So it seems you cannot go with me. But if you're sincere in your offer, I will, while in town, speak to a married missionary whose wife needs help. Your own fortune will make you independent of the Society's aid. And so you may still be spared the dishonor of breaking your promise and abandoning the group you agreed to join."
Now, I had never, as the reader knows, made any formal promise or entered into any commitment. This language was far too harsh and far too dictatorial for the situation. I replied—

"There is no dishonor, no broken promise, no abandonment here. I am under no obligation whatsoever to go to India—especially with strangers. With you I would have risked a great deal, because I admire you, trust you, and love you as a sister. But I'm convinced that wherever I went, and with whomever, I would not survive long in that climate."
"Ah! You're afraid of yourself," he said, curling his lip.

"I am. God did not give me my life to throw away. To do as you wish would be nearly the same as suicide. And besides, before I make any final decision about leaving England, I need to know for certain whether I can't do more good by staying than by going."
"What do you mean?"
"It would be pointless to explain. But there's a question that has tormented me for a long time. I can't go anywhere until it's resolved."

"I know where your heart turns and what it clings to. The attachment you cherish is sinful and unsanctioned. You should have destroyed it long ago. Now you should be ashamed even to mention it. You're thinking of Mr. Rochester."
It was true. My silence confessed it.
"Are you going to look for Mr. Rochester?"
"I must find out what has become of him."

"Then it remains for me," he said, "to remember you in my prayers and to earnestly ask God that you may not become lost. I had thought I recognized in you one of the chosen. But God sees differently from man. His will be done—"
He opened the gate, passed through, and walked away down the glen. He was soon out of sight.
Back in the parlour, I found Diana standing at the window, looking thoughtful. Diana was much taller than me. She put her hand on my shoulder and, bending down, studied my face.

"Jane," she said, "you're always pale and upset now. I'm sure something is wrong. Tell me what's going on between you and St. John. I've been watching you from the window for half an hour. Forgive me for spying, but for a long time I've had a feeling—I hardly know what. St. John is a strange person—"
She paused. I didn't speak. Soon she continued—
"My brother has special views of some kind about you, I'm sure. He has singled you out with an attention and interest he's never shown anyone else. To what end? I wish he loved you—does he, Jane?"
I pressed her cool hand to my hot forehead. "No, Diana. Not one bit."
"Then why does he follow you with his eyes, and get you alone with him so often, and keep you constantly at his side? Mary and I both decided he wanted to marry you."
"He does—he has asked me to be his wife."
Diana clapped her hands. "That's exactly what we hoped and expected! And you'll marry him, Jane, won't you? And then he'll stay in England."
"Far from it, Diana. His only reason for proposing is to find a suitable partner for his work in India."
"What! He wants you to go to India?"
"Yes."
"Madness!" she exclaimed. "You wouldn't survive three months there—I'm certain. You must never go. You haven't agreed, have you, Jane?"
"I've refused to marry him—"
"And that upset him?" she suggested.
"Deeply. He'll never forgive me, I'm afraid. But I offered to go with him as his sister."

"That was reckless, Jane. Think of the task you'd be taking on—constant exhaustion, the kind that kills even the strong. And you're not strong. St. John—you know him—would push you to impossible limits. He'd allow no rest during the worst heat. And unfortunately, I've noticed, whatever he demands, you force yourself to do. I'm amazed you found the courage to refuse his hand. You don't love him then, Jane?"
"Not as a husband."
"Yet he's a handsome man."
"And I'm so plain, Diana. We'd never suit."
"Plain? You? Not at all. You're much too pretty, as well as too good, to be roasted alive in Calcutta." And again she urged me to give up all thoughts of going with her brother.

"I must," I said. "Just now, when I repeated my offer to serve as his assistant, he was appalled by my lack of propriety. He seemed to think I'd done something indecent in proposing to travel with him unmarried—as if I hadn't always hoped to find a brother in him and regarded him as one."
"What makes you say he doesn't love you, Jane?"

"You should hear him on the subject. He has explained again and again that it's not himself but his mission he wants to pair with a wife. He has told me I'm made for work, not for love—which is true, no doubt. But in my view, if I'm not made for love, it follows that I'm not made for marriage. Wouldn't it be strange, Diana, to be chained for life to a man who saw you only as a useful tool?"
"Unbearable—unnatural—absolutely out of the question!"

"And then," I continued, "though I feel only sisterly affection for him now, if forced to be his wife, I can imagine developing an unavoidable, strange, agonizing kind of love for him. Because he is so talented, and there's often a certain heroic grandeur in his look and manner. In that case, my life would become unspeakably wretched. He wouldn't want me to love him. And if I showed my feelings, he'd make me understand they were unwanted and excessive. Superfluous. I know he would."
"And yet St. John is a good man," said Diana.

"He is a good and great man. But he forgets, mercilessly, the feelings and needs of ordinary people when pursuing his own grand vision. It's better, therefore, for the small to stay out of his way—or be trampled underfoot. Here he comes! I'll leave you, Diana." And I hurried upstairs as I saw him entering the garden.

But I was forced to face him again at supper. During the meal he appeared just as composed as usual. I had thought he would barely speak to me, and I was certain he had abandoned his marriage plan. The rest of the evening proved me wrong on both counts. He addressed me exactly in his usual manner—or what had lately become his usual manner—carefully polite. No doubt he had called on the Holy Spirit to subdue the anger I'd provoked, and now believed he had forgiven me. But I saw he had not. It was there in every measured word and controlled gesture. The forgiveness was a performance. Beneath it, the steel remained.

For the evening reading before prayers, he chose the twenty-first chapter of Revelation. It was always a pleasure to listen to his voice read the Bible. Never did it sound so sweet and full—never was his manner so impressive in its noble simplicity—as when he delivered the words of God. Tonight that voice took a more solemn tone and his manner a more thrilling quality. He sat amid his household circle—the May moon shining softly through the window—and read of the new heaven and new earth. Of the river of the water of life, and the tree with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding fruit every month. Of the city with no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God was its light.
The words that followed thrilled me strangely—especially as I felt, by a slight, indescribable shift in his voice, that in speaking them his eyes had turned to me.

"He that overcomes shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. But"—he read slowly, distinctly—"the fearful, the unbelieving, and so forth, shall have their part in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death."
From that moment, I knew what fate St. John feared for me.

A calm, subdued triumph—blended with yearning earnestness—marked his reading of the last glorious verses of that chapter. He believed his own name was already written in the Lamb's book of life. He longed for the hour that would admit him to the city to which the kings of the earth bring their glory and honor. The city that needs no sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God lights it, and the Lamb is its lamp.

In the prayer that followed, all his energy gathered and all his stern passion awoke. He was in deep earnest, wrestling with God, determined to prevail. He begged for strength for the fainthearted. He asked for guidance for wanderers from the fold—for a return, even at the last moment, for those being lured from the narrow path. He pleaded for a brand snatched from the burning. Earnestness is always deeply solemn. First, as I listened, I was moved. Then, as the prayer went on, I felt troubled. Was this prayer for me? Was I the one being prayed for? A shiver ran through me.

The prayer over, we said our goodbyes. He was leaving very early in the morning. Diana and Mary kissed him and left the room—prompted, I think, by a whispered hint from him. I offered my hand and wished him a pleasant journey.

"Thank you, Jane. As I said, I'll return from Cambridge in two weeks. That time is yours for reflection. If I listened to human pride, I would say nothing more about marriage. But I listen to my duty, and I keep my first aim firmly in view—to do all things for the glory of God. My Master was patient, and so will I be. I cannot abandon you to ruin. Repent—decide, while there's still time. Remember, we're told to work while it is day—warned that the night comes when no one can work. Remember the fate of Dives, who had his good things in this life. God give you strength to choose the better part which shall not be taken from you!"

He laid his hand on my head as he spoke these last words. He had spoken earnestly, gently. His look was not that of a lover gazing at his beloved, but that of a pastor calling back his wandering sheep—or better, a guardian angel watching over the soul in his care. All men of talent, whether they feel deeply or not—whether they are zealots or despots—if only they are sincere—have their moments of mastery, when they command and rule. I felt reverence for St. John. I felt his power. But the power was not mine to submit to. I would follow him to the ends of the earth. I would not give him my hand.

I stood motionless under my guide's touch. My refusals were forgotten—my fears overcome—my resistance paralyzed. The impossible—my marriage to St. John—was rapidly becoming possible. Everything was shifting with a sudden sweep. Religion called—angels beckoned—God commanded—life rolled together like a scroll—death's gates opening, showed eternity beyond. It seemed that for safety and bliss in the next world, everything in this one could be sacrificed in an instant. The dim room was full of visions.

"Could you decide now?" asked the missionary. The question was put gently. He drew me to him, also gently. Oh, that gentleness! How much more powerful it was than force! I could resist St. John's anger. But I grew soft as a reed under his kindness. Yet I knew—if I gave in now, I would still be made to regret my earlier resistance. His nature had not changed in one hour of solemn prayer. It was only lifted up.
"I could decide if I were only sure," I answered. "If I were only convinced that it is God's will that I marry you, I could vow to do it here and now—come what may afterward!"

"My prayers are heard!" St. John exclaimed. He pressed his hand more firmly on my head, as if claiming me. He put his arm around me—almost as if he loved me. I say almost—I knew the difference. I had felt what it was to be loved. But, like him, I had now pushed love aside and thought only of duty. I struggled against the dimness clouding my vision, behind which something still churned. Sincerely, deeply, urgently, I longed to do what was right—and only that. "Show me, show me the path!" I begged of Heaven.

The house was completely still. I believe everyone except St. John and me had gone to bed. The single candle was dying out. The room was full of moonlight. My heart beat fast and hard—I could hear its throb. Suddenly it stopped, seized by a feeling beyond description. The feeling was not like an electric shock, but it was just as sharp, strange, and startling. It acted on my senses as if they had been asleep until now, and were suddenly jolted wide awake. They rose, expectant—eye and ear waiting. The flesh trembled on my bones.
"What did you hear? What do you see?" asked St. John. I saw nothing, but I heard a voice somewhere cry—
"Jane! Jane! Jane!"—nothing more.
"Oh God! What is it?" I gasped.

I might have said, "Where is it?" For it didn't seem to come from the room—nor the house—nor the garden. It came not from the air, nor from under the earth, nor from above. I had heard it—but from where, it was impossible to know! And it was the voice of a human being—a known, loved, well-remembered voice—the voice of Edward Fairfax Rochester. And it spoke in pain and sorrow, wildly, eerily, urgently.
"I am coming!" I cried. "Wait for me! Oh, I will come!" I flew to the door and looked into the passage—it was dark. I ran out into the garden—it was empty.
"Where are you?" I called out.
The hills beyond Marsh Glen sent the answer faintly back—"Where are you?" I listened. The wind sighed low in the fir trees. All was moorland loneliness and midnight silence.

"Down, superstition!" I told myself, as that phantom rose up dark beside the black yew tree at the gate. "This is not deception, nor witchcraft. It is the work of nature. She was stirred, and she performed—no miracle—but her finest work."

I broke away from St. John, who had followed and would have held me back. It was my turn to take command. My powers were awake and active. I told him not to question or comment. I told him to leave me alone. I must and would be alone. He obeyed at once. Where there is energy to command well enough, obedience never fails. I went up to my room, locked myself in, fell on my knees, and prayed in my own way—a different way from St. John's, but effective in its own fashion. I seemed to reach beyond the visible world, as it were—very near a mighty Spirit. And my soul rushed out in gratitude. Not through words. Through something deeper. I rose from my knees. I knew what I had to do.

chapters.title: Chapter 36
paragraphs: Daylight came. I rose at dawn. I spent an hour or two arranging my things in drawers and wardrobe—in the order I'd want to leave them during a short absence. Meanwhile, I heard St. John leave his room. He stopped at my door. I feared he would knock—no, but a slip of paper was pushed under the door. I picked it up. It read:

"You left me too suddenly last night. Had you stayed a little longer, you would have placed your hand on the Christian's cross and the angel's crown. I shall expect your clear decision when I return in two weeks. Meanwhile, watch and pray that you do not fall into temptation: the spirit, I trust, is willing, but the flesh, I see, is weak. I shall pray for you hourly.—Yours, ST. JOHN."

"My spirit," I answered silently, "is willing to do what is right. And my flesh, I hope, is strong enough to carry out Heaven's will, once that will is clearly known to me. At any rate, it shall be strong enough to search—to inquire—to find a way out of this cloud of doubt, and reach the open day of certainty."

It was the first of June, yet the morning was overcast and cold. Rain beat hard against my window. I heard the front door open and St. John walk out. Looking through the window, I saw him cross the garden. He took the path over the misty moors toward Whitcross—where he would catch the coach.
"In a few hours I'll follow you on that road, cousin," I thought. "I too have a coach to catch at Whitcross. I too have people to see and ask after in England before I leave forever."

It was still two hours until breakfast. I filled the time walking softly around my room, pondering the experience that had given my plans their new direction. I recalled the sensation I had felt—for I could recall it, with all its indescribable strangeness. I recalled the voice I had heard. Again I asked where it had come from, as uselessly as before. It had seemed to be inside me—not in the external world. I asked myself whether it was just a nervous impression—a hallucination. I couldn't believe so. It seemed more like an inspiration. The extraordinary effect on me confirmed this. I felt as though I had been called—not by mortal voice, but by something higher.
"Before many days," I said, ending my reflections, "I will know something of the man whose voice seemed to summon me last night. Letters have failed—I will go in person."
At breakfast I announced to Diana and Mary that I was going on a journey and would be away at least four days.
"Alone, Jane?" they asked.
"Yes. I need to see or hear news of a friend I've been worried about for some time."

They might have pointed out—as I'm sure they thought—that they'd believed I had no friends but them. I had often said as much. But with their genuine tact, they held back from commenting. Diana only asked if I was sure I was well enough to travel. I looked very pale, she observed. I replied that nothing was wrong except anxiety, which I hoped to relieve soon.

It was easy to make my arrangements. No one pestered me with questions or suspicions. Having explained that I couldn't yet share my plans, they kindly and wisely respected my silence. They granted me the freedom I would have given them under similar circumstances.

I left Moor House at three in the afternoon. Soon after four I stood at the Whitcross signpost, waiting for the coach that would take me to distant Thornfield. In the silence of those lonely roads and empty hills, I heard it approaching from far away. It was the same coach from which, a year ago, I had stepped down on this very spot—utterly lost, hopeless, and purposeless! It stopped at my signal. I climbed in—this time not forced to hand over my last coins for the fare. Once I had been penniless. Now I had means. The coach carried me away.

It was a journey of thirty-six hours. I had set out from Whitcross on a Tuesday afternoon. Early Thursday morning the coach stopped to water the horses at a roadside inn, set amid scenery whose green hedges, broad fields, and gentle hills—how mild compared to the stern moors of Morton!—greeted my eyes like the features of a once-familiar face. Yes, I recognized this landscape. I was sure we were near Thornfield. "How far is Thornfield Hall from here?" I asked eagerly.
"How far is Thornfield Hall from here?" I asked the stable hand.
"Just two miles, ma'am, across the fields."

"My journey is over," I thought. I got out of the coach and left a trunk in the stable hand's care, to be held until I called for it. I paid my fare, tipped the coachman, and was ready to go. The brightening day shone on the inn's sign, and I read, in gold letters: "The Rochester Arms." My heart leapt—I was already on my master's own land. Then it sank again, as a thought struck me:

"Your master himself may be across the English Channel, for all you know. And if he is at Thornfield Hall, who else is there? His wife—his mad wife. And you have no business with him. You dare not speak to him or seek him out. You've wasted your trip—you'd better go no further," urged my inner voice. "Ask the people at the inn. They can tell you everything you need to know. They can settle your doubts at once. Go up to that man and ask if Mr. Rochester is at home."

The suggestion was sensible, yet I couldn't force myself to act on it. I so dreaded an answer that would crush me with despair. To prolong doubt was to prolong hope. I might yet see the Hall one more time beneath the morning sky. There was the stile before me—the very fields I had stumbled through, blind, deaf, driven half-mad with anguish, on the morning I fled from Thornfield. Before I fully knew what I'd decided, I was in the midst of them. How fast I walked! How eagerly I strained my eyes toward the familiar landscape!

At last the woods rose up. The rookery clustered dark. A loud cawing broke the morning stillness. Strange joy filled me. On I hurried. Another field crossed—a lane threaded—and there were the courtyard walls and the back buildings. The house itself, the rookery still hid. "My first glimpse shall be from the front," I decided, "where the bold battlements will strike my eye at once, and where I can pick out my master's window. Perhaps he'll be standing at it—he rises early. Perhaps he's walking in the orchard, or on the road in front. If so, I could meet him this very minute. Is there not a chance? A possibility?"

I had followed the lower wall of the orchard and turned the corner. There was a gate opening into the meadow, between two stone pillars topped with stone balls. From behind one pillar I could quietly peer around at the full front of the house. I crept forward carefully, wanting to check whether any bedroom blinds had been raised yet. Battlements, windows, the long frontage—all were within my view from this sheltered spot.

The crows sailing overhead may have watched me taking this survey. I wonder what they thought. They must have noticed I was very cautious and timid at first, and that gradually I grew bolder. A peek, then a long stare. Then a departure from my hiding place and a drift into the meadow. Then a sudden stop, full in front of the grand house, and a long, hard look straight at it.
Let me give you an illustration, reader.

A lover finds his beloved asleep on a mossy bank. He wants to catch a glimpse of her face without waking her. He creeps softly over the grass, careful to make no sound. He pauses—thinking she's stirred. He retreats. Not for anything would he be seen. All is still. He advances again. He bends over her. A light veil rests on her features. He lifts it, bends lower. His eyes anticipate the vision of beauty—warm, blooming, lovely in sleep. How quick was his first glance! But how it freezes! How he recoils! Not just a veil was lifted—a mask was removed. What he sees is not his beloved's face—but a skeleton. A death's head, cold and grinning where warmth and beauty should have been.
I looked with fearful hope toward the stately house. I saw a blackened ruin.

No need to hide behind a gatepost now! No need to peer up at windows, fearing someone was stirring behind them! No need to listen for doors opening—to imagine footsteps on the gravel walk! The lawn, the grounds were trampled and overgrown. The front door gaped open and empty. The front of the house was, as I had once seen it in a dream, just a shell—a very high, fragile-looking wall, full of paneless windows. No roof, no battlements, no chimneys—all had collapsed.

And there was the silence of death around it—the solitude of a desolate wasteland. No wonder that letters sent here had never been answered. You might as well have mailed them to a tomb. The black grimness of the stones told how the Hall had fallen—by fire. But how was it started? What story lay behind this disaster? What losses beyond wood and stone and plaster had followed? Had lives been ruined as well as property? If so, whose? Terrible question—one I dreaded having answered, yet felt compelled to ask.

Wandering around the shattered walls and through the devastated interior, I gathered evidence that the catastrophe was not recent. Winter snows had drifted through that empty arch. Winter rains had beaten in through hollow windows. Among the soaked piles of rubble, spring had encouraged new growth—grass and weeds sprouted between the stones and fallen beams. And where, in the meantime, was the unfortunate owner of this wreck? In what country? Under what circumstances? My eyes wandered over the grey, neglected ruins. Then they instinctively turned toward the sky above the ruins, as if searching for something more.

I needed answers. I could find them only at the inn. I returned there before long. The innkeeper brought my breakfast to the parlour. I asked him to close the door and sit down. I had questions. But when he did as I asked, I hardly knew how to begin. I dreaded the possible answers so much. Yet the scene of destruction I had just witnessed had partially prepared me for bad news. The innkeeper was a respectable-looking, middle-aged man.
"You know Thornfield Hall, of course?" I finally managed to say.
"Yes, ma'am. I lived there once."
"Did you?" Not during my time, I thought. You're a stranger to me.
"I was the late Mr. Rochester's butler," he added.
The late! The words hit me with the full force of the blow I'd been trying to dodge.
"The late!" I gasped. "Is he dead?"

"I mean the present gentleman, Mr. Edward's father," he explained. I breathed again. My blood flowed once more. Those words fully assured me that Mr. Edward—my Mr. Rochester, God bless him wherever he was!—was at least alive. Was, in fact, "the present gentleman." What comforting words! It seemed I could now bear whatever came next—whatever the revelations might be—with relative calm. Since he was not in the grave, I could endure hearing he was at the other end of the earth.
"Is Mr. Rochester living at Thornfield Hall now?" I asked, knowing what the answer would be, but wanting to delay the direct question about where he actually was.

"No, ma'am—oh no! No one's living there. I suppose you're a stranger to these parts, or you'd have heard what happened last autumn. Thornfield Hall is a complete ruin. It burned down around harvest time. A terrible disaster! So much valuable property destroyed—hardly any furniture saved. The fire broke out in the middle of the night. By the time the fire engines arrived from Millcote, the building was a mass of flames. It was a terrible sight. I saw it myself."
"In the middle of the night!" I murmured. Yes, that was always the fateful hour at Thornfield. "Was it known how the fire started?" I asked.

"They guessed, ma'am—they guessed. In fact, I'd say it was proven beyond doubt. You may not be aware," he continued, pulling his chair closer to the table and speaking low, "that there was a lady—a lunatic—kept in the house?"
"I've heard something about it."

"She was kept in very strict confinement, ma'am. For years, people weren't even certain she existed. No one saw her. They only knew by rumor that such a person was at the Hall. Who or what she was, nobody could figure out. They said Mr. Edward had brought her from abroad. Some believed she had been his mistress. But then a strange thing happened about a year ago—a very strange thing."
I was afraid of hearing my own story. I tried to steer him back to the main point.
"And this lady?"
"This lady, ma'am," he answered, "turned out to be Mr. Rochester's wife! The discovery happened in the strangest way. There was a young lady, a governess at the Hall, that Mr. Rochester fell in—"
"But the fire," I prompted.

"I'm coming to that, ma'am. Mr. Edward fell in love with her. The servants said they'd never seen anyone so smitten. He followed her everywhere. They used to watch him—servants do, you know, ma'am—and he was devoted to her beyond everything. Though nobody but him thought her all that beautiful. She was a little, small thing, they said—almost like a child. I never saw her myself, but I heard Leah the housemaid talk about her. Leah liked her well enough. Mr. Rochester was about forty, and she was barely twenty. When he proposed to her, you can bet there were plenty of raised eyebrows. But he was determined, and he was the master."
"You'll tell me that part another time," I said. "Right now I particularly want to hear about the fire. Was it suspected that Mrs. Rochester had anything to do with it?"

"You've hit it, ma'am. It's quite certain it was her—and nobody else—who started it. She had a woman looking after her called Mrs. Poole—an able woman in her line, very trustworthy, except for one weakness. A weakness common to many nurses—she kept a private bottle of gin, and now and then had a drop too much. That's understandable, given the hard life she led. But it was dangerous, because when Mrs. Poole was passed out from the gin, the madwoman would get the keys from her pocket, leave her cell, and wander the house doing whatever wild mischief came into her head. They said she had once set fire to the room next to her husband's bed. But this time she went up to the third floor and set the governess's old room on fire—the room directly above. Then she went down to a lower floor and set fire to the hangings in the room where her husband was sleeping. But he had already woken—the whole floor was blazing. He got up and managed to save the servants. Then he went back for her."
"What! He didn't leave England?"

"Leave England? God, no! He wouldn't so much as cross the doorstep—except at night, when he'd walk like a ghost around the grounds and through the orchard. As if he'd lost his mind—which, in my opinion, he had. Because before that slip of a governess crossed his path, you'd never have met a more spirited, bolder, keener gentleman. He wasn't a man given to drinking, gambling, or horse racing, as some are, and he wasn't especially handsome. But he had courage and a will of his own, if ever a man did. I knew him from a boy, you see. He was quite fond of me too—I've often thought more should have been done to stop him from going wrong. He was no saint. But he was not the devil people made him out to be either."
"Then Mr. Rochester was at home when the fire broke out?"

"Yes, indeed. And he went up to the attics when everything was burning above and below. He got the servants out of their beds and helped them down himself. Then he went back to get his wife out of her room. And then they called up to him that she was on the roof. She was standing there, waving her arms above the battlements, shouting so loud they could hear her a mile away. I saw her and heard her with my own eyes and ears. She was a big woman, with long black hair. We could see it streaming against the flames as she stood there. I heard Mr. Rochester call to her. I saw him climb through the skylight onto the roof. We shouted for him to come down—it was too dangerous. He approached her. Then she yelled, and with one leap she was over the edge—"
The next moment she lay smashed on the pavement.
"Dead?"
"Dead! As dead as the stones her brains and blood were scattered on."
"Good God!"
"You may well say so, ma'am. It was horrifying!"
He shuddered.
"And afterward?" I pressed.
"Well, ma'am, afterward the house burned to the ground. Only some bits of walls are standing now."
"Were any other lives lost?"
"No—perhaps it would have been better if there had."
"What do you mean?"

"Poor Mr. Edward!" he burst out. "I never thought I'd see the day! Some say it was God's judgment on him for keeping his first marriage secret and trying to take another wife while she was alive. But I pity him, for my part."
"You said he's alive?" I exclaimed.
"Yes, yes, he's alive. But many think he'd be better off dead."
"Why? How?" My blood ran cold again. "Where is he? Is he in England?"
"Yes—he's in England. He can't get out of England, I imagine—he's stuck now."
What agony! And the man seemed determined to draw it out.
"He is stone-blind," he said at last. "Yes—stone-blind is Mr. Edward."
I had feared worse. I had feared he was mad. I summoned strength to ask what had caused this.

"It was his own courage, and you might say his kindness, in a way, ma'am. He wouldn't leave the house till everyone else was out. As he came down the great staircase after Mrs. Rochester threw herself from the battlements, there was a massive crash—everything collapsed. He was pulled from the ruins alive, but badly injured. A beam had partly protected him, but one eye was destroyed, and one hand was so crushed that the surgeon, Mr. Carter, had to amputate it immediately. He lost the other eye too. He's now helpless—blind and crippled."
"Where is he? Where does he live now?"
"At Ferndean, a manor house on a farm he owns, about thirty miles away. Quite a desolate place."
"Who is with him?"
"Old John and his wife. He wouldn't have anyone else. He's quite broken down, they say."
"Have you any kind of vehicle?"
"We have a chaise, ma'am—a very fine chaise."
"Have it ready at once. If your driver can get me to Ferndean before dark today, I'll pay you both double the usual rate."

chapters.title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: Ferndean Manor was a building of considerable age, moderate size, and no architectural ambition, buried deep in a wood. I had heard of it before. Mr. Rochester often spoke of it and sometimes visited. His father had bought the estate for its hunting grounds. He would have rented the house but could find no tenant, because of its remote and unhealthy location. So Ferndean remained empty and unfurnished, except for two or three rooms fitted up for Mr. Rochester's occasional overnight stays.

I reached this house just before dark on an evening marked by grey skies, a cold wind, and steady, penetrating rain. The last mile I walked, having dismissed the carriage and driver with the double payment I'd promised. Even when I was very close to the manor, I could see nothing of it—so thick and dark were the trees of the gloomy wood around it. Iron gates between granite pillars showed me where to enter. Passing through them, I found myself among trees. There was no clear drive visible, no smooth lawn or broad walk. The growth of the surrounding woods had crept right up to the very doorstep. They were wild and untrimmed.

I thought I had taken a wrong turn and lost my way. The darkness of nature and forest gathered around me. I looked for another path. There was none—only interwoven branches, thick trunks, and dense summer foliage. Not an opening anywhere.

I kept going. At last the trees thinned a little. Soon I made out a railing, then the house—barely distinguishable from the trees in the dim light, so damp and green were its decaying walls. I entered through a door fastened only with a latch and stood in an enclosed yard from which the wood curved away in a half circle. There were no flowers, no garden beds—only a broad gravel walk circling a patch of grass, set in the heavy frame of the forest. The house presented two pointed gables in its front. The windows were latticed and narrow. The front door was narrow too—one step led up to it. The whole looked, as the innkeeper had said, "quite a desolate spot."
"Can there be life here?" I asked.
Yes—life of some kind was there. I heard a movement. That narrow front door was opening, and some shape was about to emerge.

It opened slowly. A figure came out into the twilight and stood on the step—a man without a hat. He stretched out his hand as if to feel whether it was raining. Dark as it was, I recognized his strong shape and features. I nearly revealed myself—but I held back. I was not yet ready to meet him. I had still a thing or two to think through. I needed to prepare myself for the shock—and to prepare him.

I stayed where I was, barely breathing, and watched him—studied him, unseen, and sadly invisible to him. It was a meeting in the dark. I held back the tears that threatened and willed my heart to steady itself.

His form was the same strong, powerful build as ever. His bearing was still upright. His hair was still raven-black. His features were still sharp and firm. Not in one year's time had decay advanced so far as to alter either. But in his face I saw a change—a look of desperate brooding that reminded me of some wronged and chained wild animal. The sightless eyes were tragic to behold. They were dark, and wild, and hopeless.

And, reader, do you think I feared him in his blind fury? If you do, you don't know me. A gentle hope blended with my sorrow. I could feel his heart was still warm, still beating, still mighty. I was sure I could bring him comfort. I just needed to find the right approach.

He stepped down from the doorstep and moved slowly, gropingly, toward the grass. Where was his bold stride now? He felt his way cautiously, as one who walks in darkness. He stopped. He stood still. Then he stretched out his right hand—the hand that had no fingers—toward the sky, the trees, the rain. He seemed to gather the elements in that mutilated grasp. He tried to see with those blind eyes. He let his hand fall, then turned and went back inside.
"Will you take my arm, sir?" said a voice. It was John. "There's a heavy shower coming on. You'd better go in."
"Leave me alone," was the answer.
John withdrew without noticing me. Mr. Rochester tried again to walk about—in vain. Everything was too uncertain. He groped his way back to the house and re-entered it. I heard him close the door.
I now approached and knocked. John's wife opened for me. "Mary," I said, "how are you?"

She started as if she had seen a ghost. I calmed her. To her flustered "Is it really you, miss, come at this late hour to this lonely place?" I answered by taking her hand. Then I followed her into the kitchen, where John now sat by a good fire. I explained in a few words that I had heard everything that had happened since I left Thornfield, and that I had come to see Mr. Rochester. I asked John to go down to the inn at Millcote and fetch my trunk, which I had left there. I then sat down to collect my thoughts and consider how best to approach my master.
"When you go in," I said, "tell your master that a person wishes to speak to him, but don't give my name."
"I don't think he'll see you," she answered. "He refuses everybody."
When she returned, I asked what he had said.
"You are to send in your name and your business," she replied. She then proceeded to fill a glass with water and place it, with candles, on a tray. I noticed her hand was shaking.
"Is that what he rang for?" I asked.
"Yes. He always has candles brought in at dark, even though he's blind."
"Give the tray to me. I will carry it in."
I took it from her hand. She pointed me toward the parlour door. The tray shook as I held it. The water sloshed from the glass. My heart pounded. Mary opened the door for me and shut it behind me.

The parlour looked grim. A neglected handful of fire burned low in the grate. Leaning over it, with his head propped on his hand, sat the blind tenant of the room. His old dog, Pilot, lay on one side, curled up as if afraid of being accidentally stepped on. Pilot pricked his ears when I came in. Then he jumped up with a yelp and bounded toward me. He almost knocked the tray from my hands. I set it on the table, then patted him and said softly, "Lie down!" Mr. Rochester turned mechanically to see what the commotion was, but since he saw nothing, he returned to his brooding.
"Give me the water, Mary," he said.
I approached him with the now only half-filled glass. Pilot followed me, still excited.
"What is the matter?" he asked.
"Down, Pilot!" I said again. He paused with the glass halfway to his lips, and seemed to listen. He drank, and put the glass down. "This is you, Mary, is it not?"
"Mary is in the kitchen," I answered.

He put out his hand quickly, but not seeing where I stood, he didn't touch me. "Who is this? Who is this?" he demanded, seeming to try to see with those sightless eyes. An expression of pain and bewilderment crossed his face.
"Will you have a little more water, sir? I spilled half of what was in the glass," I said.
"Who is it? What is it? Who speaks?"
"Pilot knows me, and John and Mary know I am here. I came only this evening," I answered.
"Great God!—what delusion has come over me? What sweet madness has seized me?"
"No delusion—no madness. Your mind, sir, is too strong for delusion, your health too sound for madness."
"And where is the speaker? Is it only a voice? Oh! I cannot see, but I must feel, or my heart will stop and my brain will burst. Whatever you are—whoever you are—let me touch you, or I cannot live!"
He groped. I caught his wandering hand and held it in both of mine.
"Her very fingers!" he cried. "Her small, slight fingers! If so, there must be more of her."
The strong hand broke free from mine. My arm was seized, my shoulder—neck—waist—I was pulled close and gathered to him.
"Is it Jane? What is it? This is her shape—this is her size—"
"And this her voice," I added. "She is all here—her heart, too. God bless you, sir! I am glad to be so near you again."
"Jane Eyre!—Jane Eyre," was all he said.
"My dear master," I answered, "I am Jane Eyre. I have found you out—I have come back to you."
"In truth? In the flesh? My living Jane?"
"You touch me, sir. You hold me, and tightly enough. I am not cold like a corpse, nor empty like air, am I?"

"My living darling! These are certainly her limbs, and these her features. But I cannot be so blessed, after all my misery. It is a dream—such dreams I have had at night when I clasped her once more to my heart, just as I do now. And kissed her, as thus—and felt that she loved me, and trusted she would not leave me."
"Which I never will, sir, from this day on."
"Never will, says the vision? But I always woke and found it an empty mockery. And I was desolate and abandoned—my life dark and lonely—my soul thirsting, and the cup always snatched from my lips."
"There, sir—and there!"

I pressed my lips to his once-brilliant, now sightless eyes. I swept the hair from his brow and kissed that too. He suddenly seemed to trust that I was real. A look of grateful joy broke over his worn face.
"It is you—is it, Jane? You have come back to me, then?"
"I have."
"And you do not lie dead in some ditch? And you are not a starving outcast among strangers?"
"No, sir! I am an independent woman now."
"Independent! What do you mean, Jane?"
"My uncle in Madeira is dead, and he left me five thousand pounds."
"Ah! That is practical—that is real!" he cried. "I should never dream that. Besides, there is your particular voice—I could never mistake that. Jane Eyre—Jane Eyre," he repeated.
"Quite rich, sir. If you won't let me live with you, I can build a house of my own close to your door, and you may come and sit in my parlour whenever you want company in the evening."
"But as you're rich, Jane, you must now have friends who will look after you and not let you devote yourself to a blind man like me?"
"I told you I am independent, sir, as well as rich. I am my own mistress."
"And you will stay with me?"

"Certainly—unless you object. I will be your neighbor, your nurse, your housekeeper. I find you lonely. I will be your companion—to read to you, to walk with you, to sit with you, to wait on you, to be eyes and hands to you. Stop looking so gloomy, sir. I will not let you be sad."

He didn't answer right away. He seemed deep in thought—withdrawn. He sighed. He half-opened his lips as if to speak, then closed them again. I felt a kind of panic stir in me. I began to wonder if he was going to refuse me.

"No—no—Jane; you must not go. No—I have touched you, heard you, felt the comfort of your presence—the sweetness of your consolation. I cannot give up these joys. I have little left in myself—I must have you. The world may laugh—may call me absurd, selfish—no matter. My very soul demands you. It will be satisfied, or it will take deadly vengeance on its frame."
"Well, sir, I will stay with you. I have said so."

"Yes—but you understand one thing by staying with me, and I understand another. You perhaps could bring yourself to visit the blind man in his cell and sit beside him—to cheer him—and come again tomorrow. But to consent to stay always with this poor, dark, desolate creature—that is another thing entirely."
"I will think whatever you like, sir. I am content to be only your nurse, if you think it better."
"But you cannot always be my nurse, Janet. You are young—you must marry one day."
"I don't care about being married."
"You should care, Janet. If I were what I once was, I would try to make you care—but—a sightless block!"
He fell back into gloom. I, on the contrary, grew more cheerful and took fresh courage. These last words gave me an opening. I felt it would not do to let the conversation drift into despair.

"It's time someone undertook to bring you back to life," I said, parting his thick, long, uncut hair. "I see you are being turned into a lion, or something of the sort. Your hair reminds me of eagle feathers—whether it has been combed lately I cannot tell."
"On this arm, I have neither hand nor nails," he said, drawing the mutilated limb from his chest and showing it to me. "It is a mere stump—a ghastly sight! Don't you think so, Jane?"
"It is a pity to see it. And a pity to see your eyes—and the scar of fire on your forehead. And the worst of it is, one is in danger of loving you too much for all this and making too much of you."
"I thought you would be revolted, Jane, when you saw my arm and my scarred face."
"Did you? Don't tell me that—or I might say something unflattering about your judgment. Now, let me leave you for a moment to find a better fire than this dead pile of ashes."
"Yes—with the right eye I see a glow—a reddish haze."
"And you see the candles?"
"Very dimly—each is a glowing cloud."
"Can you see me?"
"No, my fairy. But I am grateful enough to hear and feel you."
"When do you have supper?"
"I never have supper."
"But you shall have some tonight. I am hungry—so are you, I expect. Only you've forgotten it."

I called for Mary and soon had the room in better order. I prepared him a comfortable meal. My spirits were high, and I was happy to be active and useful. He seemed astonished, even a little overwhelmed, at the rapid change from loneliness to company, from darkness to warmth.

After supper, he began asking me many questions—where I had been, what I had been doing, how I had found him. But I gave him only brief answers. It was too late for long stories. Besides, I wanted to keep certain things back until another time.
"You are altogether a human being, Jane? You are certain of that?"
"I truly believe so, Mr. Rochester."

"Yet how, on this dark and gloomy evening, could you so suddenly appear at my lonely hearth? I reached out my hand to take a glass of water from a servant, and it was given me by you. I asked a question, expecting Mary's voice to answer—and your voice spoke to my ear."
"Because I had come in, in Mary's place, with the tray."

"And there is enchantment in this very hour I am spending with you. Who can tell what a dark, hopeless life I have dragged through since I last saw you? And suddenly, you appear. I stretch my hand and touch what I dreamed would never be real again."
A plain, practical reply, cutting against the current of his troubled thoughts, was, I was sure, the best comfort I could offer.
"What use is it to do me good, benevolent spirit, when at some moment you will desert me again—passing away like a shadow from my grasp?"
"Have you a pocket comb about you, sir?"
"What for, Jane?"
"Just to comb out this shaggy black mane. I find you rather alarming at close range. You talk of my being a fairy, but I'm sure you look more like a brownie yourself."
"Am I hideous, Jane?"
"Very, sir. You always were, you know."
"Hmph! The mischief hasn't been taken out of you, wherever you've been."
"Yet I have been with good people—far better than you. A hundred times better. People with ideas and views you never entertained in your life. Much more refined, and with much better manners."
"Who on earth have you been with?"
"If you twist around like that, you'll make me pull the hair out of your head. And then I think you'll stop suspecting I'm a phantom."
"Who have you been with, Jane?"
"You won't get it out of me tonight, sir. You must wait until tomorrow. Leaving my tale half-told will, you know, be an excellent way to ensure you let me come back."

"You mocking creature—fairy-born and human-raised! You make me feel as I haven't felt in twelve months. If Saul could have had you for his David, the evil spirit would have been exorcised without the need for a harp."
"There, sir—you're tidied up and made presentable. Now I'll leave you. I have been traveling for three days, and I believe I'm tired. Goodnight."
"Just one word, Jane: were there only ladies in the house where you've been?"
I laughed and made my escape, still laughing as I ran upstairs. "A good idea!" I thought with glee. "I see I have the means of teasing him out of his melancholy for some time to come."

Very early the next morning I heard him up and moving about, wandering from one room to another. As soon as Mary came down, I heard the question: "Is Miss Eyre here?" Then: "Which room did you put her in? Is she up? Go and ask if she wants anything. And when she'll come down."

I came down as soon as I thought breakfast might be ready. I entered the room very softly. I had a view of him before he discovered my presence. He sat in his chair, his old dog at his feet. Pilot's head rested on the mutilated hand—he was trying to caress the animal, but could not manage it well. The look on his face was one of grief and lonely longing—painful, almost unbearable to witness. Yet I held back my tears. This was not a time for tears. I would be upbeat—relentlessly.
"It is a bright, sunny morning, sir," I said. "The rain is over and gone. There is a soft glow after it. You should feel it through the open window. Can you see the light?"
His features lit up at once.

"Oh, you are really there, my skylark! Come to me. You are not gone—not vanished? I heard one of your kind an hour ago, singing high over the wood. But its song had no music for me, any more than the rising sun had brightness. All the melody on earth comes from one voice. All the sunshine from one presence."
The tears stood in my eyes at this confession of his need—just as if a royal eagle, chained to its perch, had been forced to beg a sparrow to be its provider. But I held firm. I would not weep now.

Most of the morning was spent outdoors. I led him out of the wet and wild wood into cheerful open fields. I described the sky and the landscape for him. I let him sit on a comfortable seat and feel the sun. I helped him navigate the uneven ground. I was careful and patient. I was also very happy.

"Cruel, cruel deserter!" he exclaimed at one point. "Oh, Jane, what did I feel when I discovered you had fled from Thornfield? When I couldn't find you anywhere? When, after searching for hours, I knew you were truly gone?"

Prompted by his urgency, I began the story of my experience over the past year. I softened considerably what related to the three days of wandering and starvation—because telling him those things in full would have been torture to him. His loving spirit could not have borne it. The hunger, the cold, the exhaustion—I touched on them lightly, emphasizing instead my rescue.

He said I should not have left him that way, without any means of making my way. I should have told him my intentions. I should have trusted him. He would have found a way to set things right without separation. He swore he would never have forced me to remain at Thornfield. He'd have been happy to know I was safe, even far away.

"Well, whatever my sufferings had been, they were very short," I answered. And then I told him how I had been taken in at Moor House. How I had obtained the position of schoolmistress. The inheritance and the discovery of my relatives followed in due order. Of course, St. John Rivers' name came up frequently. When I had finished, that name was immediately seized upon.
"This St. John, then, is your cousin?"
"Yes."
"You've spoken of him often. Do you like him?"
"He was a very good man, sir. I couldn't help liking him."
"A good man. Does that mean a respectable, well-behaved man of fifty? Or what does it mean?"
"St. John was only twenty-nine, sir."
"Still young, then. Is he a short, dull, plain man? The kind whose goodness lies more in the absence of vice than in any real strength of character?"
"He is tirelessly active. Great and noble deeds are what he lives for."
"But his mind? Probably rather soft? He means well, but you'd shrug listening to him talk?"
"He speaks very little, sir. What he does say is always to the point. His mind is first-rate—not easily swayed, but powerful."
"Is he an able man, then?"
"Truly able."
"A thoroughly educated man?"
"St. John is an accomplished and profound scholar."
"His manners, I think, you said aren't to your taste? Stuffy and preachy?"
"I never mentioned his manners. But unless I have very bad taste, they must suit me. They are polished, calm, and gentlemanly."
"His appearance—I forget how you described it. Some sort of raw young curate, half-strangled by his white collar and tottering on thick-soled boots?"
"St. John dresses well. He is a handsome man—tall, fair, with blue eyes and a Grecian profile."
"Damn him!" (Aside.) Then to me: "Did you like him, Jane?"
"Yes, Mr. Rochester, I liked him. But you asked me that before."

I could see what he was doing, of course. Jealousy had seized him. It stung—but the sting was healthy. It gave him a break from the gnawing fang of melancholy. So I didn't immediately soothe the snake.
"Perhaps you'd rather not sit on my knee any longer, Miss Eyre?" came the next, somewhat unexpected remark.
"Why not, Mr. Rochester?"

"The picture you've just painted suggests a rather overwhelming contrast. Your words have sketched a graceful Apollo—tall, fair, blue-eyed, with a Grecian profile. Your eyes rest on a Vulcan—a real blacksmith, brown, broad-shouldered, and blind and lame into the bargain."
"I never thought of it before, but you certainly do resemble Vulcan, sir."
"Well, you may leave me, ma'am. But before you go"—and he held me with a firmer grip than ever—"just answer me a question or two." He paused.
"What questions, Mr. Rochester?"
Then followed this cross-examination.
"St. John made you schoolmistress of Morton before he knew you were his cousin?"
"Yes."
"You would often see him? He'd visit the school sometimes?"
"Daily."
"He would approve of your plans, Jane? I know they'd be clever, because you are a talented creature!"
"He approved of them—yes."
"He would discover many things in you he hadn't expected? Some of your accomplishments aren't ordinary."
"I don't know about that."
"You had a little cottage near the school, you say. Did he ever come there to see you?"
"Now and then."
"In the evenings?"
"Once or twice."
A pause.
"How long did you live with him and his sisters after the family connection was discovered?"
"Five months."
"Did Rivers spend much time with the women of his family?"
"Yes. The back parlour was both his study and ours. He sat near the window, and we sat by the table."
"Did he study a lot?"
"A good deal."
"What?"
"Hindustani."
"And what did you do in the meantime?"
"I studied German, at first."
"Did he teach you?"
"He didn't know German."
"Did he teach you anything?"
"A little Hindustani."
"Rivers taught you Hindustani?"
"Yes, sir."
"And his sisters too?"
"No."
"Only you?"
"Only me."
"Did you ask to learn?"
"No."
"He wanted to teach you?"
"Yes."
A second pause.
"Why did he want to? What use could Hindustani be to you?"
"He intended me to go with him to India."
"Ah! Now we reach the heart of the matter. He wanted you to marry him."
"He asked me to marry him."
"That's a lie—an outrageous invention to torment me."
"I beg your pardon, it's the plain truth. He asked me more than once, and was just as stubborn about pressing his case as you ever were."
"Miss Eyre, I repeat, you may leave me. How often must I say the same thing? Why do you remain planted on my knee when I've told you to go?"
"Because I'm comfortable here."

"No, Jane, you are not comfortable—because your heart isn't with me. It's with this cousin—this St. John. Oh, until this moment I thought my little Jane was all mine! I believed she loved me even when she left me. That was a drop of sweetness in the bitterness. For all the time we've been apart, for all the hot tears I've wept over our separation, I never imagined that while I was mourning her, she was loving another! But it's only natural enough. You said he was young, handsome, talented. And I—what am I now?"
"Shake me off, then, sir—push me away. I won't leave on my own."
"Jane, I've always loved your voice. It still gives me hope—it sounds so true. When I hear it, it carries me back a year. I forget that you've formed a new attachment. But I'm not a fool—go—"
"Where must I go, sir?"
"Your own way—with the husband you've chosen."
"Who is that?"
"You know—this St. John Rivers."

"He is not my husband, and never will be. He doesn't love me. I don't love him. He loves—as much as he can love, which is not the way you love—a beautiful young woman called Rosamond. He wanted to marry me only because he thought I'd make a suitable missionary's wife, which she would not. He is good and great, but severe. And for me, cold as an iceberg. He is not like you, sir. I am not happy at his side, nor near him, nor with him. He has no hold on my sympathy or warmth. I do not long for his company. I am not drawn to his approval. No warmth rises in me at his approach."
I shuddered involuntarily, and pressed closer to my blind but beloved master. He smiled.
"What, Jane! Is this true? Is this really how things stand between you and Rivers?"

"Absolutely, sir! Oh, you have no reason to be jealous! I wanted to tease you a little, to make you less sad. I thought anger would be better than grief. But if you want me to love you, could you but see how much I do, you would be proud and satisfied. My whole heart is yours, sir. It belongs to you. And with you it would stay, even if fate exiled the rest of me from your presence forever."
Again, as he kissed me, painful thoughts darkened his face.
"My ruined sight! My crippled strength!" he murmured with regret.

I stroked his face to soothe him. I knew what he was thinking and wanted to speak for him, but didn't dare. As he turned away for a moment, I saw a tear slide from under the sealed eyelid and trickle down his cheek. My heart swelled.

"I am no better than the old lightning-struck chestnut tree in Thornfield orchard," he said after a while. "And what right would that ruin have to ask a flowering vine to cover its decay with fresh green?"

"You are no ruin, sir—no lightning-struck tree. You are green and full of life. Plants will grow around your roots whether you ask them to or not, because they delight in your generous shade. And as they grow, they'll lean toward you and wind around you, because your strength offers them the safest support."
Again he smiled. I was giving him comfort.
"You speak of friends, Jane?" he asked.
"Yes, of friends," I answered, somewhat hesitantly. I knew I meant more than friends but couldn't find another word. He helped me.
"Ah! Jane. But I want a wife."
"Do you, sir?"
"Yes. Is that news to you?"
"Of course. You said nothing about it before."
"Is it unwelcome news?"
"That depends on circumstances, sir—on your choice."
"Which you shall make for me, Jane. I'll accept your decision."
"Choose then, sir—her who loves you best."
"I will at least choose—her I love best. Jane, will you marry me?"
"Yes, sir."
"A poor blind man, whom you'll have to lead by the hand?"
"Yes, sir."
"A crippled man, twenty years older than you, whom you'll have to wait on?"
"Yes, sir."
"Truly, Jane?"
"Most truly, sir."
"Oh! My darling! God bless you and reward you!"

"Mr. Rochester, if I ever did a good deed in my life—if I ever thought a good thought—if I ever prayed a sincere and blameless prayer—if I ever wished a righteous wish—I am rewarded now. To be your wife is, for me, to be as happy as I can be on earth."
"Because you delight in sacrifice."

"Sacrifice! What do I sacrifice? Famine for food. Waiting for fulfillment. To be allowed to put my arms around what I treasure—to press my lips to what I love—to rest against what I trust: is that a sacrifice? If so, then yes—I delight in sacrifice."
"And to put up with my weaknesses, Jane. To overlook my flaws."
"Which are nothing to me, sir. I love you better now, when I can truly be useful to you, than I did when you were proud and independent—when you'd accept no role but that of the giver and protector."

"Until now I've hated being helped—being led. From now on, I think I shall hate it no more. I didn't like putting my hand into a hired servant's. But it's a pleasure to feel Jane's little fingers around it. I preferred total loneliness to the constant presence of servants. But Jane's quiet care will be a perpetual joy. Jane suits me. Do I suit her?"
"To the very core of my being, sir."
"Then we have nothing in the world to wait for. We must be married at once."
He looked and spoke with eagerness. His old fire was rising.
"We must be joined without delay, Jane. There's only the license to get—then we marry."
"Mr. Rochester, I've just noticed the sun is well past noon, and Pilot has actually gone home for his dinner. Let me look at your watch."
"Fasten it to your belt, Janet, and keep it. I have no use for it."
"It's nearly four in the afternoon, sir. Aren't you hungry?"
"The third day from now must be our wedding day, Jane. Never mind fine clothes and jewels—none of that matters."
"The sun has dried up all the rain, sir. The breeze is still. It's quite warm."
"Do you know, Jane, I have your little pearl necklace around my neck at this moment, tucked under my collar? I've worn it since the day I lost my only treasure—as a reminder of her."
"We'll go home through the wood. That will be the shadiest way."
He pursued his own thoughts without hearing me.

"Jane! You think me, I'm sure, a godless man. But my heart swells with gratitude to the merciful God of this earth right now. He sees not as man sees, but far more clearly. He judges not as man judges, but far more wisely. I did wrong. I would have stained my innocent flower—breathed guilt on its purity. The Almighty snatched it from me. I, in my stubborn rebellion, nearly cursed the punishment. Instead of bowing to the decree, I defied it. Divine justice followed its course. Disasters came thick upon me. I was forced to pass through the valley of death. His punishments were heavy. I acknowledged their justice. I began to experience remorse, repentance, the wish for reconciliation with my Maker. I began sometimes to pray—brief prayers, but very sincere."

"Some days ago—four days, to be exact—last Monday night, a strange mood came over me. Grief replaced frenzy. Sorrow replaced bitterness. I had long been convinced that since I couldn't find you anywhere, you must be dead. Late that night—perhaps between eleven and midnight—before going to my miserable bed, I begged God, if it pleased Him, to take me soon from this life and admit me to the next world, where there was still hope of reunion with Jane."

"I was in my room, sitting by the open window. The mild night air soothed me. I could see no stars—only by a faint, luminous haze did I know the moon was out. I longed for you, Janet! Oh, I longed for you with soul and flesh! I asked God, in anguish and humility, whether I had not been desolate and tormented long enough. Whether I might not soon taste peace and happiness again. I admitted I deserved everything I'd endured. I could hardly expect mercy. But I begged for it—urgently. Then I cried out: 'Jane! Jane! Jane!'"
"Did you speak those words aloud?"
"I did, Jane. If anyone had heard me, they'd have thought me insane. I said them with such desperate force."
"And it was last Monday night, near midnight?"

"Yes. But the time doesn't matter. What followed is the strange part. You'll think me superstitious—there's some superstition in my blood, and always has been. But this is true—at least it is true that I heard what I'm about to tell you.

"As I cried 'Jane! Jane! Jane!' a voice—I cannot tell where it came from, but I know whose voice it was—replied, 'I am coming: wait for me.' And a moment later, the wind carried a whisper: 'Where are you?'

"Let me try to describe what those words created in my mind—though it's hard to express. Ferndean is buried, as you see, in heavy woodland where sound falls flat and dies without echo. 'Where are you?' seemed spoken among mountains. I heard a hill-sent echo repeat the words. At that moment the wind felt cooler and fresher on my brow. I could have believed that, in some wild, lonely place, Jane and I were meeting. In spirit, I believe we must have met. You—wherever you were—must have felt it at the same moment."

Reader, it was on Monday night—near midnight—that I too had received the mysterious call. Those were the very words with which I had answered it. I listened to Mr. Rochester's account but said nothing in return. The coincidence struck me as too strange and awe-inspiring to discuss. If I told anything, my story would inevitably make a deep impression on his mind—and that mind, already too prone to dark thoughts from suffering, did not need the added weight of supernatural mystery. I kept these things in my heart.

"You can't wonder, then," my master continued, "that when you appeared before me so unexpectedly last night, I had difficulty believing you were anything more than a voice and a vision—something that would dissolve into silence, as the midnight whisper and mountain echo had dissolved before. Now, I thank God! I know otherwise. Yes, I thank God!"

He set me down from his knee, rose, and reverently lifted his hat from his head. Bending his sightless eyes toward the earth, he stood in silent devotion. Only the last words of his prayer were audible.
"I thank my Maker that, in the midst of judgment, He has remembered mercy. I humbly beg my Redeemer to give me strength to lead a purer life than I have lived until now!"

Then he reached out his hand to be led. I took that dear hand, held it a moment to my lips, then let it rest around my shoulder. Being so much shorter than he, I served as both his support and his guide. We entered the wood and made our way home.

chapters.title: Chapter 38 — Conclusion
paragraphs: Reader, I married him. A quiet wedding we had—just he and I, the parson, and the clerk. When we got back from church, I went into the kitchen of the manor house, where Mary was cooking dinner and John cleaning the knives, and I said—

"Mary, I married Mr. Rochester this morning." The housekeeper and her husband were both the kind of calm, steady people to whom you can safely announce remarkable news without having your ears pierced by a shriek or your head stunned by a flood of amazed chatter. Mary did look up, and she did stare at me. The ladle she was using to baste a pair of roasting chickens did stop in midair for about three minutes. Then, without comment, she resumed her basting. When she had finished and put the ladle down, she said—
"Have you, Miss? Well, I never!"

A short time later she added: "I saw you go out with the master, but I didn't know you'd gone to church to be married." And she went back to her basting. John, when I turned to him, was grinning from ear to ear.

"I told Mary how it would be," he said. "I knew what Mr. Edward"—John was an old servant who had known his master since boyhood, so he often used his first name—"I knew what Mr. Edward would do. And I was certain he wouldn't wait long either. And he's done right, in my opinion. I wish you joy, Miss!" And he politely touched his forehead.

"Thank you, John. Mr. Rochester told me to give you and Mary this." I pressed a five-pound note into his hand. Without waiting to hear more, I left the kitchen. Passing the door a short while later, I caught the words—

"She'll likely do better for him than any of the grand ladies would have." And again: "If she's not one of the handsomest, she's no fool and very good-natured. And in his eyes she's beautiful—anyone can see that."

I wrote to Moor House and to Cambridge immediately, explaining what I had done and fully laying out my reasons. Diana and Mary approved the step without reservation. Diana announced she would give me time to finish the honeymoon, and then she would come and see me.

"She'd better not wait that long, Jane," said Mr. Rochester when I read her letter to him. "If she does, she'll be too late—for our honeymoon will last our whole lives. Its light will only fade over your grave or mine."

How St. John received the news, I don't know. He never answered the letter in which I told him. Yet six months later he wrote to me—without, however, mentioning Mr. Rochester's name or my marriage. His letter was calm and, though very serious, kind. He has kept up a regular, if not frequent, correspondence ever since. He hopes I am happy and trusts I am not among those who live without God in the world and think only of earthly things.

You haven't quite forgotten little Adele, have you, reader? I hadn't. I soon asked and received permission from Mr. Rochester to visit her at the school where he had placed her. Her wild joy at seeing me again moved me deeply. She looked pale and thin. She said she was unhappy. I found the school's rules were too strict and its coursework too demanding for a child her age. I took her home with me. I had planned to be her governess again, but soon realized that was impractical. So I found a school with a more relaxed approach and placed her there. She settled in well, made good progress, and eventually grew into a pleasant and kind young woman. A good education corrected whatever flaws her French upbringing had given her, and when she left school I found her a faithful and agreeable companion.
My story draws near its close. One word about my experience of married life, and one brief glance at the fortunes of those whose names have appeared most often in this narrative, and I am done.

I have now been married ten years. I know what it is to live entirely for and with the person I love most on earth. I consider myself supremely blessed—blessed beyond what words can express—because I am my husband's life as fully as he is mine. No woman was ever nearer to her husband than I am. We are truly bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh. I never tire of my Edward's company. He never tires of mine, any more than we each tire of the heartbeat in our own chests. We are always together. To be together is for us to be at once as free as if we were alone, and as content as if we were in company. We talk all day long. To talk to each other is only a more animated and audible form of thinking. His presence is all I need. Mine, he says, is all he needs.

Mr. Rochester continued to be blind for the first two years of our marriage. Perhaps it was that circumstance that drew us so close—that bound us so tightly. For I was his eyes, as I am still his right hand. Literally, I was—as he often called me—the apple of his eye. He saw nature and books through me. I never tired of gazing on his behalf and putting into words what I saw—field, tree, town, river, cloud, sunbeam. The landscape before us, the weather around us. And impressing by sound on his ear what light could no longer stamp upon his eyes.
One morning, at the end of those two years, as I was writing a letter to his dictation, he came and bent over me and said: "Jane, have you a glittering ornament around your neck?"
I had a gold watch chain. I answered "Yes."
"And have you a pale blue dress on?"
And have you a pale blue dress on?
I had. He told me then that for some time he had thought the darkness clouding one eye was becoming less dense. Now he was sure of it.

He and I went to London. He consulted an eminent eye specialist and eventually recovered the sight of that one eye. He cannot see very clearly now. He cannot read or write much. But he can find his way without being led by the hand. The sky is no longer a blank to him—the earth no longer a void. When his firstborn was placed in his arms, he could see that the boy had inherited his own eyes, as they once were—large, brilliant, and dark. On that occasion, he acknowledged once more, with deep gratitude: "God is merciful! He sees that I have earned the right to a little happiness, and He grants it."

My Edward and I are happy. And the more so because those we love most are happy too. Diana and Mary Rivers are both married. They visit us once a year, and we visit them. Diana's husband is a captain in the navy—a brave officer and a good man. Mary's is a clergyman, a college friend of her brother's, and worthy of the connection in every respect. Both Captain Fitzjames and Mr. Wharton love their wives and are loved by them.

As for St. John Rivers, he left England. He went to India. He entered on the path he had chosen for himself, and he follows it still. A more determined, tireless pioneer never struggled through hardship and danger. Firm, faithful, and devoted, full of energy, zeal, and truth, he works for humanity. He clears their painful way toward progress. He cuts down prejudices of creed and caste like a giant felling trees. He may be stern. He may be demanding. He may be ambitious still. But his is the sternness of the warrior who guards his captain's tent. His is the ambition of the servant laboring in his Master's vineyard. He is a man willing to lay down his life for the truth.

St. John is unmarried. He never will marry now. He has been enough, by himself, for the work. And the work draws near its end. His glorious sun is hastening toward its setting. The last letter I received from him drew human tears from my eyes yet filled my heart with divine joy. He anticipated his sure reward—his imperishable crown. I know that a stranger's hand will write to me next, to say that the good and faithful servant has been called at last into the joy of his Lord. And why weep for this? No fear of death will darken St. John's last hour. His mind will be unclouded, his heart will be unshaken, his hope will be sure, his faith will be steadfast. His own words are a pledge of this—
"My Master," he says, "has forewarned me. Daily He announces more distinctly—'Surely I come quickly!' and hourly I more eagerly respond—'Amen; even so, come, Lord Jesus!'"
